summaries on either side [doubtful], and the sufficiency of the
bringing alleged in turn on account of the prorogation that had
intervened, was not determined — the court of the conditional offices
binds the said parties to the completing of a more sufficient
bringing, according to the prescription of the tribunal's decree,
and the communication [doubtful] in the nature of the documents,
and that in this instant. The parties brought the documents
comprehended both in the summaries, under their own hands and
subscribed by the judges, and also beyond the summaries, existing in
the archive of the Most Illustrious Magnificent Prusimski, starost
of Niszczewice, and communicated them to one another; and the
Magnificent Ignacy Zakrzewski, ensifer Przedecz, corroborates the
summary subscribed by the Magnificent Kazimierz Zakrzewski, judge
territorial of Brześć in Kujawy, parent, with his own subscription;
and the Most Illustrious Magnificent Prusimski, starost of
Niszczewice, attached some documents to his own summary and subscribed,
and on account of the non-persistence offered the oaths again in
this bringing; which oaths the court of the conditional offices,
declaring them admissible, decrees that they avail to this effect:
that all the documents generally, pertaining to the present cause,
the masses of the substances, as much the paternal Prusimski as the
maternal Golinski, left by the late Magnificences Paweł and Antoni
Prusimski, sterile ones, as the loads hanging on the same substances,
elucidating [them], they really brought; and that they conceal
nothing of them to the damage and prejudice of party by party — so
they swore, God and the passion of Jesus Christ aiding, to the
down-treading of the oath. The oath was taken by the Magnificent
Ignacy Zakrzewski, ensifer.

The said one only — and to the actors, and the Most Illustrious
Magnificent Prusimski, starost of Niszczewice — after which the courts
of the conditional offices pronounced those parties free of further
bringing; to these parties he bids induce the business. In the
induction, the resolution of the category against the Most
Reverend Abbot and Venerable Convent of Ląd, introduced by the
original actor party, being suspended, he commands the original
agent parties to proceed further in the [word doubtful: read by its
sense as "principal"] business. In proceeding: the controversies of
the parties, namely of the Magnificences Zakrzewski, Tomicki,
Taczanowski, Kołaczkowski and Tworowicz, in respect of the

app53170koningr119-8:
Done in Konin on Wednesday next after the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, being 15 September 1784.

On behalf of His Honour Prusimski, Starost of Niszczewice — Requisition

To the office and present records of the Konin Municipal Court, appearing in person, the Honourable Leon Maszewski, Commissioner of the Trąbczyn estate district, in the name and by special commission of the Illustrious Right Honourable Antoni of Kolno Prusimski, Starost of Niszczewice, heir of those same estates, his principal — requested of the present office and petitioned for the extraction of the relatio of the citation issued for the Ordinary General Sessions of the Piotrków Crown Tribunal, on behalf of the Right Honourable Stanisław Scibor Chełmski, Treasurer of Wschowa, to the estates of Trąbczyn, exported by a court summoner on Thursday after the Feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the current year — whether it is found recognized in the present records or not.

To which requisition the present office, granting it and having reviewed the Protocol of Relationes from the Thursday last past, makes public certification of the non-existence of the aforesaid relatio.

Leon Maszewski, in the name of the Most Honourable Prusimski
app53170koningr120-1:
Done at Konin on 14 March in the Year of the Lord 1785

The Hard-working Andreas Kinos of Trąbczyn filed an obduction

Coming personally, Laboriosus Andreas Kinos, from the goods of the village of Trąbczyn, adhering to the common law, showed to the present office the bruises written below, namely: the right eye suffused with blood all around; under the same eye the flesh swollen and livid; likewise the left eye suffused with blood through the middle and livid; likewise the entire face swollen; likewise the right shoulders swollen. Which aforementioned injuries he asserted, himself the same one filing this report, to have been inflicted and visited upon him by force and violence with fists and a stick by Right Honourable Martinus Sarzyński on the public road, while departing from home to the town of Pleszew, cutting off his path in the village of Obory, on the most recent past Saturday.
app53170koningr120-2:
On the part of Right Honourable Chełmski against His Worship Prusimski — Return of Service to the Tribunal

Coming personally, Providus Sebastianus Biegański of the village of Słask, General Royal Summoner, sound [of mind], acknowledged that he had cited [with] authentic citation letters issued for the Ordinary General Sessions of the Crown Tribunal at Piotrków below-written, of the following tenor:

Stanisław August, by the Grace of God King of Poland, etc. To you, the Illustrious Right Honourable Antoni Prusimski of Kolno, starosta [district administrator] of Niszczewice, Knight of the Order of Saint Stanisław, regarding your goods We command that at our Ordinary General Sessions of the Crown Tribunal of Piotrków, properly within four weeks from the date and delivery of this present citation, or at such time when the present cause, called and proclaimed for judgment from the register competent to it, shall fall due, you appear personally and lawfully, at the instance of Right Honourable Stanisław Chełmski, skarbnik [treasurer] of Wschowa, plaintiff, who cites you to the prepared, connected and competent inscriptions, to see and hear yourself — to the production of a specific document, namely the contract for the sale of oak woodland, entered into and concluded with the Honourable Joannes Trachultz,

remaining with you, the oath having been administered beforehand, to be bound, or the same presentation to be fulfilled at the designated place, to be prescribed. Now indeed in our Court, with penalties against you the cited party — both with respect to the remission procured from the Condescensorial Court to the Plenary Court, and thereafter from our Plenary Court to the Tribunal Court, and contrary to the decrees duly and legitimately passed accepting a condescension designating the institution of terms and of the cause not yet decided in the lesser bench, extended separately to the Court of Supreme Instance of Evocation, and from the circumstances of the matter and the cause occurring — the Land Court Decrees of Kalisz, passed in the jurisdiction of the Konin district, the whole matter having been suspended with the consent also of you the cited party, [decrees] designating a condescension to be carried out, to be arranged; all manner of satisfaction to be found for the plaintiff and ordered to be rendered; the rest according to the conclusion to be put; and the earlier terms of the plaintiff to be decided and resolved.

Given at Piotrków on 2 October in the Year of the Lord 1786.

In the manor court of the goods of the village of Trąbczyn, on the table of the heated room, with the representative of the cited party present, on the 2nd day of the month and year expressed in the act above, [he states that he] placed [it] and left [it] notified.
app53170koningr121-1:
Done in Konin, on 9 June in the Year of the Lord 1788.

On behalf of the Most Honourable Prusimski — Presentation of Livestock and a Horse with a Cart joined to the same.

Coming in person to the present Municipal Court Office and Records of Konin, the Honourable Ludovicus Żurawski, serving the Most Honourable Antoni in Kolno Prusimski, Starost [district administrator] of Niszczewice, hereditary owner of the estate of Trąbczyn, and adhering to the common law, presented to the said Office a cart — with two front wheels, bare, that is without an iron plate placed on top, that is with bare front wheels; but with the rear wheels having an iron plate placed on top, that is with rear wheels shod with iron — together with two rear oxen: one of yellowish coat, that is of pale coat; and the other of mixed colour, that is of mottled, overly-white coat; and also a cow of striped coat, that is of dun mottled coat; and a chestnut mare harnessed to the above-mentioned cart with its cart stanchions — the oxen and cow in a yoke, that is in yokes, the mare in reins, that is in traces, all pulling the same cart — [all found on] the Peasant Martin Gryndel from the estate of Łomowo of the Right Honourable Scibor Chełmski, Treasurer of Wschowa, hereditary owner of the said estate, belonging to the more principal hereditary estates of Łukom of this Right Honourable Scibor Chełmski, Treasurer of Wschowa; the serf [found in] the pine forest belonging to the estate of Trąbczyn of the above-mentioned Most Honourable

Antoni in Kolno Prusimski, Starost of Niszczewice, Knight of the Order of Saint Stanislaus, and belonging and pertaining to his hereditary estates, and not subject to any dispute regarding the hereditary estate at any time; while [the serf] was riding into the said pine forest and already transporting from it a cut tree — suitable and fit for buildings — to the aforementioned estate of Łomowo, to his own home; [all of the foregoing] intercepted in this very pine forest by the Guardian of the Forests of Trąbczyn, and by reason of the presentation that followed in the manner set forth above, driven and brought to the present Municipal Chancellery of Konin. Which oxen, cow, and mare, with the cart harnessed to the same, standing before the Chancellery, [he] presented. The same presenter, the Honourable Ludovicus Żurawski, left the said [animals] at the present Municipal Chancellery of Konin for the purpose of the extradition of the same to the above-mentioned Peasant Gryndel, requesting the immediate extradition of these following the aforementioned Presentation — (as the aforesaid Quietance of Extradition pertaining to the matter of his Chancellery Office, drawn up in the Act on this day, having followed, sets forth more fully) — and left, and leaves [them], by these presents.

adwl85-1:
The village of Trąbczyn,

in which there is a church. Its parish priest is the Reverend Józef Zurkowski, born in the diocese of Poznań, as his baptismal record shows, in the year 1740, on 9 July. He was ordained priest by the Most Illustrious and Reverend Ignacy Augustyn Sariusz [uncertain: Kozierog] Kozierowski, Bishop Adratyński, in the year 1767, on 24 February, having first had letters dimissory for receiving the orders of the diaconate and the priesthood from the Most Illustrious and Reverend Teodor Czartoryski, Count of Klewań and Żuków, Bishop of Poznań, given to him on 17 December 1766. He was instituted to this church in the Illustrious Consistory of Gniezno on 21 February 1785, on the presentation of the Most Illustrious Antoni Prusimski, Starost of Niszczewice, Knight of the Order of St Stanislaus, heir and patron of these estates. He was approved to hear confessions for one year at the time of the retreat, in its appointed place and term, in

Konin, held in the present year on 15 October. A fund for a vicar, an organist and a schoolmaster is found in the documents, but none of them is at the church.

The state of this church.

This church, in the village of Trąbczyn, the hereditary property of the Most Illustrious Antoni Prusimski, Starost of Niszczewice, Knight of the Order of St Stanislaus, lies in the voivodeship of Kalisz, in the district and deanery of Konin, in the archdeaconry and officialate of Gniezno. It is 6 miles from the metropolitan city of Gniezno, 21 miles from Łowicz, 5 miles from His Royal Majesty's city of Kalisz, and 2 miles from Konin, the district town. By parish right it takes in the said village of Trąbczyn, in which the church stands; Mariantów, Porąbki, the farm called [uncertain: Uła], the new and old Olędry, Łazy, Osiny, Nowawies. These villages lie from the church: towards the winter sunrise 8 furlongs; towards the forenoon likewise; towards the afternoon half a mile; towards the sunset a quarter of a mile; to the west 10 furlongs. All of them are the hereditary property of the Most Illustrious Starost.

The parish extends a good half mile. In the whole parish 760 souls are counted in all, that is 170 men, 191 women, 95 boys coming to communion for the first time, 99 girls; of dissidents 63 men, 60 women, 40 boys, 42 girls. In the past year 1790, according to the entries of the registers, children baptised

of the male sex 13, of the female sex 15; couples married 10; men died 10, women 15, children of both sexes 4; all of which may be seen in the following table.

This church is in the form of a cross, with two wooden chapels, and has a new roof. The ceiling is damaged in places by leaks of rain from earlier times; the floor of planks throughout the church needs relaying in the great choir. The church faces the sunrise. The great door, to the west, closes well. It has a high choir loft, on which stands a good positive organ with seven stops and three bellows. Beside it, on the south side, a door from the cemetery to the porch, closing well, from which one enters the chapel and from it the church. The sacristy is of wood and needs its windows repaired and a new floor;

in it a table with four large drawers for the vestments and smaller ones for the chalices, veils and corporals etc., closing well; there too an old tabernacle for keeping the Most Holy Sacrament, broken; a large chest with a good lock. From this sacristy a door to the west into the library, in which a large cupboard stands for the books. Opposite the sacristy, to the north, a treasury, whose door and lock are good; a large cupboard stands there with a good lock.

The length of this church in all is 47 ells, the width 33 ells; that is, the presbytery is 14 ells long and 9 ells wide; the great choir 33 ells long and 14 ells wide. The chapel of St Martin on the north side is 12 ells long and 8½ ells wide; in it 2 cupboards, locked, for the lights. On the south side the second chapel, of St Aloysius, 10½ ells long and 8¼ ells wide. The sacristy is 8 ells long and 5 ells wide; the library 5 ells long and 4 ells wide; the treasury 8½ ells long and 2¾ ells wide; the porch 4½ ells long and 5½ ells wide.

Windows: in the small choir 4, needing repair; in the great choir 4, good; in the chapels two each, these good; in the sacristy 2 small windows with iron grilles, somewhat damaged; in the treasury only an iron grille, without a window.

In this church are 4 good confessionals painted blue, with grilles; 20 good pews painted the same way; a railing with balusters

painted, covered with white cloths.

This church was built in part by the noble Trąmpczyński family, once heirs of the place, and later enlarged by the noble Lady Prusimska, née Rozdrażewska, the Chamberlain's wife, heiress (when, it cannot be known). Its titular patron is St Martin, Bishop. It was consecrated in the year 1546, on 26 September. The day of its consecration is kept every year on the first Sunday after the feast of St Matthew the Apostle. The cemetery has on the south, east and west side a small, recent fence, into which there is a good gate for entering from the east, and from the west a carriage gate and a gate, good, with a lock, but there are no grilles by them. There too, straight opposite the great door of the church, is the belfry, needing sill-beams and doors over half of it, as the planks have fallen off, and a roof before long; in it two bells, whether consecrated is not known; one of them is chipped. To the north of the church is an ossuary of wood, good, with a window onto the cemetery; between it and the belfry the fence leans, further on it is good.

The right of patronage, or collation, of this church is lay, and the church has always been governed by secular priests. Its patron now is the Most Illustrious Antoni Prusimski, Starost of Niszczewice, Knight of the Order of St Stanislaus. There are no mansionaries, prebends or altarages, nor any fund for them.

In this church there are 5 altars: the first, the high altar, in which a picture of the Mother of God under the title of the Scapular, with a confraternity, closed by a sliding cover, with a dress and crowns of silver

smaller 20. Cushions on the altars 5. Covers for the altars 6. Good small carpets 2. An old carpet 1.

Church books.

The first register, for entering baptisms, begun in 1597, is complete to the present year. The book of marriages from 1597 to this year. The book for entering the dead from the year 1728 to this time. The book for entering the brothers and sisters of the Holy Scapular from the year 1662. A book in which the state of the benefice in the year 1688 is described; various foundations; inventories of various times, and benefactors. Antiphonaries with notes 2. Choral book 1. Rituale Sacramentorum 1. Breviary, Agenda, Gospel books 2. Old missals 3. Vita Virorum Illustrium, Conceptus Theologicus 1. Libri duo Justini Baronii, Conciones of the Reverend Father Ozorius, Conciones of the Reverend Father Besser, Decisiones et Declarationes Concilii Tridentini, Conciones cum Evangeliis of an unknown author, Coeli seu sphaerae coelestis contemplatio, Rudolphus Godonius, Opera Sancta, a Polish chronicle, Homiliae Sanctorum, a pastoral letter, Promptuarium morale, Catechismus Romanus, Manuale Parochorum. The rest of the books that were at the visitation of the Reverend Dorposki are not set down here; the reason is that, through a trick played under the present rector of this church, and through not knowing to whom they belonged, they were given to the creditors of the late Reverend Paprocki, the pastor here. A good catafalque with a coffin, a bier, a processional cross 1, a lectern 1, a mourning banner 1,

small pennants 5, small banners 2.

Description of the rights and documents found at this church.

1662. A resignation made in court in the books of the Konin land court, of a piece of peasant land called Pierzchalińska, for the pay of the organist and the needs of the church. 1636: the first foundation sum, 1,000 Polish złoty, secured on Trąbczyn; the second, 1,500 złoty, in the year 1637, which the noble Trąmpczyński, heir, recorded at Kalisz and at Pyzdry. From these there is now due 80½ złoty each year, with the obligation of singing 52 Holy Masses a year, reading 156, and of 208 litanies sung by the organist; from this income also something for the fabric of the church. 1668: a sum of 350 Polish złoty, secured on part of Kurów and recorded there too, from the noble Mr Stefan Wardencki; likewise 250 złoty placed by the noble Mr Bogusławski; from it 21 złoty is due for saying 52 Masses. 1670: 500 Polish złoty secured on Strzałkowo, recorded at Kalisz and Pyzdry, from the noble Mr Strzałkowski; from it 17½ złoty is due, for 12 Masses. There too a sum of 2,000 złoty, recorded under the same year and act by the noble Lady Golinska on the estate of Przespolew, for saying 104 Masses every year. 1692, 16 December: a decree of the Gniezno consistory, taken from its archive, by which the tithe from the farm of Dręzgi, and likewise from the farm called Nowina, is awarded. 1694: the inn, confirmed by a decree of the Most Illustrious Official of Gniezno, with the right to sell beer and spirits in it; in the same decree a house for the school is named, which

now has the name of the organist's house. Likewise, in the same decree, a piece of the parish land: a separate pine wood, by which the peasants, with the parish priests' leave, cleared fields and small meadows for themselves; this clearing has the name Porąbki, and three cottagers now live on it; likewise a large meadow beyond the wood and Porąbki, belonging to the parish. The estates Kamionna and Kolno lie in the province of South Prussia, in the department of the Royal Government at Poznań, and in its Międzyrzecz district.

These estates stand in a single economic connexion, and are distant 3 miles from the district town of Międzyrzecz, 3 miles from Swerin, 1/2 mile from Birnbaum, 1 1/2 miles from Zircna [uncertain: Zircna], 2 miles from Pinne, 9 miles from Poznań, and 3 miles from the Neumark frontier, namely towards Driesen.

The nearest river is the Warta at Birnbaum, and the produce which is not consumed on the estate itself has been disposed of and sold in that town.

Kamionna borders to the east upon Mechnach, to the south upon Groß-Munche and Grolewo, and to the north upon Kolno.

Kolno borders to the east upon Prusim and Mechaiz, to the south upon Groß-Munche and Grolewo, to the west upon Bilski, Gorozin and Skrilewo, and to the north upon Popowo and Rzeitun.

Most Serene Prince, Gracious Lord!

Your Serene Highness has, by Cabinet Order of the 23rd of this month, received as a gift from His Majesty, in heredity and full property, the town of Kamionna, together with the market town of Kolno in the Poznań district, the villages of Trąbczyn, Szetlewek, Nowawies, Łazy, Old and New Laske, Osiny, Hauland Trąbczyński in the Konin district, and the village of Brzyce with its appurtenances in the Cujavian district; and His Most High Majesty commands me to make the necessary notifications upon the proposals that have been made, concerning the most high intention of his will in the matter.

I rejoice exceedingly to be able to [uncertain: convey] to Your Serene Highness this proof of the Royal favour, and I am this very moment conferring with the Feudal Department, in order to see the deed of donation for the same expedited soon. Since these estates belonged to a principal insurgent, von Prusimski, and since it is necessary to know the debts that may be charged upon these estates, so as to free them from the same so far as possible, I am likewise making the necessary arrangements on that account with the Government at Poznań.

According to the preliminary reports, these estates yield at least an annual return of 4,000 Thalers; and should the same be duly valued and appraised by Your Serene Highness's command, then I know

no better manager to propose to the same than the Royal Chamber Councillor Peucker at Fraustadt, who, should the occasion arise, would with his acquaintance among the South Prussian nobility find a buyer for these estates, in case [uncertain: Your] Serene Highness should not be pleased to retain them for himself. The Colonel von Sanitz has received the von Prusimski estates lying in the Wegrowietz district, namely Pawlow, Dzwonow and Beerenbusch. With true pleasure I look forward to the glad tidings that Your Serene Highness, amid his great exertions, finds himself in the desired good health. For it is exceedingly agreeable to me to persist in the most reverential sentiments. Your Serene Highness's most obedient servant, Hoym

Wrocław, the 30th of July 1796.

Mellentz[?] Upon various orders received from His Majesty, to bring forward proposals of vacant estates granted by royal favour (Gratial-Güter) and of confiscated insurgents' estates for the benefit of sold-off full officers, I have rendered the enclosed report of the 14th of this month, and His Most High Majesty has been pleased to approve all the proposals in accordance with the cabinet order of the 23rd of this month, which is here enclosed with the most humble request for its return.

Since the content of the donation charters hitherto drafted may be entirely identical with those which are now to be despatched, inasmuch as only the names of the persons favoured, and the estates assigned to them, make the essential difference, I have not first drawn up particular drafts for the donation letters in question, but leave it most humbly to Your Excellency whether you will be pleased to have them despatched in the Fiefs Chancery, and to send them to me by way of a joint report for my counter-signature and further conveyance to His Majesty. I note besides that with the estates the addition: cum appertinentia, or appurtenances, will always have to be inserted, because, in the absence of any system of mortgage registration in Suprensten, it is too difficult to obtain speedy and thorough information of the relations of the estates belonging together, and otherwise the beneficiaries would easily suffer a disadvantage contrary to His Majesty's intention, if in future, through strict specifications in the donation charters, appurtenances which belong to the principal estates were to remain not delivered over to them.

Thus, for example, there are reckoned to the Duninow estates the villages of Duninow, Tolenczna, Szadow, Nowawies, and Krzement

and designated merely by the expression: the Duninow estates granted by royal favour, of 1,500 Rthl. in yield. But if the donation charter is framed in general terms, then upon the future delivery of possession all those estates may be reckoned to it which the former holder by royal favour or private proprietor possessed in this or that district, and which by that measure are to be transferred by His Majesty to the present recipients. Since each of them would wish soon to have the donation instrument put into his hands and the estates delivered over, I may all the more humbly request Your Excellency to have the issue of the charters expedited as far as possible. Wrocław, the 30th of July 1796. Hoym

Lieutenant General of Infantry, Chief of a Regiment of Foot, Governor of the capital city of Wrocław We Friedrich Wilhelm by the Grace of God King of Prussia (tot. tit.) do declare and make known by means of this Our open letter, for Ourselves and Our successors in the Crown, the Electorate and Our remaining lands, and hereby graciously give to know to each and every one whom it concerns: that, as We are, out of inborn favour and clemency, much inclined to acknowledge and requite the good and profitable services rendered to Us and to Our Royal House by particular marks of Our Royal good will, We have considered the important, distinguished and useful services rendered for many years past to Us and to Our Royal House in Our Royal Heimath by the High-Born Prince, Our kindly beloved uncle, Friedrich Ludewig, reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, Our (the character of the Prince in the Royal service to be inserted), Knight of Our Orders etc., and have resolved, in order to give to the said Lord Prince a mark of the recognition of his excellent merits and of Our Royal gratitude, to bestow and convey upon him, heritably and in property, the following estates which have fallen in to Our Most High disposal, namely: the town of Kamionna, and the market town of Kolno, in the district of Poznań; the villages of Trąbczyn, Szetlewek, Nowawies, Lazy, Old and New Laske, Oszny, Hauland Trąbczyński, in the district of Konin; and the village of Brzyce, together with appurtenances, in Kuyavia; with all their belongings, by whatever name they may be called, heritably and

in property.

This We also do herewith and by virtue of these presents, out of Royal power and plenitude, for Ourselves and Our descendants and successors in the Crown, the Electorate and Our remaining lands, in such wise and manner that Our aforesaid kindly beloved uncle, the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, shall from now on for eternal times have, possess and enjoy the above-named estates, with all rights and privileges attaching thereto, as such have hitherto been exercised or may lawfully be exercised, no less than with all their appurtenances and other belongings, by whatever name they may be called, just as the same have hitherto been used or may of right be used, as a well-acquired and unencumbered property — yet subject to the reservation of the sovereign taxes and other public dues to be laid upon them like other estates of Our South Prussian [uncertain: territories] — for himself and his descendants and heirs, irrevocably from Us and Our successors, and the power shall likewise be vested in him to dispose thereof at his pleasure, unhindered by any man. We therefore command and enjoin all Our South Prussian Governments and Chambers of War and Domains, as also all other authorities whom it concerns, herewith as graciously as earnestly, that they shall in no way hinder or impede either the [uncertain: aforementioned] Lord Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen in the heritable and proprietary possession, granted to him, of the above-named holdings and estates together with their appurtenances and belongings, nor him or those upon whom, by virtue and in force of this Our letter of donation, he may bequeath the same therein or otherwise lawfully convey it by other acts inter vivos or mortis causa, but shall rather let him, and eventually also them, enjoy the same freely and peaceably, doing nothing themselves against it, nor occasioning or permitting that such be done by others, upon pain of Our Most High disfavour and unfailing severe punishment. In witness whereof We have caused this present letter of donation to be signed with Our own Most High hand and Our Royal great seal to be appended thereto. Thus done at Berlin, 9 August 1796.

The Polish gentleman Antoine Prusimski having presented himself at my house in a truly ruined state of health, and affected almost to stupor by the death of his wife, asking me for a certificate of his sad situation and of the impossibility in which he was, for the present and in this season, of being able to set out on a journey, I did not think I could refuse it to him; for if he was wearied to the point of prostration in passing from one house to another, how could he have set out on a journey to pass from one country to another?

[Written by the receiving office:]

Mr von Raumer

Presented the 2nd of January 1797.

16 Feb. 1797

Promemoria

By the laws, many of the authors of and participants in the South Prussian rebellion would have incurred death, and the rest confiscation and lifelong imprisonment in a fortress.

But this legal severity has been exceptionally mitigated by special most-high dispositions.

Several letters of pardon, and repeated amnesty patents, especially those of 24 September and 10 December 1794, have withdrawn the greatest part of its victims from justice altogether.

Above all, however, the Immediate Instruction of 3 April 1795 laid down:

1, that only 6 or 8 of the chief ringleaders were to be punished with the rigour of the laws, but even these not with death;

2, that the rest were to be subjected only to certain fines, to be assessed by a finance commission in Poznań; and

3, that only against those who would not submit to the decrees of the commission, or could not raise the fines imposed, were temporary sentences of fortress imprisonment to be pronounced.

The justice had no share at all in any of these ordinances; they were merely sent to it to be complied with.

The chief ringleaders, Niemoiewski, Wybicki, Xaver Dombrowski, Mniewski, Prudzinski [Prusimski], Krupecki, Jetzierski [Jezierski], Rokittnicki etc., have saved themselves by flight. One has therefore had to be content with confiscating the property they left behind, and no example of punishment could be made on their persons.

Other chief promoters of the rebellion hastened to settle with the finance commission at Poznań by paying fines, and thereby to free themselves from all further claims of the justice.

Hence it has come about that of 387 insurgents who have been freed

307 merely paid fines,

49 were sentenced to shorter fortress imprisonment, not exceeding 3 years,

26 to long,

2 to lifelong fortress imprisonment, and only 3 to death; of whom, however, one received a pardon under the gallows, and a second saved himself by flight. = 387.

Should His Royal Majesty be inclined to extend His most high grace still further towards these leniently punished participants in the insurrection, this could nevertheless be advised only in the following measure.

1, the confiscation imposed on the rebels who have left the country should simply be allowed to stand, since in particular over the

confiscated estates disposition has for the most part already been made.

2, the fines imposed would nevertheless have to be collected, even if they were still in arrears, because these monies are already counted on for various necessary expenses of the province.

3, The insurgents condemned to the fortress for only a shorter time have for the most part already served their sentence. Those who are still sitting could be remitted the rest of their time of arrest entirely.

4, those who are condemned for a longer time, according to the enclosed list, might be remitted about half of the sentence pronounced.

But von Pratzmowski, sub num. 7, von Ryczewski, sub num. 12, and von Maruczewski, sub num. 13, would have to be excepted from this, because they incurred the sentence pronounced not merely as insurgents but chiefly as highway robbers.

5, As regards the insurgents condemned for life according to this same list, the sentence pronounced should simply be left as it stands in the case of Nowicki, sub num. 2, because the death sentence already pronounced on him has been remitted, and in the case of Sobolewski, sub num. 3, because he has been condemned chiefly as a participant in various murders and highway robberies. On the other hand, in the case of von Stockowski, sub num. 1, who seems to have sinned more from simplicity and vanity than from evil intent, a pardon down to 10 years might perhaps take place, and the settlement of a pension or dowry out of the confiscated estates for his daughter, who is under age and stripped of all property of her own.

A few investigations are still pending against insurgents who have only recently presented themselves in answer to the public summonses issued.

Against these, judgment would have to be given under the rules hitherto in force, but when the rescripts of confirmation are submitted

regard would be had to the principles now laid down.

Should His Royal Majesty most graciously deign to accept the above proposals, then

1, a public notice concerning the amnesty granted under 3 and 4,

2, the necessary order to the Minister of State Count von Hoym and to the Grand Chancellor would have to be laid before His Majesty for most high signature.

Berlin, 16 February 1797.

Goldbeck

[Written in another hand:]

After close consideration of the crimes[?], I find none of the condemned[?] worthy of a reduction of the punishments; rather, those who have been condemned to money fines must be held to the payment of them, or, where[?] they are not able to pay it, be brought to an arrest in proportion to it.

Fr. Wilhelm

We Friedrich Wilhelm, by the Grace of God King of Prussia, do by this Our open letter attest and declare, for Ourselves and Our descendants and successors in the Crown, the Electorate and Our remaining lands, that, it having been submitted to Us in all humility in what manner Our intention — namely to give to the High-born Prince, Our friendly beloved uncle Friedrich Ludw., Reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, by the grant of the estates which had belonged to the absconded former Starost von Prusimski, a token of the friendship and goodwill We bear towards him, as also of Our Royal gratitude for the distinguished and beneficial services rendered to Us and to Our house — was not achieved entirely as We had willed it, because the said estates were burdened with many debts, We have most highly resolved to relinquish, to grant and to convey to His Lordship the hereinafter named formerly ecclesiastical estates, namely: the villages of Pszczew, Świechocin, Stoki, Łowyń, Głażewo, Tarnowo, Zagórów, Skokum, Świątniki, Kopojno, Olesnica, Drzewce, Grądzyń, Wrąbczyn, Wieniecz and Wolica, together with all their appurtenances, by whatsoever name they may be called, in hereditary and full ownership, against payment of

1) the sovereign dues hitherto discharged therefrom, as a fixed and unalterable canon, and

2) the maintenance allowance due therefrom to the ecclesiastical corporations or foundations.

We also do so hereby and by virtue of this present instrument, out of Our Royal power and plenitude, for Ourselves and Our descendants and successors in the Crown, the Electorate, and Our remaining lands, in such manner and wise that Our aforementioned friendly beloved uncle, the Reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-

Ingelfingen shall from now on and for all eternity, for himself and his heirs and descendants, irrevocably have, possess and enjoy the abovenamed estates with all rights and entitlements attaching thereto, as these have hitherto been exercised or may in law still be exercised, and no less with all appurtenances belonging to him and other accessories, by whatsoever name they may be called, as the same have hitherto been used or may in law be used, and with all the lands appertaining thereto in fields, woods and meadows, in ponds and waters, as a true, well-acquired and unrestricted property from Us and Our descendants and successors; and that the power and authority shall likewise be vested in him to dispose thereof at his pleasure under the above-mentioned conditions, unhindered by any man. We do therefore command and enjoin all Our Superior Provincial Boards, as also all other authorities whom this concerns, hereby as graciously as earnestly, that they shall in no manner hinder nor obstruct the said Prince etc. in the hereditary and proprietary possession of the abovenamed estates, together with their appurtenances and accessories, granted to the same, nor those to whom he may one day bequeath the same or otherwise transfer them in lawful manner by other acts inter vivos aut mortis causa, but shall rather let His Lordship, and eventually them also, enjoy the same freely and peaceably; shall themselves do nothing against this, nor occasion or permit that such be done by others, on pain of Our Most High disfavour and unfailing severe reprimand.

In witness whereof etc. Given at Berlin, the 19th of June, 1797. Friedrich Wilhelm

Instrument of grant for the Reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, for the hereditary and proprietary possession of the villages: Pszczew, Świechocin, Stoki, Łowyń, Głażewo, Tarnowo, Zagórów, Skokum, Świątniki, Kopojno, Olesnica, Drzewce, Grądzyń, Wrąbczyn, Wieniec and Wolica, together with appurtenances.

Copy.

Friedrich Wilhelm etc. In the taking-over and delivery, commanded of you, of the South Prussian estates of your department granted to His Lordship the Prince of Hohenlohe, it has been Our will and intention that the same should at once, and as far as is in any way possible without prejudice to the rights of a third party, be left to His Lordship's free disposition, and hence also to his husbandry and improvement as he shall please. Notwithstanding this, We come to learn that the delivery carried out has consisted merely in a superficial ceremony, and that the remark made in some places, that His Lordship is to settle all debts charged upon these estates, has confirmed various persons in the false notion that they may seat themselves in the estates and frame all manner of claims. Both in the confiscated noble and in the ecclesiastical estates granted to His Lordship the Prince there are said to be persons seated who have indeed produced pledge or lease contracts, but in respect of which it was not at all thoroughly investigated at the delivery whether these contracts were in themselves validly concluded, and, even were that the case, whether the holders thereof also really have a real claim upon this or that estate, and whether rather mere personal obligations were not contracted. It is said even to be already proven that some of these persons have false pledge contracts, and on that account the suits are said to be already pending before the Governments. But you yourself perceive that if His Lordship the Prince of Hohenlohe must first laboriously and through all instances conduct suits of this kind, Our Most High intention of putting His Lordship soon into the full enjoyment of the granted estates is thereby entirely delayed. Also the Treasury is bound, in pursuance of the deeds of grant, to procure for each donee as far as possible an unencumbered estate (fundum liberum). The delivery commissioners ought therefore also to have

more closely ascertained those claims which have been made upon these estates by outside persons, and to have left in possession of such an estate only those claimants who were able at once to prove a real right in one or the other estate and have exercised such real right by actual possession of the estate, and not to have acted so superficially, and to have conceded to many persons the continuing possession and further use of these estates even when they had by no means laid down undoubted proofs of their right. Now, in order not to burden His Lordship with unnecessary and protracted suits, yet also not to injure anyone in well-acquired rights, you are yourselves to take every pains to examine and settle the various demands upon these estates as soon as may be, to have these estates, so far as can in any way lawfully be done, handed over to the princely mandatories for the sole disposition and free husbandry of the Prince, to compose all disputed points amicably so far as ever possible — the more so as His Lordship himself, with sacrifice of his own interest, shews every inclination thereto — and, in those cases where it absolutely cannot be otherwise arranged without great danger to the Treasury and without legal proceedings, to take the shortest ways, and, according to the circumstances, to have the suit conducted either by the fiscal officers alone, or by them as assistants of the princely mandatory. For the complete settlement you will have to examine most exactly the circumstances of each single estate, and then to set the further matter in train upon the constant presupposition that His Lordship be at once in

stalled in all rights and powers that can in any way be lawfully transferred by the Treasury. Also, since the detailed valuations of all the ecclesiastical estates have already been remitted to you with approbation, you will very easily and soon be able to determine the dues and the competence monies which His Lordship the Prince of Hohenlohe has to pay; and since the discontent of the clergy grows ever greater the longer you delay the fixing and advance payment of these competence monies, you are to ascertain the same with the utmost despatch and to make report thereof to Us. In general you are to report to Us fully upon the settled business of delivery of possession of these estates, and what difficulties have arisen therein, and, according as the estates belong together or are separate, to report upon them severally; wherein We hold Ourselves assured that you will carefully order everything according to this Our will and intention, and will urge the Domains Establishment Commission, the delivery commissioners and the office of the Treasury, each in its own relation, to the speedy fulfilment of what has been ordered. [uncertain: Sinde G.] Wrocław, the 20th October 1797.

A. S. B. signed Count von Hoym. To the p Chamber at Poznań and Petrikau.

We Friedrich Wilhelm, by the Grace of God King of Prussia etc., do hereby certify and declare, and by force of this Our open letter, for Ourselves and Our descendants and successors in the Crown, the Electorate and Our remaining lands, that We, out of the particular friendship and affection We bear toward the High-Born Prince, Our kindly beloved Uncle Friedrich Ludewig, reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, as also in order to give him a fresh proof of Our Royal gratitude for the distinguished and beneficial services rendered to Us and to Our Royal House, have found Ourselves moved to make over, grant and convey to His Lordship, in heritable and proprietary form, the appurtenances belonging to those estates already conferred upon him by the instrument of the 19th of June of this year, namely Pszczew, Zagórów and Wieniec, to wit:

1. at Pszczew, the villages of Stołuń, Kuligowo, Szarcz, the bailiwick of Zielomyśl and Silna, together with the Hollander holdings, the Pomherr Hollander holding and Heidemühle;

2. at Zagórów, the little village of Swięcia; and finally

3. near Wieniec, Konty, Szedlemin, Bątkowo and Karczyn — against payment:

1. of the sovereign dues hitherto discharged by the said villages, Hollander holdings and parcels of land, as a fixed

and unalterable canon; and

2. of the competence due therefrom to the ecclesiastical corporations and foundations.

This We also do hereby and by force of these presents, out of Royal power and plenitude, for Ourselves and Our descendants and successors in the Crown, the Electorate and Our remaining lands, in such manner and wise that Our above-mentioned kindly beloved Uncle, the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, shall irrevocably have, possess and enjoy the above-named appurtenances belonging to the estates of Pszczew, Zagórów and Wieniec, with all rights and prerogatives attaching thereto, as the same have hitherto been exercised or may lawfully be exercised, with all lands pertaining thereto, in fields, woodlands and meadows, likewise in ponds and waters, according to the lawful boundaries and bounds, just as all has hitherto been used or may by right be used, from now on for everlasting time, for himself and his descendants and heirs, as a true, well-acquired and unrestricted property, from Us and Our descendants and successors; and that there shall likewise be conferred upon him the

power and authority to dispose thereof at his pleasure under the above-mentioned conditions, unhindered by any man. We therefore command and enjoin all Our Supreme Provincial Colleges, as also all other authorities whom this concerns, herewith as graciously as earnestly, that they in no wise hinder or impede either the Lordship of the oft-mentioned Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen in the heritable and proprietary possession thus conferred upon him of the above-named appurtenances belonging to the estates of Pszczew, Zagórów and Wieniec, nor him or those upon whom he may one day pass the same by inheritance, by force of this Our letter of grant, or may otherwise lawfully transfer them by other acts inter vivos aut mortis causa; but rather that they let His Lordship, and eventually also them, enjoy the same freely and quietly, doing nothing against it themselves, nor causing or permitting such to be done by others, on pain of Our supreme displeasure and of unfailing severe punishment. In witness whereof etc. Berlin, the 1st of December 1797.

Friedrich Wilhelm

Letter of grant for the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, for the heritable and proprietary possession of the appurtenances belonging to the estates of Pszczew, Zagórów and Wieniec.

1798. 3 September.

Letter of Tadeusz Kościuszko

Citizen!

I have received your letter, Dear Citizen, from Dresden, dated 10 Aug. of the
present year, addressed to me. I read in it the expressions of your goodwill
towards me with the same courtesy as in those which reached me in America from
You. I regret deeply that events did not allow me to see You in London. It
would have pleased me to make Your acquaintance in person.

Be assured, Citizen, that when circumstances point out to us the time for
regaining the national independence — which I do not yet see, and which hope
alone makes sweet to long for — I shall stand inseparable from every Pole who
has a truly Republican soul, and therefore from all those who fought together
with me against the enemies of our country. In that time we shall found the
ways of common defence and the nation's true happiness upon the principles
which You mention in Your letter.

Today, Dear Citizen, care must be taken not to expose them to the persecutions
of the enemies through premature steps, while happier events are awaited.

Keep this letter for Yourself; for my part I shall preserve Your friendship,
and I accept the sincere expressions of goodwill and respect shown to me.

T. Kościuszko.

Most gracious Lord!

To Your Majesty I [have] rendered my most humble and most reverent thanks for the gracious sentiments expressed toward me in Your Majesty's most high letter of 4 Dec. Only this one thing troubles me, that according to the report rendered by the Minister of State von Voss I appear in a light as though I had made to Your Majesty proposals prejudicial to the interest of the State in the exchange, most humbly applied for, of my South Prussian estates against the lordship of Krotoszyn; and therefore I may expect pardon from Your Majesty's grace toward me if I permit myself to make the following observations against that report.

I. First[?] I must most humbly state that, when it was disclosed to me by various persons that the additional payment of 30,000 Rthl in cash, toward the exchange offered for Krotoszyn and Polajewo, would meet with difficulties, because a domain estate may indeed be exchanged but not alienated, I voluntarily notified the Minister von Voss that I wished to restrict my request merely to the exchange of my estates for Krotoszyn, whereby the alienation of Polajewo would fall away. It would betray little good will toward me if the Minister should not have brought this modification of my petition to Your Majesty's notice, as appears to emerge from his letter sent to me and from Your Majesty's order.

II. When Your Majesty, upon my most humble petition, charged the said Minister von Voss to examine whether the proposed exchange could take place, it was surely the first thing I might expect that he would obtain exact intelligence of both of the objects to be exchanged. Of this, however, so little was thought that it was not even held worth the trouble to set so much as a pen to it; rather the report was rendered upon the one-sided statement of the Councillor of War Nöldichen, and of Kro-

toszyn that high yield was assumed without ground - a yield which, as is known to me, was straightway, by the Minister von Voss's own reports to the Majesty of the late blessed King, and [as] rumoured [uncertain: reported] in many letters in the Minister von Struensee at the time of the transfer of the estates from the Maritime Trading Company to the Poznań Chamber, after several local investigations made at that time to himself, reduced to about 28/m Rthl.

It therefore remains striking to me how he now speaks of a yield of 49,043 r., and thus seeks to demonstrate a loss to the State of 17,400 Rthl. as against my estates.

It is founded in truth that Krotoszyn at present pays 30,100 Rthl in rent, and it would be much if, given the prevailing prerogatives of the town, which rob the manorial lordship (Dominium) of every prospect of improvement, the yield could ever really be brought up to 36,000 Rthl. My estates yield, after the old debts paid in by me and still to be discharged, which I had to guarantee merely in order to come into possession, 41,500 Rthl., for which I can give Your Majesty warranty of title. From this it follows, surely, that the advantage is on the side of the State, inasmuch as a clear revenue of 11/m Rthl. accrues to it. If the Minister von Voss will reckon the stated yield upon improvements yet to be undertaken, then I believe I may freely maintain against this that improvements are far more likely to take place in my estates than at Krotoszyn, inasmuch as the number of villages, and likewise the area of surface, are far more considerable than in the former.

Were, however, the data adduced as to the value of Krotoszyn founded throughout in truth, then I should have importuned Your Majesty with prejudicial proposals in the exchange offered. But I owe it to myself to avoid even the suspicion that I

were capable of it; and this therefore makes it my duty most humbly to beg that my petition be not left unheard: "to charge an impartial commissioner with investigating the value of my estates and of the Krotoszyn estates, to draw up a balance of the yield of both, and to report the result to Your Majesty." I should presume most reverently to propose for this the Minister of the Estates Count von Hoym, who knows the circumstances most exactly, were it not that it might have the appearance as though he, in justification of his own administration, were speaking in support of my assertions. To Your Majesty I leave it to give this charge to a commissioner whom Your Majesty shall most highly think good, and I beg Your Majesty imploringly and urgently "not to deny me the requested inquiry and reports for the rescue of my honour, and most graciously to require the same." My intention was chiefly and solely to negotiate a capital upon the Krotoszyn estates, in order to pay my debts as soon as possible according to Your Majesty's will. It would also have given me pleasure, since they are not at the time far removed from my government, to see to their management myself, and in this regard I would even take upon myself a loss as against my own estates, whereas it can be indifferent to the State where it has its domains situated, provided only that they afford the yield fixed by the establishment.

I remain, until death,

Your Majesty's

Right Honourable Sir,

The said exchange of estates has taken a more than disagreeable turn for me, so that I find myself in a lamentable situation. My purest intention was, without falling burdensome to the State in any manner whatsoever, to rid myself [uncertain: himself] of the debts oppressing me, in order to devote my services to the King undisturbed, and without being plagued with domestic cares, for so long as my powers should last. The estates conferred upon me by the most highly blessed Monarch turned out, after I had expended some 50/m Rthl upon them, so productive that I at once formed the resolution to employ the greater part of them to borrow a sum upon them, in order to pay the debts made during my term of service. Every attempt, however, miscarried with me, since unspeakable obstacles were sought out, especially on account of the resistance of the Chambers, so that I should never have attained my purpose. A South Prussian nobleman of the name of Karnhowsky, who was willing to advance 90/m #, declared frankly "that he could give nothing upon all my estates, which were in part confiscated and for the greater part taken from the clergy. If, however, I could furnish him for his security with estates such as the Krotoszyn ones, he would be willing and ready to advance me this and a still larger sum." Hereupon the wish grew lively in me to bring the Krotoszyn estates into my possession. On the part of the Poznań Chamber it was believed that Polajewo was inseparable from Krotoszyn, and therefore I made to the King, as Your Excellency knows, the proposal that was made. Several men, however, thought on the other hand that Polajewo could not be ceded to me for ready money, and I at once wrote to Minister von Voss that I would renounce Polajewo, and wished to exchange only the Krotoszyn estates alone for those conferred upon me. The King gave only [uncertain: me] a gracious answer, and all other men versed in the matter regarded the thing as done, until at last first Minister von Voss, and afterwards the King, only wrote [uncertain: wrote to me] "That this exchange is to the disadvantage of the State, inasmuch as the Krotoszyn estates yield 17,400 Rthl more than mine do." In this affair I now appear in a light as though I had wished also at the cost

of the State to enrich myself and to play a dishonourable, self-interested part. I cannot and will not rest content in this, until the matter has been wholly cleared up and this false appearance [uncertain: rectified]. I gladly renounce all good fortune; only in my honour can I not know myself injured. In the matter of the exchange I have done nothing without having first put myself fully in the picture [uncertain: au fait] concerning everything.

I had the assurance from the Chambers and from all the world that Krotoszyn could never really yield more than 30,000 Rthl, because the town holds too many prerogatives prejudicial to the manorial lordship (Dominium). I heard that Minister von Voss would by no means undertake the administration of these estates if he were to pay over from Krotoszyn 30 and from Polajewo 20/m Rthl annually.

Minister Count von Hoym further assured me that this was a noble proposal on my part, one truly suited to the Royal interest, because by it the King would see himself covered for the future on account of the guarantee given to the Maritime Trading Company, and would at bottom be rid of a matter which, sooner or later, were it to remain in Royal hands, might yet be censured in the ugliest manner by Goerne and his heirs and take a disagreeable turn. I learned besides that many boundary suits were still pending, and especially with General Count Kalckreuth, which look so unpromising that through them a great part of Krotoszyn might yet be torn away. However dreadful some of these pictures may always appear even to myself, I nevertheless formed the resolution to propose this exchange to the King all the more readily — since it was said that I was acting nobly and in accordance with the Royal interest.

It is now more than striking to me that Minister von Voss told the King

that the State would lose some 17,400 Rthl annually thereby. I cannot and will not rest content with this portrayal by Mr Voss; I renounce, as I have said, Krotoszyn, if it be believed that I gain anything further by it than the opportunity of negotiating moneys upon it.

It is demonstrable that Krotoszyn yields no more than 30,100 Rthl, and that, according to the statement of the councillor of war von Coeln, it can at the utmost one day be brought by every art to 36,000 Rthl. My estates, in which, however, I must still pay some 70 to 80/m Rthl to two creditors, already yield some 41,500 Rthl, for which I should have given the King my warranty until his departments had themselves been convinced of it; and in this way the State would have gained annually over 11,000 Rthl, for which I pledge my princely word. More than hard and oppressive to me, therefore, is the treatment by Minister von Voss, who, upon the one-sided advice of the councillor of war Nöldichen, without instituting the least local inquiry into the one or the other estates, rendered to the King that report, which for the greater part rests only upon far-fetched and shallow speculations; and I have therefore, for the vindication of my honour, this day begged the Monarch to have this matter investigated by an impartial person — and to have laid before him from Minister von Struensee the files containing the correspondence concerning the taking over of the Krotoszyn and Polajewo estates between the most blessed King, Minister von Voss, von Struensee and Count Hoym, from which the rest will then at once appear.

Wrocław, the 7th December 1798.

The error on the part of Mr von Voss is very great, and it ought not to be difficult, with the batteries now laid, to shoot his follies full of holes, so that one may press in upon him and bring the ravings of his Nöldich to light.

In general my plan is that the King should absolutely appoint a Commissarius, or else determine the matter at once decisively and promise Your Serene Highness the estates in such a way that the business should be settled according to equal yield and value.

The manner of handling and the carrying out of my idea is then, firstly, with respect to Your Serene Highness's estates. Of these Glenck is general lessee / for he must for the present remain in play there, so that he may carry through the business at the estates, since otherwise other spirits may work knaveries and cause Your Serene Highness cost and vexation.

Glenck has a 9-year lease contract and pays annually, inclusive of the ascertained forest revenue, 44,500 Rthl. All sub-leases depend upon him; he has the liberty to clear land, to dismember, and, as concerns the profit of the estates, to do and to leave undone freely what he will. To this end he has, with his associates, given a caution of 10/m Rthl — next to this, Your Serene Highness has paid him the first sums for putting the estates in condition and for other matters etc. to the amount of 67/m Rthl., successively, and has also assigned him funds for the settlement of what still rests upon the possessors Broniewski and Trąpczynski — for which Your Highness holds his receipts, and need trouble Yourself no further as to how

he has applied and employed this or that — With this contract and with the receipts Your Serene Highness comes forward, hands these over, gives warranty of title for them, and has nothing further to do than to look upon the pen-heroes with pity when in their anguish they gnaw their nails.

2. With regard to the Krotoszyn estates. Here Mr von Voss's favourite says / for he himself does not appear in the end at all / that Krotoszyn is to bring 49,000 Rthl — the lease contract, to be sure, states only 30,000 Rthl, and the valuations no more than 23–25 and 27/m Rthl; nevertheless it is known that it had brought 49,000 Rthl — to which the answer is: whereby is this to be proved? For the declaration of Minister von Struensee states only the highest figure, which was established by Mr von Voss's manifold results, at 27 or 30/m Rthl. Then the Nöldich answers: Here I have the accounts of the rent-master Schmiedel, who kept them at the time of the Triebenfeld administration; these state so much or less, and the remainder one thinks to make up by improvements —

Then Your Serene Highness's authorised representative demands that T. too might be asked.

T. appears and asks, with irony, what is desired. The talk is then of the revenues received from Krotoszyn — It is said that these amounted to 40 or 50/m Rthl. — He answers that it may well be so; he had applied himself to it with a glowing zeal, to arrange large and considerable receipts at his rent-office — in doing so he had always cherished the ardent wish that this might be trumpeted abroad as much as possible, in order to find somebody who should thereafter hanker after the lease of Krotoszyn and take it off his hands — many and large outgoings, on the other hand, he had defrayed in silence, letting his [uncertain: Cassini] know nothing of them, so that the latter, without coming too near his already troubled conscience, might be able to assure every inquisitive person of a large revenue — for at bottom he had never, as lessee, had cause to give anybody information or to answer for profit or loss — Meanwhile his plan had succeeded:

he had got somebody who not only wished himself into his place, but moreover gave him a sum for standing down, and who, if the contract were prolonged, would in the latter years pay the King annually some 5,000 Rthl. more — this the King himself approved by cabinet order, at once accepting estates from the new lessee in place of payment, having the sum for standing down paid to T. in advance, and afterwards recovered out of the estates.

For the rest, however, he, T., must — if one called upon him to speak upon duty and honour — assure them that it must fall hard upon anyone to render up the lease raised by him to as much as 35/m Rthl. The under-lessees appointed by him, meanwhile, could not maintain themselves either — for he, T., when he engaged them at the high rents, had constantly sought thereby to make the discharge of the

Your Most Serene Highness's

true, humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

from which Your Serene Highness may [uncertain: draw] so much good [uncertain: spring] which washes away every affliction and suffering into total oblivion; and then, if Providence grants this my truly honest wish, then, most gracious Lord, preserve me in your grace and goodwill, which I shall always strive with the most ardent zeal to deserve.

Concerning the journey to Öhringen I have also spoken with the Colonel this morning. — The Colonel wishes that Your Most Serene Highness would write to His Majesty with the greatest haste and petition for the leave of absence.

My counsel therefore is that Your Highness, immediately upon receipt of this, write to the King and transmit the letter to me by express courier; I shall attend to this and then hasten it back, so that Your Serene Highness may then take your route here by way of Berlin and be able at once to thank the King besides. This is, beyond myself, the counsel of the worthy Colonel von Köckritz, and particularly that Your Serene Highness should not take your tour by way of Bohemia but over Berlin.

I reckon now that my letter will be in Your Serene Highness's hands early on Friday. May Your Highness deign within the hour to write to the King for the leave of absence, and send me the letter by express courier; I shall receive it on Sunday towards midday, give it the same day to the Colonel, on Monday I receive the answer, and with this I arrive in Wrocław on Wednesday.

With regard to the secularisation business I shall then lay before Your Serene Highness my opinions, submitted without prejudice. At present there is nothing to be done here in that respect, and I think that here too [uncertain: it can hardly be] the place for pressing this business forward. — His Serene Highness the Prince of Hesse-Darmstadt commends himself to your favour. At bottom Your Serene Highness has only three true friends here, and these are the King, Colonel von Köckritz and the Prince of Hesse-Darms[tadt]; all the others think very nearly like the man in Wrocław. But among all the rogues Wedel in Wrocław still remains the greatest, for this wretched man has given, concerning the Krotoszyn affair, a report or opinion such as can only have been hatched in the brain of an arch-liar and villain. — Upon this opinion the other gentleman, who will have it that he has done so much, then likewise delivered his opinion in writing, namely that Krot[oszyn] could readily bear 50/m Rthl — and it is precisely these infamies alone that have cost me so frightfully much trouble to overcome. The honest Cab[inet] Councillor Beyme let me read the papers in the Cab[inet] itself.

retain, and to Your Serene Highness all brain, and believe every man out of policy what he finds it good to lie.

In deepest respect I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

most humble and faithful servant

von Triebenfeld

Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Lord!

most conveniently remain here 3 to 4 days — The Monarch must have no good grounds for wishing Your Serene Highness's route to be laid here by way of Berlin. The King is greatly incensed at it, and this contributes much to his indisposition; the Queen, however, keeps moving from one chamber to the other — Yesterday evening the Princess was stripped of the dignity of Royal Highness, her household was withdrawn, other arrangements made concerning the children, and now she is to depart in haste with her husband, who is being transferred as a major with the hussars to Ausbach — that this causes a mighty terror at court, Your Serene Highness can

For that very reason I was glad that the King invited Your Serene Highness here so flatteringly — for then the B — will tremble again — because their conscience will torture them — Do not say anything to the Princess Sacken, Serene Highness, Your Serene Highness

nothing of it here, that I have disclosed to You the wicked tricks of Hoym and Wedell — And let nothing be noticed of it there either — As to the secularisation business, pray say nothing at all, Your Serene Highness — this is a mere farce — Prince George strongly advises against it — if anything can ever be done in the matter, we will do it in Vienna — I promise Your Serene Highness to work there with Prince George in its proper season just as here — for from our side nothing is being done — and if You can obtain something and enlarge Your realms, it is all one whether You obtain it from there or through action here — Settled it remains — if You have much to that end, the more compliments they will pay You.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

My warmest wishes are still only these, that Your Most Serene Highness may have arrived right happily and contented [uncertain: u] Öhringen; the affairs which otherwise lie upon my heart will surely be concluded in the best manner and everything brought [uncertain: ann] to the desired end. Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Lord!

According to several reports, the Minister von Voss, His Excellency, is to arrive in Krotoszyn in about 3 weeks in order to examine the business in question. God grant that the matter be concluded as we wish. If only Mr

Prittwitz would then take the trouble and go there himself, the matter would proceed very quickly. Chełmski has lost in the 2nd instance as well, and now I await only what he will do further. The matter will soon be concluded.

With Broniewski I can come to terms at any hour; meanwhile I shall not do so until I see how things turn out with Krotoszyn — I have now once more dissected the whole business in Poznań, and everyone now finds that not a single Groschen ought to come out of it for the [uncertain: Patri]. In the meantime, however,

in order to neglect nothing, the dismemberment there will be drafted completely and firmly; the exchange will be made along with it; so I shall settle with Broniewski for some few thousand Rthl and give order for the dismemberment — After the survey of Kamionna and Kolno, Glenck already brings out nearly 6,000 Rthl in interest, and in that fashion it will proceed proportionately with each estate — Only on account of Brzyce have I had much uproar in Poznań; they wanted to seize it at once for the Prusimski daughter, and with every imaginable exertion I have been able to obtain a term of 6 weeks — My humble advice is that the Grand Chancellor now be written to, and an extension of the term by 5 months requested — This I shall see to, for I still have blank forms. Thereafter the matter may turn out strangely — for the Treasury has applied to the Minister Hoym to have the decree of confiscation published against the Prusimski woman as well. But the Minister has ordered the files to be laid aside in secret, so that something might be

turned to the girl's advantage — since Your Serene Highness might otherwise not consent to anything at all — This turn of his is peculiar in its way — for first he did after all report these estates to the King as confiscated, and proposed them for Your Serene Highness — in law he must answer for this shortfall — He is altogether a singular man. For the rest, it may be that other means of rescue will yet be found; I shall assuredly leave nothing untried. Over the Wieniec forest the Chamber is making a great commotion; I shall meanwhile shortly go there myself and sort out the Poles — As soon as I have finished with Prince George's affairs, which may be within 5 weeks, I shall hasten to Berlin to prepare everything for von Voss's return — The letter to Mr von Prittwitz Wildeganst will deliver today, and the one to [illegible] shall likewise be handed over. Everything is also very well said; meanwhile I do not believe that Weigel is to blame for it — With Schlabrendorff I shall manage the matter one way or the other. In the end he shall himself lend me the money for the payment of the

interest — Wildeganst takes every imaginable pains to conduct this in a delicate manner. The news about the war is truly sad; meanwhile I hope that matters there will go better than is believed. With the Russians it looks bad, for there they plunder greatly, and as I have observed all of South Prussia is turning that way — It is a true misfortune that nobody in South Prussia keeps watch over the people. Everything already looks quite like a band of robbers.

May God only keep Your Serene Highness in health. In deepest submission I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

most faithful and most humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 6th of March 1799.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

In the Broniewski matter I have as yet done nothing further, because the term for the taking of evidence is set for the 14th of this month. The patron is now very willing to settle, and I believe that he would for the present be content with some 20/m Rthl. But the real proofs newly furnished by Rapacki testify clearly that not a Groschen belongs to him — this is the reason why I am still deferring the settlement. If the Government accepts these grounds, then no settlement will take place — unless the Krotoszyn exchange should require it, for the sake of which I would at need sacrifice a few thousand, and in order to come at once into possession. His anxiety is already very great, for he offers even to accept a bond which I hold from the Minister on Kępno. From Mr Schlabrendorff I shall have news today, whether he is satisfied with my bill of exchange at one year. In any event I shall seek to pacify him.

The Chełmski suit has been won in the second instance — it now remains to be seen whether he will proceed further — through Rapacki and Kordaszewcken I shall presumably obtain real intelligence concerning the Brzyce estates; also arrange-

ments have been made for me to get into my hands the documents concerning the Wieniec forest; these will no doubt at once refute from the ground up the foolish babble of the witnesses — the Chełmski and Broniewski matters will be brought to a good end; only the Brzyce and Wieniec ones demand every attention — because behind them stands the worst web of malice — Above all, I am now sitting over a description of the estates bestowed upon Your Most Serene Highness. A quarrel between Prittwitz and Glenck, and likewise the constant carping of the Minister — as though Your Serene Highness had received, quite contrary to the his of the King, too many estates, in which Prittwitz seems to concur — give me occasion for it.

Out of the one, envy bellows; out of the other, a clumsy ignoramus. For if one takes it that the King ordered estates to be given to Your Most Serene Highness bearing 7 to 8,000 Rthl of revenues, then this has only been punctually fulfilled in every part. The confiscated Prusimski estates, which were given first, were to answer to the King's will; but the valuations of the chamber councillor Beukerts, chosen by the Minister himself,

proved that twice as much debt still rested upon those estates as the value of the same was ascertained to be from the yield by Beukert.

In order now to cloak the evil intention previously entertained, and to comply with the his of the Monarch, the Minister then proposed the various ecclesiastical estates, which were to bring 8,640 Rthl of revenues.

The Prusimski estates are now to be regarded as bought, because they must first be vindicated at law and fought for step by step, and considerable sums must still be paid in upon them. They are therefore no gift at all, and stand upon the same footing as purchased allodial estates, with which one often fares more happily than with these. Meanwhile the yield thereafter falls out in the following manner:

1. from Kamionna and Kolno = 6,000 Rthl.

2. from Trąbczyn = 8,400 Rthl.

3. from Szetlewek = 1,600 Rthl.

4. from Brzyce = 4,000 Rthl. is in sum 20,000 Rthl.

The estates now actually bestowed, in respect of which, as alleged, the King's will has been exceeded, have been valued how many times over, and were to bear = 8,640 Rthl; through [uncertain: seren] sums paid and three years' revenues applied therein, a surplus of about = 14,000 Rthl has been brought out; this makes together = 22,640 Rthl, in all 42,640 Rthl.

NB to the 8,640 Rthl there come further about 1,400 Rthl of building moneys, which may be deducted from the 14,000; so they are improved only by about 12,000 Rthl of yield.

The yield of the bestowed estates is therefore now raised by something more than the double, through diligence, expense and industry. This, however, is no wonder to the clear-sighted man; still less does the least offence lie here, but merely spiteful envy, grounded in the daily [uncertain: Gepkerr] of men. For take the Bischofswerder estates: these were, according to 4 valuations, to bear at most 1,500 Rthl — I sold them for 207,000 Rthl. The Zastrow estates were, [illegible], to bear about 2,000 Rthl; they indisputably bring some twenty thousand. The Dolf estates were to bear about 500 Rthl; Treskow — is now selling them for 360,000 Rthl. Those of General Rüchel were to bear 940 Rthl yearly; they were sold for 140,000 Rthl. Of all these not a word is spoken; only in the case of Your Serene Highness's estates does one indulge the vice of envy, and carp without knowing what. Sad enough for the State that men are constantly paid salaries who [uncertain: mir] act out of passion, who dwell upon trifles and upon the everyday chronique scandaleuse, but never take the whole to heart.

Glenck shall meanwhile lay this representation of the matter before Prittwitz under his own name, and after that one shall indeed see what sheepish faces the one or the other will show. God grant that Your Serene Highness may soon return to me in health; if not, I shall doubtless come from Berlin to Öhringen, Ansbach, or wherever I may find Your Highness. The wretched war has then truly broken out after all — rather is this, however, a wholesome poison — I remain, until death, Your Most Serene Highness's

faithful servant

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 13th of March 1799.
