Most Serene etc. Poznań, 19 March 1799. Suit of Stanisl[aus] von Chełmski of Łukom near Pyzdry v. the Starost Anton v Prusimski of Trąbczyn, concerning 12,000 ducats on the strength of a handwritten bond (ex chirographo).

On 16 June 1794 I had to advance to the Starost Anton von Prusimski of Trąbczyn, Nowawies, Osiny and the Trąbczyn Hollanders 12,000 ducats for one year, namely until St John's Day 1795, for which he handed me the blank note enclosed in copy, in the presence of Jacob von Bieńkowski of Mierzewo near Gniezno and of Antonius v Przeradzki. At the loan itself it was agreed between me and the defendant debtor, in the presence of those witnesses, that if the repayment of these 12,000 ducats did not follow on the date fixed for payment, I might treat the said

blank note as a contract of antichresis (contractus antichreticus) and take possession of the estates listed as a pledge. Payment did not in fact follow on the date agreed, namely at St John's Day last year, and I therefore took possession of these estates at that time.

Meanwhile my debtor was charged by the Fiscus with taking part in the insurrection that broke out in this province in 1794, and because he has not even yet returned, his property was to be seized by the Fiscus in the month of May last year, which I had forestalled only by taking possession of the said estates in the month of June.

The Fiscus did then bring a suit for eviction before Your Royal Majesty on 7 December 1795, and a hearing on it was set for the 27th

27 February this year before Your Most High Government; but at it the following settlement was reached between me and the Fiscus: that I am to sequestrate the oft-mentioned estates, first deduct the interest for delay at 7 per cent from the income, but then render account, while still pursuing my claims at law.

Before Your Royal Majesty I therefore bring my suit against the Starost Anton von Prusimski for these 12,000 ducats, with the request that a hearing to take evidence be appointed, and that the defendant be not only summoned to it but also condemned both to pay the 12,000 ducats owed and to pay interest for delay at 7 per cent, with costs.

In proof of the correctness of the loan, and that he stipulated taking possession of the pledge in

case of non-payment on the fixed date, I refer also to the witnesses proposed above, whom I at the same time most humbly[?] ask to have examined, and that this my suit be deemed sufficiently substantiated. who am etc.

Your Royal Majesty

etc.

v Chełmski.

Most Serene, Most Mighty, Most Gracious King and Lord! Kalisz, 8 October 1799.

In the year 1794 I gave the Starost von Prusimski a loan of 12,000 ducats in gold against a written undertaking, which he promised to repay at St John's Day 1795. Before the date of payment came, however, von Prusimski became a fugitive, and through the sentence of confiscation passed against him his property was seized by the Fiscus.

After consulting with him, von Prusimski, I did take possession of the estates of Trąbczyn and Nowawies belonging to him, but I had to give them up to the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, to whom these estates had been given by Your Royal

Majesty's own Most High Person, upon the opening of the judgment of revision, and was referred with my said claim to the Fiscus.

I then sued the Fiscus for payment of it on 6 September this year, but by the decree of the 10th of the same month, which I enclose in copy, I was told that before my suit could be admitted the real character of the said claim must first be proved.

Since by the judgment of revision mentioned above the contrary was already established, and since moreover I demand my satisfaction not from the

Prince of Hohenlohe but from the Fiscus as possessor of the whole of von Prusimski's property, the suit in this matter was not inadmissible on the ground that the claim in question is merely personal. Referring to the Most High Cabinet Order of 14 September 1796, I pressed repeatedly for a hearing to take evidence to be appointed; against my expectation, however, I was once more dismissed with the suit by the decree of the 27th of the same month, which I likewise present in copy.

As I cannot rest content with these adverse rulings,

I see myself compelled, for the following reasons, to have recourse to Your Majesty's Most High court. By the Cabinet Order just mentioned, No. 2, it is indeed ordained that the Fiscus, in respect of compensation for damage, takes precedence over all personal creditors of an insurgent, and that it shall then rank after them with the penalty of confiscation. It is thus clear that the Fiscus must give satisfaction from the confiscated property for a personal claim on the insurgent, if its correctness is proved from elsewhere (aliunde), otherwise than by my mere written undertaking; and that there is therefore no sufficient ground in the present case for dismissing the suit because

the claim is merely personal.

The declaratory Court Rescript of 17 September 1796 can find no application here, since on the one hand it interprets the Cabinet Order, the Most High will of Your Royal Majesty Yourself, extensively and against its clear content, which belongs solely to Your Most High[?] Person and not to the Chief of Justice; and on the other hand it touches on matters of substance.

But even the said Rescript lays down that personal suits against the Fiscus are to be admitted without question at the parties' request, but that a certified

statement of the damage done by the insurrection, for which by legal principles the insurgents are liable jointly and severally (in solidum), might be laid before such a plaintiff by the Fiscus, from which it should appear that the confiscated property of the insurgents is far from sufficient to cover these damages.

I will gladly accept that procedure, but reserve my objections to such a liquidation of damages, and most humbly ask Your Royal Majesty

to grant me a hearing at law, and to instruct the Government at Kalisz to open the taking of evidence on the suit I have brought against the Fiscus.

I who remain, until death, in deepest reverence Your Royal Majesty's most humble Stanisl v. Chełmski, in his own hand

Kalisz, 1 December 1799.

Most Serene etc. As early as 9 October this year my client, the landowner v Chełmski, submitted to Your Royal Majesty a complaint against the Government here over the improper dismissal of a suit brought against the Fiscus concerning a claim of 12,000 ducats, and most humbly asked for a hearing at law. As no preliminary ruling has followed yet, I make bold to petition Your Most High Majesty again on this matter. The decrees of the Government plainly rest on a misunderstanding, in that they confuse the suit that v. Chełmski first brought against the Prince of Hohenlohe, as present owner of the Trąbczyn estates confiscated from Prusimski, with the present one, which is directed against the Fiscus alone.

That the claim of 12,000 ducats cannot be sued for against the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, my client understands of himself. On the other hand the Court Rescript of 17 September 1796 in no way prevents him from claiming the said capital from the Fiscus, under the clear provision of the Most High Cabinet Order of the 16th of the same month and year.

If, moreover, the Government follows the letter of the Court Rescript, which is not binding in itself, it nonetheless cannot refuse v. Chełmski a hearing at law in this matter, since this very Rescript expressly lays down that if the party does not rest content with the dismissal by decree, the taking of evidence is to be opened and the matter formally adjudged. This, in my opinion, must happen in every legal matter where

the party cannot be convinced that the dismissal was lawful.

I enclose a copy of the suit with the bond on which it rests (ex quo), which my client had already brought before the Government at Poznań, - only I must remark that he had first sued v Prusimski before the judgment of confiscation had been passed.

On the resumption of the proceedings against the Fiscus nothing was changed but the person. So that the matter may not be delayed any longer, and the plaintiff may at last be satisfied, I most humbly ask Your Royal Majesty to have a preliminary ruling given him without delay. I who etc.

Your Royal Majesty etc.

Mondro

criminal-court councillor.

Most Serene: The Prince of Hohenlohe's further most humble submission concerning the exchange of his estates situated in South Prussia for the lordships of Krotoszyn and Polajewo. From a letter addressed to me by the Privy Minister of State von Voss, dated the 1st of December, I learn that he has not found the exchange of my estates in South Prussia for Krotoszyn and Polajewo, which I most humbly offered to Your Majesty on the xxxxx th of xxxxx, consonant with Your Royal Majesty's interest. The grounds adduced in this regard are:

I) that in the case of this district office the true principles of husbandry have not been followed, because

a) the lessee has been granted unusual and unwarranted great advantages, by way of a so-called Reservations Fund, whose annual capital amounts to 9,540 Rthl.

b) that an entire demesne farm, which yields 1,500 Rthl. of rent, was not brought into the valuation and was passed over altogether.

c) that the very profitable mast in the woodlands has been made over to the councillor of war Triebenfeld by way of indemnification for the small sum of 3,327 Rthl. in super-inventory monies paid to his predecessor upon his entering into the lease.

II) that by an altered arrangement in the forests, which hitherto have yielded no return whatever, a considerable income could now already be obtained; and therefore, by adding these items to the existing lease sum of 30,100 Rthl., which I wished to take as the basis of the exchange, that sum would have to be raised as high as 60,000 Rthl.

III) that these district offices, being domains, afford me just as little security as the estates already received from His Majesty.

To refute the above grounds the Count von Hoym would indeed be better able than I, since these estates have hitherto stood under his supervision, inasmuch as an unfavourable light is thereby cast upon the previous administration; yet through my acquaintance with the locality and with the lessees of that time I shall be in a position to refute these assertions thoroughly, and in what follows to lay most humbly at Your Royal Majesty's feet a plan still more advantageous to Your Highest interest, more in order to remove the appearance

that I wished to enrich myself at the expense of Your Majesty's treasury, than for the sake of my own advantage. On point I, concerning the excessive advantages of the present Krotoszyn district lease: on a) the Privy Minister of State von Voss appears still too new to and unacquainted with the constitution of the district office, when he has quite incorrectly asserted that the fund of

9,543 Rthl.

of the Reservations Fund could accrue to the lease sum, and when he will not distinguish between gross and net yield. The gross yield does indeed consist of 39,643 Rthl. From this, however, the necessary outlays have not been deducted at all, and there always remains to the Royal treasury only the surplus of 30,100 Rthl.

Now, since I took the latter sum as the basis of the exchange, it goes without saying that I have undertaken to bear those outlays.

These outlays consist of

24 per cent land contribution = 2,722 Rthl.

Salaries for the judicial officials of the district office = 1,234 Rthl. For remissions to the subjects, reckoned one year with another, = 2,000 Rthl. = 5,956 Rthl.

There accordingly still remains over = 3,587 Rthl.

This remaining amount is far from sufficient to maintain the buildings of the district office yearly, and to this item would have to be added all those advantages which forest and mast may perhaps afford.

On b) it is just as incorrectly asserted that an entire demesne farm has hitherto been left out of the valuation. The case is quite otherwise. This is no demesne

farm, but 1 Hollander Hufe, which von Triebenfeld acquired from the possessors of two Hollanders as far back as Polish times. A demesne farm has indeed been laid out by him upon it, and the same ceded to the present lessee; nonetheless it cannot be regarded as an appurtenance of the manorial lordship (Dominium). And even supposing that von Triebenfeld had acquired it illegitimate modo, it would be the former possessors, and not the Treasury, who could vindicate it. On c) the Privy Minister of State von Voss can never have seen the Krotoszyn woodlands.

It is notorious that they have already been devastated by the ex-minister von Goerne, who for a year and a day had stave-cutters, six hundred persons of them, at work therein; and although the terrain is indeed large enough, yet a whole century must first pass before it becomes serviceable again, if one will but consider that all the subjects receive free timber for building and firewood, whence it comes that neither forest nor mast usage has hitherto been of any importance.

If therefore the Privy Minister of State von Voss asserts that Krotoszyn must in future yield 60,000 Rthl., then I most humbly and most urgently beg Your Royal Majesty to hold him to his word at the end of the lease in 1800, should nothing come of my offer; and I shall not fail then to remind Mr von Voss of it. The meliorations to be looked for, however, are not to the point here, inasmuch as a large capital outlay is required for them.

On 3, the [uncertain: Kan.] Voss betrays no knowledge whatever of the matter, inasmuch as the district offices of Krotoszyn and Polajewo are no domains at all, but at best may after 36 years develop into such, which likewise I do not doubt.

These estates are originally of noble quality; they were bought by Minister

Goerne qua tales, and thereupon sequestrated for the account of the Maritime Trading Company, to which von Goerne owed [uncertain: nearly] 1 million thaler.

When South Prussia was occupied, the Maritime Trading Company was eager to cover that capital together with the interest, and exerted itself to bring about that the estates should be handed over to the Poznań Chamber in administration on the condition that an amortisation amount of 50/m Rthl. should be discharged yearly.

At that time this plan was entirely repugnant to Mr von Voss, and for that reason I cannot now explain his contradiction to myself either, since the matter stands this very day just as it stood then.

After Mr von Voss had lost the department, the plan of the Maritime Trading Company was confirmed by a cabinet order of the 4th of March 1795, but it was at the same time laid down therein that only after 36 years, when that burden of debt had been discharged, should these estates assume the character of domains. Until then they are to be regarded as private estates, which is sufficiently proved already by the fact that they bear the burdens of noble estates, such as the 24 per cent dues.

Having sufficiently refuted the assertions of Mr von Voss, I cannot forbear adding the following, which

Mr von Voss has probably passed over in silence deliberately:

1. Krotoszyn has lost the propination rights in the town of Krotoszyn, whereby the revenue is reduced by 4,000 Rthl. according to the valuation.

2. The most important part of the forest is in a boundary dispute with the manorial lordship of Kozmin.

3. The Jews have brought it about by judgment and law that

they have been reduced to lower dues.

4. Polajewo is leased at 6,000 Rthl. higher than it was valued, on which account sequestration has already been set in motion there three times, and the lessee, Count von Flotow, has thereby been ruined, who, as I am prepared to prove, has already sunk 20,000 Rthl. in it.

5. Polajewo is so totally ruined that the costs of restoration have been put at

300,000 Rthl.; to which [uncertain: there is added] that the forest is stripped of all building timber; and

6. I pledge my honour that Polajewo must come down to a net yield of 12,000 Rthl. net if the restoration is to be effected out of the revenues.

I appeal to the opinion of the Poznań Chamber that this is the true state of the matter. Now may it please Your Royal Majesty most graciously to have my further proposal most humbly laid before you.

1. I renounce the possession of Polajewo. But because the [uncertain: district office] is not in a position to afford the present yield any longer, I am willing to undertake to pay 8,000 Rthl. yearly on that account, and to be content that the same be transferred onto Krotoszyn, of which therefore the net yield would be 38,000 instead of 30/m, whereby I afford more than if I were, on my first offer, to take over Polajewo as well.

2. I undertake, as goes without saying, all the public burdens (onera publica), buildings, remissions etc. charged upon Krotoszyn, which have hitherto been paid out of the Reservations Fund.

3. My estates must be valued, or my lease contracts taken as the basis of the exchange, and from these the net yield

be constituted; this is to be balanced against the net yield of Krotoszyn, reckoned to capital at 5 per cent, and whatever Krotoszyn is worth more than my estates I will pay in cash to the Maritime Trading Company, whereby then the yearly amortisation amount is proportionately reduced, which Krotoszyn and Polajewo have hitherto discharged at 50/m r. yearly, and which in future Polajewo and my estates will discharge.

The advantages which I gain thereby are:

1. those already adduced in my submission of the —

2. that I obtain a rounding-out of my estates, which hitherto lie scattered in South Prussia

3. that Krotoszyn lies only 8 miles distant from Wrocław, and can be managed in the neighbourhood of my domicile. The advantages which Your Royal Majesty gains are:

1. it can be a matter of indifference to Your Royal Majesty whether my estates lie scattered, since they do after all border one upon the other domains.

2. Pszczew contains building timber, firewood and meadow growth; this is wanting to the intendancy of [uncertain: Buck] and Międzyrzecz,

3. Polajewo is relieved by 8,000 Rthl.

4. The amortisation amount is reduced. Since I am firmly convinced that Your Royal Majesty, as well as I, gains by this exchange, and since my point of honour suffers when the matter is represented otherwise by Mr von Voss, I must most humbly beg:

that Your Royal Majesty may be pleased to direct the Poznań Chamber by cabinet order to have the investigation carried out by 2

members of the Chamber who are acquainted with the matter, whose vote should circulate among the remaining members of the collegium, each of whom should then add his own vote, from which the correctness of my statement will certainly appear; at the same time I also beg that a report be required of the Count von Hoym, and I remain, until death, in deepest fidelity,

Your Royal Majesty's.

We Friedrich Wilhelm, by God's Grace King of Prussia etc., do by means of this Our open letter, for Ourselves and Our successors to the Crown of the Electorate and Our remaining lands, attest and declare, and hereby graciously give to know to each and every one whom the same concerns: that, inasmuch as We are by inborn favour and clemency much inclined to acknowledge and requite the good and profitable services rendered to Us and to Our Royal House by particular marks of Our Royal benevolence, We have [considered] the services rendered by the High-Born Prince, Our

affectionately dear Uncle Friedrich Ludwig, reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, Our Lieutenant-General of Infantry, Chief of a Regiment of Foot, Governor of the capital city of Wrocław, Knight of Our Orders etc., the important, distinguished and useful services rendered for a considerable number of years to Us and to Our Royal House, weighed in Our Royal mind; and that, in order to give the said Lord Prince a mark of the recognition of his excellent merits and of Our Royal gratitude, We have resolved to confer and convey to him, heritably and in full property, the below-named estates which have fallen to Our All-Highest disposition, namely:

Kamionna, the town, with the market-town of Kolno

of the Poznań district; the villages of Trąbczyn, Szetlewek, Nowawies, Łazy, Old and New Laske, Osiny, Hauland Trąbczyński of the Konin district; and the village of Brzyce together with its appurtenances in Cujavia, with all their belongings, by whatever names they may be called.

This We also hereby do, and by force of this present instrument, out of Royal power and plenitude, for Ourselves and Our successors and heirs to the Crown of the Electorate and Our remaining lands, in such manner and to the effect that the above-mentioned Our affectionately dear Uncle, the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, shall have the above-named estates with all rights and jurisdictions attach-

ing to them as the same have hitherto been exercised, or may lawfully be exercised, and no less with all their appurtenances and other belongings, by whatever names they may be called, in such manner as the same have hitherto been enjoyed or may lawfully be enjoyed, as a well-acquired and unrestricted property - yet subject to the reservation of the sovereign taxes and other public dues to be laid upon them in like manner as upon the other estates of Our South Prussian vassals - for himself and his successors and heirs, from now on unto eternal times, irrevocably from Us and Our successors, to

have, hold and enjoy; and that there shall likewise be vested in him the power to dispose thereof at his pleasure, unhindered by any man.

We accordingly command and enjoin all Our South Prussian governments and Chambers of War and Domains, as also all other authorities whom the same concerns, herewith as graciously as earnestly, that they in no wise hinder or trouble either the aforementioned Lord Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen in the heritable and proprietary possession, conferred upon him, of the above-named holdings and estates together with their appurtenances and belongings, nor him or those to whom he may in time, by virtue and in force of this

Our deed of donation, bequeath the same, or otherwise lawfully transfer it by other acts inter vivos aut mortis causa; but rather shall let him, and eventually also them, enjoy the same freely and quietly, doing nothing themselves against it, nor occasioning or permitting that such be done by others, on pain of Our All-Highest displeasure and unfailing severe punishment.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

The affair with Prince George grows ever more alarming, and the distress on my side ever greater. President v. Schuckmann writes me that he duly delivered my letters to the Prince; notwithstanding this the Prince answers not a syllable, and sends no remittances either. The Jew Kuh has sued me over the 5,800 Rthl; he already has a decree of execution, and on Friday I am to pay or be arrested — on that account I was yesterday at Dyhrenfurth, where the minister assured me that he would be in Wrocław today and would calm the Jew. Just now I was at his residence, and there it is said that he will not come until Thursday. It is truly dreadful how the Prince treats me. In Berlin he borrowed 120,000 Rthl upon the estates — then he drew through Schuz 55,000 Rthl — here he has drawn, according to the accursed bills of exchange, about 23,000 Rthl.

The costs etc. 8,000; these are in sum 206,000 Rthl. Now there stand upon the estates a further 64,000 Rthl of debt.

In this way the dear Prince has already encumbered the estates with 270,000 Rthl of debt — I sold them to him for 280,000 Rthl, and the remainder is 10,000 Rthl.

Right Honourable Sir; Most Highly Honoured Lord Grand Chancellor! Your Excellency will forgive me if I take the liberty of accompanying my petition with these few words.

My trust in Your Excellency's goodwill towards me is far too great for me not to look forward with complete confidence to the granting of my most urgent request: "that Your Excellency might deign kindly to give orders in accordance with the contents of the petition".

The following reasons have moved me to my request,

among others:

The very proposal for a settlement which the commissioned judge (Deputatus) made at the last hearing makes me anxious that the Government at Poznań may not set about drawing up the judgment with the impartiality that is due. The life interest which the plaintiff's father, who is still living, had to exercise in the property of his late wife is surely plainly a part of the property confiscated from him, and by the confiscation of the entire present and future property of

von Prusimski the Treasury (Fiscus) has surely plainly made the life interest subject to itself. It therefore struck me greatly that the commissioned judge, in his proposal for a settlement, could raise the strange doubt against the validity of the life interest, that it would not belong to the Treasury because the plaintiff's late mother had not contracted with the Treasury concerning the life interest. This, and likewise the circumstance that the guardianship board, which pursues the case with so much zeal, is at the same time to be judge in it, and no less other reasons bearing solely on my individual conviction, have therefore raised in me a misgiving about having the case decided by the Government at Poznań. I therefore once more most urgently beg Your Excellency kindly to entrust the decision of the case either to the Government at Kalisz or to any other South Prussian court. May Your Excellency deign to accept the assurance of the un

bounded reverence with which I shall remain for life Your Excellency's most obedient servant, F[riedrich] L[udwig] P[rince] of Hohenlohe.

Most Serene Prince, Gracious Lord!

It is exceedingly agreeable to me that Your Serene Highness has been pleased, by Your most honoured letter of yesterday's date, to put me fully in the picture concerning the affair of Your South Prussian estates.

Mere misunderstanding lies at the bottom of it if Your Serene Highness has been in the least disquieted concerning their transfer, and in proof of this I need only append herewith a copy of the dispositions issued to the respective Chambers at Poznań and Petrikau, and despatched by express couriers for the expediting of the matter, of the 26th of last month, in order to convince Your Serene Highness that I have most conscientiously ordered the speediest taking-over and transfer of all the estates, so as to see everything set right, if possible, during the time of [the] presence in the province. I have accordingly acted in this not only on Your behalf, as [I have] for the named gentlemen donatories, but have even instructed the respective Chambers as to the transfer earlier than the instrument of grant concerning the last estates was made out. Your Serene Highness may therefore also, and indeed from Midsummer of this year onward, regard Yourself simply as sole lord and proprietor [uncertain: his own] of the same, of the [uncertain: ecclesiastical] estates reserved to Yourself by His Majesty. For the hitherto ecclesiastical possessors have since the 1st of June 1796 no longer been sitting on their own account but on account of the Treasury, in these estates already at that time drawn in to His Majesty's revenues. As soon as they receive their competence according to principle, they must vacate the estates any day, for they are already now sitting upon competence moneys and [illegible] them, and must pay out to the Treasury everything that goes beyond such. There is only this difference, that the clergy, who have hitherto remained in the

natural possession of the estates up to now, do not yet know, up to now and before the taking-over of their estates, how they are to receive their competence, and the reason lies in this, that with so great a quantity of such estates the valuation assessments could not all be prepared within this short time, nor the consolidations for the new domain offices be completed. The Bishop of Cujavia would therefore likewise have had to vacate the estates of Wieniec and Wolica, had Your Serene Highness not been graciously pleased to declare Yourself willing to leave them still to him. Probably, however, the following circumstance has given occasion to the misunderstanding: according to the first plan, all the estates in South Prussia which had been declared drawn in for the royal account already since the 1st of June 1796 were to have been taken from their then possessors on the 1st of June 1797; this was not possible for the reasons adduced above, and because through the numerous donations of estates the establishment of the domain offices was constantly [uncertain: delayed], and therefore the general determination was made that these hitherto possessors might continue to manage such estates until June 1798 in the manner hitherto, that is, for the account of the Treasury. Various of these possessors have made use of one estate or another by leasing it out, and if their lessees are de facto evicted, these demand compensation from their lessors, namely the clergy, and if these excuse themselves on the ground that not they but the Treasury threw them out of the lease, then the Treasury must compensate such lessees, and thereby the most prejudicial lawsuits arise for the royal treasury. Now the clergy may indeed be [in the case] of long-term lease contracts, but since they received only the authority to manage the estates, in the manner hitherto allowed, until Midsummer 1798, neither can the Treasury lawfully be expected to declare these leases valid for longer than up to this term. Perhaps in the whole body of estates which have been granted to Your Serene Highness there is no case in which a valid lease contract

exists between the hitherto possessors and a lessee; but should such a case nevertheless be found here or there, the lessee will probably be brought by amicable means to vacate. If this cannot be effected without disadvantage to You, then Your Serene Highness will Yourself be inclined rather to leave him in the lease until June 1798 and to receive the lease money instead, since otherwise the royal treasury would not only lose the revenues but would also have to hold the lessee harmless. Only with regard to the competence moneys is it to be observed that their determination, according to the [uncertain: Hohlinschen] surveys, turns out so low that particularly in the case of the monasteries the monks [illegible] could not subsist at all. His Majesty has therefore also commanded by cabinet order that the valuation assessments be taken as the basis, and since these are already low as against the true yield, the clergy thereby already suffer loss, inasmuch as by the royal declaration concerning the drawing-in of the estates everything has been assured to them that remains of the yield after deduction of 15 per cent administration costs and 50 per cent [uncertain: dues]. This detail lays before Your Serene Highness an exact survey of the established principles, and, with Your good way of thinking, You will find them just and equitable. Should You desire any special dispositions to the War and Domains Chamber, I most obediently beg to be informed of it, and it shall be exceedingly agreeable to me to be able to act entirely in accordance with Your wishes. For Your Serene Highness has proofs enough that it has for many years been my endeavour to be of service to You, and thereby also to lay down the most perfect veneration, in which I remain, until death,

Your Serene Highness's

most obedient servant Hoym

Wrocław, the 3rd of October 1797.

to convey.

as graciously as earnestly, that they shall in no wise hinder or impede the oft-mentioned Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen in the hereditary and proprietary possession, conferred upon him, of the above-named possessions and estates together with their appurtenances and belongings, nor him or those to whom he may one day, by virtue and in force of this Our letter of donation, bequeath the same or otherwise lawfully transfer it by other acts among the living or by reason of death; but rather shall let him, and eventually also them, enjoy the same freely and undisturbed, shall themselves do nothing against it, nor occasion or permit such to be done by others, on pain of Our All-Highest displeasure and of unfailing severe punishment.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord, just now my tenant from Świniary has sent in and begs me urgently to come out for a moment and to bring the peasants into order, who will not obey him but mean to refuse their services. I must now hasten thither to prevent mischief. Your Most Serene Highness will most graciously forgive me that today, on account of this matter, I do not appear at the midday meal. With the Minister I have spoken today concerning Schlabrendorff. Frankly said, he seems to take it somewhat amiss that Your Most Serene Highness will tell him nothing, for I believe he expected that yesterday — [uncertain: rech] but I find it good that Your Highness tells him nothing; one can first see what he will do.

He has written to Schlabrendorff that on the 15th of the [...]

month he is to be here; he has to speak with him in the matter in question — for the present he lays it on his heart to withdraw all complaint at once, for people are watching him so closely that not the least thing would remain undiscovered, and if one were to find a Groschen's worth of blemish in the affair he could be assured that it might go badly for him.

He, the Minister, could not afterwards save him, Sch:, even with the best will; indeed he would then have to deny outright that he is related to him by ties of blood, etc.

Asch he had with him today and told him all this by word of mouth, so that it might be laid further upon the heart of the Count in Stolze, whither Asch goes the day after tomorrow; in particular he is by all means to prevail upon Schlabrendorff to be here on the 15th of this month.

I go tomorrow to Lądek, but shall quite certainly be here again on the 15th too, and then I shall harness Hirsch in alongside — In deepest submission I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

faithful humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Instrument of valuation of the estate of Szetlewek, belonging to the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, Friederich Ludewig, Serene Highness, situate in the Province of South Prussia, in the Department of the Royal Government at Kalisz, in its Konin district and the parish of Rzgow.

The estate of Szetlewek, situate in the Province of South Prussia in the Department of the Royal Government at Kalisz, in its Konin district and the parish of Rzgow, lies 1 1/4 miles from Zagórów, 3 miles from Konin, 2 miles from Pyzdry, 2 miles from Slupce, 5 miles from Kalisz, and 1 mile from the river Wartha. It borders towards the east upon Podbiele and Grabienice, has a corner[illegible]boundary with Grabienice, Świątniki and Kurow; towards the south upon Kurow and Biskupice; towards the west upon Łukom; and towards the north upon Trąbczyn. and the surface content thereof ascertained at 1,724 M. 2 R. For the purposes of this valuation the parcels have been graded for quality, with the assistance of the surveyor Chwalowski and two sworn [uncertain: Bautners], and according to the grading register they comprise

We Friedrich Wilhelm, by the Grace of God King of Prussia etc., do hereby attest and declare by this Our open letter, for Ourselves and Our descendants and successors to the Crown, to the Electorate, and to Our remaining lands, that whereas it has been most humbly laid before Us in what manner Our intention — namely, to give to the High-born Prince, Our kindly beloved uncle, Friedrich Ludwig, reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, by the grant of the estates that had belonged to the absconded former starosta von Prusimski, a mark of the friendship and goodwill We bear towards him, as also of Our Royal gratitude for the distinguished and beneficial services rendered to Us and to Our Royal House — has not been attained entirely as We had willed it, because the said estates were burdened with many debts, We have most highly resolved to make over, grant and convey to His Lordship the hereinafter-named formerly ecclesiastical estates, namely the villages of Pszczew, Świechocin, Stoki, Łowyń, Głażewo, Tarnowo, Zagórów, Skokum, Świątniki, Kopojno, Olesnica, Drzewce, Grądzyń, Wrąbczyn, Wieniec and Wolica, together with all their appurtenances, by whatever name they may be called, against payment of,

1.) the sovereign dues hitherto discharged therefrom, as a fixed and unalterable canon, and

2, the competence due therefrom to the ecclesiastical corporations or foundations.

to be left over to him hereditarily and in full property, granted and conveyed.

We do so likewise hereby and by virtue of this present, out of Royal power and plenitude, for Ourselves and Our descendants and successors to the Crown, to the Electorate and to Our remaining lands, in such wise and so that Our aforesaid kindly beloved uncle, the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, shall from now on and for all time, for Himself and His descendants and heirs, irrevocably have, possess and enjoy the above-named estates with all rights and liberties attaching thereto, as these have hitherto been exercised or may lawfully be exercised, and no less with all their pertinences and other appurtenances, by whatever name they may be called, as the same have hitherto been used or may lawfully be used, and with all the lands belonging thereto, in fields, woods and meadows, likewise in ponds and waters, as a true, well-acquired and unrestricted property, from Us and Our descendants and successors; and that there shall further be conferred upon the same the power and authority to dispose thereof at pleasure under the above-mentioned conditions, unhindered by any man.

We therefore command and enjoin all Our Supreme Provincial Colleges, as also all other authorities whom this concerns, herewith as graciously as earnestly, that they in no wise hinder or impede the Lordship of the oft-mentioned Lord Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen in the hereditary and proprietary possession of the above-named estates granted to Him, together with their pertinences and appurtenances, nor him or those upon whom He may one day bequeath the same, or may otherwise lawfully transfer them by other acts inter vivos aut mortis causa, but rather shall let His Lordship, and eventually them also, enjoy the same freely and quietly, shall themselves do nothing against it, nor cause or permit that such be done by others, on pain of Our Most High disfavour and unfailing severe punishment. In witness whereof etc. Given at Berlin, the 19th of June 1797. Deed of Grant.

Friedrich Wilhelm

for the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, to the hereditary and proprietary possession of the villages of Pszczew, Świechocin, Stoki, Łowyń, Głażewo, Tarnowo, Zagórów, Skokum, Świątniki, Kopojno, Olesnica, Drzewce, Grądzyń, Wrąbczyn, Wieniec and Wolica, together with appurtenances. E. W. v. Rösch — between the special authorised representative of His Most Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, Forest Inspector Rochlitz, as seller on the one part, and Martin Honrichs and Valentin v. Kwasieborski, as purchasers on the other part, there has, with due deliberation, been agreed and concluded under today's date the following points of contract, for the purpose of a formal judicial contract of purchase and sale to be concluded hereafter concerning the noble estate of Witów.

The said Forest Inspector Rochlitz sells, in the name of His Most Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, the aforesaid his Lord and principal, the noble estate lying in the Royal South Prussian Kalisz Government Department and in its Warta district, namely the village and village mayor's holding of Witów with all appurtenant rights and privileges, nothing thereof excepted, just as the same was, pursuant to the Most High deed of donation of the most blessed King Frie-

-drich Wilhelm the Second, conferred upon Colonel von Schlieben, and by his widow and heirs, pursuant to the judicial contract of purchase of 22 October 1799, conveyed to His Most Serene Highness — to the said Martin Honrichs and Valentin v. Kwasieborski, and this for a purchase price deliberately agreed and fixed between the contracting parties of 16,000 Rthl, in words sixteen thousand Reichsthaler Prussian Courant. 2: this purchase price the purchasers bind themselves to pay in solidum, that is to say, one for both and both for one, to His Most Serene Highness in the following instalments, namely at St John the Baptist of this year 4,000 Rthl, say four thousand Reichsthaler; at Christmas of this year 6,000 Rthl., say six thousand Reichsthaler; and at Midsummer 1804 the remainder with 6,000 Rthl., say six thousand Reichsthaler; and until the arrears are fully paid, to pay interest on the same at 5 per cent.

3. His Most Serene Highness affords the purchasers warranty of title only for those parcels of land actually held in possession and to be handed over to them at the

delivery of possession. In respect of those 1,016 składy of arable which may be evicted at the suit of the burgesses of Warta, and which are not in the possession of His Most Serene Highness, no warranty of title is afforded; rather it remains the purchasers' affair alone to vindicate the said fields at their own entire risk and cost, against which, however, His Most Serene Highness relinquishes all claims as against the purchasers, should they in fact recover these składy of arable against the burgesses of Warta, whether in whole or in part.

4. The handing over of this sold estate to the purchasers shall take place 14 days after Midsummer of this year, at which time, concurrently and against each other, the first instalment of the 4,000 rtll. must be paid, since until this is done the handing over cannot take place.

5. At this handing over there shall be handed over as well such ground [text as transcribed: "Grund zuverloren"] and livestock and implements as are found upon the estate

and is specified in the judicial deed of transfer on the part of the tenant Knoblauch to von Bloch of Blotniz of 10 and 11 July of last year, excluding the surplus inventory in horses and oxen taken away at that time by Knoblauch pursuant to the deed of 11 July, which for that very reason are no longer to be found upon the estate and for that very reason cannot be handed over with it.

6. The seller promises to procure the consent to the purchasers' acquisition of this estate if possible at the latest by St John's of this year; should the same however not be forthcoming, then the present purchase falls away.

7. Should the final resolution regarding the said consent be delayed longer than 14 days after St John's of this year, in such wise that the handing over has already taken place and the first instalment of the purchase price has already been paid, but the resolution in the matter should then turn out

negative, then the contracting parties, to avoid all disputes concerning the revenues drawn, have agreed that the purchasers shall retain possession of this estate for one year, namely until 14 days after St John's Day 1804, by way of lease, but shall for that year pay to the seller a rent of 800 Rthl., say eight hundred Reichsthaler, and shall likewise discharge all public dues concerning this estate, by whatever name they may be called, upon the assessment ex Propriet, without being permitted to bring anything thereof into account against the seller; and the purchasers, in this last event, renounce any and all remissions and other demands whatsoever, by whatever name they may be called, but bind themselves, subject to the most summary execution, to vacate the estate of Witów 14 days after St John's 1804 in good husbandry condition, and submit themselves in this

regard to the process of execution with all its legal consequences; it being however of course understood that in such event, upon their vacating the estate, the 4,000 Rthl. paid must be repaid to them by the seller, after deduction of the stipulated lease rent of 800 Rthl and of such public dues and costs as they could not show to have been paid at their departure.

8. The estate shall be handed over to the purchasers with the winter and summer sowing fully carried out, and the purchasers hereby declare that they accept the winter sowing as duly sown, and expect only the like in respect of the summer sowing.

9. The documents concerning this estate shall be delivered over to the purchasers immediately upon the arrival of the consent to their acquisition [uncertain: Frühige].

10. Finally, the contracting parties renounce all objections and evasions running counter to these points of purchase, by whatever name they may be called, and in particular the purchasers renounce the plea of injury in and beyond the half; and they set, for the case of non-performance or non-fulfilment of this contract, a vadium or conventional penalty of 1,000 rtll, say one thousand Reichsthaler, which the contravening party shall be bound to pay to the other, and nonetheless to perform the contract.

11. The costs of this contract both parties assume by halves; those of the rectification of the title of possession in the purchasers' names, the latter alone.

Both parties have, this instrument of purchase points having been read by them themselves — which was explained to the co-purchaser v. Kwasiborski by his socius Honrichs in the Polish tongue — after prior

approval, executed the same with their own signatures manual.

Kalisz, 21 April 1803. At the signing, both parties observed to me that, in respect of the buildings standing upon the village mayor's holding, which the tenants there claim to have built themselves, no warranty of title is afforded to the purchasers by the seller; but that, in case the tenants' statement should prove correct, the purchasers must come to a separate settlement with them on that account.

Copy

Your Royal Majesty has most graciously been pleased to send us, for a report, the enclosed original representation of the former Starost von Prusimski and of Xaver von Jezierski, who left the country because of their part in the South Prussian insurrection and have now asked from Dresden for leave to return to their fatherland.

The files required from the Government at Poznań having come in, we can now most humbly report the following.

1., Anton von Prusimski was accused of having gone on 2 August 1794, before the outbreak of the South Prussian insurrection, from his estates near Kalisz to his Smiłowice estates in the district of Kuyavia, which now belongs to the department of the Government at Poznań; of having received daily visits there from the neighbouring nobility; and of the so-called Kuyavian insurrection having been brought to completion at his house on 21 Aug., and the act of confederation drafted and executed. He is also said to be among those South Prussian noblemen who met at Dresden in the winter of 1793/94 on account of the changes in the Polish state. All these accusations, however, rest for the most part only on a so-called Memoire raisonné, drawn up from the statements of some unnamed trusted Poles and officials, and have not been closely examined.

Nor did the Government think them sufficient to order against him the criminal proceedings against absent offenders, as was done in respect of some chief insur

gents, but, at the instance of the fiscal, only instituted the confiscation proceedings, because he had not returned in accordance with the general ordinances issued.

The fugitive was duly summoned in public; he did, from Italy, where his wife, who also died there, allegedly had to stay at the time to recover her health, hold out hope of his return and seek to avert the confiscation; but as he did not appear after all, the sentence of confiscation was drawn up, and after it had become final, his Trąbczyn estates were given to the Prince of Hohenlohe, his Pawłów estates to the present Major General von Sanitz, and his Smiłowice estates to Lieutenant General von Bischofswerder. Besides these he held no other property in the country.

2., The second petitioner, Xaver von Jezierski, was a canon in Włocławek and parish priest at Neustadt. He was named, partly in the Memoire mentioned above, partly by persons who were named, as one of those who stayed most often with von Prusimski at Smiłowice before the outbreak of the Kuyavian insurrection and worked most actively to bring this insurrection about. He is said to have drafted the proclamations to the people, to have

raised men, and to have been a member of a security commission set up by the insurgents at the time.

Against him too, who did not return from his flight, only the confiscation proceedings were instituted, and confiscation of his small property was decreed with final effect; it consisted only of the income of his benefices, taken into sequestration and since filled otherwise, of which he was also deprived by the sentence.

Neither of the two petitioners has been declared to have forfeited his nobility, nor has any capital punishment otherwise been fixed or reserved against them.

In proportion to their part in the insurrection, they have been punished, by the confiscation of their property, at which it must remain unalterably /: a point on which I, Count von Haugwitz, refrain from expressing an opinion, since it is not of my department :/, and by a 9 years' banishment from their fatherland, more harshly than many others who returned and submitted to a moderate fine or a term in a fortress. Nor is their part of such a kind that it would mark them out as dangerous men before others who stayed in the country or returned to it later; and since their petition is directed only

at leave to return, we are most humbly of the opinion:

that it might well be granted;

which, however, we most devotedly leave entirely to Your Royal Majesty's most high judgement.

Berlin, 30 April 1803

Goldbeck. Haugwitz

To His Royal Majesty.

Your Most Serene Highness, I would gladly lay myself personally at [uncertain: your expense] and obtain your most high commands concerning the sale of the estates, but I am very ill and cannot come out of my room. The Poles continually choose me as their arbiter, only I do not always know what I am to say, because no [uncertain: lower] plan has been made, but the matter is presented now one way, now another. Thus it is said, for example, that 150,000 Rthl of debts are secured upon Trąbczyn, which Walichnowski is to take over, and that notwithstanding this he is to take on 56,000 Rthl and a canon of 5,000 Rthl annually.

What there is in the matter I cannot judge, but I hold it to be a misunderstood piece of gossip, and I only fear that Your Serene Highness's honour will suffer by it. For if debts are secured upon the estates, then it is not necessary that this be told to every Pole who wishes to take the

estates in hereditary lease. My unpresumptuous proposal is this: that Walichnowski be told that he must pay 60,000 or 80,000 Rthl of hereditary purchase money at once, and for all time 4 to 5,000 Rthl annual hereditary quit-rent, and that Your Serene Highness would give orders as to whom he is to pay the rent, which would remain secured upon the first mortgage. This would then be a firm word from which there must on no account be any departure.

I know the Poles thoroughly — if one shows a firm tone and resolution, and scorns their offers, especially all bribes, then one is at once at one's goal with this brood.

I have proved this sufficiently in the case of Dombrowska[uncertain: Dąbska]. Forgive, most gracious Prince and Lord, my frank representation. It is, however, truly well meant. May Your Serene Highness also deign to take to

heart this further request, and by no means let this note be seen by [uncertain: Wünstere] or by others — it would sooner do harm than good — men are often too covetous, so that, when an honest man meets them on this path, they [uncertain: slander] him and do him harm. Command me by two lines in secret as to how you wish it to be, and then reckon, most gracious Prince, upon my faithful zeal, which will yet be ten times greater and go more to my heart than my truly painful illness. Walichnowski has a genuinely real will to acquire the Trąbczyn estates.

In deepest submission I remain, until death, Your Most Serene Highness's

most faithful and most humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 11th of December 1803

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

At this very moment a certain Kunkel presented himself to me with 2 colonists from Oleśnica.

The people are willing to pay 1,500 Rthl, but in return wish to have a contract executed.

I have sounded these men out and sought to examine whence they mean to take the monies for the payment of the 17,000 Rthl due at Martinmas and Midsummer. They are, as I find, fortune-seekers who build upon shallow speculations, who in the end will not be able to pay, and with whom one will get endless lawsuits.

Should Your Most Serene Highness nevertheless command that a contract be concluded with these people, [uncertain: despite] these gloomy prospects, then I shall have the contract drawn up and shall hold them here until Your Most High return. For the rest, I have already brought Kunkel to such a disposition that he will let the matter be turned as shall be most suitable to Your Most Serene Highness's interest.

Kunkel has a commission from a certain Chief District Steward Nerlich, that he is to procure for him Trąbczyn or Zagórów in hereditary lease.

Nerlich has 80,000 Rthl in cash for this purchase, which he can pay out in full within one year.

Kunkel is willing to bring this about, in order to earn more by it than by the colonists.

May Your Most Serene Highness deign most graciously to instruct me how I am to handle the matter.

Walichnowski has just written and wishes to know in detail what he is to give, so that he may incur no unnecessary travelling costs. Otherwise, however, a certain Urbanowski has sent by express for the Trąbczyn valuation. He promises for certain to come and to bring a good deal of money with him at once — should he come sooner than Walichnowski, then I shall conclude with [uncertain: him] according to the instruction given me.

In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

most faithful servant

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 10th of February 1804.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Mr Weigel, now that I have first of all furnished him with a guarantee, is zealously endeavouring to smooth the matter over entirely. But until the rights have been ceded (jura cessa) by von Grotowski, the Bank will not discount.

I have therefore persuaded Mr Weigel to write at once to Mr von Grotowski and to give him the assurance that the 30/m Rthl as well as the interest are lying ready with him; but that, before the monies can be paid, Mr von Grotowski must execute the instrument of cession for the 30/m Rthl there with all speed before the court, whereupon the monies shall immediately be remitted to him. So as to fail in nothing here that may serve to bring the matter about most swiftly, I drove to Court Councillor Ebersbach and had him draft the instrument as von Grotowski must execute it, which Mr Weigel sends off in the accompanying letter to von Grotowski for prompt execution before the court.

I hasten to convey this letter, enclosed, to Your Most Serene Highness [uncertain: derstest] by the orderly now departing. May Your Highness be pleased only to send it on at once to Mr von Grotowski by express, so that he may execute the instrument of cession, whereafter I shall immediately finalise the matter. The sudden death of the honest Captain von Müllern has deeply shaken me

He was truly a good man and a genuinely faithful adherent of Your Most Serene Highness.

But may Your Serene Highness be pleased to take this sudden death to heart — think, in these critical times, of Your own preservation, and do not press so hard upon Your health — such rapid marches make even the most iron-firm man falter — Morgenbeßer too died yesterday evening at 7 o'clock — Now, most gracious Prince and Lord, I appeal to Your heart. That, for the rest, the gallant Nelson caught the French as they meant to slip away from Toulon and unite with the Brest fleet, took 2 ships of the line of 74 guns together with many boats, and sank several more, Your Most Serene Highness will doubtless already know. In Vienna this news has caused a quite extraordinary sensation; the people cheered aloud, and it has everywhere been let to be marked all too plainly that the Court and the nation take England's part. That [uncertain: Siderung] Smith is burning Flushing and also the small fleet that was there is indeed reported from Vienna, though it is said therewith that the official notices on this are still wanting. With Bernhardi I have arranged everything according to Your Most Serene Highness's [uncertain: Willens Mann] — he wrote by yesterday's post to Mr Stössel and is from now on honestly endeavouring to lead the water onto the wheel, which sets the departments in motion, whereby the good cause will be quickly brought to its goal.

In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

Wrocław

29 Feb. 1804. most faithful and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld
