I shall accordingly disclose my opinion to the Prince. The messenger from Zagórów is back and has brought the enclosed pieces. If this is not some imaginary artefact of our good Glenck's, then it surpasses the boldest wishes I have cherished for Your Serene Highness's good fortune. For according to this table we should indeed have some 31,000 Morgen of true manorial lands to dismember, and the peasant lands would remain for further disposal — indeed even a piece of forest for town and country remains over. Now, in order to make this great work properly brilliant and worthy of the labour, I have a plan of my own, which Your Serene Highness may be pleased to examine.

The surveyor Cabanis, three years ago, divided up the little estate of Betsche below Strehlen and handed it over to a number of Hussites; the people paid for 23 Hufen a full 25/m. rt. in cash and

took over all burdens — They begged Cabanis that he might point out to them districts in South Prussia where they could buy themselves in and settle in large bodies. If Your Serene Highness permits it, I shall at once send Cabanis to the Hussites and have some 500 husbandmen recruited — These are people of means and industrious, with whom anything can be done. Moreover the affair is a very good one and will make a stir with the King, inasmuch as people would be drawn out of Bohemia into the country.

The Rapacki prospective purchasers are not worth much; the fellows want far-reaching terms of payment, and it is not proper to enter into that — the messenger has come back with the matter unsettled.

The Hussites are more to my liking, for I shall afterwards beg Your Serene Highness for the patent as bishop of this flock, as soon as some 500 and more husbandmen shall have been engaged. Schöneich deciphers out of a plan of just the same kind his only salvation — he means to give over his whole M[uncertain: s]tower estates to people of this sort.

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 29th of March 1804
oe1bu9454-120:
120 Cabanis came back yesterday with the good news that the Hussites wish to buy.

In Husinich, Rentsch and the neighbourhood there are already a considerable number who have at once shown the best will; since, however, the number of Hufen is too great for these, they have immediately sent an express to their Moravian brethren in the faith. They have found the price of 300 Rthl per Hufe and 15 Rthl. yearly rent a fair one, and believe that, notwithstanding that the oppression in Bohemia has ceased, they will soon, on account of the acceptable price, have the requisite number of farmers together. Within a fortnight at the latest they mean to appear in a body — God grant His blessing — Cabanis is nevertheless to [uncertain: travel out] again, in order to encourage the people, through the clergyman at Hussinitz, to press the matter forward as quickly as possible. The messenger from Countess Schlabrendorff is back as well — here the answer does not correspond to Your Most Serene Highness's wishes — She [uncertain: flatly] refuses to give out the instru[uncertain: ment] any sooner, until she has received the other 50/m Rthl. The term to the 1st of January 1805 Homuth is procuring. But he will draw up the receipt in

such form that Your Serene Highness may use it separately — the acceptance for the second term is also to be so drawn up that no mishap can occur any more. Kunkel I await with longing — he does indeed write to his mother that he will arrive here in these days with several persons; meanwhile the time does grow somewhat too long — I wish he were here already — Kunkel's mother lives here in the greatest destitution; should Your Serene Highness be pleased to do a work of mercy on this present day, then send me a couple of Thaler for this poor woman, who lies sick and wretched — I do indeed give her a little, but this does not go far towards keeping herself in these dear times.

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 2nd of April 1804.
oe1bu9454-122:
122 The enclosed note I received early this morning — it had by an oversight been left lying at my old lodging — Mr Homuth has just now sent to me again on this account and begs most earnestly that this post be settled soon, so that he may at once, by the messenger, report the receipt of the 166 Rthl. 16 Groschen as well — Cabanis is at this very moment setting off by post for Hussinitz — I promise myself from that quarter the swiftest and happiest success. From Berlin or Frankfurth I have not received a syllable today.

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 6th of April 1804.
oe1bu9454-123:
123 Late yesterday evening I received by express courier the enclosed letter from Kunkel, which I herewith [uncertain: lezt] submit to Your Most Serene Highness, requesting Your instructions as to how I am to conduct myself. It is indeed necessary to come to an arrangement with von Otocki, and if this could be brought about by an amicable settlement, such that Otocki were content with 1500 or 2,000 Rthl., it would be an advantageous and desirable thing. I leave it to Your Most Serene Highness's supreme judgement — whether the power of attorney for the settlement is to be given to Kunkel.

That Kunkel and Jentsch, moreover, appear to be acting so much against one another arouses my great apprehension — I fear that Kunkel, by his vehement conduct, will do foolish things, and that Jentsch, out of malice, will make intrigues, which may prove prejudicial. My humble counsel is to instruct these men well and to keep them within their bounds.

Glenck did not come to me again yesterday, and has even left the Konotop accounts behind here, which gave full information upon everything in this matter.

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 23rd of April 1804
oe1bu9454-124:
124

To Your Most Serene Highness I submit herewith the reply to Kunkel; may Your Highness deign to look it through, whether it accords with Your Highness's will and intention. At the same time I beg that someone be allowed to make fair copies of the two letters, for I am as though crushed, and, since my good wife is being laid to rest today, I have withdrawn with the children to my brother-in-law's.

In my letter, which I send along to Kunkel, I shall set everything out thoroughly — I must first seek to compose myself somewhat. A map of Kopojno, Skokum and Świątniki I have here von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 24th of April 1804
oe1bu9454-125:
125 To His Most Serene Highness. The people from Oleśnica have arrived with the monies — they wish to be with Your Most Serene Highness at 4 o'clock. I have negotiated something with them here, upon which I shall make my report to Your Serene Highness this afternoon — I believe it will not be displeasing to Your Serene Highness. von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 28th of April 1804.
oe1bu9454-126:
126

To His Most Serene

Highness. Cabanis is back with the Hussites — the people liked it exceedingly; they now wish to hurry back, gather their fellow believers together and settle everything within 14 days. But Cabanis has brought back a great deal of news, about which I must speak with Your Serene Highness. It becomes most extremely necessary that someone go there at once, to bring everything into the best track.

I am here working with the Oleśnica people — would Your Serene Highness be so gracious as to come to me for a quarter of an hour from the parade, for then Your Highness could hear all these persons yourself, and at once issue Your Highness's commands as to what is further to be done.

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 30th of April 1804
oe1bu9454-127:
127 All pleading is of no avail, I am to and must pay. The Prince, as the enclosure shows, has not settled so much as a single Groschen of interest.

I must therefore pay the = 700 Rthl. promised by the Prince for the inventory under my guarantee, and the interest since 1799 amounting to = 175 Rthl., likewise court costs = 35 Rthl.

in all = 910 Rthl.

My funds are exhausted, for I already paid out 1,537 Rthl 12 Groschen yesterday in the Nudnich matter — which the Prince, according to fourfold court documents, so solemnly promised to settle — Wildegans and Heyman Pincus promise to settle everything — only God knows when — Meanwhile I must pay, if I am not to have distraint in the house. Can Your Serene Highness help me with the 900 Rthl? Then have the goodness to do so — At Midsummer I can again support Your Serene Highness with the timber monies.

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 2nd of May 1804
oe1bu9454-128:
128

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Even were my loyal attachment to Your Most Serene Highness and my zeal exemplary, I am nevertheless not able to remedy all the confusions that have [uncertain: crept in / been bargained in] here, as I at first believed I might —

1. There are lawsuits, 11 in number, in which hearings have just now [text lost: been adjourned by some parties] — I have petitioned for prorogation, have obtained it, and hope to bring several of them, which in part amount to 6 and 15 Rthl annually, to the best possible end by settlement.

2. The tenants have been stirred up to the point of madness, and none will yield without an enormous sum for quitting — to arrange this and to bring it into good order according to Your Serene Highness's wishes, I must [uncertain: exercise] every possible patience, so as to press the people toward the goal by forbearance and kindness, but it will not be got through without sacrifices. With Otcibi I have just now come to terms; he receives 3,000 Rthl for quitting, 2,000 Rthl security,

and 1,000 Rthl for additional seed-corn and housing costs, which latter two items will be recovered again.

3. With Flörken and Ribbeck I have got so far that they are willing to settle. The people show that they have paid 12,600 in cash; next to that they liquidate for buildings etc. some 8,000 Rthl. Now even though the liquidated sum of 6,905 Rthl has been accepted for the present, still in a lawsuit, which might run some 3 years, the sum of 8,000 Rthl will certainly be awarded to him. By this calculation Your Serene Highness would already have 2,000 Rthl to pay; the sum for quitting stipulated in the contract is 500 Rthl a year, which likewise amounts to 7,000 Rthl; the surplus inventory may come to 2,000 Rthl, after which then the people must absolutely have 11,600 Rthl, if judgment is given according to the letter. The contract is badly drawn, serves only the tenants, and is in every point disadvantageous to Your Serene Highness. Bad as this matter looks, I still hope to settle it in the best way, namely that the people vacate and renounce all claims. To attain this end I have petitioned for execution, and have caused the sequestration to be undertaken for the tenants' account. Under this pressure I think they will vacate.

4. I shall conclude with von Rudnicki, or else set the matter on the footing that he is to depart at Midsummer. The contract with him too has been concluded in a peculiar manner.

5. As soon as I have finished with these people I shall proceed to the leasing

of them. Jetzinger [uncertain: and] consorts are [uncertain: here now], Ca[banis]: with the help of the district councillor, who is more than active, I think I shall soon be done with these too. The old subjects give throughout 1 Rthl per Hufe in ground-rent — the district councillor himself concludes with them, so that the Chamber must be silenced. An astonishing deal has thereby been gained, and it makes the newer colonists take pause. Just now the 3 B. offered to annul the Oleśnica contract and to see to the general dismemberment. There are 6 persons for it. They demand 3 Rthl per Hufe as brokerage and 9 Hufen free altogether — This I shall in the end concede, for now everything can be brought to a happy conclusion. The district councillor is entirely my man and helps to overcome the most difficult matters. He deserves a great reward. Through his help I shall be done with the tenants here — through his efforts I have today obtained purchasers for 87 Hufen, and were Midsummer not at the door, or were there not some want of money, he would get me Mennonites who would at once buy everything up dear and pay in cash — he has even obtained the Chamber's permission for it — Glenck has written to the district councillor and mocks me, saying in particular that no more stupid stroke could have been made than the Oleśnica contract. He goes on to say that it is true, he did indeed make a preliminary agreement with the people, but this was

only in jest; at that time he had just then needed 1,000 Rthl, and the fellows ought to have sacrificed these, but how could he ever have meant to give away the estates in hereditary lease like that — He calls upon the district councillor now only to see to it that Kunkel be got rid of; he has another man whom he would send here, who would comply with all the district councillor's orders. In general he requests the district councillor to come to an understanding with him so as to do business with him. He [uncertain: sits] now at the gold-spring, where gold is to be had and gold to be [illegible]. He asks that the district councillor should enquire in his own and the neighbouring districts whether the nobility have need of money — he could obtain as much as he wished — the district councillor need only have strong brokerage stipulated, and he would then faithfully share with him after deduction of costs. It is a sad thing to hear so much [uncertain: argus Zeugt], whereby Your Serene Highness is in the end compromised. I shall redress what I can, and so I should certainly settle several lawsuits at once and preserve for Your Serene Highness that which is already lost — As for money, I hope a strong sum should come together by Midsummer. How much, however, I cannot yet determine. In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

faithful servant

von Triebenfeld

Trąbczyn, the 8th of May 1804
oe1bu9454-129:
129 Today I have letters neither from Berlin nor from Frankfurt an der Oder. My anxiety therefore increases hourly. If Your Most Serene Highness has anything from Glenck that affords comfort, may you deign to communicate it to your servant. As to Kolzig I had great hopes — but Amelang does not answer. Had a ray of hope appeared there, I should have advised that all sale of Konotop be forbidden — but if Amelang continues to keep silent about the plan laid before him in this matter, then I must believe that Beyme does not [uncertain: gantirt] him; and in this regard the sale of Konotop would have to be pursued zealously. To that end I have summoned Bernhardi here and intimated to him that he, as tenant, should recommend and represent the estates in the best light to every prospective purchaser — for on this sort of

people much depends. For

1. such a creature, in order to remain secure in his tenancy, could easily hinder the sale by hideous descriptions; and again such a man could

2. out of [uncertain: ſolcht] gain easily let himself be bought, and act to the seller's disadvantage; therefore I have had him come here, and to forestall all this. Now I am [uncertain: sending] her off again at once, so that when Ludolff and Stubenrauch arrive he may not only receive them well, but also describe everything to those people truthfully and from the best side.

This afternoon I shall bring out what is to be sent to South Prussia — now I must first arrange my business, of which I have found a great deal awaiting me. von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, 15th May 1804.
oe1bu9454-130:
130

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord, some 2 hours ago I [uncertain: am] arrived here and heard, to one's vexation, that Glenck had travelled to many, and also that Leixner was absent and is not expected until today. In all of it, however, nothing has unfortunately been done yet, and as I see, the one does not trust the other. Meanwhile I have made the agreement with M. Bernhard "that I am to bring the Pszczew matter to a conclusion, that the estates are to remain in Your Serene [uncertain: Highness's] name — that Leixner will then take Kamionna, and that this shall stand either in Your Serene Highness's or in my name, for as I have said, so it has been done. — Leixner is hard pressed. He [uncertain: thereupon] will not apply further for the Incolat. Count Schulenburg has got onto his roof — Meanwhile

he is content if I lend him my name. I have therefore sent an express courier after Glenck so that he may be here again on Saturday; I go to Berlin today to sound everything out there, and when I return on Saturday I shall settle everything here, go from here to Pszczew, and with Heaven's help finish everything there too, and then hasten to Your Serene Highness, for to live longer in uncertainty would be the torment of hell — I do not know what Glenck is thinking; Midsummer is indeed far too near — The post is about to go; more from Berlin. In deepest reverence I remain, until death, Your Most Serene Highness's faithful and most obedient [uncertain: servant]

von Triebenfeld

Frankfurt an der Oder, the 17th of May 1804.
oe1bu9454-131:
131

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

I have been here in Berlin since yesterday and have already searched out everything where springs of comfort were supposed to flow. Unhappily, however, I find nothing but puddles, out of which swindling and malice well up — All the prospects and views painted here are devilish lies — Your Most Serene Highness would, had I not come here, have been taken in for ever. — For from here there was not a heller to be counted upon.

Things now stand thus — Tomorrow evening / that is, the 20th / I go back to Frankfurt an der Oder and conclude, if everything else remains as it is, with Leixner concerning Kamionna, and secure the monies needful on account of Koszęcin, though I should have to pledge my salvation along with it. Here I shall set everything in train so that Your Serene Highness obtains Koltzig or the loan. More hope, however, is given for the estates, since the King has no inclination to give money away / for Russia absolutely wants war /. Matters stand here so strangely that every honest man shakes his head. Meanwhile more than everything can be contrived

As to the Broniewski affair, matters have come so far that, if the causae arresti are proven, the arrest is to be accepted — In this matter too as good as nothing has been done, notwithstanding how highly the thing is cried up — Upon the causae arresti it cannot [be done] without 2,000 Rthl in Friedrich d'or — had Mell[uncertain: itz] and Glenck long since called this by its right name, then this would long since have been decided and known without all the business. The post is about to go; I shall faithfully settle everything for the best, which is averred by

Your Most Serene Highness's

most faithful servant

von Triebenfeld

Berlin, the 19th of May 1804.
oe1bu9454-135:
135

Right Honourable Sir,

Most highly honoured Chamber Director. When I received from the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe, through his General authorised representative, Mr Glenck, Building Councillor, the commission to sell his estates Kamionna and Kolno situated in South Prussia, I received from His Highness the same, enclosed herewith, binding written undertaking concerning 2 per cent commission, which I most obediently submit to Your Right Honourable [uncertain: Hochverabschriften] and entirely identical with the original. Since I have now learned with certainty that the transaction has been brought about through Chamber Councillor Ludolff, you would nevertheless be obliged, on the ground of this written undertaking, to pay the stipulated commission of 2 per cent, and that for the reason that I should have pointed out the purchaser, to pay. Even though this pointing-out can be fully proved by me, since in the month of December of this year I brought forward these estates Kamionna and Kolno [...] in proposal, and also Mr Glenck, Building Councillor, as [uncertain: his authorised representative] through Your Right Honourable personally present, yet the manner of thinking of the authorised representative — not of the Prince, who as is well known possesses the most excellent character — makes me apprehend that the obligation to pay this commission of 2 per cent stipulated to me might be disputed under this or the like pretext, and that with the intention of bargaining down a considerable sum from this honorarium settled upon me. I have therefore hereby wished to take the surest course and most obediently to report this proceeding to Your Honour by communicating a copy of the princely written undertaking, the original of which I am at all times ready to produce, and to append the most humble and obedient request: to arrange most graciously for this commission of 2 per cent, stipulated to me in such wise and assigned upon the first purchase moneys, to be paid out of those first purchase moneys, and to my order. I am to expect with certainty from Your Honour's just and equitable character that, since Your Honour directs this business of sale, it is impossible that I should be deceived on the part of Mr Glenck, Building Councillor, with regard to these my just claims upon the purchase moneys to be paid to His Serene Highness — and that therefore, in the event of an actual sale of these estates, I shall not have need to extract a judicial arrest upon the purchase moneys. Your Honour has hitherto shown himself as my patron and friend. You are also acquainted with the unhappy fates which I and my family have suffered, particularly with the hereditary Count von Stollberg, with whom I lost 30/m Rthl. Unhappily, after such sacrifices, I must maintain myself and my family, known to you, by the laborious working-up of business of this kind, of which perhaps one in a hundred succeeds. I therefore apprehend, since Your Honour [uncertain: directs] this business, that I am [uncertain: exposed] to chicanery on the part of Glenck, and, through Your Honour's favour, to obtain the wages of labour assured to me on the part of His Serene Highness under his princely seal, for which I shall be especially thankful and grateful — may I most obediently beg to be informed in a few lines: how high the agreed purchase sum for Kamionna and Kolno amounts to?

I remain with all reverence,

Your Right Honourable's

most obedient servant,

the

Cabinet Councillor Werner

Berlin, 19 May 1804.

Neue Schönhauser Straße No. 13.

If Chamber Councillor Werner in Berlin shall point out to me, directly or indirectly, a purchaser for my estates Kamionna and Kolno situated in South Prussia, with whom I come to terms of bargain, then I promise the same, or him to whom he may give order and to whom he may assign his rights out of this written undertaking, for this his pointing-out, his exertion, and the service thereby rendered to me, a voluntary remuneratory compensation for exertion, 2, in writing two, per cent of the sum of the purchase price upon which I may come to terms with the purchaser. These shall be paid immediately after conclusion of the contract out of the first purchase moneys, and shall be paid by the seller in payment to the bearer hereof, who has received order from Mr Werner.

This I promise to fulfil under my princely signature and seal. Wrocław, the 17th of December 1803 (L. S.)

Friedrich Ludwig of Hohenlohe, Prince.

Your Honour will permit that I follow up my oral conference of the day before yesterday with a written enquiry also, respecting the purchase and sale of the estates Kolno and Kamionna.

Since my Prince, His Serene Highness, presses on that account for a speedy sale of his estates Kamionna and Kolno, because he must have, 8 days from the next coming Midsummer, over and above the 100,000 Rthl needed for the cancellation of the present Broniewski protestation, a further 60/m Rthl for other use — but the purchase of these estates cannot be effected so speedily, inasmuch as a thorough investigation is first to precede; I therefore most submissively enquire — in case, upon the present investigation of the value of the estates Kamionna and Kolno by Mr Ludolff, Councillor of the Order's Commission, it should be found that these can have a true value of 200/m Rthl, whether Your Honour would then be pleased, behind the above-mentioned 100/m Rthl, to lend 60,000 Rthl on a second mortgage in such wise that it can be paid 8 days before Midsummer on my Prince's, His Serene Highness's, account; whereby it is understood that my Prince [illegible] must acquiesce in the restrictions of free disposition demanded in return, as also that he can further sell these estates to no one other than the lender of these 60/m Rthl.

I await your command hereupon, as to when I might have the honour of making my personal attendance once again.

Your Honour's

most entirely devoted servant,

Glenck

the 12th of May 1804

at the Golden Eagle, the Square No. 32.

Your Most Noble Honour, I return herewith enclosed all the papers of the estate purchase offered to me. I add to these a note just received from a certain Werner, whom you will kindly put off, because I never engage with people of this sort. In general I regret being unable to serve Your Honour in this matter, inasmuch as these estates, through the manifold offering-about by brokers of every kind, have come into a very ill repute.

Stubenrauch

Berlin, the 22nd of May 1804.
oe1bu9454-132:
132

My dearest Friend, I am just now on the point of stepping into the carriage and returning to Wrocław. It has been enough to drive me mad, to sit here so long [uncertain: to sit] waiting upon Mr Glenck, and in the end to accomplish nothing. The result is always that people fish in troubled waters and want to profit barbarously at the Prince's expense. At Pszczew the people have gained thirty thousand Rthl in so short a time, without having to put themselves to the least trouble. The subjects merely buy themselves free and give 30,000 Rthl more than the purchasers gave. Meanwhile the latter pocket this sum. Spoiled by that transaction, at Kamionna still more than this was to be gained at once, and yet God knows what screws were then to be applied to the Prince — into this I cannot intervene, and so I depart with nothing accomplished — Now, my dear Friend, see to it that [uncertain: the gentleman] Director Stubenrauch buys the estates and furnishes the money. — I will stand surety to the man for a clear and perpetual revenue, if I am permitted to dismember the estates, of = 10,000 Rthl yearly — this would amount, reckoned at 5 per cent, to a capital of 200/m Rthl. But since Mr Glenck has been assured that the Order's capital is content if

[uncertain: it] has 4 per cent clear interest from its capitals, then the value of the estates might be taken at 250,000 Rthl. Now, however, the Prince, since he needs money, would be very well content with 180,000 Rthl, consequently [uncertain: the chapter would gain] 70,000 Rthl in cash by this purchase. You might further urge this, that the chapter or the Order's Chamber, if still more were to be got out of it, would have to give a bonus proportionate to the matter.

In case the Lord Director Stubenrauch will agree to this, have the kindness to send me an express courier; I [uncertain: hasten] then straight back to Berlin, conclude the matter and provide the warranty of title.

Had I known the business thus sooner, everything would already be settled, and much might have been gained by it. As it is, one always learns everything too late.

Mr Glenck has all along reckoned on a purchase money of 500 Rthl per Hufe, which the people were to pay — With this in view he [would] assume a light hereditary quit-rent of 10 to 12 Rthl per Hufe, and the value of the estates was thereby diminished; but if I now take no entry money, the subject willingly pays 50 Rthl per Hufe yearly. By this means an enormously high value now comes out, so that I am still able, out of old rents and for the beer and brandy excise, to bring out a perpetually

subsisting [uncertain: revenue] of 12,000 Rthl, and consequently a value at 4 per cent of 300,000 Rthl; on which footing the Order's Chamber would profit to the extent of 120,000.

Take this to heart, and seek to move that worthy good man the Chamber Director Stubenrauch to make the purchase and to furnish the moneys for it by Midsummer of this year. In the matter of the Koltzig estates, or in the business of compensation, seek to bring about the best that may be, but do go cautiously with the Lord Cabinet Councillor, for at present I fear that man extraordinarily.

With the most faithful heart and the greatest attachment I am unceasingly

Your

most faithfully devoted servant

von Triebenfeld

Frankfurt an der Oder, 23 May 1804.
oe1bu9454-133:
133

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

I could almost despair over all the wretched business that I find here at every turn, and God knows whether I shall be able to redress it all and steer it to the best.

1. In all of it nothing has been done, and Glenck is not in a position to show me one Rthl's worth securely.

2. Leixner has been secretly at Pszczew, and on account of all the fraud and trickery prevailing there is so shy of the thing that he would gladly give up the contract and renounce everything at once — only with the greatest effort can he be made to stand by the remainder and now to keep to the payments engaged for.

3. He will on no account enter into any connection concerning Kamionna; I am to furnish him the warranty of title against eviction for a profit of 30/m Rthl and also to procure the right of residence for him. This I cannot promise. I am willing to guarantee against all loss if he gives 160/m Rthl for Kamionna, but with that he is not content.

4. He wishes the partnership contract entered into with Glenck

contract at the Pszczew sale to be cancelled — for Glenck has had a third of the profit and a demesne farm secured to himself in the most permanent manner for the Baron von Brandenstein; this I simply cannot promise, and for that the people release nothing at all.

5. With the Chamber of the Order nothing has happened, and therefore nothing is to be paid upon it.

6. The Harlem purchase is likewise not to be thought of, for this plan appears to be wholly at home in the world of ideas.

7. As for the loan of the 100/m Rthl from the Invalids' Fund there is likewise no security, but everything rests upon [illegible] But now, in order to attempt the last, I am going back to Berlin, having sat here three days in vain at Frankfurt an der Oder and waited for Glenck.

I shall see whether, with the assistance of Amelang, I can conclude something with old Stubenrauch — he is an honest man and I hope the matter should go forward, if I furnish him the warranty of title against eviction for the shortfall —

Further, I will see for myself whether the loan from the Invalids' Fund may be obtained in any manner whatever. — If I withdraw in Berlin, then G. and the Frankfurt partnership associates may break their necks — For the rest, things looked bare in Berlin — Mr Beyme had laid the compensation petition before [the King] — At the presentation his address was short: A part of the estates which had been conferred upon the Prince of Hohenlohe have been taken from him again. He asks for compensation. He wants estates; those Your Majesty cannot give him — In place of that he wants 100,000 Rthl as a gift, or he wants 200,000 Rthl lent for 20 years without interest — the request for money Your Majesty will not be able to grant in the present course of the times, since one does not know how everything will turn out. Cases might easily arise in which Your Majesty might need all the money more than most urgently.

My counsel is that Your Majesty compensate him in this fashion: The Prince still owes His Majesty a large sum of more than 200,000 Rthl, which he borrowed for Dutch claims that were refused — Let Your Majesty make him a gift of this

then you will receive nothing back in your lifetime, and the important business of compensation is settled.

Old Köckritz, please, who greets Your [Serene Highness] most cordially, has told me this between four eyes — the answer was being worked up in that sense. I have, God be thanked, turned it about, and Köckritz votes for Koltzig-Rohde[?]; he will say everything about this [himself]. as purchasers and takers-up, the following contract has been advisedly agreed and concluded.

parties in halves. Thus done at Zagórów, the 26th of May, one thousand eight hundred and four.

Kunkel, special authorised representative of His Most Serene Highness of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

The loan with the Invalids' Fund, which the building councillor Glenck assured so positively, has likewise failed, and for the following reasons. The Invalids' Department demanded that the Otto valuation be once again revised and recast according to the principles of the South Prussian Chamber. Glenck, who thought to take the shortest road to this, turned, on the advice of a certain Captain Lange, to the Court Councillor Leugnich; the latter promised to have the valuation quickly recast for 25 Fr. Glenck believed this, departed, and only requested Leugnich to have the new valuation delivered to Councillor Seelmann. The latter has been done, but to my horror I learned yesterday on my arrival that the newer valuation had been reduced to 78/m Rthl and that it had been handed over in that form.

Your Most Serene Highness may gather the consequence — but the saddest thing of all is now that by this mutilated valuation the estates are wholly degraded in worth, and that the sale of them will be made very, very much harder. Even in Frankfurt an der Oder, since those people were counting on a loan of 80 to 100/m Rthl,

everything will now fail, for since Leixner must [garbled] Your Most Serene Highness for the sake of the loan, he must also see the instruments, and in that way he gets the lower valuation before his eyes, which, had the loan not been necessary, one [uncertain: um] have been permitted to show. If I now still obtain 60,000 Rthl lent from somewhere on the lower valuation, it will be extremely damaging to the sale and perhaps hinder it altogether. My only hope is now cast upon Stubenrauch, to whom I have promised to furnish eviction and every conceivable guarantee. This evening he intends to give his declaration — if this plan fails, then all here is lost, for all the other projects are not worth a single Groschen either, and are merely drawn up by a certain Dietz, Werner, the Jew Borchart,

Mr Lange and such rabble, who have neither head nor credit, and who only needed written undertakings from Glenck in order to be able to borrow something on them, so as not to perish of hunger. It is a sad thing that Glenck reckoned on the swindles of this brood and so very culpably frittered away the time

God is my witness that I cannot sleep for grief. [uncertain: My] most heartfelt wish is that Heaven might but govern Stubenrauch's heart, for then things will go well — gladly would I pledge him my goods and my poor afflicted soul.

Yesterday Beyme had the Privy Councillor Amelang called to him, and told him that His Majesty could give Your Serene Highness neither South Prussian estates nor money. Your Serene Highness, however, owed the King very considerable sums, apart from a loan from the Duke of Courland, for which the King had hitherto paid the interest. Since His Majesty doubted of recovering a single Groschen of the sums lent and of the interest paid by way of advance, His Majesty was willing, out of particular grace, to make Your Serene Highness a gift of these sums, as also of the interest hitherto paid to the Courlanders, as a compensation for the lost Brzyce estates. In return for which, however, Your Serene Highness might from now on satisfy the Courlanders both as to capital and as to interest. This was not His Majesty's [uncertain: ner] notion. With the best heart, and the love that he bears Your Serene Highness, he had not been able to bring about more than this. He was also to have given Your Serene Highness this resolution at once, but as he did not know whether such would be agreeable to Your Serene Highness, he had

held it back for the present, and wished that Amelang might first sound out Your Serene Highness on the matter. Amelang then answered him: he knew that Your Serene Highness wished to have nothing given to you by the King, that you would faithfully pay His Majesty everything that you rightfully owed him, that Your Serene Highness demanded nothing but what you could rightfully claim, and that you believed you had the first right, when you pressed, directly and indirectly, for a compensation for the estates taken from you, for which Your Serene Highness had to pay many thousands in [garbled: Charger Stempel um andere Gebürz], and where in addition you had had much money standing. Amelang then proposed to him that the Kolzig estates confiscated from Count Schlabrendorff might be given to Your Serene Highness as a compensation — to this he replied that the estates had not yet been sequestered, that the King would probably rather keep these estates himself, since His Majesty had a distaste for the frightening away of estates, carried over from the previous government; yet in this matter the first possibility was still present, of obliging the Prince — Amelang knew all of it, however, for it [uncertain: träst] word for word with what the honest General had said. — It was particularly

too plain that through his mediation the fine answer had been held back. All this raised Amelang's courage, and, being prepared, he spoke more freely. Amelang also now lives in the first hope that they will be civil and give no coarse resolution, but will hold it back altogether — and also that they will hasten to execute the confiscation, or the judgment to that effect, in order to be able to confer the Kolzig estates upon Your Serene Highness.

Braun will keep the General Köckritz in play and guide the matter along that road — Amelang will do the like with Beyme in his own manner — but neither knows anything of the other, and according to this plan both must in the end, without having known it, meet at one and the same point.

For the rest, Amelang will draft a letter to Beyme and perhaps to the King, which Your Serene Highness is to execute and send off. I grow dizzy when I think of the near term, and when at one stroke the last spark of hope too is extinguished. It is now 1 o'clock in the night — I can neither rest nor repose for anguish, and the beast in human shape sleeps without a care — O righteous God, what is a man without true sense of honour?

O had the unreasonable man but not, to the very greatest misfortune, let the Otto valuation be so destroyed and mutilated, then I, with Amelang — who shows himself active and who now gains credit through Beyme — should still have found much counsel, and could have procured the money on my name or on bills of exchange / since I am held to be rich /. The valuations of the Zagórów estates are only 124/m Rthl, and these are burdened with 56,000 Rthl, thus encumbered above the half — for that the estates are worth four times as much I know — but the valuations tell against it, and consequently it is not to be counted upon. Kolno and Kamionna are bungled, for the present valuation is 118,000 Rthl, and 66/m Rthl have been awarded to Broniewski, so that there too no fund remains upon which money might be taken or demanded with security,

I shall now still attempt this — I shall try whether anyone will lend 120/m Rthl on Konotop and Zagórów, for which I shall further offer a bill of exchange. If this went through, then everything might still be [uncertain: redressed], for then one would have time to conclude the Kamionna business solidly and to see to a good sale, and also to dismember the Zagórów and Trąbczyn estates at leisure. If I accomplish nothing, then I hasten quickly to Frankfurt an der Oder and try there once more [garbled: man heil]. In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

most faithful servant

von Triebenfeld

Berlin, the 26th of May 1804

future be raised, can demand no compensation from His Serene Highness the Prince of Hohenlohe; the communities also assume the contribution of 50 Rthl. which His Most Serene Highness promised to render to the town school here for 1 year.

§ 12. Both contracting parties bind themselves to have this contract published before the competent authorities and to seek its confirmation; and His Most Serene Highness hereby makes himself bound to exert himself as best he may, that this contract be confirmed by the competent authorities, and that the consent to the further dismemberment of what has been made over to them be granted to the communities.

§ 13. As soon as the delivery of possession of the Obra demesne farm here

takes place, there shall at the same time be handed over to the town and village communities that livestock and farm inventory which is sold along with the purchase and hereditary-tenure sum, in the same number as the tenant von Bornstädt received it in the year 1800 at the handing over.

§ 14. This contract shall be binding for all time upon His Most Serene Highness the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen for himself and his most high heirs and successors, as also on the part of the town and village communities. And the yearly canon or ground-rent of 1,000 Rthl. to be paid shall be rendered in half-yearly instalments of 500 Rthl., namely each time at the term of Christmas and the term of Midsummer, annually, on pain of execution, and sent carriage

free.

§ 15. So long as the communities do not alienate or dismember the lands and rights made over to them, the status possessivus remains in its present condition. But as soon as the demesne farm is dismembered, the hereditary purchasers are bound to have the intabulated items transferred onto the several plots and struck out in the name of His Most Serene Highness.

§ 16. For the stipulated canon of 1,000 Rthl. yearly all the communities are liable in solidum, and consent to the entry thereof in the mortgage book against their lands; just as conversely His Most Serene Highness consents that this present contract

be entered in the mortgage book of the manorial lordship (Dominium) of Pszczew and its appurtenances.

§ 17. Finally the contracting parties renounce any and every objection, by whatever names they may be called; in particular the town and village communities renounce the objection of lesion beyond the half, which was explained to them to mean that, if the agreed purchase and entry sum exceeded the true value of the lands and rights made over by double, they would be free to withdraw from the contract.

§ 18. His Most Serene Highness reserves to himself the supreme oversight of the forests, which he will entrust to the Royal head forester Feller; and the communities bind themselves to indemnify him for

his trouble and to come to an agreement with him thereupon.

Whereupon, since nothing further was to be brought forward, the proceedings were closed, the protocol read out, interpreted by the sworn interpreter Echaust for the deputies of the town and village communities not fully conversant with the German language, who had requested the keeping of a separate side protocol in the Polish language, approved and signed; whereby it was further noted by the contracting parties that the costs of the recording, issue, publication and confirmation shall be borne in half by both parties. We, the Princely Hohenloh-Ingelfingen court and of the lordship of Pszczew, do hereby make known and declare to each and all, but particularly where it is needful to know, that there appeared before Us.

1. the Princely Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, his estates director and general attorney, the building councillor Johann Wilhelm Glenck, on the one part

2. Likewise the authorised representatives of the town and rural communities, namely of the town of Pszczew, the village of Stołuń, Schaertzig, Świechocin, Stoki, Łowyń and Kuligowo,

a) the burgess and town representative Matheus Młynkiewicz

b) the free village mayor Johann Chmara, and that they have concluded a hereditary-lease contract over the estates of the lordship of Pszczew, as the proceedings of the 28th of July of the current year, as also the supplement of the 29th of July of the current year, set out more fully, reading thus: Actum Pszczew, the 28th of July 1804. There appeared

1., the Princely Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen general attorney, the building councillor Glenck, whom His Most Serene Highness the Councillor of War and Forests von Triebenfeld, hereditary lord of Świniary,

and Konotop, as His most highly esteemed friend and assistant, has been assigned to him

2. The burgess and town representative Matheus Młynkiewicz, as authorised representative of the burgesses of Pszczew,

3. The free village mayor Johann Chmara of Stołuń, as authorised representative of the village communities of Stołuń, Kuligowo, Szarcz, Stoki, Świechocin and Łowyń, with the motion to record a contract between His Most Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, the burgesses of Pszczew, and the village communities named above, upon the basis of the points settled, dated Alt Szarcz the 16th of July 1804. The Princely Hohenlohe authorised representative, the building councillor Johann Wilhelm Glenck, produced the said power of attorney of the Prince of Hohenlohe of the 26th of April 1803, by which the same is authorised to conclude contracts in valid form, of which power of attorney a certified copy was taken to these acts.

In like manner Młynkiewicz handed in a judicially issued power of attorney of the 5th of April 1804, by which he is authorised to conclude, in the name of the town, a contract with His Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe over all the parcels of land and profitable rights belonging to the lordship of Pszczew.

Likewise Chmara handed in a judicially issued

power of attorney of the 5th of April 1804, by which he is, on the part of the communities of Stołuń, Kuligowo, Szarcz, Stoki, Świechocin and Łowyń,

in like manner as Młynkiewicz, authorised to conclude a contract.

After negotiations conducted on both sides, and after the points settled of the 16th of July 1804 had been brought in, and the personal capacity of the parties appearing to conclude contracts was subject to no doubt, the contract was recorded as follows.

§. 1. His Most Serene Highness the reigning Prince Friedrich Ludwig of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, Governor of Wrocław, Inspector General of the Infantry and Knight of the Great Royal Prussian Orders, as hereditary lord of the lordship of Pszczew situated in the district of Międzyrzecz, makes over to the burgesses of the town of Pszczew and the inhabitants of the villages of Kuligowo, Stołuń, Szarcz, Stoki, Świechocin, Łowyń all the demesne farms belonging to him, fields, gardens, meadows, marsh, lakes, ponds, pond-sites, rivers, pastures, heaths, fallows, forests, woods, coppices, thickets, money and rents in kind, the propination rights, brewing

and distilling rights, brick and lime kilns, the Obra demesne farm — in short each and every profitable right and privilege which His Serene Highness the Prince of Hohenlohe has hitherto used and enjoyed as proprietor, and can, may and shall enjoy, as a whole, by whatever name they may be called, and in particular also the right of pre-emption over the village mayors' holdings and demesne farms granted out on hereditary quit-rent tenure, excepting the jurisdiction and transfer fees (Laudemium) and the hunt, which His Most Serene Highness, as superior proprietor and perpetual ground-lord of Pszczew, reserves for Himself and His most high successors — to be their true hereditary property, in such manner and so that the said town commune of Pszczew and the aforementioned villages may deal with it as with their true property, may sell, redeem and give it away, can, may and shall do so, for a

§ 2. duly agreed purchase and hereditary-tenure sum of one hundred and eighty thousand Reichsthaler

in Royal Prussian Courant according to the coinage standard of 1764, and an annual ground-rent of one thousand Reichsthaler in Courant according to the same coinage standard.

3. With the payment of the purchase and hereditary-tenure sum it is to be held in this manner. The town and the remaining village communities take over, ad Rationes Practii, the mortgage debts named below, intabulated against the lordship of Pszczew in the mortgage book of the Royal Government at Poznań, namely

1, 48,000 Rthl entered for the building councillor Glenck, of which sum 36,000 Rthl have been ceded to the banker Salomon Nathan junior at Berlin and 12,000 Rthl to the banker Meyer Bernhard at Frankfurt an der Oder.

48,000 Rthl

2, 2,000 Rthl which are entered for the merchant Abraham Moses Hirschel at Wrocław.

3, 5,000 Rthl which are intabulated for the Baron von der Marwitz of Budnik and have been ceded to the banker Meyer Bernhard at Frankfurt an der Oder.

4, 5,000 Rthl which are intabulated for the widowed chief district councillor's wife Christiana Dorothea Michaelis née Eichborn.

5, 5,000 Rthl which are intabulated for the building councillor Johann Wilhelm Glenck and have been ceded by him to the banker Meyer Bernhard at Frankfurt, which several items from No. 2 to 5 have already been called in by the creditors and are payable at Christmas of the current year.

Whereby it is noted that the interest on the 48,000 Rthl has been settled up to the 2nd of July of the current year, but on the remaining capitals up to the 26th of July.

65,000 Rthl

6., 72,000 Rthl which are already intabulated for the banker Meyer Bernhard at Frankfurt an der Oder, and the interest at 5 per cent has been settled up to the 26th of July

of the present year, as with the remaining capitals; and they promise to settle these sums with the creditors and to come to agreement with them thereupon.

7, 137,000 Rthl. The deputies stipulate to pay over forthwith, out of the remainder of the purchase and hereditary-tenure sum, thirty-five thousand Reichsthaler to His Most Serene Highness at Wrocław, carriage free, but the remainder of 8,000 Rthl at the term of Midsummer of the coming year, together with 5 per cent interest, without fail, if it is called in at the proper time.

The aforementioned 35,000 Rthl are to be paid in this manner: tomorrow, the 29th of July, 7,000 Rthl, and a week from tomorrow the remaining 28,000 Rthl will be paid, and the 7,000 Rthl are to be sent to Wrocław carriage free at the cost of the payers.

[Since] among the moneys to be paid there are heavy Dutch milled ducats, these are to be accepted at 4 Groschen agio per piece. Should the communities not pay the 28,000 Rthl a week from tomorrow, that is on the 5th of August, then the whole contract concluded today lapses, and the communities are bound to pay the costs occasioned, but receive the 7,000 Rthl back again, though without interest.

§. 4. The handing over follows as soon as the 28,000 Rthl which are to be paid on the 5th of August have been paid; but since the former tenant von Bornstädt is still in possession of the demesne farm here, and a suit for his eviction is pending, the communities do not insist that possession of the demesne farm be made over to them forthwith, but are rather content that he remain therein until the judgment of eviction has legal force, and that he be evicted only when the judgment of eviction has legal force; but the communities shall for this be given a fair and suitable compensation proportionate to the matter by His Serene Highness the Prince.

As regards the forests, on the other hand, these shall be closed forthwith, just as

they already are now, and the timber felled therein, in so far as it has not been felled for the use of the farm, remains the property of His Serene Highness the Prince of Hohenlohe.

§. 5. All the manorial dwelling, farm, forest and other buildings are likewise made over to the communities in hereditary property; but the communities are bound to leave the foresters their lodging in one room in the foresters' houses until Michaelmas of the current year, as also the use of their gardens. His Serene Highness also reserves to himself the castle, for the seat of the court, the dwelling of the court servant, and a dwelling for His Highness himself or his commissioners, and also a stable for 2 horses, which they shall themselves maintain in good repair. In the case of building work on this edifice the communities are bound to let His Serene Highness the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen and his successors have the bricks at cost price, and to furnish the timber for the building free of charge out of the heath. The communities are likewise bound to furnish, free of charge out of the heath, the wood needful for the heating

of the court room and of the court servant, and to cart it thither. In like manner the communities are also bound, when His Most Serene Highness or his commissioners are present here, to furnish the needful firewood free of charge and to cart it thither.

§. 6. As regards the timber-purchase contracts concluded between His Most Serene Highness and certain merchants, His Highness promises to settle with the timber purchasers without the communities making any contribution thereto.

§ 7. The town and village communities mentioned at the outset bind themselves, on alienations of their parcels of land, to pay 10 per cent transfer fee (Laudemium) on the purchase sum to His Most Serene Highness and his successors in possession. From this transfer fee, however, those holdings are excepted which the

communities now wish to lay out anew; but if these are sold in the future, the transfer fee is likewise to be paid thereon at 10 per cent.

§. 8. Further, His Most Serene Highness reserves to himself:

That, should He himself, or his successors in possession, come hither, or should they send their commissioners hither, the communities are bound to furnish the relay carriages to a distance of 4 miles, out and back.

§. 9. Further, His Serene Highness reserves to himself, should he obtain the right of patronage over the church at Pszczew, that right of patronage; but the town and village communities shall have the right to choose the clergyman and to put him forward in nomination, which clergyman so nominated His Most Serene Highness promises to present to the episcopal consistory.

§. 10. The suits between the community of Stoki and the Prince of Hohenlohe over the ownership of the Stoki marsh; between the

Prince of Hohenlohe and the possessor of Zie lomi[uncertain: pat], concerning the right of redemption; and between the district councillor von Schmaling as possessor of the demesne farm in Głażewo and the Lord of Hohenlohe, His Serene Highness, concerning confirmation of the privilege; as also the suit between the Prince of Hohenlohe and Hertzig in Łowyń concerning the restitution of the [uncertain: Schales tro] — these the communities take over at their own risk and cost, and whatever they may win at law or obtain by way of composition falls to the communities, without His Serene Highness having the least claim thereto.

§. 11. The competency taxes and other public and further dues and burdens, by whatever name, hitherto paid by His Serene Highness as manorial lordship (Dominium) of Pszczew — among which belong also the carriage of the sick to Schillner and Punctner Hauland, as also the carriages for fetching and conveying away the court, and by whatever other name they may be called — are taken over by the said town and village communities; and the latter cannot, should these dues be increased in the future, demand any compensation from the

Prince of Hohenlohe, His Serene Highness. The communities also take over the contribution of fifty Reichsthaler which His Most Serene Highness had promised to render to the town school here for 1 year.

§. 12. Both contracting parties bind themselves to have this contract published before the competent authorities and to seek its confirmation; and His Most Serene Highness hereby makes himself liable to exert himself to the best of his ability that this contract be confirmed by the competent authorities, and that consent be granted to the communities for the further dismemberment of the parcels of land made over to them.

§. 13. As soon as the delivery of possession of the demesne farm here and of the Obra demesne farm takes place, there shall at the same time be handed over to the town and village communities that livestock and farm inventory which is sold along under the purchase and hereditary-tenure sum, in the same number as the tenant von Bornstädt received the same in the year 1800 at the handing over.

§ 14. This contract shall be binding for all time upon His Most Serene Highness the Prince of Hohenloh-Ingelfingen for himself and his most high heirs and successors, as also on the side of the town and village communities. And the canon or ground-rent of 1,000 Rthl to be paid annually shall be paid in half-yearly instalments of 500 Rthl, namely each time at the term of Christmas and the term of Johannis Baptista, yearly, sub paena executiones, and sent to Wrocław carriage free.

§. 15. So long as the communities do not alienate or dismember the parcels of land and rights made over to them, the statement of liabilities remains in its present condition. But as soon as the demesne farm is dismembered, the hereditary purchasers are bound to have the intabulated items transferred onto their parcels of land, and to have them cancelled in the name of His Most Serene Highness.

§. 16. For the stipulated canon of 1,000 Rthl yearly all the communities are liable in solidum, and they consent to its entry in the mortgage book against their parcels of land; just as, on the other hand, His Most Serene Highness likewise consents that this present contract be entered in the mortgage book of the manorial lordship (Dominium) of Pszczew and appurtenances.

§. 17. In conclusion the contracting parties renounce each and every objection, by whatever name they may be called, and in particular the town and village communities renounce the plea of injury beyond the half, which was explained to them to this effect:

that if the agreed purchase and hereditary-tenure sum exceeded the true value of the parcels of land and rights made over by double, they would thereby have

the right of withdrawal from the contract free to them.

§ 18. His Most Serene Highness reserves to himself the superior oversight over the forests, which he will confer upon the Royal Chief Forester Feller, and the communities bind themselves to indemnify the latter for his exertions, and to come to agreement with him thereupon. Therewith, nothing further being to be brought forward, the proceedings were closed, the protocol read out, interpreted by the sworn interpreter Echaust to the deputies of the town and village communities, who are not perfectly conversant with the German language and who had forbidden the keeping of a separate subsidiary protocol in the Polish language, approved and signed; whereupon it was further noted by the contracting parties that the costs of the recording,

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

From all the vexation I have contracted a severe gall fever and must keep to my bed here in Poznań.

Matters are all so confused that at every turn one meets with so many obstacles as keep pushing one back from the goal. Such I found the situation here with regard to the Broniewski business — Not enough that they have concluded the accursed settlement. No! It is so defective that it afforded not a Groschen's worth of security — all this is to be cleared away and altered, and for that Broniewski's wife is required, and she is God knows where; now it is said she is in Kollo, now she is in Warsaw. In short, these people are out for nothing but to cheat Your Serene Highness.

And, frankly confessed, I hold Wunster to be the worst rogue of all — He is forever in collusion with Broniewski and Guderian, assuredly gets a couple of thousand d from the former, and has therefore contrived the most disadvantageous settlement, slipped the same into Glenck's hands so that he had to conclude it — but he himself has prudently taken himself off out of the dust, so as afterwards to be able to shift everything onto the simple-minded Glenck. The Jew M[eyer] Bernhard is here with Simon. These swindlers mean to pay Your Serene Highness only 6,000 Rthl instead of 13,000 Rthl — but that shall not succeed for these knaves — First Broniewski alone shall furnish sufficient security, which is promised for tomorrow — then Glenck shall press for the depositing of the full 66,000 Rthl with Melzer, against which

Broniewski shall at once concede the delivery of possession of the estates before the court — then the Jew and consorts are satisfied in this matter. Thereafter Broniewski takes his 53,000 Rthl and Glenck the 13,000 for Your Serene Highness. In Pszczew the Jew wished to undertake a like seizure and to confuse the people's heads — meanwhile he shall succeed there as little as here — My resolve is absolutely to bring Your Serene Highness the whole 30,000 Rthl out of Pszczew and the full 13,000 Rthl from here. Thereafter [uncertain: Your Highness] may pay out according to desert — The base fellow Wunster I scarcely get to see at all. He has his woman here, has placed her at the theatre, and gives balls for the whole gang, that they may take the buck's hide among themselves — that costs much, and therefore the knave must strike out every road to snatch something. As regards Glenck, Your Serene Highness does me great [uncertain: wrong] — I am no cringing sinner, but go willingly straight and open — What I write to Your Serene Highness, I say to him — indeed he reads everything I write. This, I believe, justifies my conduct. In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Poznań, the 4th of August 1804

Be it known and understood that between His Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, Governor of Wrocław etc., on the one part, and the building-bank cashier Herr Leixner at Frankfurt an der Oder, the following contract of sale and purchase has been deliberately, freely and irrevocably agreed, concluded and executed.

§ 1. His Most Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, Governor of Wrocław etc., namely sells His Highness's estates lying under the Department of the Government at Poznań in the

district of

Kolno and Kamionna, together with all the appurtenances and mills belonging thereto, rights and privileges, with all residents, fields, forests, lakes and waters, with the rents and the propination rights, the labour services, the hunt and the jurisdiction, also all remaining rights and appurtenances, just as His Most Serene Highness received the said estates and their appurtenances delivered over from the Royal Commission by virtue of the deed of donation, of which a certified copy is to be handed over to the purchaser, and for the correctness and truth of which His Serene Highness furnishes eviction with regard to the estates Kolno and Kamionna, and has possessed and enjoyed them, and can use and enjoy them, with everything as it stands and lies, and finally also with all the rights which His Serene Highness may have against the

inhabitants and subjects of these estates, which they have arrogated to themselves and believe they may claim, to His Honour the Royal bank cashier Herr George Conrad Leixner at Frankfurt an der Oder, for a fixed purchase sum of One Hundred and Forty-Two Thousand Reichsthaler Royal Prussian 64-piece Courant, as his complete property.

§ 2. Today's purchase of the estates Kolno and Kamionna is made without valuation, as a whole; therefore His Most Serene Highness furnishes eviction only with regard to the survey register taken up by the Royal Commission and the real properties listed in the [uncertain: Tan], which are to be handed over at the delivery of possession. All revenues and farming yields the purchaser must take over as they exist, and according as they may hereafter increase or diminish, with which the purchaser likewise declares himself content.

His Most Serene Highness has caused a settlement to be concluded with the cavalry captain von Broniewski on 3 July of this year, according to the contents of which the same wishes, upon receipt of a sum of 53,139 Rthl.

13 Groschen 8 4/5 Pfennig, to give back the estates Kolno and Kamionna forthwith and to restore the [text lost] to His Highness. Now since the merchant Herr Simon, as authorised representative of Herr Leixner, has agreed with Herr

von Broniewski at Poznań on the 6th of this month, that the payment of the 53,139 Rthl. 13 Groschen 8 4/5 Pfennig shall be made on 8 September at Poznań, but the delivery of possession in kind of the estates on 10 September at Kolno and Kamionna, His Serene Highness promises to send an authorised representative to Poznań and to Kolno and Kamionna at the said time, in order to be present at these acts; and since a Government Commissioner from Poznań will carry out the handing over in kind, His Serene Highness stipulates that the estates Kolno and Kamionna shall be delivered over to the purchaser immediately on the 10th of September.

§ 4. Both in the settlement of 3 July and also in a later declaration, Herr von Broniewski has bound himself to redeem all his intabulations upon Kolno and Kamionna completely, and thereby to have these estates cleared of all obligations charged upon them on his account. The purchaser accordingly receives these estates entirely free of debt.

§ 5. Herr von Broniewski retains all the usufructs of the estates up to 24 June of this year. From that day onward all usufructs and burdens pass over to the purchaser, and Herr von Broniewski will, at the handing over in kind, render the account thereof, just as he will at the same time restore the stock of field, cattle and farming inventory which von Broniewski received on taking over the estates in the year 1786 as the lordship's

stock, as the delivery-of-possession instrument of that time states. We Friedrich Wilhelm, by God's Grace King of Prussia etc., Margrave of Brandenburg, Arch-Chamberlain and Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, sovereign and supreme Duke of Silesia, sovereign Prince of Orange, Neuchâtel and Valangin, as also of the County of Kłodzko, Duke in Geldern, at Magdeburg, Cleve, Julich, Berg, Szczecin, Pomerania, of the Cassubians and Wends, at Mecklenburg and Krosno Odrzańskie, Burgrave of Nuremberg above and below the mountains, Prince of Halberstadt, Minden, Camin, Wenden, Schwerin, Ratzeburg, East Frisia and Meurs, Count of Hohenzollern, Ruppin, of the Mark Ravensberg, Hohenstein, Tecklenburg, Schwerin, Lingen, Bühren and Leerdam, Lord of Ravenstein, of the Lands of Rostock, Stargard, Limburg, Lauenburg, Bütow, Arlay and Breda etc., do by this Our open letter attest and declare, for Ourselves and Our descendants and successors in the Crown, the Electorate and Our remaining Lands, that, whereas it has been most humbly laid before Us in what manner

Our intention of giving to the High-Born Prince, Our friendly beloved Uncle, Friedrich Ludwig, reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, by the grant of the estates formerly belonging to the absconded former Starosta von Prusimski, a mark of Our friendship and goodwill borne toward him, as also of Our Royal gratitude for the distinguished and beneficial services rendered to Us and to Our Royal House, has not been achieved entirely as We had willed it, because the said estates were burdened with many debts; We have most highly resolved to leave over, to grant and to convey to His Lordship, in heritable and proprietary right, the hereafter named formerly ecclesiastical estates, namely the villages of Pszczew, Świechocin, Stoki, Łowyń, Głażewo, Tarnowo, Zagórów, Skokum, Świątniki, Kopojno, Olesnica, Drzewce, Grądzyń, Wrąbczyn, Wieniec and Wolica, together with all their appurtenances, by whatever name they may be called, against payment

1., of the territorial-sovereign dues hitherto discharged therefrom,

of the territorial-sovereign dues, as a fixed and unalterable canon, and

2.) of the allowance due therefrom to the ecclesiastical corporations or foundations, in heritable and proprietary right.

This We also hereby do, and by force of this present instrument, out of Royal power and plenitude, for Ourselves and Our descendants and successors in the Crown, the Electorate and Our remaining Lands, in such manner and to this effect, that Our aforesaid friendly beloved Uncle, the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, shall have the above-named estates with all rights attaching thereto

and prerogatives, as these have hitherto been exercised or may lawfully be exercised, and no less with all their pertinences and other appurtenances, by whatever name they may be called, as the same have hitherto been enjoyed, or may lawfully be enjoyed, and with all the lands belonging thereto, in fields, woods and meadows, likewise in ponds and waters, from henceforth for all eternity, for himself and his heirs and descendants, as a true, well-acquired and unrestricted proper-

ty, irrevocably from Us and Our descendants and successors, to hold, possess and enjoy; and that the power and authority shall also be attached thereto of disposing of the same at pleasure under the conditions mentioned above, unhindered by any man.

We therefore command and enjoin all Our supreme provincial colleges, as also all other authorities whom this concerns, herewith as graciously as earnestly, that they in no wise hinder or impede the Lordship of the much-mentioned Lord Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen in the heritable and proprietary possession of the above-named estates, together with their pertinences and appurtenances, granted to him, nor

Thus done and given in Our Residence City of Berlin, the nineteenth day of the month of June after the birth of Christ Our Lord, in the one thousand seven hundred and ninety-seventh, and of Our Royal reign in the eleventh year. Friedrich Willhelm. Hoym. Reck.

Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Lord!

Having broken my carriage and very nearly my neck along with it, I have nevertheless arrived here in Kalisz safe and sound, though somewhat shaken about. The greatest loss is the time I require for the repairing of my carriage, in order to be able to travel further with it. Court Councillor Grimm lies miserably ill; meanwhile he will work up [uncertain: verarbeiten] the matter for von Radzinski, for which, however, the contracts would be required.

With Honrichs things look bad — the man does not pay the 4,000 Rthl, notwithstanding that everything has been receipted, cancelled, and put in order with the consent of the Board of Wards.

Grimm wishes to compel him to payment at once by process of law — but he lacks the contract and a power of attorney — Rochlitz has the contract, and he has also had a power of attorney for the pursuit of this matter.

May Your Most Serene Highness be pleased to issue the order that the contract be demanded back from Rochlitz with the utmost haste and sent off, together with a power of attorney, to Mr Grimm. In Trąbczyn, I hear, orders are being given which run directly counter to my plan. Thus one of those in command has lent out 100 bushels of grain to somebody, whereof Your Serene Highness will never receive one of them [...], and a great part of the fields has likewise been sown. As soon as my carriage is mobile I shall hasten thither, in order then to report the rest to Your Serene Highness. In reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Lord!

From the enclosed letter of Pankratz Your Most Serene Highness will be pleased to satisfy yourself that the Mennonites will buy. Pankratz is one of their principal elders, and what he promises every member of this sect is bound to abide by. I shall therefore travel tomorrow to Lunau and try my fortune. The verbal assurance given by Pankratz to the old district messenger is that the Mennonites wish to buy the Zagórów and Trąbczyn estates as a whole and to divide them among themselves at the price fixed for them by Your Serene Highness. May God now grant it further prosperity. For the rest, I greatly fear that I shall return with a second bilious fever. The only honest man who is here is the justice-burgomaster Schenck. His valuation will turn out well, and in case of need money can at any time be raised upon it. He lacks only the contract with the miller's wife in Trąbczyn — Mr Glenck has that one — Then again, there stands against them the contract concluded on the 5th of September with the building councillor Mr Glenck, in which 300 Morgen of manorial land and the settlement of all dues from the bailiff's holding are promised to him. Glenck has sent this contract here

on to Tappert, so that he should make it public. Tappert at once laid the contract before the valuation commission and protested that they should not there bring the said lands into the valuation. The Gemeinde has taken alarm at this and protests against the removal of these lands, a part of which belongs to it as pasturage — and this now hinders the commission, so that it cannot proceed further, the more so since Tappert also produced a contract of sale of Glenck's, by which Glenck has sold along with it the komornik holdings in the whole of Wrąbczyn to a certain v Malachowski — It would be necessary for Glenck to issue a written undertaking in which he declares that he has given the 300 Morgen back to Your Serene Highness, and also declares that he was not able to sell the komornik holdings and that this was an error. Then again, all the negotiations with the Swięcia people are missing here — perhaps Glenck has something of them there; so too the contract of the miller's wife from Wrąbczyn would be there, as also the contract with the Swięcia Hollanders; and if Glenck were willing to issue the written undertakings, may Your Serene Highness be pleased most graciously to convey them to me by this express, so that the matter might be put in order —

The dismemberment will in any event be brought to a happy conclusion, for a great many persons, whose names have been noted down here, are ready to buy at any [uncertain: Wird], and besides the Mennonites they have presented themselves here, so that one may pick and choose. Still, I wish to conclude with the Mennonites, because from them I obtain the most money and go the most securely.

Otherwise they have merely played the fool and sown the fields after all — v. Otocki has followed this example at Kopojno, and there will not be much left over to sell. These are worse than wicked men — I thought to get a great deal out of it; what is to become of it now? It is remarkable that when a German comes to Poland he is at once corrupted to the very blood — thus, for example, the surveyors have not yet finished the map, and yet the [uncertain: fäulste] has not, the man Leopold has already had 368 Rthl. paid out to him — which was in fact given to the wretch as well — Wollenhaupt is a sly rogue; but I shall dispatch this scoundrel so neatly that he will not know how he got out of Trąbczyn.

Landrath v Blomberg is the worst pettifogger there ever was on earth — if one did not need the miserable

scoundrel so exceedingly in the dismemberment, I would spit the fellow in the face — Meanwhile I shall treat him with coldness and such liberty as is possible until I no longer need him — Your Serene Highness may rest assured, however, that he shall do you no harm, for I have provided against that in every way. To set down his knaveries here, and what base cunning he again employed in order to [uncertain: learn the cash-boxes] here, would be too long-winded; I shall relate them to Your Serene Highness by word of mouth. Enough that he is a bad fellow, better fitted to stand at the head of a band of robbers than to be a Landrath — I must summon up all my patience so as not to betray myself.

In the matter of Przespolewski the Government has sent execution here, that Your Serene Highness is to pay 6,500 Rthl. forthwith. I have at once had the necessary objection lodged against it.

1. Przespolewski has ceded the claim to a certain Magnuski

2. Szczucki has laid an attachment upon it

3. The document has been lost; nothing can be struck off and consequently nothing can be paid either, for Honrichs too would pay nothing sooner than when everything had been struck off. This here the government well; how can it proceed so infamously in this matter? In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's most humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Lord!

I have completed the most toilsome journey I have ever made in my life, to West and East Prussia. The Mennonites wish to [uncertain: purchase] and have assured me in their fashion that, with some money, they will arrive in Wrocław on the 19th of December and there conclude the contract. I could have drawn up a memorandum of heads of agreement with several of them on the spot, only it would have been too little for me, in a single place, since these people dwell singly, scattered about, and I could not bring them together, because the weather was too bad and the roads bottomless. Besides which, they expressly wished to have the propination rights included in the present valuation, and this moved me to depart and to summon them to Wrocław.

Since, however, the Biblical lawgivers taught — to prove all things and to hold fast that which is good — I have today sent for the Landsberg and Oder-Bruch men, am letting them come, and shall hear what they can effect — if these are better, I shall conclude at once and commend the Mennonites to the H[?]. I am no weakling — but the road to the H. — sons has nevertheless become too [uncertain: seinen], I have wrestled with life and death, and in the end the H. made me new strangling-bands — So if these people show themselves willing, I shall conclude and let the [uncertain: hypocrites] go their way.
