Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Lord!

Still I await the arrival of the people from the Oder and Netze marshes. From Wednesday onward they will probably present themselves in whole troops, and then I hope to be swiftly at the goal of my wishes. Several plots which the Swięcia people had [uncertain: marked out], and which lay about as waste corners along the border, I have sold very advantageously; I not only place well with a purchaser the soil that was held in no regard at all, but likewise the figure, so as now to be able to conclude better with the large purchasers for regular parcels. From the plan I once drew up I do not depart, and I stand surety that no Hufe shall be given away under 600 Rthl / that is, ground-money and rents taken together /. If it has succeeded with the very worst plots, then it will not fail me with the [uncertain: better ones]. The valuation will probably be finished this week and, as I hope, will come out at over 400,000 Rthl for the Zagórów estates. By this means defiance is bidden to all ill-will; I take in

Berlin as much money as is needed for the payment of Schlabrendorff, Lichnowski and other pressing creditors, and pay them. Gradually the money for these plots comes in, and that debt is paid off again; in this way nothing is lost through precipitancy and the great aim is attained. It goes hard, very hard, for much has been spoilt by the easy earlier sales; yet my perseverance will prevail, for that I answer.

The late vexation with Glenck, where the man tells me to my face that I mean to wrest his property from him, and the annoyance with the hereditary leaseholders stirred up by the Oleśnica people, have brought upon me a frightful colic which compelled me to keep my bed for 3 days; I am still very poorly.

For the rest, the Wrąbczyn subjects have protested against their contract and refuse to render the rent. Their complaint is that Glenck threatened [uncertain: them] to take their plots away and to give them others in their place; besides this they complain that Glenck's clerk compelled them to serve through the whole year still, and that he, being unable to use all the services on the village bailiff's holding, sent the subjects to Zagórów, where they must work for the burgesses, and for which

the steward has himself paid 4 Groschen daily per person / of whom there are 18 /. The subjects find this too hard, that they should be sold like slaves to serve other, strange men. The steward has moreover made it known to the people that he will draw all 18 householders entirely to the village bailiff's holding, and that Glenck means to sell them along with it to von Marowecki, who on those terms gives 15,000 Rthl for the village bailiff's holding.

The subjects implore that Your Serene Highness might not permit this; they will gladly give one rthlr per Morgen of their fields and render everything else that lies within their power. I have referred the people with their petitions and lamentations to the justice-burgomaster Schenck, and have requested him to quiet them and to bring the matter to a clear issue, so that Glenck may not cry out again that I mean to wrest from him his well-acquired property.

In deepest esteem I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

most humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

I have the honour to have just now received Your Most Serene Highness's two letters of the 30th of November and the 2nd of December. It gladdens me most heartily that Your Highness has in Mr von Nothardt so genuine a friend, through whom much good will be able to be effected. That he was to become Director I did indeed already know, but the particular manner of it was unknown to me. The business with Mr von Harlem and the councillor of war Nöldichen is meanwhile causing much terror — and Mr von Nothardt has every reason to pray to Heaven that Mr von Voss does not avenge his favourite upon him. — Things go very badly for me here — It seems as though Heaven were setting itself against all business — the Mennonites are here in Trąbczyn and wish to buy both estates together. I am having the people provided for and every kindness shown them, so that I may keep them in good humour — Meanwhile, on account of the great snow, which lies more than a foot deep, nothing can be undertaken. One hundred Hufen of the Grądzyń and Drzewce forest I am selling for [uncertain: perpetual] rent. This amounts to 3,000 Rthl in rent and consequently to 60,000 Rthl of capital. Which, in case I do not do the latter, then the poor grounds remain to me, and the valuation would turn out very low

especially as such dreadful shortfalls are appearing. For Swięcia yields, instead of 1,800 Rthl in rent, only 918 Rthl in all; Wrąbczyn, instead of 1,500 Rthl, only 1,123 Rthl.

Upon the forest, with timber prices so low, very little is to be reckoned; I must therefore think upon artificial funds, so that a value proportionate to the matter may be arrived at in the valuation, inasmuch as by means of the loan, so that nothing here be squandered away, all ill will may be forestalled and the principal debts paid.

The valuers had at first taken the matter according to the tableaux, but when it came to the examination of the people, whereby the revenues were to be proved, everything fell so far short that we must alter the whole valuation.

Lichnowski has laid an arrest upon a part of the ten thousand Rthl which the Oleśnica people are to pay at Christmas, so that only some 6,000 Rthl will thereby be received. With the Wrąbczyn people I must deal very warily, for, as Nerlich tells me, they refuse to pay the Christmas instalment. Even if in truth no snow were lying, it would still be very inexpedient to proceed now with the measuring out of the lands. Meanwhile at Wrąbczyn nothing remains over for Your Serene Highness, and the fine village brings in nothing further than the sum censured above, which, according to the area contained, if the Morgen were reckoned at 1 Rthl, ought to amount to 2,958 Rthl.

These however are matters which now can no longer be altered — I meanwhile shall give away no Morgen at under 1 Rthl rent, however poor the land may be, and in the case of lands and meadows, with the good marshes, nothing goes for less than 300 Rthl in ready money and 15 Rthl annual rent; for this I stand surety. Were the weather not so very much against me, I should perhaps already be finished; as it is, however, I must let God rule, and hold to the drawing up of the valuation.

The interest to the Lichnowski party is being paid here — Your Serene Highness will nevertheless receive from here about 8,000 Rthl at Christmas. For the Schlabrendorff and the Lichnowski principal sums I must fetch the capital from Berlin, which can then, when the Mennonites pay, be paid off again.

What good will and human powers can accomplish, I shall exert, in order to guide everything, in spite of the frightful weather, to the best end. In deepest reverence and esteem I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

most humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Trąbczyn, the 7th of December 1804

Each Hufe contains thirty Morgen, and each Morgen one hundred and eighty square rods Magdeburg measure.

6. The hereditary lessees one hundred and fifty Reichsthaler per Hufe, making for 10 Hufen 1,500 Rthl, say One Thousand and thereupon a Hundred Reichsthaler. As an annual hereditary canon the hereditary lessees pay, and that from Martinmas of this year onward, per Hufe 22 Rthl 12 Groschen, say twenty-two Reichsthaler twelve good Groschen, making for 10 Hufen 225 Rthl, say two hundred and twenty-five Reichsthaler, in two instalments, namely the half with 112 Rthl.

12 Groschen, say One Hundred and Twelve Reichsthaler 12 Groschen, at Midsummer, and the second half likewise with 112 Rthl. 12 Groschen, say One Hundred and Twelve Reichsthaler 12 Groschen, at Christmas, each time postnumerando, in cash and in Courant, into the manorial treasury; but they are wholly freed for perpetual times from all and every manorial labour service and delivery in kind to the ground lordship.

begin with the past Midsummer of this year and end at Midsummer One Thousand Eight Hundred and Eight, so that from this uncultivated land they shall render the first rent at Christmas One Thousand Eight Hundred and Eight; and the objection that one or another of them had not yet brought his land under cultivation shall then not be admitted.

§. V. Besides the annually stipulated hereditary rent, however, the hereditary lessees shall further, for themselves and their descendants, bear in perpetuity all and every royal and other public tax and due falling upon these ten Hufen, by whatever name they may be called.

§. VI. Since in the first § there are

granted to the hereditary lessees in all ten Hufen ten Morgen, it is here noted that they have received the ten Morgen for their building plots free of charge, and need pay neither purchase money nor rent for them.

§. VIII. Their establishments must the present hereditary lessees, as well as the remaining future takers, for the present and for times to come

always carry out at their own cost, and they shall receive for this neither remission of the hereditary rent nor any other building assistance; they may, however, employ for this the timber standing on the Hufen received in hereditary lease, as being theirs in property, all of it and without any exception.

§. IX. These Hufen taken in hereditary lease shall, as soon as the weather permits, be duly measured out to the hereditary lessees and delivered into their possession, and at the same time it shall be ascertained how much the surface content amounts to of the land already now under cultivation, from which

the rent is paid.

§. X. The hereditary lessees renounce entirely, for themselves and their successors, any building timber, firewood or pasture in the remaining manorial woods and fields, and they may not overstep the boundaries of their holding.

§. XI. The present hereditary lessees, as well as the remaining future takers, are at liberty to alienate their holdings in any manner they please; but upon every change of possession, whether by sale or by exchange, the tenth Groschen of the purchase money or of the exchange sum must be paid to the ground lordship as a transfer fee (Laudemium),

and in this regard the same shall always hold to the new acquirer, whose business it remains not to pay out the purchase money to the seller before the transfer fee has been settled. On inheritances or cessions to children and collateral relatives no transfer fee is paid, and likewise the first takers from the present hereditary lessees are wholly exempt from it.

§. XII. The hereditary lessees are at liberty to redeem the stipulated hereditary rent by payment of the capital sum; that is to say, each of them may pay down to the ground lordship fifty Reichsthaler, one hundred Reichsthaler or one hundred and fifty Reichsthaler, which capital

shall then remain the property of the ground lordship, and five per hundred of it shall be written off from their annual rent; yet it is expressly laid down that this redeemable sum may in no case exceed, per Hufe, the sum of one hundred and fifty Reichsthaler, and that accordingly [uncertain: fifteen Reichsthaler] of annual rent per Hufe shall remain standing irredeemable for perpetual times.

§. XIII. The hereditary lessees and their descendants remain forever wholly free of all hereditary subjection, but are without exception subject to the jurisdiction of the manorial lordship (Dominium).

and brandy the hereditary lessees and their successors in possession must always take from the manorial brewhouse and distillery or from the tavern, and for every quart of brandy brought in from other estates they shall pay one Reichsthaler, and for every barrel of beer five Reichsthaler, as a penalty to the ground lordship.

The hereditary lessees hereby expressly renounce, for themselves and their successors, all and every remission in cases of misfortune, whether these arise from fire from heaven, arson by evil people, crop failure, hailstorm, flood, cattle plague, war, or pestilence, and in whatever manner they may arise; and

on that account no compensation or remission of the hereditary rent shall ever accrue to them.

§. XVI. The costs of this contract, of its confirmation and of the official copy, the hereditary lessees undertake to settle.

So long as the hereditary lessees and their successors in possession fulfil the obligations described above, they shall be protected in their rights by the ground lordship in every respect, and be defended and held harmless against any man's real claim. Should they, however, remain in arrears with the annual hereditary canon for longer than two years, they shall thereupon forfeit this hereditary lease, and the ground lordship shall be entitled to let the same out elsewhere, in

which case only their improvements need be made good to the hereditary lessees.

cunning persuasion, of undue haste, of the impossibility of raising the rent out of the property, of matters otherwise agreed than written down or not rightly understood; and it is expressly consented by His Most Serene Highness that the hereditary lessees may, on the ground of this contract, have the title of possession to their holdings entered in their own names.

Further, on the part of His Most Serene Highness the hereditary lessees are granted the liberty of fetching, free of charge, the clay for their whole first establishments from the Trąbczyn territory; yet this liberty ceases entirely as soon as they shall have built their buildings. Also

Right Honourable Sir, Highly Honoured Sir, Councillor of War and Forests!

I have the honour to communicate to Your Right Honourable a few further items which have come in by today's riding post from Mr Glenck. His Serene Highness believes that it may be of use to you. no longer perceptible. We all hope for the best. Mining Councillor Bernhardi has arrived here, though, as I myself saw yesterday — not altogether in health — His Serene Highness sent me to reassure him on that account, since on account of his continuing indisposition he has not yet been able to pay his respects. Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Lord, the Minister von Voss has, in the most despotic expressions, forbidden all revision of the valuations; whatever names they may bear and to whomsoever they may belong, the Chamber is to reject them. Now I await only Amelang's answer — whether they will be content with the revision by the Landrath. If this too is refused — then I must think of other means — and set light against despotism. The dismemberment is [...] submitted; the President is sending a councillor to Zagórów [uncertain: um] Trąbczyn, who is to inspect everything, whereupon the consent will then be granted. The revision on account of the dismemberment I shall know how to turn to use — With Mr Meierowitz I have concluded, as the figure shows, and I am endeavouring to dislodge Honrichs — I think the matter will give Your Serene Highness pleasure: you recover your 4,000 Rthl and profit yearly by 500 Rthl canon, or 10,000 Rthl in cash for it. Weigelt receives out of the eight thousand, over and above his 4,000 Rthl,

6,000 Rthl, Schliefen, and Honrichs 6,000 Rthl; that makes 20,000 Rthl of purchase money. Szetlewek Radzinski will not let slip. Both [uncertain: facienden] therefore already ask cash money of 14,000 Rthl without the canon — and Radzinski's claim is extinguished and all the lawsuits are quashed.

With the Oleśnica people I shall soon be done — I now have important help — My opinion is now to have the fellows thrown out. To take the 10,000 Rthl from the newer subjects and let them be settled, because they have already paid 10,000 Rthl. Thereafter to come to terms with the old peasants, to bring together so much land that the demesne farm is restored, and then to let out Oleśnica anew, according to the mind of the Chamber,

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Your Most Serene Highness will receive the free pass for Hohenlohe wines at the earliest, and likewise I hope to be able to remit the 25,000 Rthl shortly. Right Honourable Sir, Highly Honoured Sir, Councillor of War and Forests! To Your Right Honourable I report, by command of His Serene Highness the Prince: that I was today in person with the Chancellor Hohmuth concerning the Schlabrendorff payment, and spoke with you regarding a longer deadline. The result of this conversation was not very comforting. Should this be done soon, with 25/m Rthl, then he would prevail upon the countess to wait yet some time for the

remaining half of 25/m Rthl — of an obligation for the latter payment he would hear nothing whatever, nor did he venture to make any proposal to that effect, inasmuch as he will have it that he is positively convinced the countess would never enter into such a thing. Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Lord!

If I had been able in any way whatever to obtain the 25,000 Rthl without making the great transaction, I should long since have brought it about with the most glowing zeal.

But if I take the lesser sum, it costs, and my hands are tied, because I must pledge the heavy papers for the small loans just as much as for the large ones. As yet I have no first assurance [uncertain: when] I am to receive the capitals. The papers are found good and the security sufficient, but there is delay, God knows why.

I am certainly doing everything of which human powers are capable, and neither rest nor repose, [uncertain: in order] to reach the goal of all wishes. Only here nothing can be forced. Twice already we believed we had the money for certain, but an evil man has thwarted it; as I think,

it is young Eysenhardt — who claims to have 18,000 Rthl to demand of Your Serene Highness as well; for these the Court Councillor Meyer will offer him the 20,000 Rthl and take over the debt — I have declined this for the present — because the lawsuit concerning the [uncertain: jewels] is not yet decided, and because the 9,000 Rthl are registered on Szetlewek, so that he must be content with the interest, for the payment of which I have myself given an assurance. I shall do the same with the Ziemecki matter. Of Bernhardi's conduct I say nothing — for he was minded to treat me worse than the greatest usurer in the state, and by an eleven-day delay put me in the very greatest embarrassment — God be praised, I have concluded the business as happily as I could have imagined, and let the peasant run.

Should the Schlabrendorff woman be unmannerly, then everything here is provided for, and she would have every cause to repent a foolish conduct.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Lord, at last, through the mediation of the venerable General von Köckritz, it has been achieved that the Invalids' Department has now declared itself willing to advance 150,000 Rthl, without my having to seek the permission of His Majesty the King, which is otherwise the course of business. The Department gives for the present, upon the mortgage and my bill of exchange, 50,000 Rthl; then the Chamber must still revise the valuations, and after these the Department pays the 100,000 Rthl, which, of the interest being duly paid, can stand for 50 years.

The wards' deposit fund, the widows' fund, and still less the Bank or the Maritime Trading Company, pay not one Ezer more into South Prussia either, but are striving to call everything in — this causes a fearful stoppage in all business and spreads such Ah! and Oh! among the people that one's hair stands on end. I too should have obtained nothing, had the Braun General not taken up my cause in the most active manner. The

bankers here now themselves give, merely to keep themselves afloat, 10 to 12 per cent proximaticum for 5 to 6 per cent interest; besides which Liep: Meyer Wolff fest each his aim — he alone still has money, and thinks of those seeking money whatever is agreeable to him. Whoever now falls into the hands of this sort of men is irretrievably lost. God and the honest friend be heartily thanked that here He appointed a better, and truly the most desirable, lot — As soon as I now receive the money I shall pay the [uncertain: ſehen] demanded 10,000 Rthl and send in haste to Your Serene Highness the sum remaining after deduction of the costs.

With the Girard and Hauk matter I am done; tomorrow I pay the arrears of interest out of my own money, and then someone takes over the debt, which can stand quietly for 4 years. The suit over the proxenetica that were taken I do not find well advised — the thing damages Your Serene Highness's credit anew, and frightens off all those so-called men of business who are in league with one another. This was even cast up at me in the course of this very business, and appeal was made to it, that Seebald should sue and demand the proxenetica back;

The Biron matter has struck fear and terror into everyone — the moral lecture which Your Serene Highness writes merely on account of the Schlabrendorff matter I did not deserve. Every breach of my word is foreign to my heart, and shall remain so to my last breath. I do not indeed know what I wrote in that agonising moment; yet I must have expressed myself mistakenly, in giving answer to Your Serene Highness's letter — Honour remains in all my dealings the first motive spring; to it I sacrifice effort, means and health. And the truth which I then spoke in the Pro Memoria upon the whole Schläbe dorff matter is, by my way of thinking, no piece of knavery — I should curse all my dealings, and withdraw — to which I am much inclined — into the last corner of the earth, far from all men, if I were in the end to be judged so.

The Mennonites I shall answer definitely according to Your Serene Highness's command. Wollenhaupt's opinion regarding the dismemberment of the estates is too insignificant for one to be permitted to say a word further about it. Should Your Serene Highness deign to give him the commission and promise him a few Tausendtstäd, he warrants he will dismember half the world — I have the samples

still before me — I shall forward the Rochlitz matters on my return to Kargowa. The free pass for the wines must by now already be there. What the Pszczew subjects want I do not understand — there must again be some store lurking in the background. Meanwhile the date of this letter is of the month of June, and indeed earlier than that of the contract.

Next Wednesday I go back from here, in order to direct at Kalisz the revision of the valuation, so as to obtain the 100,000 Rthl the more quickly, and then to be able to dismember in peace. humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Berlin, the 26th of January 1805

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Lord!

An order of the General Finance Department, issued a fortnight ago to all the Chambers here, hinders the course of my business extraordinarily, and it may be long before I reach my goal with the revision of the valuations, if indeed it is permitted at all. The cause of these new difficulties is Prince George together with the councillor of war Korn here. The former, some time ago, petitioned the Kalisz Chamber for Korn as reviser of his valuations of the estates situated in this, the Poznań, and other departments; and the Chamber granted this. But since, unhappily, the judicial valuations which were to be revised had been drawn up by Korn himself, and were contested in the [uncertain: Abord], this had to be laid before the head of the Department; and, indignant at this swindling — that a member of the Chamber should revise the valuations which he himself had made, and against which so many objections are raised, and make the Chamber answerable for them — the Minister issued the order

that no Chamber should any longer be permitted, without the prior knowledge of the General Finance Department, to order the revision of a judicial valuation; whereby the revision of Prince George's affairs was at once forbidden for ever. His Excellency the President von Goldbeck has, however, written at once to the Department and sought permission. I have sent this to Berlin by express courier, and at the same time have asked Amelang and Langens[illegible] to help procure the permission and to see to it that the same be dispatched here with all speed. It now remains to be seen whether the spiteful Voss will concede the revision.

Meanwhile I must lie here at anchor and await the answer. In the interim I shall submit the dismemberment plans for approbation, and level everything in this matter. Mr von Goldbeck was at first very [uncertain: Bau], and at the last he reproached me that I had not helped him to the Starostey Strehlitz, which afterwards Dolfs obtained, and which the Minister had promised him so firmly. The proof that I had done everything for him was not difficult for me to furnish,

and we were reconciled again. He wishes very much to have, as soon as possible, three bronzed busts, which he means to set upon his bookcase. Likewise he has asked me to procure him a washstand as soon as may be, so as to be able to wash his ailing lower abdomen daily. May Your Serene Highness have the grace to let three busts of that kind, and a washstand also, be bought, and send me these hither by the first post. The washstand is to be had in the joiners' warehouses.

I should dearly like to surprise the good man with it quite promptly. The Oleśnica matter has, through the friendly mediation of Mr von Hussarzewski, been sent back to the patrimonial court for decision; this is for us a great satisfaction — I shall now bring about the swiftest prosecution of the matter, and in the interim calm Lichnowski, so as to be able to dismember at leisure. Heaven grant only that I obtain the permission for the revision of the valuations as soon as possible; the cursed swindles of Prince George have already caused much terror, and will yet arouse much misfortune and mistrust. He is a frightful man indeed — I cannot praise God enough that I am parted from the man. In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's faithful, humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Kalisz, the 24th of February 1805.

Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Lord!

Your Most Serene Highness's gracious letter I have received by express courier, and yesterday I had the answer delivered to the Oleśnica people.

Tomorrow the term of hearing in this matter falls at Trąbczyn, and I hoped to see the business finalised shortly.

The lads say that they have no wish to litigate against Your Serene Highness, and yet these fellows, in league with the district councillor, already nine months ago lodged protests here and sought to set the matter up so that they should never have to hand over the 10,000 Rthl. — Now that they see their cause stands badly, they come crawling and try their luck another way — From Berlin I look for the answer at any hour — God grant that it turns out as we wish.

Szetlewek is what the von Otocki wishes to take in hereditary lease — He offers already 10,000 Rthl of [uncertain: bustands] money and 1,500 Rthl annual canon. Glenck valued the estate at 40,000 Rthl, but he had promised 800 Morgen of woodland from Trąbczyn — if I can get these 40,000 Rthl without it, I shall close, for then Your Serene Highness profits 16,000 Rthl against the valuation. Further, Otocki wishes to take on lease the propination rights of both estates. He offers 3,000 Rthl annually; but under 4,000 Rthl I will not let them go, and then only for 3 years. The propination rights of all the estates are valued at 2,700 Rthl, so here likewise 1,300 Rthl annually are gained; the rent he pays half-yearly in advance, and indeed

soon now, which would then amount to a capital of 12,000 Rthl and would come in by Easter. If matters succeed with the Oleśnica people, 11,000 Rthl more will be added shortly. I have instructed Titz to buy out the old peasants in Swincin. There are 13 of them, each holding 2 1/3 Hufe; if he can dispose of the fellows with 2,000 Rthl, then I shall take up money here, pay them out at once, and sell the already built-up holdings for about 1,600 Rthl; in this way again some 9,000 Rthl in cash would be gained, and here too ready money may sooner be hoped for than from the old subjects.

With Honrichs things look bad — the fellow does not pay — He says the contract states that Your Serene Highness must apply for the concession on his behalf. But it does not state that Your Highness guaranteed to procure it for him. I shall write to the Department on that account and see to it that it is refused — then the contract must be rescinded quickly. As soon as this is done, it will be bought by that same Meierowitz who at first was so eager to buy it but was turned away by Glenck. Meierowitz gives 13,000 in ready money and a thousand rthl canon annually. In this way Your Serene Highness would profit 10,000 Rthl on the estate. A wretched 100 ducats have deprived Your Serene Highness of this profit and cast you into vexation. Perhaps God will grant that I may redress it. Grimm too wishes to buy the estate of Witów in the name of his son-in-law; but he offers no more than

2,000 Rthl, which he promises to pay out at once in cash — with that, to be sure, only a clear 4,000 Rthl would be saved against the present wretched sale — I therefore refuse Grimm nothing as yet, so that he may help me quickly to get Honrichs out — afterwards I shall examine and keep what is best. May Your Serene Highness be pleased only to command Glenck that he absolutely procure without delay the points of agreement concluded by von Rochlitz, together with the Grimm supplement and the power of attorney given to Rochlitz for that purpose, so that action may quickly be taken against Honrichs. Szczucki and Czizewski must [uncertain: Gemein] today sue as the warrantors in the Przespolewski matter, for these fellows have taken the money to themselves under the Polish Tribunal's decree and by receipt — they have had the use of it these 18 years; they must either hand it out at once, or else set Your Serene Highness ex nexu. It is infamous of such a scoundrel that he lets the matter lie so long until one has the mounted constable on one's neck. It would be necessary that one sat here always and thrust such [uncertain: Massette] into his ribs, so that he does not lie idle and in the end let himself be quite outflanked — With the old and the young Lichnowski I have everything in the clear; the latter has much respect for me and runs after me like the billy-goat after the lump of salt. The old one begs imploringly for 1,390 Rthl — he writes that he is in the greatest distress — then he will wait as long as may be until he can be paid further. For that, counsel must now be found.

If Your Serene Highness has that much there, then send it to the old fellow soon; I will procure it — on my honour let it be assured — straight back again. The Chamber President here is a spiteful [uncertain: beast] and monstrously hungry — His only society is with the chamber cashier Deter, the latter's wife, and the councillor of war Zerboni — the last is his shadow and steers him as he pleases. These are bad prospects again — if only I could soon send into the fellow's house the wash-basin and the three busts by Kips, which however must be coated so as to look as though they were of bronze, then he would at once become very pliant. Let Your Serene Highness only see to it that I get these pieces here soon. In deepest reverence I remain, until death, Your Most Serene Highness's. Otocki also wishes further to take 20 to 30 Hufen of woodland, arable and meadow in hereditary lease, and to pay as the colonists do — many are applying again for plots, and when I [...] here with it, the same will be quickly disposed of. The bilious fever has seized me again; already I can scarcely drag my legs after me — the vexations are too many and various. most humble and faithful servant, von Triebenfeld

Kalisz, the 1st of March 1805

Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Lord!

From Berlin no resolution has yet been forthcoming; I do not know what I am to think of Amelang's diligence. Men are all cut from one last — only do not always stand behind them, or clear the way oneself, or [uncertain: ober füllt] the rapacious claws so, and they let everything go at their snail's pace. If the review is made difficult for me by the Finance Department, then I shall have the district administrator review, attest and guarantee the valuations; that is indeed more than is demanded. It therefore comes down solely to this, that I be given a decision from Berlin.

The chicaneries over the review of the valuations are entirely new and arise solely from Prince George's and General Kalckreuth's impetuous conduct — neither Amelang nor still less I knew anything of it in Berlin; the [uncertain: Zand] was solely with Minister von Voss, by whom all the orders were swiftly given, and since the matter was not dealt with in collegial session, no one could know anything of it. [uncertain: Unfuhr] this pretty ordinance first in Wrocław from young Count Kalckreuth. Meanwhile so much [uncertain: Ehe] has been set aside that here too a way out must be found.

NB Amelang has himself given notice to the Jew [uncertain: Itzig] on the 18,000 Rthl which he has secured elsewhere. The Jew has believed that this was done only for appearance's sake, and thought to write to Your Serene Highness with a judicial notice — but it remains with my plan[s?] — the interest I have duly paid, and hold a receipt for it, so that Your Serene Highness's honour could not be [uncertain: compromised] —

Here everything so far goes as one would wish, and I hope to bring together a heavy lump of money. With Otocki I think to conclude today. He promises 10,000 Rthl within a short time, as well as 2,000 Rthl as the

half-yearly propination rent in advance. If I am rid of Honrichs, as I firmly hope, then Meierowitz will pay 20,000 Rthl in cash 8 days before Midsummer, and will lay down an annual canon of 500 Rthl in perpetuity.

What has happened with Swięcia, and whether my plan will succeed, I shall learn today from Nerlich.

For the purchase of the grounds which are [uncertain: me]hhn to be dismembered altogether, many persons have already come forward, and among them several noblemen, who wish to buy many Hufen and to pay in cash at once. Meanwhile I press only for the issuing of the consent, so that no impediment of any kind can be put in my way.

The Chamber had entrusted the investigation to the district administrator and prescribed the norm according to which Your Serene Highness may dismember; [illegible] this has been strictly complied with, everything set aside, and everything submitted to the Chamber, so that all chicaneries have been met and the ways to the throne made smooth, [uncertain: war] one wished to draw a new barrier across our nose, for I should lay before the King those dispositions which had been given, as well as all the contracts concluded in accordance with them, and the minutes, and should then there demand the concession with full right, without having to beg. The President v. G. is entirely of one mind with me in this. By the next post I shall send Your Serene Highness a copy of all these proceedings. With the Oleśnica fellows everything will be remedied very gradually.

There has long existed with the Chambers here (of which, however, as God lives, I have not known one jot) an edict, according to which

1. no peasant or non-noble may be granted a noble estate in hereditary lease without special royal consent

2. even to noble hereditary lessees there may not be handed over, or left to the hereditary lessees,

a. not the jurisdiction

b. not the [uncertain: Zad]

c. not the beer and brandy revenue, and

d. not the power to drive out the old subjects, or to disturb them in their livelihoods

Already under the 23rd of December 1803 the Chamber here made this known to the building councillor Glenck and to the district administrator v. Blomberg. More than punishable is it of the former, that he failed Your Serene Highness in this and permitted that a contract was nevertheless concluded with the Oleśnica fellows. But base is it of the latter, that he nevertheless wished to conclude a settlement between the 3 Oleśnica rogues and the old subjects, and to have Your Serene Highness guarantee the same. God, what sort of men are these, and in whose hands has Your Serene Highness been until now — By high disposition the whole of the Chamber files have been given to me; I am having all the fine pieces extracted, so that Your Serene Highness may for once be convinced

Now I must hold firmly and purely to the performance of the contract not now kept by the Oleśnica people, so that these scoundrels do not get through with any counter-claim, for otherwise we should have to fear a lawsuit of years' duration. More than devilish it is that Glenck said not a word of the two Chamber dispositions or resolutions of the 23rd of December 1803 and the 24th of January 1804, and allowed a contract of the 22nd of February 1804 to be concluded out of them, which runs bolt straight against the edicts and rescripts of the Chamber that had been made known to Glenck. I now count upon Schenck's good will and adroitness, which I had already called upon beforehand.

From Dombrowski I learn just now that the Prusimski compromise stands in the Kowal archive, and that the receipts are also inquired into there, that Prusimski has paid. The proceedings run to some seventy sheets; I have asked Dombrowski to have them extracted with haste, then one will indeed get on the track of the matter, for [if] the recesses and actual resignations of Brzyce had also been stolen out of the archives, those persons would yet be able to demand nothing, but would rather have to pay out, since we do not have Brzyce. [uncertain: im] Ribbeck and Floricke Your Serene Highness need not trouble yourself, for these dogs I shall chastise jointly with Lichnowski. If only my health were not so shattered that I could [uncertain: gagen] about in all places, then everything should go more briskly; as it is, I must too often keep to my room in bed, there I lack all care, and the constant vexation wears me quite away — Meanwhile I remain, until death,

Your Serene Highness's

most faithful servant

von Triebenfeld

Kalisz, the 4th of March 1805.

The wash-stand has given very much pleasure — the bust of bronze, however, I am bringing back — the friend wishes only three to 4 large ones of plaster, and those coated so as though it were bronze. Echtler has perhaps such in stock. Might I have them here by the next post?

Between the Royal Councillor of War and Forests and also general attorney of His Most Serene Highness the reigning Prince and Lord of Hohenlohe, Peter Friederich August von Triebenfeld, and Franz Meierowitz, the following heads of agreement have been negotiated and drawn up.

§. 1. Von Triebenfeld undertakes, as general mandatary of the Prince of Hohenlohe, to make over to Meierowitz, in hereditary and absolute ownership, the estate of Witów situated in the Warta district, with all residents and all appurtenances, taverns, lands, the village mayor's holding, waters, buildings and inventory, with all rights and usufructs, by whatever name they may be called, nothing thereof excepted, just as the same was purchased from the widowed Colonel von Schliesen; as soon as the sale with Honrichs, who is neither capable of possession nor still less solvent, has been annulled, for which purpose what is required has already been set in train before the competent authority.

§. 2. The sale is made as a whole, and at the conclusion of the contract no further warranty is given by the seller

is given.

§. 3. Meierowitz pays on St George's Day, that is to say the 23rd of April of this year, for the above-named estate a cash purchase price of twenty thousand Reichsthaler in Courant, namely on St George's Day, that is to say the 23rd of April of this year, eight thousand Reichsthaler, and on the coming Midsummer of this year twelve thousand Reichsthaler.

§. 4. Besides this purchase money stipulated and fixed in § 3, the purchaser Meierowitz pays to the Serene Highness of the seller, or wherever His Highness shall direct, yearly and indeed for all time a canon of five hundred Rthl in Courant.

§. 5. This canon is paid in half-yearly instalments post numerando by the purchaser, on pain of the coercive measures laid down in the territorial law.

§. 6. Should, however, the purchaser be minded, and find it convenient to his interest, to pay ten thousand Rthl of capital in place of the canon of five hundred Rthl fixed in § 4, in order to rid himself of this burden of debt - which as a purchase residue that cannot be called in is to be entered upon this estate of Witów as a first mortgage - then this is conceded on

the seller's part; only, if the purchaser wishes to redeem the canon by payment of the ten thousand Rthl, six months' notice must first be given.

§. 7. Although it is laid down in § 3 that Meierowitz will pay eight thousand Reichsthaler on the 23rd of April of this year and twelve thousand Reichsthaler on Midsummer of this year, it is further agreed here that, in case the Colonel von Schliesen's widow should wish to let the six thousand Reichsthaler still coming to her according to the mortgage book stand on further, His Serene Highness will allow this to happen and will, with the canon of five hundred thalers to be paid yearly, stand behind and grant the priority to the Colonel von Schliefen's widow.

§. 8. The eight thousand thalers mentioned in § 3, however, must be paid promptly on the 23rd of April of this year, to which the purchaser most earnestly binds himself.

§. 9. The drawing up and execution of a judicial contract over the estate of Witów shall take place as soon as the purchase with Honrichs has been annulled. The complete taking-over from Honrichs, however, and the delivery to the purchaser, cannot, however the matter may go, take place earlier than Midsummer of this year, because otherwise, with

the payments of interest, many entanglements might arise.

§. 10. Since the purchaser cannot at present establish his capacity to possess noble estates, the seller undertakes to contribute everything, as soon as the purchase with Honrichs is annulled, towards obtaining the concession to possess the estate of Witów, and to intercede on that account with His Majesty the King himself. All the costs of procuring the concession, however, the purchaser bears alone.

§. 11. All the costs occurring in purchases of this kind, by whatever name they may be called, both parties bear by halves.

§. 12. Both parties bind themselves to hold fast to these heads of agreement, renouncing all objections by whatever name.

Done at Kalisz, the 9th of March 1805. Peter Friedrich August von Triebenfeld. Franz Meierowitz. Friedrich Willhelm Eger as witness. Bezuer[uncertain: Bezuer] qua testis.

Right Honourable Sir, Highly Honoured Sir, Councillor of War and Forests! In accordance with the command of His Serene Highness the Prince, I rode last Saturday to Your Right Honourable's hereditary estate Świniary, in order to speak there with the district administrator Käufer and the forester bezold. The former I did not find there, for he had ridden early to Wrocław, and had not yet returned from there. To the latter I set out the charge I had to lay upon him entirely in the manner in which it had been written to me by [text lost]; he did not appear taken aback by it, but rather enquired who might have placed him in an unfavourable light with His Serene Highness, whereupon I said to him that I did not know this myself, and that I could only admonish him to the strictest probity and attentiveness in his service, since he saw that with a contrary manner of proceeding one was never secure, and that such conduct would one day be severely punished. He assured [uncertain: me]

that he exerted all his powers for the lordship's interest, and was not in a position to do more. I then rode back, and sought out the district administrator here, whom I did indeed find, and who answered me to approximately the same effect, only with the addition that he had the best testimonials from the most trustworthy [illegible], and that his good name was worth much to him, which in his present situation he certainly did not deserve to lose. Of this he would give proofs, and he could look forward calmly to an investigation of his actions. Your Right Honourable, I report all this likewise upon His Serene Highness's command, and permit myself only to add further that the crates go off today by the carriage post. In the most perfect veneration:

Your Right Honourable's

humble and obedient servant

A. Hahn

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Since yesterday I have been here at Trąbczyn, in order to press forward the dismemberment business with zeal. A great many people are already here, but as many more are still expected, I have accordingly postponed the principal hearing until next Monday, when I certainly intend to conclude the contracts for all the plots. President v. Goldbeck is now [uncertain: münt] himself noble and upright — He has written to Minister Voss for eight days' leave, in order to go to Wrocław and be able to arrange his household affairs; and on that occasion he says to Mr v. Voss: With regard to the district councillor's minutes submitted to Your Excellency concerning the dismemberment business of the Prince of Hohenlohe, I must yet most humbly observe that the matter has already advanced too far and could not be undone. Upon [uncertain: üherer] examination I have found that the Chamber has already consented to the dismemberment and has issued to the district councillor v. Blomberg the principles pertaining thereto under the 2nd of September of last year. Both in this and in the latter report the departmental councillor, the councillor of war zur Höllen,

has incurred unpardonable errors and compromised the collegium; whereas the princely manorial lordship (Dominium) has conducted itself better and done more than was required by the Chamber at that time, so that only in a few instances has there been action contrary to the norm.

In the name of the collegium I beg Your pardon, but at the same time I pledge that, if You will be pleased to grant the consent to the dismemberment of the princely estates, the gross errors of the departmental councillor shall be rectified so far as possible, etc. etc. etc.

That is indeed all that an honest man can do, and with his approval I am now to proceed briskly and dismember everything at once; for even if Mr v. Voss should wish to raise [uncertain: querden], the Chamber must keep its word and press for the consent. This role has been played masterfully through all the proceedings. With the Oleśnica men I think I shall soon be finished, for today [uncertain: Mona] Kunkel was fetched away by the mounted district constable and, through the mediation of [uncertain: Schencis], put into custody for a considerable time. Now it will be easy play with the 3 lads.

On account of Szetlewek I shall have a warm day of it tomorrow; God grant success, as in other cases.

Today the Winnicki heirs have again brought suit and demand a further 1,300 Rthl. of outstanding surveying costs. It is truly dreadful how things have been carried on here: the revenues have always been consumed and not a soul has been paid.

By this carriage may Your Serene Highness be pleased to have the 6 tables and 30 fruit trees conveyed to the President. I have instructed the man to be sure to say that it all [uncertain: comes] from me — For the rest, may God the All-Good only grant that Amelang does good business, for then all wishes are attained. In deepest reverence I remain, until death, Your Most Serene Highness's faithful and most humble and obedient servant von Triebenfeld

Trąbczyn, the 28th of March 1805.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Lord!

The snow, lying a foot deep here, hinders all my operations; I must sit here to no purpose, without being able to do anything. The contracts with the old peasants and the securing of the dues I have these days concluded before the court, and have thereby secured to Your Serene Highness a considerable revenue for all time. I am now negotiating over Szetlewek and the propination rights with von Otocki, for old Radzinski changes his mind every moment and would gladly drag the matter out so as to be able to cheat in the end. From Berlin I have good news concerning the loan; Amelang promises to bring everything about, only I am not to hurry him. The Department still urgently requires the refusal of Minister

von Voss and of the Chamber concerning the revision of the assessments. This I shall send on by the first post to Amelang, and I hope for the best. Concerning the dismemberment, Kleur has stated that if the grounds were not sold as at Pszczew [...] for ready money but for a proportionate rent, the consent should not [uncertain: arise/fail].

The latter has for the most part been done, and the consent will assuredly follow shortly, since Mr von Goldbeck has written so handsomely. Meanwhile I have sent Amelang with all speed a description of the whole matter, so that he may demonstrate everything thoroughly to Mr von Klewitz and show him that the revenues of these estates are not being sold, but rather are by the dismemberment increased fourfold and set on a footing for all time. More than galling it is for me, however, that amid so many labours I must still do battle against a pack of villains; and were my attachment to Your Serene Highness not boundless, I should long since have grown weary in my zeal.

Mr Glenck here makes merry over my dealings, makes them ridiculous before the world, and is at pains to thwart everything. He has now made common cause with Wollenhaupt, engaged him as his mandatary, and promised him all the kingdoms of the world. The three Oleśnica lads and a certain Meyer are likewise in this plot, and when purchasers come, all these scoundrels take pains to talk the people out of it. Altogether Glenck's conduct is [uncertain: haab] and vindictive, and it is all one to him whether he helps to cheat Your Serene Highness of several thousand Rthl, so long as he attains his purpose and, with the plot, hinders everything. All is in the greatest confusion, and no one can find either beginning or end — thus, for example, the

Wieniec heirs have now again sued for 1,300 Rthl of surveying costs.

Chwalowski demands 850 Rthl.

Sprengel, what Mr Glenck now certifies, 61 Rthl. Wollenhaupt 800 Rthl.

[uncertain: total] is 3,011 Rthl.

These people have already received large sums, and notwithstanding that, there is nothing substantial on hand from Glenck, nor any survey register; rather everything must be surveyed and allotted anew. In the Wieniec matter, however, nothing will come of it, for I know the curator; Chwalowski will have to content himself with the half; Sprengel must have his money, since Glenck has certified to him the claim of 61 Rthl. for his present exertions. With Wollenhaupt, however, it will look foolish. The fellow demands, as said above, 800 Rthl. I proved to him that he has worked elsewhere these 2 years and left Your Serene Highness's works quite untouched, whereby 600 Rthl. fell away.

Further, that for 4 years he had appropriated to himself 5 Hufen of land and used them all; this amounts yearly to 150 Rthl, consequently for 4 years 600 Rthl, which makes 1,200 Rthl.

He must therefore still hand back 400 Rthl.

To this Wollenhaupt replies that the building councillor Glenck had granted him leave to undertake works outside, wherever he knew of them and was able, for it would indeed be an honour to the Prince if his people were sought after.

With regard to the 5 Hufen he made use of, the same man says likewise that

Mr Glenck had given him leave to use them freely and to draw the revenues of Mariantów / that is, rent from the inhabitants / and everything.

The dwelling, too, the fellow will not vacate, for he says that both Mr Glenck and also Your Serene Highness had assured him the dwelling for so long as until he should be otherwise provided for. Schenck is hanging his lip over this, since he cannot move in, and will probably give up his engagement and the justiciary's office — I must now cajole this fellow too as far as possible — but if he grows too defiant, he may go to the devil, [text lost] now I have pretty well [uncertain: worked my way through], and for that post we shall find a hundred for one — but it is enough to drive one mad, to have to struggle about with all these lads amid works already beyond surveying, and to keep the rogues always in eye so that they do not do too much damage — Schenck insists absolutely on 4 [uncertain: Herren] of land and on the liberty to choose an actuary himself. I shall make oral report to Your Serene Highness upon it.

With boundless fidelity I remain, until death,

Your Serene Highness's

humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Trąbczyn, the 31st of March 1805

The old subjects of Swięcia I have bought out for a trifle, and have just now concluded a contract with other people for all 28 Hufen; they give 400 Rthl in cash per Hufe and 15 Rthl yearly in interest, bear all burdens like the others, pay 10 per cent transfer fee (Laudemium), and pay on St George's Day a sum suited to the matter. Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Lord!

The building councillor Glenck has assured the criminal-court councillor Grimm that the punctation concluded between Rochlitz and Honrichs concerning Witów, together with the beginning, around the power of attorney given to Rochlitz, lies in the Trąbczyn archive, of which I am said to have taken the key into my keeping.

I at once gave the old Titz and the justice-burgomaster Schenck the commission to look through all the papers present there, to see whether the mentioned punctation and power of attorney were really to be found in that archive. Unhappily, however, not a syllable of these papers has been discovered, and for that reason I cannot move a step forward with this affair, so finely set in train — Let Your Serene Highness have but the one grace of commanding Glenck that he absolutely and with the utmost dispatch procure these pieces from his Rochlitz — for otherwise you, most gracious Lord, risk losing for ever the advantage gained of 14,000 Rthl, and moreover, since Honrichs pays neither capital nor interest, you might have much vexation with Weigel and the Schleifen.

From Amelang I have letters today — he writes that I should only have the proper justification given to the valuations, and then everything would fall into place

A good general, he says, always thinks of a fortunate retreat, and more of the like. Although the windbag says nothing more substantial, I nevertheless believe that people will be content with the district councillor's review, his attestation and his guarantee; for this was my own proposal, in order to lay it upon those men's hearts — So I must now drain the cup of suffering and do the business with the wretched Blomberg. But the base fellow will not touch a pen unless I pay him 1,000 Rthl in advance — for the reports he has submitted, and for his minutes at the dismemberment plan, I have already had to pay him 900 Rthl in cash, and if everything is to come out clean, then I must find means and fill the fellow's [uncertain: gullet]. The cashier Deter here is so good as to advance me the money. Next Monday I go with a councillor from the Chamber to Trąbczyn; he reviews the locality according to the dismemberment plans submitted by the district councillor, and on the strength of these I obtain the concession without having to approach the King.

If only everything succeeds, as it now has the appearance of doing, then we gain

1. the surplus last reported from Oleśnica, Szetlewek, Witów etc. of 50,000 Rthl.

2. through the dismemberment, in cash, 200,000 Rthl.

3. the loan still to be hoped for, some 100,000 Rthl, making 350,000 Rthl.

With this modest little sum many a bear may yet be redeemed, and, as I reckon,

everything be [uncertain: smoothed over]. To be sure, I shall have many a sleepless night yet and many an hour full of care before I can reach the goal; meanwhile, if my health in any way permits it, I shall labour on untiringly until I have attained the goal.

As to Szetlewek, I would conclude everything this very week, and thereby clear a great stone of stumbling out of the way. With Oleśnica everything is set in train, and I hope to be finished with the matter very quickly and to be able to secure for Your Serene Highness the profit last reported to him.

For the propination rights I have many tenants; I shall choose the one who offers most, and press for the greatest possible security. According to the dismemberment plan submitted by the district councillor, 8 new villages are to be established — May Your Serene Highness deign to send me the names for them by this messenger, for I must submit this to the Chamber. Between the Royal Councillor of War and Forests von Triebenfeld, general attorney of His Most Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, and the hereditary leaseholders subscribed at the end, the following heads of agreement were this day arranged and concluded, subject to the approval of His Serene Highness.

1. His Most Serene Highness, through his general attorney, makes over to the subscribed hereditary leaseholders, out of the grounds belonging to his estates of Trąbczyn, Łazy, Osiny, Neudorff and Przybysław, consisting of fields, meadows and woods etc., the superficial content of 270 Hufen, say two hundred and seventy Hufen Magdeburg measure, the Hufe reckoned at thirty Morgen and the Morgen at 180 rods.

2. As purchase money the hereditary leaseholders named below shall pay to His Serene Highness, for each Magdeburg Hufe, 300 Rthl, say three hundred Reichsthaler Royal Courant.

3. Each hereditary leaseholder, and his successors in possession, shall pay yearly for each Magdeburg Hufe a clear money rent of 15 Rthl, say fifteen Reichsthaler in Courant, to the manorial treasury, and that in half-yearly instalments at Midsummer and Christmas, each time seven before twelve good Groschen.

4. The hereditary leaseholders or takers are at liberty to make over these acquired Hufen in several separate parts to others, and to come to such agreement with these new takers, to their own advantage, as best they can.

5. It is however expressly laid down that when the hereditary leaseholders wish to make over parcels to other takers or successors, this shall at once be notified to the lordship, so that in regard to arrears and to debts charged upon the grounds no error may arise and everything may be kept in good order. Every sale concluded without the lordship's prior knowledge shall be held wholly invalid and as not concluded at all.

6. Both the present hereditary leaseholders and the future takers must effect their establishments, for now and for the future, at their own cost, and they shall receive for this neither remission of the hereditary rent nor any other building assistance; they may however employ for this purpose the timber standing upon the Hufen received in hereditary lease, which belongs to them in property, all of it and without any exception.

7. These Hufen taken in hereditary lease shall be measured out to the hereditary leaseholders forthwith and delivered into their possession.

8. Upon the arable land and meadows the rents shall be duly paid even in this current year; upon the woodland, however, and upon the other grounds, four free years are allowed, by the end of which time each taker must have cleared and brought under cultivation the woodland grounds purchased by him, so that after the lapse of the four free years the rents upon these grounds must likewise be paid at fifteen thaler per Hufe, and discharged to the manorial treasury in half-yearly instalments of 7 Rthl 12 Groschen.

9. Besides the yearly hereditary rents, the hereditary leaseholders undertake, for themselves and their descendants, to render all royal and other dues charged upon these estates, by whatever name they may be called, and such shall be laid upon the Hufen and duly apportioned.

10. Since all the grounds are dismembered and let out against rents, the hereditary leaseholders may make no claim to any rights of pasture or of timber, but must graze their cattle upon their own grounds alone, and must seek to grow and conserve their own timber.

11. The hereditary takers are granted the liberty to set up a brick-kiln upon their grounds and to burn for themselves the bricks needed for the first building, without anything having to be paid for this to the ground lordship.

12. The hereditary leaseholders must divide the two hundred and seventy Hufen Magdeburg they have taken among themselves

in the best possible manner themselves, without the ground lordship taking the least part therein, since it is bound only to allot to them the total of the Hufen; the ground lordship does however undertake to bear the whole costs of this allotment.

13. The present hereditary leaseholders, as also the other takers, are at liberty to alienate their holdings to others in any manner they please; but upon every change of possession, whether by sale or by exchange, the tenth Groschen of the purchase money or of the exchange sum must be paid down to the ground lordship as a transfer fee (Laudemium), and the lordship holds itself always to the new taker, whose business it remains not to pay out the purchase money to the seller until the Laudemium has been settled.

14. No redemption of the hereditary rent shall take place; the fifteen Reichsthaler hereditary rent per Hufe once fixed remain irredeemable for everlasting times. 15. The hereditary leaseholders, their subsequent purchasers and their descendants remain for ever entirely free of all hereditary subjection, and may not render the ground lordship the least manorial service, nor deliver any produce in kind; they are however without exception subject for ever to the jurisdiction of the manorial lordship (Dominium).

16. Besides the Hufen upon which they pay rent, there shall be allotted to the newly established communities, once and for all, namely

1. for the schoolmaster 6 Morgen

2. for the village mayor 6 Morgen

3. for the church [uncertain: Hust] 1 Morgen; accordingly for each new village which shall keep a village mayor and a schoolmaster thirteen Morgen Magdeburg, free of charge and free of rent.

17. The hereditary leaseholders are bound to lay out and build the new villages according to regulation in two even lines.

18. Their drink, in beer and brandy, the hereditary leaseholders and their successors in possession must always take from the manorial brew- and brandy-house or tavern, and for every quart of brandy brought in from outside estates they shall pay down to the ground lordship a penalty of one Reichsthaler, and for every barrel of beer five Reichsthaler.

19. The hereditary leaseholders renounce, for themselves and their successors, any and every remission in cases of misfortune, by whatever name these may be called, and no compensation or remission of the hereditary rent can ever accrue to them.

20. The costs of the contract, of its confirmation and of the official copy, the hereditary leaseholders undertake to settle.

21. So long as the hereditary leaseholders and their successors in possession shall fulfil these obligations described above, they shall be protected by the ground lordship in their rights in every quarter, and defended and held harmless against every man's real claims. Should they however remain in arrears with the yearly hereditary canon for longer than two years, they shall thereupon forfeit this hereditary lease, and the ground lordship is entitled to call it in without contradiction and to let it out otherwise.

22. For the correct and prompt payment of the purchase money and of the fixed hereditary rents the hereditary leaseholders and the future takers, as also their successors in possession, are liable in perpetuity, one for all and all for one, that is to say jointly and severally.

Both parties promise to keep the foregoing hereditary-lease contract firmly and inviolably, and renounce all legal evasions available against it, particularly the objection of an injury suffered above or below the half, and have signed themselves below in their own hands. §. I. His Most Serene Highness grants, namely, from the demesne farm Drzewce

18 Hufen, in words eighteen Hufen, of clear arable land, and near Wrąbczyn

2 Hufen, in words two Hufen, of Magdeburg meadows, together therefore 20 Hufen, in words twenty Hufen Magdeburg measure, to the building inspector Johann Wilhelm

Wollenhaupt, from now on for perpetual times in hereditary quit-rent, and there are at the same time herewith also

1. the dwelling house and

2. the brewhouse in Drzewce transferred to him in property.

The hereditary lessee binds himself, for these twenty Hufen acquired, from Midsummer of this year onward, to a perpetual hereditary quit-rent, which may never be raised or reduced, per Hufe Magdeburg measure of 15 Rthl, in words fifteen Reichsthaler, thus for 20 Hufen 300 Rthl, in words three hundred Reichsthaler, in Courant cash, and that yearly in two

instalments, at Christmas and at Midsummer, each time with

By the Grace of God, Friedrich Wilhelm, King of Prussia. Our friendship, royal grace and good will beforehand, High-born Prince, particularly dear Friend and dear Faithful Subject! In pursuance of the notification issued on the 5th of February of this year upon Your Lordship's petition submitted on the 31st of December of last year for permission to let out the lordship of Pszczew on lease to the burgesses there and the remaining rural residents, We hereby give Your Lordship, with the return of the hereditary-lease contract submitted, upon the ground of the rescript of Our South Prussian Finance Department of the 15th of last month issued to Our Chamber in conformity with a Most High Cabinet Resolution of the 11th of last month, the following decision: that the hereditary letting in question has been found wholly inadmissible, and that the consent sought thereto cannot be granted to Your Lordship; for, firstly, if this consent had not been refused Your Lordship, several landed lordships would venture similar applications, and thereby the possessions of the nobility, which is so numerous in this province and upon whose conservation regard must be had, would be diminished, and the opportunities for the acquisition of estates would be taken from it. Even if, however, this considerable obstacle did not already stand in the way of Your Lordship's design, the aforementioned letting could not be approved

because, secondly, the appropriate management of the Pszczew forest — which, since this forest is the only considerable one in that district, merits every regard — could not take place, inasmuch as, if free use of it were left to the hereditary lessees, even the best supervision could not wholly prevent its devastation; thirdly, there is also this circumstance to be weighed, that if Your Lordship's application were deferred to, the lands to be taken in hereditary lease by the residents could not even be managed in an orderly fashion, since every resident, and likewise every burgess of the town of Pszczew, possesses as much land as he requires for a proper husbandry; and moreover, as regards the burgesses, care is to be taken that they apply themselves rather to the pursuit of urban trades than to that of agriculture, most of the residents being besides too lacking in means to be able to raise the sums of money required for the management. In which We remain well disposed toward Your Lordship with friendship, royal grace and good will.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Lord!

Soon I shall have to succumb after all to the [uncertain: nameless] intrigues of the finance department; that a minister should raise as many difficulties as Minister von Voss does in the business of dismemberment is unheard of. Several landed proprietors who dismembered as much as two years ago must restore everything again to the status quo, and are thereby brought to the beggar's staff. Here he has had everything inhibited, and to that end has ordered the Chamber to send a commission which is to examine whether everything has already been dismembered — whether it may not be possible to thwart this matter; in particular it is now to inquire precisely whether the principles have in any way been acted against; whether all the money has not been drawn off, and the public burdens (onera publica) therefore, as at Pszczew, were no longer covered.

On the presumption that this last would certainly be the case, everything was to be inhibited forthwith, and in that event the strictest measures taken. The commission departed today; I have indeed prevailed,

but money and health have been spent on it. I have meanwhile demonstrated that I have done nothing without the foreknowledge of the provincial authority,

2. that I have acted strictly in accordance with the prescription,

3. that everything is sold, so that without a complete derangement of the whole no annulment or reversal of the dismemberment could take place.

4. that the most real revenues of the manorial lordship (Dominium) would now amount to 8 times as much as the revenues hitherto, whereby the public burdens (onera publica) would be covered tenfold.

5. That His Serene Highness the Prince applied the entry moneys to nothing else than to the discharge of the debts which encumber the estates, in order to make the estates clear, and that

6. These estates were to remain an entailed estate of the princely family, which last His Majesty had already most graciously sanctioned himself.

The commission has found all this substantiated, and has withdrawn the inhibition, the more so since with the old peasant too everything has already been concluded judicially, and since here as well it was not possible even for envy to find matter for founding new intrigues — The clear annual revenues acknowledged by the commission are 31,000 Rthl. It had to determine this precisely in order to cover the public burdens (onera publica). This the Chamber will now confirm, and the

finance department will grant us the concession for it — As soon as I receive this instrument, neither assessment nor anything further is needed, but one can quickly obtain 3 to 400,000 Rthl upon it at any treasury, and then all distress is at an end.

The 180,850 Rthl still to come in can then be taken for the extinction of all the household and other debts. The only fatal thing is merely the accursed procrastination, for in the first moment all the purchasers ran off once that cursed inhibition became known, and I must now strike very gentle notes so that I may entice the people back again. Enough: Your Serene Highness will come happily through with the dismemberment, and will in a few years be [uncertain: free of the village mayor's dues] here — for if for several years together you assign the revenues to the absorption of the debts of the estates here, then in 9 years the estates will be quite clear, will yield you a revenue of 40/m Rthl, and you will besides draw out of the estates, little by little, a capital of 220,000 Rthl — this I believe I can now assure Your Serene Highness firmly and solemnly. But now, most gracious Lord, I am worn out — I have laboured with truly glowing zeal, and every man who knows the matter marvels at this thing brought so far. I cannot hold out here any longer — both my health and my fortune are being spent on it, and I shall leave beggars behind me — Also for some time past one misfortune after another has struck

Thus in the last couple of months I have lost 2 lawsuits which cost me some 6,000 Rthl.

In another I am held in contumacy, and shall have trouble to redress the same and to save a further 6,000 Rthl. Today I receive the news that the hail has beaten down everything on my Świniary estates; there I shall again have some 5,000 Rthl of damage. At Konotop, as I hear this very moment, a tenant has become insolvent; there I suffer a further 2,500 Rthl of loss — in a short time this comes to 19,500 Rthl. It is as though all blessing had departed from there and had followed me hither. Now I must go back to save what is there, for otherwise I go to ruin.

I tremble, to be sure, when I go away from here and let the guiding thread out of my hands, that everything will come to a standstill again — but necessity presses me — I must hasten for some time to Świniary and Konotop, for otherwise I risk a new and still greater loss.

Since everything here is understood, I shall instruct Schenck and a few more people to collect in the moneys. But I cannot vouch for it whether the people will hold to the execution of my dispositions with the same zeal, because every brute would far too gladly see the affairs continue in confusion through a whole generation, as has otherwise happened. In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Serene Highness's

humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Trąbczyn, the 29th of July 1805.

Right Honourable Sir, Highly Honoured Sir Councillor of War and Forests! To Your Right Honourable I hereby most obediently report that yesterday afternoon at 6 o'clock the news arrived by express courier of the decease of the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Neuenstein, Serene Highness. his pious and praiseworthy life. Attempts were made on the part of the Princes of Langenburg and Kirchberg to exercise geheliche measures, which rest upon a certain misunderstood partition treaty, but from the Aufaenger of the Ingelfingen side manly resistance was offered, the troops were turned back, and the Ingelfingen patents of the taking of possession—

were posted up; also, where on the opposing side they let themselves beygehen — which to post up, these were taken down again and Ingelfingen ones put up in their place.
