The Princely Hohenlohe Patrimonial Court hereby makes known that before it, between His Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, through his general mandatory the Councillor of War and Forests von Triebenfeld, as lessor on the one part, and Mr Maciej von Niedźwiecki as lessee on the other part, the following lease contract concerning the estate of Kopojno has been declared ad Protocollum, which reads word for word as follows: Actum Trąbczyn, the 17th of August 1805. Before the undersigned justiciary of this place there appeared in person, 1st, the Councillor of War and Forests von Triebenfeld as the known general authorised representative of His Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, hereditary lord and lord of the court of this place, and

2nd, the local holder of the propination rights lease, Mr Maciej von Niedźwiecki.

The appearing parties are personally known to the undersigned, and there exists no doubt as to their capacity validly to perform judicial acts. They declare freely and after due deliberation the following lease contract concluded between them, to be entered in the judicial protocol.

§ I. That is to say, the Councillor of War and Forests von Triebenfeld, by virtue of the power of attorney held from His Most Serene Highness, leases out the demesne farm of Kopojno, just as the same is now divided and arranged, together with the winter and summer sowing now standing, the fishery in the waters and in the Warthe stream, and all the remaining usufructs, yet with the exclusion of the brewery and distillery, as being separately leased, and without any livestock or field inventory, to Mr Maciej Niedźwiecki for

six consecutive years, namely from Midsummer Day of the present year 1805 until Midsummer Day 1811, for an annual rent of 1,500 Rthl, in writing one thousand five hundred Rthl Courant.

§ II. This rent money shall be paid annually in advance, namely each time on Midsummer Day, that is the 24th of June, in good Prussian convention money; and since the rent for the first year, amounting to 1,500 Rthl, in writing one thousand five hundred, [uncertain: not good] has already been paid in cash, receipt is hereby given for the due receipt thereof.

§ III. This lease is concluded as a whole without a valuation, and therefore no subsequent reckoning in respect of the yield takes place.

§ IV. The lessee must effect the tillage of the fields with his own draught teams

and there shall be made over to him, for hand-services only, the whole of the komorniks and cottagers present in Kopojno with their services, and these shall receive from the lessor, namely

a., each komornik, ten in number, four Morgen, and

b., each cottager, whose number is undetermined, two Morgen of Magdeburg measure, free of rent. As to the working, the lessee must come to terms with these people according to his own convenience.

§ V. Free grinding of the bread grain is likewise granted to the lessee at the mills at Tarzewo and Kopojno; the cash rent from these mills, on the other hand, as also from the rent-paying peasants in Kopojno, remains to the lessor.

§ VI. Besides the cash rent, the lessee assumes the settlement of all Royal dues in taxes,

forage deliveries and the like, as also the allowance due to the monastery of Ląd, without any compensation or abatement of the rent.

If in future these dues come to be apportioned over the entire surface area of the estates, then any resulting decrease shall accrue to the lessee's benefit.

§ VII. The lessee received for his own need 50 annually, in writing fifty cords of pine firewood, from the lordship's forest, which wood he must cart himself, and likewise have felled at his own cost, or else pay the felling-wage for it to the princely office. He also receives two cartloads of hard timber every year.

§ VIII. All dwelling and farm buildings and gardens situated in Kopojno the lessee receives for his use; he must however maintain the buildings in roof and frame at his own cost. The larger repairs, on the other hand, fall to the lessor,

as also all new buildings.

§ IX. Since the lessee for the present does not receive the fields with a determined sowing, the appearing parties have agreed between themselves that the lessee binds himself, at the expiry of the lease term, to leave behind the one field sown with winter grain, the second duly manured with summer grain, and the third field as fallow worked up in husbandmanlike fashion, without either party making any demands upon the other on account of surplus or deficient sowing. The fields shall be divided into three wholly equal parts.

§ X. This lease begins from Midsummer Day of this year and the lessee renounces all subsequent reckonings in respect of the usufructs of the various heads of husbandry hitherto foregone.

§ XI. The clearing of the field ditches and the upkeep of the bridges falls to the lessee; yet for the latter he shall receive the necessary timber free of charge, and the village people must render assistance in this.

§ XII. The lessee may make over the estate to another in sub-lease only with the foreknowledge and express consent of the lessor; in the contrary case such a sub-lease is invalid and the lessee is answerable to the lessor for all damage or detriment arising therefrom.

§ XIII. In the event of misfortunes occurring, such as fire from heaven, or arson by evil-disposed persons, total hail-strike and war, the lessee shall receive a remission such as is granted to the lessees on the Royal domains according to the principles of the Chamber.

Upon all other misfortunes, whether they arise from crop failure or in whatever manner it may be, the lessee expressly renounces claim; he also hereby binds himself expressly to make every indemnification which is caused by his own fault or that of his people.

§ XIV. The lessee must maintain the fields in good manured condition, and may not sell any straw or hay off the estate, unless he had the same absolutely in surplus.

§ XV. At the expiry of the years of lease no particular notice of termination is required from either the one side or the other; rather the lessee is bound to vacate at Midsummer Day 1811; yet there shall be allowed him the

vacating period customary in this region, up to 14 days after Midsummer Day; but he must see to the necessary carting-out himself.

§ XVI. The lessee shall have free pasture in that portion of grazing-ground and woodland which remains over for the manorial lordship (Dominium) and is not dismembered.

§ XVII. The costs of this contract and of the future re-delivery both parties shall bear by halves.

§ XVIII. For the fences the lessee shall receive the requisite brushwood, and the same shall be assigned to him upon his application. Both parties promise to hold firmly to this contract and, having been judicially instructed as to the consequences, renounce all legal subterfuges available against it, in particular the objection of an injury suffered above or below the half, of a cunning persuasion, of overhaste,

of seduction, fear, coercion, of matters otherwise agreed than written down, or not rightly understood. Most Serene and Most Mighty King, Most Gracious King and Lord! The reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Öhringen and Ingelfingen, as manorial lordship (Dominium) of the lordships of Trąbczyn and Zagórów, most obediently prays that the Government at Kalisz be most graciously commanded, in his suit against the so-called hereditary lessees Giese, Bagans and Gietzinger, to sequester his estate of Oleśnica.

Your Royal Majesty's Government at Kalisz compels me to lay a petition before Your Most High Self, of

whose lawfulness I am as entirely convinced as the damage is great and irreparable which is being inflicted merely by the hitherto refusal of the said government to grant my petition.

The matter has the following connexion, conformable to the truth and to the contents of the files.

On the 22nd of February of last year I concluded, with three persons of the common burgher estate, by the names of Giese, Bagans and Gietzinger, respecting the estate of Oleśnica belonging to my lordship of Trąbczyn and Zagórów situated in South Prussia, the hereditary lease contract appended here in copy (A), according to the contents of which /§. 4./ the hereditary lessees bound themselves to pay an entry money of 20,000 rthr. in two equal instalments of 10,000 Rthl:, and, besides the discharge of all sovereign dues and public burdens, /§. 7./ also an annual hereditary lease rent of 2,000. rthtr; likewise in two equal instalments; and at the same time acknowledged the condition that if the payments of the entry money should not follow in the manner appointed, the contract should be null and void, and that over and above a conventional penalty of 10,000. Rthl. should take place. The hereditary lessees were also indeed granted permission to sub-let the estate held in hereditary lease again in hereditary sub-lease and to dismember it, /§. 10./ yet I reserved to myself that the hereditary sub-lease contracts should not be concluded without my special consent, and that all entry monies of the hereditary sub-lessees should be paid to me directly,

in return for which I undertook to procure the requisite approbation of Your Royal Majesty's War and Domains Chamber to this contract.

Upon the ground of this contract the estate itself was now handed over to the said hereditary lessees naturaliter, though without any particular proceedings of delivery of possession, and the area of 3,338. Morgen 14. rods Magdeburg measure, which had previously been exactly surveyed and revised by three sworn surveyors, Winitzki, Chwalowski and Cabanis, was assigned to them. After they had in this manner been placed in the full natural possession, they sub-let in hereditary sub-lease and dismembered a great part of the estate to the sub-lessees named in the annexed specification (B), and out of these monies, already levied contrary to the contract and payable directly to myself, they paid me the first half of the entry money with 10,000 rthll:, and they also discharged successively the first year's lease rent. With the second half of the entry money, however, they remained in arrear, and in the second year they paid neither the hereditary lease rent nor the sovereign dues, which were thereupon levied from myself by execution by Your Royal Majesty's War and Domains Chamber to the amount of 431 Rthl;

17. Groschen 11. Pfennig and 17 Rthl. 21. Groschen. I also received from the said Chamber, upon my petition for the confirmation of the hereditary lease contract, the resolution that such could by no means take place, in conformity with the statutory provision published after the conclusion thereof in Your Royal Majesty's own most high

Cabinet Order of /: in Hoff and Mathies's juristic monthly, vol. II, p. 103. /. In this posture of the matter nothing else remained to me but to proceed by suit against the said hereditary lessees, and my then attorney, Criminal-court Councillor Mondro, thought it expedient to institute three separate suits on that account, in which, upon the ground of the clausula cassatoria contained in

§. 4., he moved for the annulment of the contract and demanded the current hereditary lease rent for two terms. In what posture these three suits at present stand, Your Royal Majesty will be pleased to see at large from the appended copy of my representation to the Government at Kalisz of the 12th of August of this year.

(C) Now while these suits pursue their course, the hereditary lessees have not only made use of all the revenues of the estate, but have also not ceased to alienate single parts of the same, and to collect the entry money coming in for them from the sub-lessees, as well as the current rent, without paying the least thing to me, and without so much as discharging the sovereign dues and onera publica. They have also fallen into gross and violent disputes with their sub-purchasers, whom they have deceived in manifold ways,

nay, they have even presumed to give themselves out publicly as hereditary lords of the estate of Oleśnica, and in the record (D) of the 6th of August to slander me in the most shameful manner, as though I caused them to be evicted arbitrarily and to be treated with violence, although the judicial attestation of the (E) 12th of August of this year proves that this calumnious allegation is an impudent and punishable lie. It could not be a matter of indifference to me that not only all the revenues of my considerable estate were withheld from me without any right whatever, and its appurtenances arbitrarily alienated, deteriorated and devastated; it must also have vexed me sensibly that I was moreover to bear all the current burdens and dues and to pay them out of my own means. This determined me to petition Your Royal Majesty's Government at Kalisz for the sequestration of this estate in two representations, which, together with the (F) (G) (H) resolutions received thereupon, I append in copy, and herewith once more solemnly assure that all the factual assertions contained in the submissions are conformable to the contents of the files.

I cannot conceive that those dismissive resolutions are conformable to the laws, because from them would follow the impossibility of restraining an insecure hereditary lessee who finds himself without any right whatever in the natural possession of an estate, and institutes prolix and vexatious suits against the proprietor, but pays nothing in rent and dues, from, during the

course of these suits, using the estate itself, alienating it, laying it waste, and inflicting irreparable damage on the proprietor. Such a means most assuredly exists in the form of process introduced by Your Royal Majesty with such infinite wisdom, and according to the opinion of all persons learned in the law, in every case where the possession and use of an immovable estate, or of a living movable thing, is in dispute, the mutual right of the parties must be secured by sequestration. The grounds which Your Royal Majesty's Government at Kalisz has adduced against this universally valid principle can convince me the less, as they already of themselves stand in contradiction with the principles of the legislature. For as concerns

I. the resolution of the 13th of August of this year, it is

a.) contrary to law in principle that sequestration is merely an executive and not also a means of security, since the General Law Code, Part I, Title

15. §. 103-105., Title 18. §. 344., Title 21. §. 140. and 244., expressly determines that sequestration shall be ordered in all cases where the possession, the detention, the administration and the use of an immovable or living movable thing is in dispute, and at the same time danger and insecurity for the contending parties is present; and consequently, under the like legal modalities, in the case of movable inanimate things, judicial deposit is

requisite.

As to b. and c., however, it remains an inward and irreconcilable contradiction when the government assumes that the opponents, upon the ground of an imperfect contract which is null and void ex clausula cassatoria, and has moreover been declared by the Chamber authority, by virtue of a special law, to be absolutely invalid, should nevertheless, and although no title of possession has been entered for them, and chiefly also no purchase money and no entry money has been paid by them out of their own means, be so far possessed as that they must be held in the legal sense to be settled, and on account of their settledness to be secure. Upon this I refer myself simply to the contents of my representation of the 12th of August of this year.

II. Equally insufficient are the grounds in the resolution of the

20th of August of this year. For

1.) it is an altogether incorrect exposition of §. 204., Title

21., Part I, of the General Law Code, when the reporting councillor assumes that sequestration according to this statutory provision could find application in respect of the arrears of hereditary rent only if such were acknowledged

by the hereditary lessee as undisputed. In such a case execution takes place, and sequestration may indeed also be ordered by way of execution, according to §. 116., Title 24., Part 1, of the General Court Ordinance. But also "for the security of the hereditary lessor" sequestration is, according to the clear determination of the law, to be ordered in via arresti, and it goes without saying that in that case only those general principles can be applied which obtain in cases of attachment generally; wherefore it is sufficient if the claims are only in some measure attested, grounds of the insecurity of the party attached are adduced, and securities are furnished by the party attaching.

2.) As incorrect as this interpretation of the law is in itself, just as contrary to the files is the assertion that no liquid arrear of hereditary rent exists. The opponents, in that suit which concerns the first arrear of the 1,000. Rthl., and which was instructed and decided before my patrimonial court, have unconditionally

admitted the correctness of this arrear; the matter has, but for a small error in the formalities of the citation, really been dealt with in an executive process, and in the first instance judgment was given against the opponents for payment of the arrears of hereditary lease rent of the 1,000. Rthl., because, as the ipsa verba of the sentence run: "they had simpliciter acknowledged their obligation to pay; their objections, however, being exceptiones ulterioris indaginis, belonged in part to the principal suit concerning the annulment of the hereditary lease contract, and in part must be referred ad separatum — ". The opponents were also expressly informed in the publication record of this sentence of the 2nd of March of this year that the appeal at once lodged by them against it had only effectum devolutivum, and that execution must nevertheless be ordered. In my most obedient judgment, execution upon these 1,000 Rthl., which I repeatedly moved for, ought therefore to have been ordered and carried out; but even if regard is to be had to the in themselves wholly immaterial errors in the formularies of the citations, and the matter is therefore to be considered as having been dealt with only in processu ordinario, still so much is beyond doubt certain, that by a condemna-

tory judgment, even if not yet in legal force, which is grounded upon an acknowledgment of the debt made simpliciter on the part of the defendant, the claim itself is at least so far sufficiently attested as the laws require in the case of a petition for attachment.

All the objections which the opponents have opposed to their obligation to pay, in the appellate stage of this suit and in the first instance of the second suit pending concerning the other arrear of hereditary rent, consist in the assertion that they had not received the contractual number of Morgen of the area of 3,338. Morgen 14. rods, and that the Chamber's consent had not been procured by me. Both exceptions are in themselves immaterial, and moreover false; for I have already shown the correctness of the area by attestations of the sworn surveyor who measured it, and have already remarked above that the Chamber's consent, repeatedly applied for by me, was refused

upon the ground of the more recent statutory ordinance in the Cabinet Order of the 10th of April of this year. In general all this belongs to the principal suit concerning the annulment of the contract. The hereditary rent is paid for the use of the estate and the collection of its continuing revenues /: General Law Code, Part

1., Title 21., §. 187. 190. /; the opponents are in possession and enjoyment of all the estate's revenues, and must therefore also pay the continuing canon until it is decided upon the nullity of the contract, or in the worst case at least deposit it. But even the deposit has not been made, although I have expressly had them called upon to do so, and it lies quite plainly at day that the opponents can as little pay as they will.

3.) The opponents are indeed highly insecure, and the alternative set up in the resolution is neither conformable to the files nor logically correct. aa, It is contrary to the files that the opponents had paid the first half of the entry monies with 10,000. Rthl. out of their own fortune, and that I am bound to repay them this sum if the hereditary lease contract were annulled. But I have already mentioned that this payment was discharged out of the

sum of 11,089 Rthl. 8. Groschen levied by them from their sub-purchasers contrary to the contract and payable directly to myself. All the contracts which the opponents concluded with the sub-purchasers, and upon which they levied those 11,089. Rthl. 8. Groschen, were concluded without my consent, expressly reserved to me in §. 10., and are for me so far not binding that I am not bound to acknowledge the payments made by the sub-purchasers to the opponents. If I chose to make use of this right, all the sub-purchasers, who for the most part have no other fortune than the entry money paid in, would in the most irresponsible manner lose what is theirs and be brought to the beggar's staff. This I would never allow, and I have already declared on the record that I reserve to myself to credit these 10,000. Rthl. 8 Groschen to the poor sub-purchasers so shamefully deceived by the opponents, pro rata of their payments, and to depart from the rigour of my right. Your Royal Majesty will certainly regard this declaration of mine as in the highest degree lawful, equitable and worthy of my person.

But if I thus credit these

10,000 Rthl. to the opponents' sub-purchasers, and thereby prevent their being fraudulently deprived of what is theirs, it is clear that I do not hold them as an object of security for the latter, and can never restore them to them. Moreover I have claimed these 10,000. Rthl. under

§. 5. of the hereditary lease contract as a forfeited conventional penalty, and this point too is litispendent in the principal suit.

bb, the second case of the alternative, that the contract should stand and be declared valid, is not conceivable at all, and is really a casus non dabilis, since on the one part the clausula cassatoria of §. 5. takes effect, because the opponents have not paid the second half of the entry money nor deposited it, and on the other part the Chamber's consent is refused, and according to the most recent statutory provisions must be refused.

cc, As concerns finally the unsettledness of the opponents, again assumed by the reporting councillor, this supposition rests quite evidently upon a manifest confusion of the legal conceptions of natural and civil possession, and

the counter-representation contained in my submission of the 12th of August has not been taken into consideration at all. I am utterly unable to see how anyone is implicitly placed in civil possession by delivery and the yielding up of natural possession; I do not comprehend how anyone for whom no title of possession is entered in the mortgage book, and who, because his contract remains void, can only be so entered, should be an estate possessor in the legal sense —; it remains inexplicable to me how I am supposed to have conceded civil possession to the opponents by having demanded of them the current hereditary lease rent for the enjoyment of the natural possession, until such time as the contract is annulled and the ejectment of the opponents realised —; and I absolutely do not understand how anyone can be held to be possessed, settled and secure who finds himself sine titulo et jure in the natural possession of an estate for which he has yet paid nothing at all out of his own means. Most Gracious King and Lord! Never would I trouble Your Most High Self with this prolix petition, in a

matter unhappily very confused, were I not quite properly compelled to it. I have absolutely no other purpose than to be secured against the manifest and wholly irreparable injuries of the opponents, who continue to alienate and lay waste my estate, while I must effect the discharge of all burdens and dues without receiving any income or revenue of the estate whatever. If there is another lawful means of securing myself than sequestration, I will gladly submit to it. But the jurists with whom I have conferred on the matter assure me that no other means exists, and therefore I must persist in my petition for sequestration. I desire nothing further than that the estate revenues which the sequestrator shall collect be paid ad depositum judiciale, and I have even offered to furnish security for the sequestrator proposed, or for another solid one. In my judgment all conceivable scruples are thereby entirely removed, and I must most humbly beg that the whole of the files be called in from the Government at Kalisz,

and that thereupon sequestration be graciously ordered, and its immediate realisation commanded to the government upon remission of the

files.

It is not unknown to me that ordinarily only a report is required in such cases as this; but I expressly beg for the calling in of the files, because a mere report would not turn out so complete, and would in no case so thoroughly demonstrate the perfect lawfulness of my petition for sequestration, as if — for which I most respectfully beg — Your Royal Majesty would be pleased to have the same laid before Your Most High Self in comparison with the court files.

The principal suit is being instructed at length; the taking of evidence on the spot and with the calling in of sworn experts will be hard to avoid, and it is only too certain that, since the matter has been introduced merely in processu ordinario, for at least two years yet there can be no thought of a judgment and of an

execution grounded upon it. So much the more must I be intent upon the hastening of my being secured, and I therefore hold myself convinced that I may look forward to a favourable resolution with that confidence and reverence with which I remain Your Royal Majesty's most humbly and most faithfully obedient

von Triebenfeld, as general plenipotentiary

Wrocław, the 18th of September 1805.

Since I know that Your Right Honourable takes an interest in news of my most gracious Lord, I take the liberty of conveying to you the assurance that His Serene Highness is almost entirely healed of the Bible in his foot, and is in other respects perfectly well; the foot is only a little swollen still, and causes no pain. We Friedrich Wilhelm, by the Grace of God King of Prussia, Margrave of Brandenburg, Arch-Chamberlain and Elector of the Holy Roman Empire; sovereign and supreme Duke of Silesia, sovereign Prince of Orange, Neuchâtel and Vallangin, as also of the County of Kłodzko, Duke of Magdeburg, Cleve, Berg, Szczecin, Pomerania, of the Cassubians and Wends, of Mecklenburg and Krosno Odrzańskie; Burgrave of Nuremberg, above and below the mountains, Prince of Hildesheim, Paderborn, Halberstadt, Münster, Minden, Cammin, Wenden, Schwerin, Ratzeburg, East Frisia, Eichsfeld, Erfurt, Essen, Quedlinburg and Elten, Count of Hohenzollern, Ruppin, the Mark, Ravensberg, Hohenstein, Tecklenburg, Schwerin, Lingen, Bühren and Leerdamm; Lord of the lands of Rostock, Stargard, [uncertain: Werden], Limburg, Lauenburg, Bütow, Arlay and Breda, etc. We do hereby make known and confess, for Ourselves and Our successors on the throne, that, whereas the Serene Prince, Our friendly dear cousin, Friedrich Ludwig of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, Our General of Infantry, Governor of Wrocław, Inspector of the Lower Silesian and Franconian Infantry Inspections, Knight of Our Red and of Our Great Black Eagle Order, has

most humbly given Us to understand in what manner, in order to preserve the flourishing of the Princely House of Hohenlohe, he has founded in his will drawn up on the 7th of October 1805 a family entailed estate and fideicommiss, for which he designates his houses in Wrocław, his park at Szczytniki, his Silesian allodial estate of Bytków, the Silesian lordship of Koszęcin purchased by him together with the estates connected therewith, Boronów, Harbultowitz, Olszyna and Cieszowa, and finally those estates which he possesses in South Prussia, namely the lordships of Zagórów, Trąbczyn, Pszczew, Wieniec and Bątkowo; with the added most humble request that, since the erection of such an entailed estate and fideicommiss cannot take place under the laws of the land without Our sovereign approbation, We might most graciously be pleased to grant him the same; whereupon We have then granted this request out of the particular royal favour and goodwill We bear towards the aforementioned reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen and his family.

Accordingly We have, the extract most humbly presented to Us

containing the above-named family entailed estate and fideicommiss, from the will of the Serene reigning Prince Friedrich Ludwig of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen drawn up under date Wrocław the 7th of October 1805, which runs word for word as follows:

Copy of an extract from the will which His Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Neuenstein-Ingelfingen deposited with the Wrocław Government Court on the 9th of October 1805.

§ XII. Already in the settlement I declared that I would likewise raise to an entailed estate various considerable portions of My private fortune, for the founding of the flourishing of My Princely House. I therefore declare first of all:

1. My houses in Wrocław, and consequently also the Schulzius house first newly purchased in the past year, which is at present joined with My older house, as it stands and lies;

2. My park and gardens at Szczytniki, including both the dwelling houses belonging thereto and also including

the garden in Szczytniki purchased by Me from the Countess von Götz, in the most solemn legal form as an entailed estate, as described above. I add to this entailed estate, and hereby declare incorporated in it, the furnishings and all the utensils to be found in My houses here and in the town and at Szczytniki, and likewise in the pleasure-houses there. Namely, all My silver plate to be found here, porcelain table centrepieces, linen, paintings, copper engravings. All this is to be well preserved by every future lord of the entailed estate, and he may indeed make improvements and alterations therein as fashion changes and so forth, at his pleasure; but the value as a whole, and the silver by weight, shall never be diminished.

My library and map-room here I likewise add to the entailed estate. My eldest son must, however, not withhold from his younger brothers whatever may be of use to them from the library and map-room for their military study.

I also make it the express duty of My eldest son, and of every successor in the entailed estate, to keep the road and the bridge to the garden always in good

repair; likewise to conserve well all the plantations in the park, and also the water features in the same, and to increase and improve them according to his good taste; in particular to have the replanting of the [word defective in the transcription: Ge…tze] commended to him, and above all to conserve diligently and in the best structural condition, for all time, the monuments set up by Me to the three Kings of Prussia whom I have served. At the same time I hereby ordain that the garden and park at Szczytniki shall, under every future lord of the entailed estate also, remain a public promenade for the public of Wrocław. Yet every possessor may in return require decent conduct of the public and faithful care of the park and of all its parts.

In this regard I also hereby address to the Wrocław Government and to the Police Directorate here the urgent request to take this place of pleasure, and this walk dedicated by Me to the general enjoyment, under their special protection and supervision.

My heir shall duly forward and convey to these high authorities a copy of the extract of the present passage of My will

in proper form.

§ XIII. Now, in order further to promote the flourishing of My Princely House, I will by the present solemn legal disposition also have the hitherto allodial estate of Bytków purchased by Me hereby made into an entailed estate, and namely have the same added to the Sławięcice ironworks department. I here make it the express duty of the lord of the entailed estate to complete, in the greatest possible extension, the establishment of a coal-fired blast furnace erected by Me but not yet quite finished, and to hold firmly and inviolably to the partnership contract concluded by Me with Mr Baildon upon this matter; also always to preserve this gentleman in his present connexion with the Sławięcice works, and to make use of his good counsel, as one who in My conviction can be of excellent service to the interest of this branch of estate economy.

§ XIV. I have also purchased the lordship of Koszęcin and the lordships connected therewith, Boronów, Olszyna, Harbultowitz

and Cieszowa, for about one million thaler. Their true value may, however, well reach fourteen hundred thousand thaler. Into these estates I have paid two hundred thousand Reichsthaler in cash; and I can therefore safely reckon that I already at present possess in them a clear property of five hundred thousand thaler, whereby I have at the same time worked towards regulating the debts still resting upon them in such a way that I cannot be incommoded by any calling-in of them, but that it depends upon the possessor whether, when, and how much of them he will successively discharge and pay off. This lordship of Koszęcin too, and the lordships connected therewith, Boronów, Olszyna, Harbultowitz and Cieszowa, I hereby make into an entailed estate, as characterised above. To My eldest son, the Hereditary Prince August, who thus succeeds Me first in these estates also, I commend the mining councillor Bernhardi, who now directs the administration. Should he, however,

in his sickliness depart this life early, then I advise My dear successor to place at the head of the Koszęcin administration also the Lasowice ironworks inspector Koenig, who is very experienced in ironworking and truly deserving; in which [administration] the best possible forestry management and the ever-increasing cultivation and improvement of the ironworks likewise founds the most solid Revencirch funds.

§ XV. Finally I also declare those estates and lordships which I leave behind Me at My death in South Prussia to be an entailed estate, namely the lordships of Pszczew, Zagórów and Trąbczyn, Bątkowo and Wieniec.

§ XXIV. Since all My entail foundations relate only to the flourishing of My House and Princely name, I have already in the settlement of 1799, § 10 no. 8, had the power conveyed to Me to dispose freely, by a particular disposition, also in respect of the Uxoral Güter made into entailed estates for My male line, for

the event of the extinction of My male line. Partly by virtue of this reservation, partly by virtue of My own right, I therefore ordain that, in case My male descent in all three lines of My beloved Princes should — which may fate avert to the latest times! — die out and be extinct, then:

1. The estates of Sławięcice, Birawa, Stara Kuźnia, Lasowice, together with the manufactories and ironworks belonging thereto, as also the estate of Bytków, and the estate of Landsberg possibly still to be purchased, [shall fall] to My eldest daughter Adelheid or her future descendants;

II. All the Saxon estates, as also the lordship of Koszęcin and the lordships connected therewith, Boronów, Olszyna, Harbultowitz and Cieszowa, to My second daughter Emilie and her future

descendants.

III. All the South Prussian estates to My third daughter Auguste and her future descendants.

IV. My houses in Wrocław and the park at Szczytniki, together with all appurtenances, to the Princess Adelheid, My eldest daughter, and her descendants, likewise alone,

shall fall and be assigned. How matters are to be handled with the Öhringen fideicommiss capital of the 200,000 fr [illegible] has already been disposed of above.

All the remainder, which is not mentioned here, becomes free allodium in the person of the last possessor and male descendant out of all three lines of My Princes. With those allotments, however, it shall be held as follows.

I. Were one of My three Princesses still living

at the extinction of the male line — which early death may fate avert — then the Princess would enjoy the usufruct of the share assigned to her for her lifetime. Thereafter, however, upon her death the same shall descend to the firstborn male descendant; and in her male descent the assigned share remains a family fideicommiss according to the right of lineal succession and of primogeniture, but in the person of the last male descendant it becomes free allodium.

II. The same shall be held if My own Princess daughter is no longer living at the extinction of My male line. Her share then falls at once to the firstborn of the first line of her male descendants, and in the further transmission it shall be held just as before stated.

III. If at the extinction of My male

line one of the Princesses has also died without leaving any male or female descent, then her share falls to the two remaining Princesses and their descendants in equal parts. But if there is still female, though no male, descent of the Princess, then the female descendants then living succeed to her share as to a free allodium; yet not in Capita but in Stirpes. That the foregoing and overleaf copy of the extract of the will of His Most Serene Highness the reigning Prince of the Empire of Hohenlohe-Neuenstein-Ingelfingen has, after careful comparison and collation, been found conformable to and agreeing with the original laid before the undersigned, is hereby on the part of the Royal Government Court here

certified and attested in attestation.

Thus done at Wrocław, the 7th of October in the year 1805. (L. S.)

Richter

We do so also hereby and by virtue of these presents, ratify and approve the foregoing extract of the will in every respect, and will that the foundation contained therein shall be valid for all time; saving, however, Us in Our rights and in the obligations which lie upon the Prince and the Princess with regard to the cabinet orders of

27 September and 25 October 1804, and likewise saving to every man his well-acquired and well-founded rights, and with the provision that the legal prescriptions, according to which none of Our vassals may reside outside the country

without Our express permission, are also to be exactly observed by each successive possessor of this entailed estate and fideicommiss. We therefore command and enjoin all Our Supreme Provincial Colleges, as also each and every one of Our vassals and subjects, of whatever estate, dignity or condition they may be, but in particular Our Silesian Supreme Provincial Governments and Our South Prussian Governments, and moreover every man whomsoever, that they conduct themselves most obediently accordingly, and leave the successors and descendants of the oft-mentioned reigning Prince Friedrich Ludwig of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen quiet and undisturbed in the operation of the family entailed estate and fideicommiss

institution most graciously confirmed by Us and duly to be entered in the relevant mortgage books; that on the contrary they neither contest, hinder nor trouble them therein, nor occasion or permit that such be done by others, upon pain of Our highest displeasure and unfailing severe punishment.

make known and hereby give to be understood that, whereas the possessor of the lordships of Zagórów and Trąbczyn, situated in South Prussia in the Kalisz Chamber Department and its Konin district, His Lordship the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, has sought permission from us, reserving a part of the demesne farm of Trąbczyn together with the manorial parcels at Mariantów, in all Seven Hundred and Eighty-one Morgen and 77 square rods, likewise Four Thousand Nine Hundred and Forty-seven Morgen of forest, the said lordships together with the remaining and greater part of the forest, namely

A. to dismember the demesne farms belonging to the lordship of Zagórów, Drzewce, Kopojno, Świątniki, Swięcia and Broniki, likewise the demesne farms belonging to the lordship of Trąbczyn, Nowawieś, Przybysław, Stara-Hutta, and a part of the demesne farm of Trąbczyn,

B. to let out in hereditary lease the demesne farm and village of Oleśnica, likewise the demesne farm and village of Szetlewek, and

C. to be permitted to convert the services and prestations of all the subjects into a fixed money rent, we have therefore, in consideration of the utility of this design

and of the profitable services rendered and still to be rendered to us in our Royal House by His Lordship the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, our General of Infantry and Governor of Wrocław, resolved by Cabinet Orders of the 22nd of October and 7th of December of last year to grant this his petition in such manner and to approve the same, only that the following conditions shall obtain therein, namely

1. that the compensation to be granted to the subjects for their hitherto existing rights of pasturage and of taking wood be more nearly determined, and that in the hereditary-rent deeds of each individual the area assigned to him rent-free be exactly noted, as also that herein generally the provisions contained in § 12 of the Edict issued for the province of Silesia on the 1st of March 1804 must be duly observed, on the basis of a special and corrected survey.

2. that none of the present peasant holdings may be allowed to lapse, but that if, upon a fire damage or other misfortune, no one is found who will restore such a holding out of his own means, the manorial lordship (Dominium) must re-erect the building at its own cost.

3. that all the dues and charges of the state at present resting upon the said estates, or hereafter still to be laid upon them,

shall as before be paid over to our treasuries appointed for the purpose at the prescribed terms, and that for their security the necessary entry be made in the mortgage book of the lands and forests reserved by the manorial lordship.

4. that the rights of taking wood belonging to the monastery and provostry of Lond be entered in the land and mortgage book upon the totality of the forests reserved from the dismemberment, and be secured in that manner; in return for which we approve that if hereafter the forests excepted from the dismemberment should be found insufficient for the rights of taking wood belonging to our Treasury in respect of the domain office of Ratyń, a compensation for them shall be ascertained by an annual canon and secured.

In witness whereof we have caused the present consent to be made out under the customary signature and the greater seal of our Chamber of War and Domains, and have executed it.

The parties appearing are personally known to the undersigned (Subscriptis), and there is no doubt as to their capacity to execute judicial acts validly.

The same declare, of their own free will and after due deliberation, the following hereditary-lease contract to the protocol.

§ I.

Namely, His Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, through his general attorney the Councillor of War and Councillor Mr von Triebenfeld, who is legitimated by the annexed power of attorney, makes over, from the forest belonging to his estate of Drzewiec, the area of 100 Hufen, in words One hundred Hufen Magdeburg measure, reckoned at thirty Morgen to the Hufe and each Morgen at one hundred and Eighty square rods, to the aforesaid residents, namely:

1. Johann Friedrich Turno — 5 Hufen

2. Martin Dikhoff — 5 Hufen

3. Johann Martin Sydow — 5 Hufen

4. Johann Gottlieb Haberland — 10 Hufen

5. Samuel Schubert — 5 Hufen

6. Michael Dikhoff — 10 Hufen

7. Gottfried Dikhoff — 5 Hufen

8. Friedrich Siering — 5 Hufen

9. Christ. Friedr. Vagel — 5 Hufen

10. Johann Wilh. Böttcher — 5 Hufen

11. Johann Büchner — 5 Hufen

12. Ephraim Fuchs — 5 Hufen

13. Johann Halbott — 5 Hufen

14. Dr. Johann Wendel Heilmann — 5 Hufen

15. Martin Dikhoff — 5 Hufen

16. Michael Just — 5 Hufen

17. Johann Luckow — 5 Hufen

18. Johann Liewert — 5 Hufen

Total as above 100 Hufen, for everlasting and perpetual time in hereditary lease, under the following conditions.

§ II.

Of entry money not a farthing is paid, since these One hundred Hufen are waste land overgrown with wood, which must first be cleared. On the other hand a perpetual hereditary canon of 30 Rthl, say thirty Reichsthaler, per Hufe Magdeburg measure, and thus for 100 Hufen in all 3,000 Rthl, say three Thousand Reichsthaler, is paid from it yearly to the ground lordship in two instalments, namely with the one half of 1,500 Rthl, say One Thousand Five hundred Reichsthaler, at Midsummer and with the other half of 1,500 Rthl, say one Thousand Five hundred Reichsthaler, at Christmas, in good Courant such as the treasuries accept.

§ III.

The hereditary lessees are free to make over these Hufen which they have acquired, in several separate

parts, to others, and to come to terms with these new takers as best they can to their own advantage.

§ IV

Their establishments both the present hereditary lessees and the other future takers must effect at their own cost, now and in future, and they receive for this neither remission of the hereditary rent nor other building assistance; they may, however, use for this the timber standing on the Hufen received in hereditary lease, which belongs to them all in property without any exception.

§ V

These Hufen taken in hereditary lease shall be duly measured out to the hereditary lessees in the Drzewiec forest district as soon as the weather allows, and delivered into their possession.

§ VI

Since, as aforesaid, the hereditary lessees must make the land arable for themselves by clearing, they receive for this, one like another, four free years, which begin at Christmas of this year and end at Christmas One Thousand Eight hundred and Eight; during these four years the hereditary lessees need pay not a farthing of hereditary rent, but they pay the first half-yearly hereditary rent of

One Thousand five hundred Reichsthaler only at Midsummer One Thousand Eight Hundred and Nine, from which time this payment of rent is continued half-yearly.

§ VII

Besides this annual hereditary rent the hereditary lessees undertake, for themselves and their descendants, to render the royal and other public dues that shall hereafter be fixed upon the One hundred Hufen, by whatever name they may go.

§ VIII

The hereditary lessees have not the least claim to any firewood or pasture in the other manorial woods; they and the other takers are, however, permitted to graze their cattle free of charge in that part of the woods near Drzewiec which the ground lordship does not sell but keeps for itself, and where there are no young plantations or plantings of timber; the right of the ground lordship to let out these remaining parts of the wood as well shall, however, not be restricted by this in the least, but the hereditary lessees' right of pasturage ceases entirely as soon as such a case of sale occurs.

§ IX

The hereditary lessees are granted the liberty to set up on their ground a brick kiln

and to burn for themselves the bricks and roofing tiles they need, without anything having to be paid for this to the ground lordship.

§ X

The hereditary lessees must divide the Hufen they have taken among themselves in the best possible manner, without the ground lordship concurring in this in the least, since it is bound only to allot to them the total of the 100 Hufen; the ground lordship undertakes, however, to bear the whole costs of this allotment in the manner determined in § I.

§ XI

The present hereditary lessees, as also the other takers, are free to alienate their holding to others in any manner they please; but at every change of possession, be it by sale or exchange, the tenth Groschen of the purchase money or of the amount of the exchange must be paid to the ground lordship as a transfer fee (Laudemium), and the ground lordship always holds to the new taker, whose affair it remains not to pay out the purchase money to the seller until the transfer fee is settled.

On inheritance, or where the holding is given up to children and collateral relations, on the other hand, no transfer fee is paid, and in the same way the first takers from the present

hereditary lessees are wholly exempt from it.

§ XII

At the end of the four free years, and at the latest at Midsummer One Thousand Eight hundred and Nine, the hereditary lessees and the other takers are free to redeem the stipulated hereditary rent of thirty Reichsthaler per Hufe up to one half, by payment of the capital sum at Five per cent; that is to say, each of them may pay off to the ground lordship in cash One, two, up to three hundred Reichsthaler per Hufe, which capital then remains the property of the ground lordship, and for every One hundred Reichsthaler paid, Five Reichsthaler of annual rent are written off for the hereditary lessees. The second half of the hereditary rent, of Fifteen Reichsthaler per Hufe, remains however irredeemable for everlasting time.

§ XIII

The hereditary lessees and their descendants remain for ever wholly free of all hereditary subjection, and need render the ground lordship not the least manorial service nor deliver anything in kind. They are, however, without exception subject for ever to the jurisdiction of the manorial lordship (Dominium).

§ XIV

Besides the One hundred Hufen on which they pay rent, there is allotted to the whole community

once and for all, namely 1. for the schoolmaster Fifteen Morgen — 15 Morgen

2. For the village mayor — 5 Morgen

and 3. for the churchyard, say one Morgen — 1 Morgen

in all 21 Morgen, say one and twenty Morgen Magdeburg measure, free of charge and free of rent.

§ XV

Their drink, of beer and brandy, the hereditary lessees and their successors in possession must always take from the manorial brewery and distillery or from the tavern, and for every quart of brandy brought in from other estates pay One Reichsthaler, and for every barrel of beer five Reichsthaler, as a penalty to the ground lordship.

§ XVI

The hereditary lessees, for themselves and their descendants, hereby expressly renounce all and every remission in cases of misfortune, whether they arise through fire from heaven, the incendiarism of evil persons, crop failure, hailstorm, inundation, cattle plague, war and pestilence, or in whatever manner it may be, and on that account neither a compensation nor a remission of the hereditary rent shall ever avail them.

§ XVII

The costs of this contract, of its

confirmation and official copy, the hereditary lessees undertake to settle.

§ XVIII

So long as the hereditary lessees and their successors in possession fulfil these obligations here written down, they shall be protected by the ground lordship in their rights in every respect, and defended and held harmless against every man's claims in rem.

Should they, however, remain in arrears with the annual hereditary canon for longer than two years, they then forfeit this hereditary lease and the ground lordship is entitled to let it out otherwise, in which case only their improvements may be made good to the hereditary lessees.

§ XIX

For the due and prompt payment of the hereditary rent fixed, the hereditary lessees and the future takers, as also their successors in possession, are liable for ever One for All and All for One, and thus jointly and severally, in such manner that the ground lordship shall be entitled on this account to hold either to the One or the Other, or else to the whole community.

Both parties promise to hold to the foregoing hereditary-lease contract firmly and inviolably, and renounce all legal pleas

that might be raised against it, in particular the objection of an injury suffered above and below the half, of crafty persuasion, of overhaste, or of the impossibility of getting the rent out of the thing, of matters agreed otherwise than written down or not rightly understood; and His Princely Serene Highness expressly consents that the hereditary lessees, each one of them, may on the ground of this contract have his title of possession (titulum possessionis) of his holding settled in his own name. The contracting parties had nothing more to state; they asked for the confirmation and the official copy of this contract, and after this protocol had been read out to them word for word, and they had also been instructed that the renunciation of the legal pleas and objections carries with it the entire loss of the same, they once more renounced them after due deliberation, and in token of their approval have subscribed and signed below in their own hand.

The Princely Hohenlohe Patrimonial Court hereby makes known that between the Councillor of War and Forests von Triebenfeld, as general attorney of His Serene Highness, as seller on the one part, and the resident Christian Friedenberger, as purchaser on the other part, the following hereditary-lease contract, concerning one Hufe Magdeburg measure of land situated in the Trąbczyn forest, has been concluded and judicially declared before us.

Actum Trąbczyn, the 25th of March 1806. There appeared the persons well known to the undersigned justiciary, namely

1. The Councillor of War and Forests von Triebenfeld, as general attorney of His Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, hereditary lord and lord of the court of this place, legitimated by the power of attorney annexed hereto, on the one part, and

2. the resident Christian Friedenberger from Szymanowicer Hauland, on the other part.

The parties appearing are in a condition to execute judicial acts validly, and declare freely and

voluntarily and after due deliberation the following hereditary-lease contract to the protocol.

§ I. His Most Serene Highness grants in hereditary lease to Christian Friedenberger one Hufe, in words One Hufe Magdeburg measure, reckoned at thirty Morgen to the Hufe and each Morgen at one hundred and eighty square rods, situated in the Trąbczyn forest, from now on for all perpetual time

in hereditary lease.

§ II. Christian Friedenberger pays for the one Hufe Magdeburg measure 100 Rthl., in words One hundred Rthaler, as purchase money; and since this purchase money is already fully paid, Christian Friedenberger is hereby receipted for it without further reservation.

§ III. Christian Friedenberger

hereby binds himself, for himself and his successors in possession of this holding, to pay to the manorial lordship (Dominium) of this place an annual hereditary canon of thirty Rthaler, in words thirty Rthaler, from this one Hufe; and this hereditary rent shall be settled yearly in two instalments, namely with the one half at Christmas and with the other half at Midsummer, on each occasion in cash and in Courant, to the manorial treasury.

§ IV. For the wholly unbroken arable the hereditary lessee receives three free years, which begin from Martinmas of the past year and end at Midsummer 1809, so that the first half-yearly hereditary rent must be paid at Christmas 1809 with 15 Rthl., in words fifteen

Rthaler.

That land which, at the measuring out, is handed over to Christian Friedenberger already as broken ground, be it much or little, bears rent from Christmas of this year, since the free years extend only to that part which has first to be made arable.

§ V. It stands free to the hereditary lessee to redeem the fixed hereditary rent of the thirty [uncertain: Rthaler] up to one half, that is to say, to pay off to the ground lordship, according to his means, one, two, up to three hundred [uncertain: thaler] of capital, whereupon for every hundred Rthaler five Rthaler shall be

abated yearly from the hereditary rent; the capital so paid off remains the property of the ground lordship, and this redemption of the hereditary rent takes place only in respect of the first half; the second half, of fifteen Rthaler per Hufe, on the other hand remains irredeemable and can never be raised or reduced.

§ VI. Besides the [uncertain: inner] hereditary rent, the hereditary lessee undertakes, for the present and for future times in perpetuity, to settle and to render all the royal and other public dues whatsoever falling upon this one Hufe, in whatever they may consist, without any exception and without deduction from the hereditary rent or any other reimbursement, and to

render.

§ VII. The hereditary lessee must build at his own cost, without receiving for this, either now or in future, timber or other building assistance; however, all the timber standing on his Hufe belongs to him in property without exception.

Likewise the hereditary lessee and his successors in possession of this holding must effect all future repairs and new buildings out of their own means, without subsidy or assistance.

§ VIII. Outside his own possession the hereditary lessee has no right to firewood or to [uncertain: pasturage] in the manorial forests and fields.

§ IX. His drink the hereditary lessee must always take from

the manorial brewery and distillery, or from the tavern; if foreign drink is brought in by him or through his people, the hereditary lessee forfeits on each occasion a penalty of 5 Rthl. for every barrel of beer and one Rthaler for every garniec of brandy, which penalty is to be paid to the ground lordship.

§ X. The hereditary lessee is subject to the milling compulsion and may grind his grain only where the estate lordship directs him.

§ XI. From all and every manorial service and deliveries in kind, without distinction, the hereditary lessee is for ever wholly exempt;

he remains, however, subject to the jurisdiction of the lordship of this place.

§ XII.

The hereditary lessee and his successors in possession are entitled to alienate their holding to another in any manner they please; but on each sale or exchange the tenth Groschen of the purchase or exchange money must be paid to the ground lordship as a transfer fee (Laudemium), and its consent obtained to every alienation, the ground lordship hereby reserving to itself once and for all the right of pre-emption.

§ XIII. The hereditary lessee, for himself and his successors in possession, renounces all and every remission in cases of

misfortune, whether they arise through fire from heaven or the incendiarism of evil persons, hailstorm, crop failure, cattle plague, inundation, war and pestilence, or in whatever manner it may be, for the present and for the future, entirely; and in cases arising neither a compensation nor a remission of the hereditary rent shall take place.

§ XIV. All costs pertaining to this contract the hereditary lessee undertakes to settle.

§ XV. His Most Serene Highness consents that the hereditary lessee may, on the ground of this contract, have his title of possession settled in his own name.

§ XVI. So long as the hereditary lessee and his successors in possession fulfil all the obligations contained in this contract, His Most Serene Highness promises to maintain them in their rights and to defend them against every man's claim in rem.

Should, however, the hereditary lessee or his successors remain in arrears with the annual hereditary rent longer than two years, or else lay waste this holding and thereby diminish the revenues of the ground lordship, then the ground lordship shall be entitled to dispose of this holding otherwise, and the hereditary lessee forfeits his whole

right and the purchase money paid in.

Actum Mariantów, the thirty-first of March One Thousand Eight Hundred and Six. There appeared the persons well known to the undersigned justiciary, namely

1. Mr von Triebenfeld, Councillor of War and Forests, as general and authorised representative of His Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, hereditary lord and lord of the court of this place, legitimated by the power of attorney annexed, of the one part

and

2. the resident Christoph Erbet of Trąbczyner hauland, of the other part.

The parties appearing are in a condition validly to execute judicial acts, and freely and after due deliberation declare to the protocol the following hereditary-lease contract:

§. I. His Most Serene [continued]

Highness lets to Christoph Erbet one Hufe, in words One Hufe Magdeburg, at thirty Morgen to the Hufe, and each Morgen reckoned at One Hundred and Eighty square rods, situate in the Trąbczyn forest, from now on for everlasting time in hereditary lease.

§. II. Christoph Erbet pays for the one Hufe Magdeburg 100 Rthl., in words One Hundred Reichsthaler, as entry money, already, and since this entry money is already fully paid, Christoph Erbet is hereby receipted for it without further reservation.

§. III. Christoph Erbet hereby binds himself, for himself and his successors in the possession of this holding, to pay from this one Hufe an annual [continued]

hereditary canon of Thirty Thaler, in words thirty Rthaler, to the manorial lordship (Dominium) here, and this hereditary quit-rent shall be discharged yearly in two instalments, namely one half at Christmas and the other half at Midsummer, each time in cash and in Courant, into the lordship's treasury.

§. IV. For the wholly uncultivated arable the hereditary lessee receives three free years, which begin from Martinmas of the past year and end at Midsummer 1809, so that the first half-yearly hereditary quit-rent must be paid at Christmas 1809 with 15 r., in words Fifteen Rthaler.

Such land as is already handed over to Christoph Erbet as cultivated at the measuring-out, be it much or little

in amount, bears interest from Christmas of this year, since the free years extend only to that part which has first to be brought under cultivation.

§. V. The hereditary lessee is at liberty to redeem the fixed hereditary quit-rent of Thirty Rthaler up to one half; that is, he may according to his means pay off to the ground lordship one, two, up to three Hundred Reichsthaler of capital, whereupon for every hundred Rthaler five Rthaler shall be taken off the hereditary quit-rent yearly; the capital so paid off remains the property of the ground lordship, and this redemption of the hereditary quit-rent takes place only in respect of the first half; the second half, at

Fifteen Reichsthaler per Hufe, on the other hand remains irredeemable, and can never be raised or lowered.

§. VI. Besides the cash hereditary quit-rent the hereditary lessee undertakes, for now and for future everlasting times, to discharge and render all the [uncertain: assessed] [uncertain: pänglichen] and other [uncertain: gleitlichen] dues falling upon this one Hufe, consist in what they may, without any exception and without deduction from the hereditary quit-rent or any other reimbursement.

§. VII. The hereditary lessee must build at his own cost, without receiving for this, either now or in the future, timber or any other building assistance [illegible] In da

However, all the timber standing on his Hufen belongs to him in property without exception. Likewise the hereditary lessee and his successors in the possession of this holding must effect all future repairs and new buildings out of their own means, without subsidy or assistance.

§. VIII. Outside his own allotment the hereditary lessee has no right to firewood or [uncertain: pasturage] in the lordship's forests and fields.

§. IX. The hereditary lessee must always take his drink from the lordship's brewery and distillery or from the tavern. If foreign drink be brought in by him or his people, the hereditary lessee shall each time incur a penalty of five Reichsthaler for every barrel of beer and one Rthaler

for every garniec of brandy, which penalty shall be paid to the ground lordship.

§. X. The hereditary lessee is subject to the mill compulsion, and may grind his grain only where the estate lordship directs him.

§. XI. From each and every manorial service and delivery in kind without distinction the hereditary lessee is wholly and for ever exempt; he remains, however, subject to the jurisdiction of the manorial lordship here.

§. XII. The hereditary lessee and his successors in possession are entitled to alienate his holding to another in any manner he pleases, but on every sale

or exchange the tenth Groschen of the purchase or exchange money must be paid to the ground lordship as a transfer fee (Laudemium), and the consent of the same must be obtained for every alienation, the ground lordship hereby reserving to itself once and for all the right of pre-emption.

§. XIII. The hereditary lessee renounces, for himself and his successors in possession, wholly and for now and for the future, each and every remission in cases of misfortune, whether the same arise through fire from heaven, arson by evil persons, hailstorm, failure of crops, cattle plague, flood, war and pestilence, or in whatever manner it may be, and upon the occurrence of such [continued]

cases neither compensation nor remission of the hereditary quit-rent shall take place.

§. XIV. The hereditary lessee undertakes to discharge all the costs attending this contract.

§. XV. His Most Serene Highness consents that the hereditary lessee may, on the ground of this contract, have his title of possession settled for himself.

§. XVI. So long as the hereditary lessee and his successors in possession shall fulfil all the obligations contained in this contract, His Most Serene Highness promises to maintain them in their rights

and to defend them against every man's claim in rem.

Should, however, the hereditary lessee or his successors remain in arrears with the annual hereditary quit-rent longer than two years, or lay this holding waste and thereby diminish the revenues of the ground lordship, the ground lordship shall be entitled to dispose of this holding otherwise, and the hereditary lessee shall forfeit his whole right and the entry money paid in.

Both parties promise to keep this hereditary-lease contract firmly and inviolably; having been instructed by the court as to the consequences, they renounce

all evasions available against it, in particular the plea of an injury suffered above or below the half, of cunning persuasion, fear, duress, of matters otherwise agreed than written down, or not understood; they moved that this contract be made out judicially, and have, after previous reading aloud word for word, in token of approval subscribed and signed below in their own hands.

If Your Royal Majesty might be pleased to grace with Your Most High attention and support a plan which, for a princely house whose head has consecrated his whole life to that same Most High Person, fulfils in a blameless manner several equally weighty purposes, and at the same time leaves no danger whatever to be apprehended for the Most High interest: then I may most humbly take comfort that the following representation will be deemed worthy of a Most Gracious consideration.

It is known to that same Most High Person with what exertion the Prince of Hohenlohe has hitherto laboured to bring the affairs of his house into order; the just hope of doing so, entertained for many years and grounded in the decease of his uncle and the inheritance from him, has for the moment been frustrated anew by political events, for the damage he suffered in the [uncertain: Weich] amounts to 532/m Rthl. Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Your Most Serene Highness's most gracious letter of the 19th and 27th of March I received so late only because the same lay a very long while in Słupca. It is more than saddening for me that I must live so far removed from Your Serene Highness and have news so seldom; it is particularly hard for me to act when Your Serene Highness leaves me so long without any answer at all. Meanwhile I do myself the honour of reporting to Your Highness most obediently how all matters have prospered.

Having put everything in order upon the estates, I betook myself here to Berlin again, in order to work here and, if possible, to finalise the business.

The dismemberment has, as Your Serene Highness knows, been approved most honourably, and His Majesty the King Himself has been pleased to grant me His high approbation. The Pszczew matter too has been approved at the Chamber, laid before the King for approbation by the General Hinrich Department, and this very day the same, executed by the King, has come in here. This matter, which threatened Your Serene Highness with great danger, is now likewise entirely in the clear. The valuations of the Kalisz Chamber are likewise concluded; they have turned out as the copy under A shows, and lie at this moment before the General Finance Department, from which tomorrow I am to receive an authentic attestation concerning the permanently established revenues of the estates

and in which the yield is fixed, after every possible examination, at 40,260 Rthl. — However, in this neither the forest nor the transfer fees (Laudemia) and jurisdictional incidents have been taken into account, but all has been left to Your Serene Highness's disposition. Yet great as the yield has turned out to be, the debts, according to the schedule appended under B, are not less great and weighty, and a series of years will be required before everything is cleanly paid off.

It was a piece of good fortune that I arrived here just at this time, for the matter of the Courland post and the interest payments was again pending, the more so since the Minister von Stein is now clearing everything up and has to that end requested the appointment of a commission, consisting of Minister von Voss, the Grand Chancellor, and himself, over against the Minister Count von Schulenburg, which is to investigate everything and have everything secured, so that light may be had especially in respect of the Bank and the Maritime Trading Company, where great deficiencies are suspected. I have conferred much on this matter with the Lord General von K[öckritz], and have in the end agreed with him thus far, to request of His Majesty the King as many treasury notes as are required for the payment of Your Serene Highness's debts altogether.

The whole sum is, as the schedule states, however 698,000 Rthl, exclusive of the items due to myself, with which I shall wait until happier events. I have wished to write on that account under my own name, as the enclosure

under Letter C shows, and the more so since the King is now according me the justice due to me. Meanwhile the Privy Cabinet Councillor B[eyme] has not yet given his fiat, and the worthy General feared, with every right, that the matter might founder altogether. Therefore that upright friend proposed that the bosom friend of Mr B. — the Court Fiscal Pochammer — should conduct this business.

With him I have only now come to an agreement; he will see to everything and demands for his pains an honorarium of like measure to that which he has been promised by the Prince of Hesse. In the meantime he must have a special power of attorney, and to that end he has this very moment sent me the form appended under Letter D, which I transmit to Your Serene Highness with the most obedient request that the same may be made out there in probative form / insofar as everything has Your Highness's approbation / and executed, and sent hither with the greatest speed, so that I may work quickly and bring everything to completion — the more so since Midsummer is at the door — and since in these most sorely pressed times not a Groschen is to be had from anywhere else, all the treasuries being especially [uncertain: barred], with which to pay the most urgent debts.

Everything will turn upon this, that Mr Pochammer so dispose the Cabinet Councillor that we obtain the monies, or treasury notes, at 3 per cent. The Prince of Orange must indeed give 4 per cent; meanwhile Mr Pochammer believes he shall entirely succeed and prise the capital loose at 3 per cent. Were this so, Your Serene Highness might count yourself exceedingly fortunate. You would be quit of all your debts at a single stroke, would have after some 30 years the cleanest of estates, and would meanwhile nevertheless draw yearly some 10,000 Rthl from the two lordships, and would be free and quit of all cares and sorrow, and especially of the vexation of the dishonouring lawsuits. — The plans of amortisation I have drawn up to that end, and particularly for Your Serene Highness's survey; they are respectfully appended here under Letter E. Deign, most gracious Prince and Lord, to examine everything, and send me above all the power of attorney for the Court Fiscal Mr Pochammer — so that this work, so exceedingly important and tending to Your Serene Highness's welfare, peace and honour, may be pursued most zealously and at length happily concluded. Most rewarding for me is it that the Monarch alone could not withhold his approbation, and that this matter has excited the astonishment even of the Cabinet Councillor Beyme; but what has pleased me most of all is that the Minister von Voss has set up my conduct as a model to his Chambers.

Now as concerns the Glenck letter of the 28th of February, I answer thereto most deeply obediently that the Prusimska matter is as foreign to Glenck as colour is to one born blind. Were it possible for me to be everywhere at once, I should pursue this affair too with equal force. But since this cannot be done without arrogating to oneself divine attributes like a madman, I must keep to the chief matters, and work upon these with honest zeal, in order to establish Your Serene Highness's peace. For the rest, I console myself with this, that Mr Glenck has merely feigned this matter with his year, in order now to have material for writing to Your Serene Highness and to recall his [uncertain: Pracheregen] to Your Highness's memory.

His purpose he has attained, in that I must now see and speak with him. — My judgement was nevertheless correct, for of the Prusimska matter he knew nothing; only the consent for the sale of his lands was the object upon which he discoursed. He vaunted his many years of service, and that he had made 42 journeys in Your Serene Highness's affairs — for which, in his opinion, he believed he had deserved a far greater remuneration than this trifle. To make an end of the thing, I asked him what he actually wanted, if he were to sell the lands back to Your Serene Highness. His answer was that he could not let them go for [illegible] under 8,000 Rthl. For he had already made a gift to Your Serene Highness of 330 Morgen of land which Your Highness had promised him besides the bailiwick and the 300 Morgen of forest — this surely was already more than reasonable, and in case one should wish to refuse him the consent, he would bring suit and demand these as well. — In order to make an end of all these [uncertain: bachensee] of Glenck's, I have promised him the 8,000 Rthl sub spe rati, and I submit myself herein to Your Serene Highness's commands — but the consent

to his sale Your Serene Highness cannot give him, unless You should prefer some 20 new lawsuits — for every peasant and cottager who has land within the 700 Morgen would be unwilling to yield, and would protest against the dismemberment and against everything. I shall now see to make it possible to raise a part of the monies and to pay Glenck off. Today I go to Pszczew, and there to set everything in order, in particular to stop the mouth of that wretched Jew Meyer Bernhard. The fellow has brought suit against Your Serene Highness, notwithstanding that I had made it known to the knave that His Majesty had approved the Pszczew

From Pszczew I go to Kalisz and Trąbczyn, arrange everything there, see what money I can gather in at that place, and hasten back here with it in order to smooth out the principal business. Eighteen days from today I expect to be in Berlin again, and if all now goes as wished, I shall then perhaps myself bring to Öhringen the sum desired by Your Serene Highness.

The constellations, moreover, are now very evil, and it is much wished here that Your Serene Highness might be quite soon entirely restored to health, and that you would take your return journey by way of Berlin. Through my long stay here I was lately very nearly placed in a favourable situation. The Głogów Government had ordered that the 30,000 Rthl of the von Wulffen lady which stand upon Konotop be paid. The mandates had been left lying in Wrocław, so that I knew nothing of it until they fell upon my neck here. In the meantime the upright General at once helped here; he gave me in cash what I needed, and the Lord Grand Chancellor had 200,000 Rthl paid upon the one mortgage, and so these two honest men provided me — Now I have full quiet and can attend to all Your Serene Highness's affairs.

With unbounded reverence I remain, as Your Serene Highness's

faithful, humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Berlin, the 17th of June 1806.
