188

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Lord!

In Berlin I succeeded in the end better than I had believed, through the help of our friends General von Köckritz and Cabinet Councillor Beyme; the Lord Grand Chancellor is giving some 176,000 Rthl out of the Justice Fund, wherewith all the burdensome creditors upon the estates, and in particular Mr Weigel here, will be paid. — Above all I am concerned to set the mortgage of 200,000 Rthl pledged with Oppenheimer afloat again.

The [uncertain: Ge] Schlabrendorff I shall pay in this manner, that I take 20,000 Rthl upon a Świniary mortgage from the councillor of war von Hellen, which I had meant to pay over to Mrs von Wulffen of Konotop, but which can for the present still stand.

If all this is attended to, then Your Serene Highness will soon be in the clear, especially as regards the 300,000 Rthl Courant debt, upon which they are willing to wait provided the interest continues to be paid.

The cursed small items of debt press the hardest of all, for these [uncertain: Kaste] creditors make the most outcry over their trifles. — Altogether I have this time been in such straits that I must thank God a hundredfold if it can all be smoothed out,

I arrived here yesterday, and this very hour I hasten on to Kalisz and Trąbczyn, in order to drive together there what is possible, so that I may be able to make out an order of payment to Your Serene Highness for a sum at Fürth. In Pszczew I have put everything in order so far, that Your Serene Highness need no longer be troubled by the creditors there. Echaust is entirely satisfied and has given a receipt before the court, and there remains for Your Serene Highness 4,000 Rthl which the deputies must pay on the 6th of July. These I already think to apply towards the 30,000 Rthl. Now it depends upon what I shall find in Trąbczyn. There the tenants had still 6,000 Rthl to pay. 60,000 Rthl were to come in as entry moneys; the Midsummer rent amounts, from the tenants alone, to 10,000 Rthl; the Midsummer interest from the peasants and hereditary purchasers amounts to some 4,000 Rthl; the Wrąbczyn and Swięcia people must pay some 1,800 Rthl; the Oleśnica people are already some 16,000 Rthl in arrear: this amounts to some 102,000 Rthl of outstanding arrears. It now depends upon whether Schenck has been a [uncertain: Can:] or an honest, industrious fellow. For he has the charge of collecting in what is possible, so that Your Serene Highness may receive a considerable sum at Midsummer.

Grattenauer is a lazy, false brute — he does nothing,

and now sits continually with the Minister, who, as I hear this very moment, has given him a post-horse pass for a journey into the mountains and Upper Silesia. How can the wretched fellow take a salary from Your Serene Highness when he serves the Minister as his agent? The rascal ought to be arrested for debt; I advanced him his salary for 1 1/2 years, and now that he has it he does nothing more. — Little by little I give up the hope of ever finding an honest man.

God grant me that all goes happily and well at Trąbczyn. — In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Serene Highness's

faithful and most obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 25th of June 1806.

The undersigned Court makes known to whom it may concern, that between the authorised representative of His Serene Highness the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, the Honourable Councillor of War and Forests Triebenfeld, and the Hollander Bogumił Sarre, the following contract has been concluded.

Actum Trąbczyn, the eighth of July, one thousand eight hundred and six. There appeared the persons well known to the undersigned justiciary, namely as

1. the Councillor of War and Forests von Triebenfeld, as general authorised representative of His Serene Highness the reigning Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, hereditary lord and lord of the court of this place, legitimated by the power of attorney here appended, on his part.

and

2. the Hollander farmer Gottlieb Sarre from the Peyserschen Hauland on the other part. The appearing parties are found to be in a condition validly to execute judicial acts, and declare freely and after due deliberation the following hereditary-lease contract to the protocol

§ I. His Most Serene Highness grants to Gottlieb Sarre, in the forest situated near Trąbczyn, 1 1/2 Hufen, in words one and a half Hufen Magdeburg measure, the Hufe reckoned at thirty Morgen and each Morgen at one hundred and eighty square rods, of waste land, from Midsummer of this present year onward, in hereditary lease for all perpetual time.

§ II. Gottlieb Sarre pays for the Hufe Magdeburg measure 100 Rthl., in words one hundred Reichsthaler, hence for one and a half Hufen 150 r., in words one hundred and fifty Reichsthaler as entry money; and since this purchase money has already been paid in full, Gottlieb Sarre is hereby receipted without further reservation.

§ III. Gottlieb Sarre hereby binds himself, for himself and his successors in the possession of this holding, to pay from each Hufe an annual hereditary canon of 30 Rthl., in words thirty Reichsthaler, hence for one and a half Hufen

45 Rthl., in words forty-five Reichsthaler, to the manorial lordship (Dominium) of this place; and this hereditary rent shall be settled annually in two instalments, namely with the one half at Christmas and with the other half at Midsummer, each time in cash and in Courant, into the lordship's treasury.

§ IV. Of the wholly uncultivated arable the hereditary lessee receives three free years, which begin at Midsummer of the present year and end at Midsummer 1809, so that the first half-yearly hereditary rent must be rendered at Midsummer 1809 with 22 Rthl. 12 Groschen, in words twenty-two Reichsthaler, twelve good Groschen.

That land which at the time of the measuring out was already handed over to Gottlieb Sarre as arable

be it much or little, bears interest from Midsummer of this year onward, inasmuch as the free years extend only to that part which has first to be brought under cultivation; and since the handing over of these one and a half Hufen Magdeburg measure has already taken place to the hereditary lessee, he renounces all claims that might be made on that account.

§ V. The hereditary lessee is at liberty to redeem the fixed hereditary rent of thirty Reichsthaler per Hufe up to one half, that is to say, he may according to his means pay off to the ground lordship one, two, up to three hundred Reichsthaler of capital, whereupon for every hundred Reichsthaler five Reichsthaler shall be struck off the hereditary rent annually

The capital so paid off remains the property of the ground lordship, and this redemption of the hereditary rent takes place only in respect of the first half; the second half, of fifteen Reichsthaler per Hufe, on the other hand remains irredeemable and can never be raised or lessened.

§ VI. Besides the hereditary rent in cash, the hereditary lessee undertakes, for the present and for future times in perpetuity, to settle and to render the royal and other public dues falling upon these one and a half Hufen, in whatsoever they may consist, without any exception and without deduction from the hereditary rent or any other reimbursement.

§ VII. The hereditary lessee must build upon it at his own cost, without his

receiving for this purpose, either now or in the future, timber or any other building assistance. However, all the timber standing upon his one and a half Hufen belongs to him in property, without exception.

Likewise the hereditary lessee and his successors in the possession of this holding must effect all future repairs and new buildings out of their own means, without subsidy or assistance.

§ VIII. Outside his own holding the hereditary lessee has no right to firewood or pasturage in the lordship's woods and fields.

§ IX. His drink the hereditary lessee must always take from the lordship's brewery and distillery, or from the tavern.

If by him or by his people foreign drink is brought in, the hereditary lessee incurs each time a penalty of five Reichsthaler for every barrel of beer and one Reichsthaler for every garniec of brandy, which penalty shall be rendered to the estate lordship.

§ X. To the milling compulsion the hereditary lessee is subject, and may grind his grain only where the estate lordship directs him.

§ XI. From each and every manorial service and delivery in kind, without distinction, the hereditary lessee is entirely and for ever exempted; he remains, however, subject to the jurisdiction of the manorial lordship of this place.

§ XII. The hereditary lessee and his successors in

possession is entitled to alienate his holding to another in any manner he pleases; but at each sale or exchange a sum of money must be rendered to the ground lordship as a transfer fee (Laudemium), and the consent of the same must be obtained for every alienation, inasmuch as the ground lordship hereby reserves to itself once and for all the right of pre-emption.

§ XIII. The hereditary lessee, for himself and his successors in possession, renounces entirely, for the present and for the future, each and every remission in cases of misfortune, whether these arise through fire from heaven, arson by evil persons, hailstorm, crop failure, cattle plague, inundation, war and pestilence, or in whatsoever manner it may be; and in the event of such cases neither any compensation nor remis-

sion of the hereditary rent shall take place.

§ XIV. All the costs pertaining to this contract the hereditary lessee undertakes to settle.

§ XV. His Most Serene Highness consents that the hereditary lessee may, on the ground of this contract, have his title of possession entered for himself.

§ XVI. So long as the hereditary lessee and his successors in possession shall fulfil all the obligations contained in this contract, His Most Serene Highness promises to maintain them in their rights

and to defend them against any man's real claim. Should, however, the hereditary lessee or his successor remain in arrears with the annual hereditary rent for longer than two years, or else lay this holding waste and thereby diminish the revenues of the ground lordship, then the ground lordship shall be entitled to dispose of this holding otherwise, and the hereditary lessee forfeits his whole right and the entry money he has paid in. Both parties promise to keep this hereditary-lease contract firmly and inviolably; having been instructed by the court as to the consequences, they renounce all

evasions available against it, in particular the objection of an injury suffered above or below the half, of cunning persuasion, fear, compulsion, of matters otherwise agreed than written down, or not rightly understood; they apply for this contract to be issued in judicial form, and, after it had first been read aloud to them word for word, have in token of their approval subscribed it below with their own hands.

von Triebenfeld Gottlieb Sarre

Ogrodowicz

191

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Lord, After I have lain here 5 weeks with the present gall [fever] and have barely escaped death, my first concern is to put Your Serene Highness au fait of everything, how your affairs stand here. I must therefore, if with the weakness still pressing upon me I shall be able to recall it all, begin from Berlin. There I departed a few days before Midsummer with the assurance that I should receive so much out of the justice fund as to be able to pay Oppenheimer with 110,000 Rthl. and to get the mortgage book clear. Then it was intended to pay Lichnowski the 40,000 Rthl. still coming to him against jura cessa; further to hand over to Grotowski the remainder, 20,000 Rthl., against the adding of his instruments.

Finally, to satisfy Haugt on the very same footing on account of his claims of 18,000 Rthl., and Secher Thoss[?] with 8,000 Rthl.,

likewise the Prusimska with 8,000 Rthl.

To Zerboni, Eysenhardt and Seehausen, the old Mr Radzinski was to be paid with 24,000 Rthl., because the villain does not render his rent but only keeps making chicanery.

It was still my trouble to raise, for the Countess Schlabrendorff, [uncertain: also] for that creature the Prusimska, 8,000 Rthl., together 33,000 Rthl., and in particular to gather something for Your Serene Highness. Also indeed to render the interest to the Invalids' Fund on the 50,000 Rthl. promptly, so that credit might be won; this must together amount to 311,000 Rthl.,

and more debts you have not here, for all the others are discharged and stand under the 110,000 Rthl. In the meantime, Your Serene Highness has on the other hand, as the table states, 184,000 Rthl. to take in by degrees, and there remain owing on the estates only the 40,263 Rthl. which would yield annually = 127,000 Rthl.

So, as said overleaf, [I went] from Berlin before Midsummer to Pszczew, to whom the Rader of the Jews, Meyer Bernhard, had brought 3 or 4 suits against Your Serene Highness, because nothing was yet known of the Royal approval concerning the Pszczew matter.

In Pszczew I communicated the news to the people, settled accounts with them, likewise paid Echaust old court costs, and after these the burgesses and residents still owed Your Serene Highness 4,000 Rthl., which they must pay at Michaelmas. Meanwhile I learned, to my horror, that an execution decree had been sent from Poznań to Trąbczyn, by which (since Metzer had noticed nothing) the Prusimska was to be paid 10,000 Rthl. dowry together with interest and costs, thus together some 22,000 Rthl.

I therefore hastened as best I could to Kalisz and proved, by the documents procured for me by Rapacki, that Prusimski had already paid that dowry in part; by this I did indeed gain time, but the matter hangs, and a year and a day may pass again before I bring it clear. Only this is certain, that even those 16,000 Rthl. entered in the tables may no longer be paid in full, let alone the 22,000 Rthl. From Kalisz I went to Trąbczyn, where I now confidently believed I should find some 30,000 Rthl. But, o heaven, how startled I was when instead of money I found a thousand confusions, knaveries, and consequently empty [coffers] — the earlier[?] ones all declared themselves insolvent — made out great accounts on account of the exorbitant deliveries, carting and quartering under the Russians and Prussians, so that the rents of 2 years would still have gone out on it.

The old peasants who had been put on quit-rents had ceased, and had, despite all judicial contracts, approvals by the Chamber and by His Royal Majesty himself, again abandoned the grounds assigned to them, and — certainly with the connivance of the tenants, so that these knaves might believe themselves entitled to make a so much the greater account — had again

appropriated their former grounds and sown them, and thereby almost dissolved the demesne farms — indeed in the end they even drove off the German colonists already settled, so that I could count neither on the stipulated entry moneys from these, still less on quit-rents. On top of all this Schand had kept silent and gave himself out for dead of gangrene when I wished to call him to account. I asked this Massette for advice as to what was to be done in the matter — his answer was to let the affair take its course, and to report it to the Government, to throw a lawsuit round the necks of the tenants and the subjects.

Question: Have you proceeded so well in the Floricke, Ribbeck and Szczucki matter?

Ans.: No, but it cannot be done otherwise. Question: How long do you believe the lawsuit can last before the matter comes clear?

Ans.: Well, some 2 to 3 years.

Question: Does the gentleman understand Russian?

He: No!

I: Well then, I will show it to him. With me one spits such lazy scribblers in the face, lets him run, and acts alone.

Upon this I went to Trąbczyn and summoned the tenant Honrichs before me with his contract.

To the question whether he could pay the rent sum now falling due, of 2,000 Rthl., and also at once render the remainder of the 800 Rthl., he answered — No. He believed, he added, that he owed nothing either, for he had over 5,000 Rthl. in claims

and I believe he is a scoundrel. He pays, or within an hour he lies with his affair over the Warthe. By this first tone the fellow was put out of countenance[?] and began to plead.

Upon this I gave way, that if he at once surrendered the lease contract, let the claims fall, and paid the 2,800 Rthl. at Christmas on forfeit of his whole property, he might still sit this year; yet it must be free to me to dismember as much, and when I pleased, of the demesne farm of Trąbczyn. To this he agreed; the contract for 6 years was annulled and in its place a one-year contract drawn up, with the condition that as soon as he had reaped I might dismember the demesne farm; whereupon Honrichs undertook himself to recruit purchasers who should give 600 Rthl. per Hufe / consequently 2 to 300 Rthl. more than hitherto /, in return for which I conceded to him that the grounds which should be [uncertain: Dummabredt] need not be improved again, and also promised him to place him in Your Serene Highness's service with 400 Rthl. yearly salary, if he would faithfully effect this and in particular help bring the peasants and the other tenants to reason. After this operation I at once had all the residents belonging to Trąbczyn summoned together. When the peasants saw that the tenant stood ready on my side already with the whip — then their courage too fell away, and within an hour this work was so ordered to Your Serene Highness's advantage that neither devil nor saint can have anything against it in eternity. The peasants soon paid their half-yearly quit-rent and vowed to lay down the other half at Christmas. Now I went with Honrichs to

Świątniki. Here sat von Zglinski with his two gaping fools of sons.

There the peasants had sown a great part of the manorial fields and, in league with the tenant, had so confused everything that I myself shuddered to penetrate into this [uncertain: Labirath]. Under the contract von Zglinski was to pay 1,500 Rthl. The contract ran for 12 years, and contained among its clauses the provision that, should the tenant not pay on the term day, the contract should at once be null and void, and the tenant bound to vacate immediately, but to pursue any claims he might have by course of law. Now I asked this Sarmatian whether he would pay; his answer was — I shall not only not pay, but shall sit here so long until I know my claims, which amount to 5,700 Rthl., satisfied; and moreover I insist that the grounds which the peasants hold in possession, but which were previously assigned to me, be handed over to me at once.

At this [uncertain: summons] all the peasants also appeared and declared that they would not give up the grounds, even if the Prince and the King himself should come; they were born and bred on these grounds and would never vacate them. I represented to the fellows that they had settled everything judicially, that the Prince had made them a gift of their freedom, had besides given them the inventory gratis, that their quit-rent was insignificant compared with that of the colonists, that even the houses and buildings had been given them into the bargain,

whereas the colonist must first laboriously [clear] all the soil and build everything at his own cost. — Meanwhile my talking availed nothing; it was much more like oil to put out a fire. Since, however, I had marked the spokesmen and had at the same time perceived which of them drew near to von Zglinski and his sons, I had one of these step forward, threw him down and had 50 strokes of the whip counted out to him — the fellow did not endure them quite to the end, for Honrichs flogs like the best Cossack general — he begged for mercy; notwithstanding, I let it go on, but at the 43rd the beast fainted. I had him doused with water, and when he came to himself had him led aside and the next one brought forward. I threw him down too; Honrichs with every stroke tore breeches and hide apart — this took effect, and he cried for mercy and promised to report. I had them stop, and to the question what he had to say he then declared that all three communities had been set on by Zglinski, Niedźwiecki and the people of Oleśnica. The [uncertain: Schatz] and several others, particularly the people of Kopojno who had likewise come in beneath, confirmed this — they confessed themselves deserving of punishment, but begged imploringly for forgiveness and declared themselves content with the grounds assigned to them. In the meantime, however, they had to complain of the justiciary: he had always turned them away when they wished to lay a complaint before him or to ask for orders of conduct; on the other hand he had always stood together with the noblemen and lived in merriment with them. After this coup of mine, which succeeded, I at once sent to Schanden and had him bidden come to me immediately, so that in his presence the peasants' ground might be properly bounded, and separated for eternity from the manorial and colonists' grounds.

He appeared in the shape of the most crushed wretch, and the work too was begun and happily completed; only Schenck remained halfway

and substituted a certain Ogrodowitz. Perhaps the scoundrel will croak and death free us from this hypocrite.

After this too had been happily settled, I went at the tenant again by the throat, who, since he was unmasked, [uncertain: took it to heart] and [saw] the complete failure of his plans; he therefore asked for pardon, which I could not give; so he surrendered the contract and withdrew in apparent [fashion] — I had his grain reaped and sold for 260 Rthl., and [I am] now [offering] the demesne farm, which consists of 30 Hufen of land and meadow, the Hufe at 600 Rthl. entry money and 15 Rthl. yearly quit-rent — now it comes to this, that Honrichs soon gets purchasers for it, for through the tenant's infamy nothing has been lost here either, but much gained. After this the tenant of Kopojno had to step forward; he, warned by those proceedings, soon asked for fair weather — his accounts likewise came to some 6,000 Rthl. He brought them down, however, to 1,125, which I had to accept, since the district councillor had all but flayed the people; but in return he too had to cancel the contract and grant it only for 1 year, for which he must pay 2,500 Rthl. at Christmas, and against which I may also at once have it dismembered. The peasants of Skokum, who had been incited by that gang of rogues from Oleśnica and Wrąbczyn, had likewise to lie down at the mark, after Honrichs, because they had secretly pulled apart the boundary mounds, but had luckily been caught by them, had counted out 30 strokes of the whip to each. Now on this side everything is in order, and the Germans are gradually coming in again.

The old malicious Titz too, who has leased Drzewce, promises to render the rent; only the fellow will bring 600 Rthl. into deduction as the 2 years' pension which Your Serene Highness is said to have assured him with 300 Rthl. for his lifetime.

I did not know what there is in this; may Your Serene Highness deign to instruct me upon it. In the records here nothing is to be found except the accompanying certified copies, which are taken from Titz's original pieces, and according to these the old [uncertain: Inachten] has nothing to demand.

All these affairs I had concluded within the space of 6 days, and I was at pains to have the Germans, who had some 40,000 Rthl. to pay, sought out together in order to obtain money to pay the interest, to satisfy the [uncertain: Schluß Arendorffen], and to gather something for Your Serene Highness. But this did not succeed — many of the old ones did indeed show themselves, but always vanished again. Newer purchasers were to come, but always drew back timorously again. At this failure of my plans I so vexed and grieved myself that of a sudden a violent gall fever came upon me, which has compelled me to keep my bed now these 5 weeks. Only these 2 days is it improving, and I can now think and work more again. Meanwhile everything still looks very motley, and prospers only so far as the long time in bed, violent headache and the great weakness permit.

[uncertain: Weigens] I shall, as soon as I am certainly back, and if possible have appeased the Schlabrendorff woman, go again to Berlin — for here it might take too long before I bring together anything appreciable. The notorious Glenck, who has hatched a true conspiracy against me and Your Serene Highness, is, as I have just learned, and what came out during my illness, talking all purchasers away with his gang — he has been staying here already over 6 or 7 weeks — he has joined himself with the three rogues of Oleśnica, with a certain Kramplich, with Flöricke, Ribbeck, with a certain Bergemann and more such rabble, in order to frustrate all my plans.

To attain his purpose he has made a lampoon upon me and given such to people who wish to buy, who have taken it with them as far as the Mark, and thereby at the same time frightened back others who wished to come here

and settle themselves. His clerk by the name of Meyer, who lives here on the Wrąbczyn village bailiwick, has fallen out with him and during my illness reported him to Schmid. The latter, perhaps to ingratiate himself again, sent me the lampoon yesterday evening.

The content is as stupid and tasteless as the fellow himself is; only the rascal has attained his purpose of hindering my plans and harming the good cause. He thinks I shall tire and go off, and then he would have to come back because nobody would be there.

The wretch is offering his estate for sale and means to dismember it himself; he always draws the people who wish to come and buy here aside to himself, talks them away from here as aforesaid, and when in the end he can give no judicial contracts, against which the peasants of Wrąbczyn always protest, then the people go back and think they would only be cheated in Your Serene Highness's estates. I am urged to denounce the fellow to the fiscal authority, or at least to throw an action for defamation round his neck — I shall not do it — the villain has harmed Your Serene Highness more than me. I therefore submit this to Your Serene Highness's judgement. For the rest, deign, most gracious Lord, to tell me whether the yearly quit-rents ought not to be demanded of the fellow. He has not yet given a single kreuzer, but assures everyone that he settles accounts on that score with Your Serene Highness alone.

The outstanding quit-rents are said to amount already to over 400 Rthl., and even this is a motive for throwing the fellow out

and taking the village bailiwick back in again, particularly if his own clerk will prove that he has for some years constantly appropriated to himself all the [grass] from the Wrąbczyn meadows, amounting to several hundred Morgen, and has even taken quit-rents from the komorniks living there.

The bailiwick itself is fully paid for with 4,000 Rthl.; the 300 Morgen would indeed be worth nearly as much, only these cannot be assured to him, for there are peasants' meadows lying in them at every turn, and then a costly lawsuit is unavoidable — the wretch has nastily misled Your Serene Highness in the granting of the 300 Morgen — the rogue has forgotten that he sold within the Wrąbczyn boundary some 10 Hufen to 4 Kashubians for a trifle and took the money; so, if the cursed contract with the peasants is to be kept, nothing remains. I greatly fear that Your Serene Highness will yet get a costly lawsuit out of this [uncertain: Schwedenstrei-], for it was just now said that Glenck has sold the bailiwick to the [uncertain: Schulweische] Giese in Oleśnica.

Now the fellow has so nastily prompted you that you sell him the 300 Morgen for 300 Rthl. and allow him to dismember — if Giese buys, then he will at once go judicially against Your Serene Highness — my advice at the time was good, to give the fellow 4,000 and let him run.

With the Oleśnica fellows the [uncertain: man] has brought Your Serene Highness into such great misfortune, and as they say he is supposed to have secretly given the [uncertain: Bessinn] testimonies by which they will win the lawsuit. For this man's sake the matter here is most disagreeable to me

As concerns the revenues and the sums which Your Serene Highness has to receive from the estates here now and in future, you will perceive these from the accompanying table. I believe you can, when all this shall have been settled, be very well content with it.

Since, for the rest, the lazy Schenck means, as he says, to croak, the councillor of war von H[e?]llen will be so good as to come here from Kalisz once every 4 weeks and look over everything that happens here, without his demanding a Groschen. Also, since Schenck now wishes to have himself brought at once to an abbot at Poznań, I shall immediately hand over the cash-box to Honrichs and Cabanis; these two shall not be permitted to do anything one without the other, and there is therefore nothing to be feared. I think too to be here again about Michaelmas, when many have now promised to pay. In deepest reverence I remain, until death, Your Serene Highness's faithful and most obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Trąbczyn, the 6th of Aug 1806.

This moment I receive in advance from the privy councillor von Tesmar in Berlin the glad news that 360,000 Rthl. are to be had. Oh, if only I could travel first. I am again today

very ill —

the 7th of Aug.
oe1bu9454-192:
192

My dear friend, there are 360,000 Rthl lying in Berlin which have been promised to me. Only I lie here and have been keeping to my bed into the fifth week; I have vexed myself here quite to ruin. Meanwhile I have now put everything here in order and entirely calmed the peasants who had been stirred up by arch-rogues, and have also driven the tenants to the devil. When God or devils and hell-brands of men play me crosswise tricks, so that I must perish of [uncertain: Argus schien] — then all glory is at an end — Glenck is here, has joined together with the Oleśnica hell-brands and has engaged for the purpose a certain Kramplitz, Bergemann and Ribbeck, the [text lost] gang of hell stirs the people up and turns the buyers away; it is too mad how it goes with me. If meanwhile my constitution recovers and I am well again, then the devil take all the rascals. The tenants are, as said before, all gone to the devil, and from Christmas and Midsummer onward everything must be so understood that only monies may be raised, and that nothing more may come up for expenditure. Mr Weigel will be paid, for which I had it, since I receive the money from the Justice Fund for Weigel and Lichnowski; these must cede their mortgages and receive their money. I have already said this to the witnesses Mr Weigel also; but while I lie here in misery I cannot act in Berlin; as soon as I recover somewhat I shall come to Wrocław and go at once with my daughters to Berlin

From here I can as yet draw nothing, but from Michaelmas onward much money should come in by degrees. It would have been easy to obtain money here if I had been willing to give away the plots of land for a [uncertain: third part] of the price, but from that God preserve me — Now the Prince will still receive 190,000 Rthl in cash and 40,000 Rthl in yearly revenues in perpetuity. The Prince has already received 10,000 Rthl from Swięcia, 10,000 Rthl from Oleśnica, 12,000 Rthl from Szetlewek, and 9,000 Rthl have been given for grounds, all of which has gone on the costs and interest and also on old debts. The peasants' revolution and the Glenck knaveries have had their use — I have indeed had to give a good deal back, but now it has turned out all the better and the more abundant for it. Enough; everything will go well — if only I am well again first — writing comes very hard to me. So only this further, that I am unceasingly.

Yours. On the whole Koszęcin affair I must suspend my judgement, for I do not know it — As it seems to me, what is wanting is a man who knows the locality thoroughly, and rather a deal of money — the [uncertain: Stös:] praise is suspect to me — Well evaded — the Pro Memoria of the Koszęcin officials give sufficient[illegible]

guidance.

The enclosed lampoon Glenck has made upon me and had distributed among the colonists who wish to buy; the original I have sent to His Serene Highness — It was drafted and dealt out by Glenck's own high hand. Trąbczyn

12th August

1806

Humble friend and servant

von Triebenfeld

To the Oleśnica [uncertain: Schluzbuben] he has, to be sure, given certificates and helped to support their cause, and for that they have promised him to sell him the bailiwick. Yesterday the judgement came down upon the fellows:

1. [uncertain: Fenſe] may not evict the fellows

2. he is to discharge the debts encumbering Oleśnica

3. he is to apply for the consent.

4. When that is given, to have the hereditary lease entered in the mortgage book,

6. but Giese is dismissed, in that the Prince may not hand over the estates to him before the consent has hitherto been issued. That is a sentence at which the dogs might howl. I shall now at once apply to the authority for the consent; then the resolution will be that such scoundrels may not possess noble estates, and the Chamber will throw them out; then all the feud will be at an end.

Right Honourable Sir,

Highly Honoured Sir, Privy Councillor!

Through the colonisation of my South Prussian lordships of Zagórów and Trąbczyn, carried out with Royal approval, a net yield of the same amounting to 40,247 Rthl has been ascertained, and after careful examination has been confirmed by the Kalisz Chamber of War and Domains.

This might put me in a position to bring my so long sought wish to fulfilment, and to arrange my debt affairs entirely. It depends, however, on whether it is possible to obtain a sum of 400,000 Rthl, namely as much as all my debts without exception amount to, in one single lot, against which I would then pledge the two aforenamed lordships, establish complete security thereupon with a first and sole mortgage, and would also fix a yearly sum for the payment of the interest and the amortisation of the capital, whereby this debt might be discharged in a few years.

I most humbly request Your Right Honourable to undertake this business and, with your extensive acquaintance, to negotiate a loan of this kind. The power of attorney necessary for the purpose I shall transmit by the first post in any form you please. I have also instructed my general attorney to deliver to the same at once all the documents needful for the prosecution of this business, and to pay out without delay, for the men of business [uncertain: Geschlußsmanner] concurring in these affairs, a [illegible]gratuity[illegible] of 5 per cent as soon as the matter [uncertain: versteht]. With the most perfect esteem I am Your Right Honourable's F[riedrich] L[udwig], P[rince] o[f] Hohenlohe. Freyberg, the 25th of September

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Lord!

An unforeseen event made it necessary that, after Your Serene Highness's departure from Berlin, I should hasten with all speed to Zagórów, because the peasants had once again stirred up a rising and would not permit the separation of the lands in the interior. This matter is now indeed settled and entirely arranged; however, much as I hurried back here again, the King had departed before I returned, and since my patron had naturally gone off with him, I could no longer reckon upon that fund. I was therefore obliged to take other paths in order to obtain the money for Weigel, for the Countess Schlabrendorff and for Your Serene Highness. This has only now, today, been assured through the councillor of justice Bucholz. This man conducts the affairs of a certain von Bredow, who has 80,000 Rthl lying with the Maritime Trading Company here, which he has ordered to be placed elsewhere / since the Minister von Stein, His Excellency, would now give only 3 per cent /.

Mr Bucholz has turned the matter thus: Upon Konotop, against cession of the two mortgages, there will be given 30,000 Rthl. Upon Świniary the 20,000. Upon Trąbczyn, for the Grotowski mortgage which Weigel holds, 30,000. Of this there are to be paid, being = 80,000 Rthl: To the Countess Schlabrendorff the 25,000 still coming to her; To Weigel the 25,000 still due to him.

To Hahn, as assistance in Koszęcin, 5,000.

To Your Serene Highness in cash 5,000.

I take for myself, for the payment of the Wulffen debt, 30,000

in return for which Your Serene Highness will then give me a note or mortgage for 30,000 Rthl, as being the amount I am raising on my own estates for Your Highness! Next to this, the privy councillor von Tesmar is pursuing a negotiation with the rich house of Nathusius at Magdeburg, in which he hopes to obtain a capital of 360,000 Rthl upon the whole of the South Prussian estates. With this all the debts are to be paid, and the mortgage of 250,000 Rthl [uncertain: refused] with Oppenheimer for 98,000 Rthl is in particular to be redeemed and cancelled. When all this shall have been seen to and brought to a clear footing, then I myself to Your Serene Highness and bring you the moneys or good orders to pay. With the sale of the lands things go somewhat slowly on account of the warlike events; meanwhile Honrichs writes to me yesterday that several purchasers had once again come forward who would buy at the newly fixed prices. Once this business at the new higher prices is properly under way, then, since all the hindrances are now removed, much money will be brought together, and an end will be made of all cares.

May God grant Your Serene Highness the most lasting health and bestow upon you (when it comes to blows, victory! This is the sole and most heartfelt wish of Your Most Serene Highness's

faithful and most obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Berlin, the 28th of September 1806.
oe1bu9454-26:
26

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

That Your Most Serene Highness has escaped with his life from the most dreadful danger I learn from a letter of Secretary Koppe. My grief on that account was boundless, the more so as so many malicious rumours were spread abroad, which gave the matter an aspect a million times worse than it now really is. I lived in the hope that all must go happily. I was on the point of travelling to Your Serene Highness, and to that end had requested 8,000 Rthl of His Excellency the Minister von Stein upon a Konotop mortgage, because at present it is hard to obtain even 10 Rthl out of South Prussia. When all at once the news came in of the defeat of our army. My sole endeavour now was to learn whither Your Serene Highness had turned. The cavalry captain von Dorville assured me that Your Serene Highness had gone to Silesia. The very same was averred by the President of the General Post Office, von Seegebarth, with the addition that Your Serene Highness had gone with few people towards Żagań. I therefore had an order to pay of 6,000 Rthl drawn on Wrocław made out to me, and took 2,000 Rthl in treasury notes, and hastened with them to that corner, where I then saw myself wholly deceived — full of grief I went

to Wrocław and was just taking counsel with Hahn as to what was to be done, when I received the express courier from Secretary Koppe out of Szczecin. My joy was now greater than my grief had been before, and I thank God only that you live.

Meanwhile, in this haste, I can do nothing further than to remit to Your Serene Highness the order to pay for the 6,000 Rthl, which His Excellency the Minister von Stein, who is assuredly your true friend, will surely have paid out there at once in cash. As soon as I then have news where Your Serene Highness is certainly to be found, I shall bring you a further 4,000 Rthl.

These, however, are not monies out of South Prussia, but sums borrowed upon the pledged Konotop mortgage. Neither do I know whether we shall soon have money out of South Prussia, where the devil has got into all their heads. I shall therefore have to approach the most upright Minister von Stein once again, that he give me money upon a Świniary mortgage of 20,000 Rthl. In short, whatever I can raise I shall bring to Your Serene Highness.

If the Russians come after this, then there is no want in Poland; there I shall take the whip of my countrymen to my aid, and there I shall indeed get money again — To the Minister von Stein I had written a letter on a blank sheet — that Your Serene Highness requested him to be obliging to von Triebenfeld whenever he should apply for anything on your most high behalf

This letter I delivered, was at once called in and asked what I wished — I handed over the petition, that 8,000 Rthl be lent me upon the Konotop mortgage of 10,000 Rthl. This the honest man granted at once, and glad at heart I meant to hasten with this little sum to Your Serene Highness when the sad tidings came in. I had had an order to pay drawn only on Leipzig for Your Serene Highness; this until I then re-write it and give the order to pay on myself to the Wrocław bank — Now I send this order to pay by express courier to Mr Koppe, so that he may quickly receive these monies and convey them to Your Serene Highness. As soon as I now learn whither Your Most High Self turns, I shall, as said before, bring more. Just now I receive news out of the Cabinet from a certain person, that Your Serene Highness's conduct and valour is praised above all things; how great a part I take in this I need not depict to Your Serene Highness at length. At the same time I have thereby gained great hope that they will give Your Serene Highness the Kolzig estates. If this succeeds for me, then I shall soon procure 100,000 Rthl, which you may apply anywhere you please; then we should have no need to seek foreign credit.

God grant Your Serene Highness further victory and keep Your Most High Self in health and well-being, and so I remain, until death,

Your Serene Highness's

faithful, most humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 28th of October 1806.
agad1174016-1:
Order for the execution of the Imperial Decree commanding the return of the Estates confiscated from the Most Illustrious Wybicki by the past Government

The Governing Commission

July the 12th

Sending to the Honourable Director of Internal Affairs, in an Authentic Copy certified by the signature of Our President, the Decree of the Most Serene Emperor of the French and King of Italy, issued at Finckenstein on 5 June of this year, which returns to the Most Illustrious Wybicki, Our Colleague, the Possession of the Estates of Maniezki, Przylepki, Boreczek and Esterpol, which had been sequestrated from him in the Department of Poznań,

and which the Prussian Government had disposed of, and which charges the Provisional Polish Government with its execution; We instruct the said Honourable Director of Internal Affairs to proceed without delay to the execution of this Imperial Decree, to order the Administrative Chamber of the Department of Poznań to hand over the Estates named above for the Most Illustrious Wybicki, and to instruct that he be put into possession of those Estates without delay. — Done at Warsaw at the Session of 12 July 1807.

Stanisław Małachowski, President

Jan Łuszczewski, Secretary General
agad11740273-2:
I have had the honour to submit my petition twice to the Governing Commission with the aim of recovering the estates: Trąbczyn in the Department of Kalisz; Kamionna, Kolno, Pawłowo, Pawłówko, the Storehouse at Wrocławku, in the Department of Poznań, confiscated from my father for the benefit of the Prussian Generals, the Prince of Hohenlo[h]e, Bischoffwerder and Zanitz; having as yet received no answer in my matter, and knowing that the Most Illustrious Wybicki has had his estates, confiscated just as mine were, given back to him by the Most Serene Emperor and King, I make bold to ask the Governing Commission to deign to intercede for me, and at the same time to give me the opportunity of obtaining the judgment of justice which the Most Illustrious Wybicki was fortunate enough to win for himself from the Most Serene Emperor.

Dresden, 20 July 1807

Michalina Dambska, née Prusimska

[Written by the receiving office:]

Presented 21 July

Whereas the matter of Mrs Michalina Dąbska, née Pru[simska], who demands the return of her hereditary Estates, confiscated under the past Government and given to someone else, has been referred to Us by the Most Serene Emperor; taking example from the justice dispensed by His Imperial and Royal Majesty to the Most Illustrious Wybicki, Our Colleague, by the Decree issued at Finckenstein on the [5]th of June, and wishing in so just a demand to preserve strict justice for everyone, We extend the Judgment of the Most Serene Emperor in favour of the Most Illustrious Wybicki both to the case of Mrs Michalina Dąbska and to those of General Niemoiewski and Mr Wichrowski, desiring that the Hereditary Estates of the Persons named above, confiscated by the late Prussian Government, should return to their true Owners. — Done at Dresden, 21 July 1807.

agad11740273-3:
Sire!

I have already taken the very humble Liberty of having the statement of my complaints and my hopes presented to Your Imperial and Royal Majesty through the Polish Government; but having so far received no news of the Decree that would reinstate me in the Lands which were confiscated for the benefit of the Prussian Generals Prince Hohenlo[h]e, Bischoffwerder and Zanitz, and being persuaded, nevertheless, that the same Justice which pronounced in the cause of Count Wybicki, reinstating him in his possessions, will be rendered to me by the Greatest and most Magnanimous of Monarchs, I dare to Beseech Your Imperial and Royal Majesty not to refuse it to me.

I am, with the most profound respect,

Sire,

Your Imperial and Royal Majesty's

Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Lord!

I hasten to convey to Your Most Serene Highness the unwelcome news that the Trąbczyn estates were taken over on the 3rd of this month by a commissary of the Court of Appeal at Kalisz, namely the appeal judge von Lipski, and have been handed over to the general attorney of Mrs von Dąbska, née von Prusimska, the canon von Jezierski.

The order that was issued states that this taking-over is done by decree of the governing Commission. I have been able to do nothing further in the matter than to protest against the taking-over by a submitted representation, and also to invoke therein that this act runs counter to the plain content of the Peace of Tilsit,

according to which all obligations of His Majesty the King of Prussia must be upheld; likewise I asked for a copy of the decree of the governing Commission by which the taking-over was ordered, in order to see the legal grounds; but this has not to this day been granted me. Lastly, by a protestation I have reserved to Your Serene Highness all remaining rights in these estates, particularly on account of the debts paid.

Your Most Serene Highness will best know what is now to be done, for with the governing Commission at Warsaw nothing is likely to be achieved, since estates have been confiscated from some of its members, and thus their own interest guides them. Next, Your Most Serene Highness has again been drawn into 2[uncertain: 2] lawsuits.

In the first, the provost Iwanski and Kuchary demand the tithe (Decem) of Swięcia, which suit he lost in the first instance in the Prussian period, as

I have informed myself from the manual records. Copy. Your Most Serene Highness's most gracious letter I received here in Berlin; I should long since have answered the same, had I not been held under arrest under strict French guard. A fate I never deserved, and one which has given my civil existence a very crooked turn.

At the end of December I was sent here from Memel with weighty commissions, and I was already near the goal of my wishes, so as to be able to depart again shortly, when, without my suspecting it, two French gendarmes were sent into my lodgings with the order "that they should hold me under strict watch and arrest until I, as general attorney of the Prince of Hohenlohe, should have paid all the arrears of interest on the 50,000 Rthl borrowed from the Invalids' Fund." Terror and shame at this occurrence nearly brought me to the most desperate resolution; the arrears of interest amounted for 2 years to 5,000 Rthl — whence was I to take these, amid the dreadful want of money, in order to [uncertain: seinehe], since there are no Royal treasuries here, and all revenues are in the hands of the French authorities. I proved, with all the jurists, that I was not the debtor. I produced the judicial instrument showing that the banker Oppenheimer had, against a discount of 7 per cent, already 3 years ago undertaken to pay this item to the Invalids' Fund, that he had had it entered in his

name, and that he must pay. I proved further that Your Serene Highness yourself had for 2 years drawn not a [uncertain: denia] from the estates, and that the Poles took cover behind the order given by Napoleon to pay nothing hither. But all of this availed nothing: the Jew, at liberty, bought himself off, and I had to sit until means were found. I had 2,000 Rthl with me; the upright Lieutenant General and Minister

von Zastrow gave surety for 5,000 Rthl in paper money, which we then converted into Courant and received 2,875 Rthl for it, but for which we must pay back 5,000 Rthl Courant on the 1st of June; and not until the last Pfennig had been paid was I freed from the execution and released from my arrest. Meanwhile, through this affair, not only have my honour, standing and credit been diminished, but the highest interest has been so far neglected that it can never be redressed. I cannot now, for honour's sake, remove myself from here until I have found means for the 5,000 Rthl together with interest and costs, for I cannot let any unpleasantness arise for the honest Minister von Zastrow. Meanwhile I know of no other course than that Your Serene Highness should, as soon as possible, send me back the bank order to pay of 6,000 Rthl which You most highly ceded to Eysenhardt,

so that I may take back the [uncertain: Kontazen] mortgage of 10,000 pledged for it from the possession, and thereby help myself. But may Your Serene Highness be pleased to endorse the order to pay over to me, or yourself to note upon it that You have drawn no money upon it and have sent the same back. I shall then press at once for the return of my mortgage, and hope in exchange to obtain the money here from a certain General's wife von Blucher, in order to satisfy the banker, or in cash. Your Serene Highness's humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

I regret nothing more than that this could not have happened 4 days earlier, since the Count was just then passing through here on his way to Erfurt, and it would have been an easy matter for me to attach myself to him and to make that tour with him. Today it is useful to set out upon the road to Erfurt, because it is quite uncertain how long the two Emperors will tarry there; besides, I also lack the ready money to make the journey thither, and with empty hands nothing can be done there. Moreover I believe that at Erfurt not everything will yet be decided; I mean that there they will only first draft everything and then deal out the cards for play — It depends upon who plays along, and whether the greatest player does not, quite as much as our Lord, lose his game codille. The alliance between England, Sweden, Austria and Turkey is considerable, and may perhaps compel Russia to steps which it does not now suspect it will take. My striving and endeavour is only that Your Most Serene Highness might be set again in the right place, and to that end I shall in quiet contribute everything possible

I was on the road to Königsberg but had to turn back hither again. Now I am seeking to borrow some thousands in money, and with these I shall watch for the return of the 2 Emperors and the Grand Duke. To these I shall attach myself and go with them wherever it may be, cost what it will. Through the Grand Duke above all I shall work on Your Serene Highness's behalf — I have gained experience, and this I shall put to use, and when the principal affairs of the monarchs have been transacted, to beg the Grand Duke so long until he advances your cause; I have too often made the observation that with great lords it is he who speaks last who carries the day — Hjostein has now sunk low, and I believe that Your Serene Highness's affairs will now shortly take the happiest turn. Before this man came forward and took the helm in hand, the King and the Queen were very well disposed towards Your Serene Highness, and at that time I hoped for the best. But as soon as Mr von Stein spoke ambiguously of the command you had conducted, the tone of the court changed also. Meanwhile I believe there will now soon be a complete want of men who can steer the helm sensibly. Therefore they will surely look about again for the one man whom nature herself has [uncertain: pult] to homage, and will have to endeavour to fetch him hither. The hypocritical Kalckreuth will to the old W. and was to step forward. There is no one in the State who has meant so honestly by the King as Your Serene Highness. Everyone joins to his actions only his own interest and seeks to line his pockets

to line. All tread softly so as to keep themselves in their places and to feed themselves well. There is none who tells the monarch the truth and goes straight at it. Count Lottom[?] and Count Palzen are a pair of upright men, but both must proceed with the utmost caution, because otherwise they might easily be laid aside in the skat — My unpresumptuous counsel is that Your Serene Highness now do nothing at Erfurt but wait to see what will happen in the great matters, for things will not remain as they are, as surely as there is a God, and everything may change in a flash — the sole endeavour of Your Serene Highness and of your adherents must now be that you first come back into your place. Why will you not go to Silesia? I should do it, and should notify the King that I was there and that I would come to him. I stake my life upon it — if the King seeks Your Serene Highness again, then everything is at once back in its track — all the more if Constantin or the Emperor shall have prepared something beforehand. You know the King: he has not the heart to propose anything to you, most gracious Lord. Besides, he now holds himself to be poor and stripped of everything; but if you can come to meet him and tell him that you will now help and advise, yet will not for a while be burdensome to him, then he will idolise Your Serene Highness — What a piece of good fortune it would be if you were at present in Königsberg when the Emperor returns. Everything would go better and would be negotiated with more courage.

The present entourage of the K. would be mightily alarmed at your appearance, but soon everyone would bow deeply before you and Triebenfeld

deeply — let Your Serene Highness take this well to heart, procure where it is possible some thousands together and then go this road courageously — You will not fail, as surely as there is a God — the South Prussian affairs are, as I have written to Your Serene Highness before, set in the best train; the French government has lifted a part of the sequestration and has ordered the revenues to be released. The matter has been sent to Warsaw to the French chargé d'affaires, so that he may make it known to the Ministry of Justice with the intimation that the moneys are to be let pass unhindered. As soon as this has been made public from Warsaw at Kalisz, I shall see to it that you receive moneys from there.

The letters to Lichnowski and Metzig are good and entirely suited to the business. Lichnowski belongs at Trąbczyn and there he must wait until the times change. To Mr Metzig I should write separately besides, and set him to rights in such a manner that he shall long remember it. The burgesses there owe inq various transfer fee (Laudemium) moneys and, of the 4,000 Rthl of remaining purchase sum, over 8 to 9,000 Rthl; why does the villain not drive it in together and report that the money is there — then it would soon be seen how it was to be got out. The rascal did, from my own hands, at that time when he helped to conduct the business with the burgesses, receive 200 Rthl[?] d'or in cash, which I gave the fellow out of my own pocket. Now he must do something for it, or he shall feel it. In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

humble and faithful servant

Peter

Berlin, the 20th September 1808

Today a courier comes from Prince Wilhelm, from whom I shall learn whether the stay at Erfurt is to be of any duration; were that so, then I should go there after all — but if the Emperor Alexander returns next week, then I shall await him at Storkow — where I shall soon be set upon by every solicitation — for the Storkow journey I have kept thirty Friedrich d'or here. — For the great journey I must have at least 400 Friedrich d'or in the cash-box, and these I shall borrow[?] here

Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

If ever a human creature has been pressed down by need and tribulation and whipped through every class of suffering, I am he now. It is now over a year since I was sent hither, in order to effect one thing and another here, and then to return from here by way of Vienna to Königsberg.

Just as I was on the point of departing hence, I was seized by French gendarmerie on the order of the General Government and for that reason placed under strict arrest, namely that I, as Your Serene Highness's authorised representative, was to pay at once to the Invalids' Fund the arrears of interest amounting to 3,521 Rthl. The affair excited a terror by which my honour and credit suffered — Against surety of the councillor of the Chamber Court von Grevenitz and the innkeeper Mathieu I was released from my arrest for 4 weeks, with the observation that within that time I should procure the 3,521 and pay the same, together with costs, in cash in hard Courant to the French Intendant Maluce[uncertain reading], failing which I, together with my sureties, should be taken into arrest anew.

During these 4 weeks, then, the money had to be procured

To obtain this sum in cash was a work of impossibility; I had to take papers at their nominal value, and in exchange promise to pay cash Courant again after 3 months. The honest Minister von Zastrow gave a pledge and no joint bill of exchange, which Grevenitz and I co-signed. The time ran out quickly and the merchant van der Lahr demanded 5,000 Rthl together with interest. For the sake of Mr von Zastrow and Grevenitz I had to find counsel quickly — I therefore took from the dyer Coste 9,000 Rthl in state papers at 6 per cent interest, which were deposited as cover, and with them the Zastrow pledge and the bill of exchange were redeemed — Coste had given me the state papers on the condition that I should return the same to him in precisely such papers. The papers stood very low at that time; I could not sell them, but pledged them, and that again cost heavy percentages and [uncertain: charges].

Meanwhile the 3,000 Rthl from Your Most Serene Highness came in; of this I paid 2,153 Rthl at once in cash to Lahr and bought papers with the remainder. Hecker gave 4,000 Rthl in paper as security; this I pledged again for 1,000 Rthl and paid interest and costs. In order, however, to profit from the speculation as all bank

bankers do, and to get out of the affair, I bought and sold papers to advantage, so that I now have the whole 9,000 Rthl for Coste together again, and nothing further is wanting but the cash interest, amounting to 340 Rthl. Once I have this, this entire sum is discharged and fully settled. Meanwhile Lahr has sued me for the 3,000 Rthl still coming to him, and is impeding my departure.

I have deposited papers for it, but I may not leave until the matter is smoothed out.

By the common law he must now be content with papers. Meanwhile I must pay the difference, and this amounts, first, upon the Coete papers, as said above, to 340 Rthl; second, interest, court and other costs, 568 Rthl.

3. For two bonds on which I still owe the whole bill of exchange, 360 Rthl.

4. For 2 bonds lying in deposit, 800 Rthl; sum total 2,068 Rthl. These 2,068 Rthl must be procured and paid; thereupon this exceedingly fatal business is lifted and settled, and I can travel where I will.

If it is in any way possible for Your Serene Highness in the world, do drive

the same together there and send them in all haste to Konotop; otherwise I cannot stir from the spot — and yet it would be very good if I were permitted to wait upon Your Serene Highness in person — for I myself do not know how to help myself — through this business of my being arrested here I lost credit and health — my creditors awoke on all sides, and to this very day are sequestrating Konotop upon me. I cannot go there myself, for I am under arrest here on Your Serene Highness's account — what pains me most is that Mathieu will in the end still hold back the remainder, since I still owe him 1,500 Rthl Münzer; 2,083 Rthl I have already paid the B —, and 1,500 Rthl still come to him, and on that account the [T?] will not let me travel.

For nearly 6 months I lay, over and above all the vexation, most wretchedly ill, and this business too costs me here some 300 Rthl, which I had to pay the doctor for all of it, and 170 Rthl which I had to pay at the apothecary's. Never has misfortune pursued me as it has this year here. Meanwhile this too will have been got through, if only I receive the 2,068 Rthl so as to be able to bring the Lahr matter entirely into the clear.

For this do find counsel, Your Serene Highness; I beg you heartily and urgently for it, otherwise I cannot get

away from here, and must sit here until help comes. From my estates I now have nothing; the taxes are too oppressive — I do not yet know how I am to be rid of the sequestrator in Konotop, and the longer I sit here the greater is my loss!

The damage I suffer is appalling. Your Serene Highness knows that I never complain, but now the water is up to my throat. I beg you, most gracious Lord, have mercy and see to it that I receive the 2,068 Rthl soon now, so that I may come into freedom. From the French General Government the order has been sent to the Ministry of Justice at Warsaw that the sequestration on account of the Invalids' Fund is to be lifted, and also that the interest extorted from one is to be repaid out of the estates — these Your [uncertain: Serene Highness] can then recover yourself against the original dispositions, and in that way you lose nothing, and may well indemnify me for the covering of the costs I have had here. As to the sequestration otherwise imposed in Zagórów, I have had the proper protestations lodged, and against the Jew Oppenheimer, who [text lost] the Bau

ceded his claim, I have here framed a suit in which I am having him proceeded against by the public prosecutor — for he reckons up to himself [uncertain: prore]netica and God knows what else — He pretends to have 105/m Rthl to claim, which is at bottom a lie — He has 72/m Rthl to claim of me, and this, once the suit is decided, will be deposited here in Berlin in papers, and then all will be in order there.

With the Invalids' Fund and all the debts, 122,000 Rthl would come out.

I have here a merchant who will take iron and other products too, and will give money. If one were in a position to raise 60,000 Rthl, one would have 120,000 Rthl, as the papers now stand, and could face everything down — Were the papers to fall again to 30 per cent, one could settle everything for 40,000 Rthl at the most — the plan has long been drawn up by me; were I only out of here first, then all would soon come into the clear.

Lay my petition to heart, Your Serene Highness, and see to it that I am rescued and set at liberty. I will willingly endure every hardship, travel day and night; only of my

liberty I will not and cannot be deprived. I am paralysed in everything; the very thought beats down all my courage again and makes me incapable of anything.

From Königsberg I have had letters of the 8th of this month; they write something consoling with regard to Your Serene Highness, and in particular General von Köckritz is said to have taken up Your Serene Highness's affairs very zealously. After the return of the post from Petersburg a good issue is promised — Whether Constantine will indeed effect any good remains to be seen. He promised much — Only I no longer put much trust nowadays in such gentlemen's promises. I have been too greatly and too often deceived; I have also suffered too much physically and morally, so that I still fear I shall become the worst of misanthropes. The Princess Sacken is said to be quite well; they have quartered General Dercke upon her, with which she is very discontented. Help speedily, Your Serene Highness, that I may get free from here, for then I shall fly to lay myself at the same's feet. In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

faithful and most obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Berlin, the 16th of January 1809.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

According to a judgment just now received from the Privy Councillor Amelang in Berlin, Lahr has been awarded, entirely contrary to the Common Law, cash money instead of papers such as he himself gave, and the 3,000 Rthl still coming to him are to be paid in [uncertain: Klag]: Courant. In the event that I cannot pay or deposit the same, I am to be arrested, since it is a bill-of-exchange suit. Amelang has indeed appealed, but how am I to save myself in the meantime? I am truly most unfortunate through this affair, and if bounds are not soon set to this distress I must go altogether to ruin. I have laboured through a whole year, and have lost health, means and credit thereby. I have also already won several advantages for Your Serene Highness thereby. But what is my reward? Hatred, persecution, and in the end prison. My inmost being rebels and my heart bursts within me when I do but think this thought. I beg and implore Your Serene Highness, pay, as is sacred, to take the matter to heart and to provide counsel swiftly, so that the monies may be deposited in cash or in state papers. According to the assurance of Grevenitz and Amelang the suit will certainly be won in the Senate of Appeals. Lahr must take papers, whereby about 1,500 Rthl., approximately, will be saved.

In this matter Your Serene Highness in the end loses nothing but the costs, which in the course of this year have indeed been very much bought up, but have meanwhile paved the way by which everything may be brought to the desired end.

The money for Lahr you will receive back, by order of the French General Government, and the sequestration will be lifted at once when [uncertain: inch] this sum, about 10,000 Rthl of interest, has been paid. To that end I have summoned the justiciary Hawich to come to me here, and shall arrange what is needful with him

The suit with Oppenheimer is proceeding in the best way, and there one may get off with papers and certainly save the half. Let Your Serene Highness only now have pity on me too and provide swift counsel for the deposit of the 3,000 rtlr., either in cash money or in as much state paper according to the exchange rate.

It is only a great good fortune that I am away from Berlin; and had I not concluded a contract with the merchant Michaelis for 600 hundredweight of iron and received 2,000 Rthl from him, in order to buy myself off to some extent, I should by now be sitting in Berlin in the Hausvogtey gaol. In this regard I beseech Your Serene Highness most imploringly by all means to give the 600 hundredweight of iron, so that I may keep my word to this man and not be brought to disgrace here as well. If Michaelis receives the iron, 300 hundredweight by the end of April and 300 hundredweight by about Midsummer, then this man may thereafter be very much relied upon. The distress and the fear that even here I shall not be left unvisited by Lahr presses me to the ground; I can say nothing further now than: save me swiftly, Your Serene Highness, and do not let me be utterly ruined for my faithful devotion, for the sake of your cause, and branded before the world. I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's — Let Your Serene Highness by all means send your letters by express messenger to Professor Rhode at Wrocław; he sends such on again from there by express — Only save me.

most faithful servant

von Triebenfeld

Konotop, the 30th of January 1809

44 My longing to be able to lay myself personally at Your Most Serene Highness's feet as soon as possible is without bounds — for impatience I could rave.

The Lahr lawsuit still holds me back, and I must see how the matter is to be managed.

Lahr still receives 3,000 Rthl, according to the judgment just now made known to me by Amelang, together with the interest.

He must take papers, and these would, at the present rate of exchange, come with the interest to about 2,000 Rthl. Now there lie pledged 2 obligations of mine at 1,000 Rthl each, for 800 Rthl.

2 at 300 Rthl for 360 Rthl, 1 at 400 Rthl for 340 Rthl; these are = 3,000 Rthl in papers for Lahr, but the costs now 1,500 Rthl, and this[?] I must have in order to be able to redeem them at once.

As soon as I have these, I am at least free. To Coste I yesterday successfully returned the 9,000 Rthl which at that time had to be deposited to cover the 5,000 Rthl which van der Lahr gave upon Zastrow, my own, and the Grevenitz bill of exchange, and I paid him 450 Rthl in interest. I also gave his bookkeeper and the broker Oldekopp 118 Rthl. These are = 2,068 Rthl.

As soon as I receive these, this dreadful business, which has robbed me of health, peace, honour and credit, is got out of the way. Your Serene Highness, however, loses little thereby, because the French Government has ordered these moneys to be reimbursed out of the Zagórów estates. My foremost Chamber is how I [may] this (also 1,500 Rthl in Courant will be saved)

2,068 Rthl quickly, and likewise how I may satisfy Mathieu — who in the end means to hold me fast for 1,000 Rthl Courant or 1,500 Rthl in coin — so as to be able to travel.

The merchant Michaelis made me the offer yesterday that, if Your Serene Highness would let him have 600 Centner of iron at 4 Rthl by the month of May, he would then at once settle the 2,068 Rthl together with interest and costs. The iron would, however, have to be delivered to him free as far as Opole.

Reckoning upon Your Serene Highness's grace, I shall, if Michaelis keeps his word, conclude this contract — the 600 Centner of bar and hoop iron must surely be a trifle for you to give, and at no cost. The lawsuit with Oppenheimer and the many messengers and other costs to South Prussia, which I have laid out here in cash, amount to 521 Rthl. These I beg to have repaid to me in cash as quickly as possible. Likewise I ask for the execution and other costs which the French gendarmerie, whom I have had to feed and pay here, have caused — these amount to 411 Rthl.

These are 932 Rthl Courant, and until I receive them I am as good as under arrest and may not stir from the spot. For the very swiftest disposition of this matter, namely the 932 Rthl in cash and the promise of the 600 Centner of iron, I beg Your Serene Highness as urgently as most heartily, and I affirm that I shall thereupon continue with the most glowing zeal to help bring all Your Most High affairs into the best course.

Answered, as desired.

3rd February 1809, to Berlin. von Triebenfeld

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Your Most Serene Highness's most gracious letter of the 8th of this month I received only today here in Konotop; the second, however, which according to Your Serene Highness's promise was to arrive at the Post Office in Berlin on the Friday following, will unfortunately miss me, because I had to leave Berlin in haste / so as not to be altogether imprisoned by Vandertahr. The decree of the first instance ordered the said Lahr to be paid the 3,000 Rthl at once in cash, or that payment be made against me under the law of bills of exchange — the former I could not do, and the latter I had to evade in order to gain time, particularly since one confidently [uncertain: hopes] that Beyme will take pains to withdraw all those confused dispositions, which run quite contrary to the provincial law and the statutes, and that the suit with Lahr will be won in the second instance, all the more so as the letter of the law is entirely on our side, and that thereby 1,500 Rthl might be recovered. The honest merchant Michaelis gave me 2,400 Rthl so that I might at least pay Mathieu and settle a few small matters, and in that way I escaped the claws of the said Lahr. Amelang has appealed against the first judgment, will write to the Grand Chancellor on that account, and will request an explanation of the cabinet order which so greatly [uncertain: impairs] the laws. Your Serene Highness's name does not appear in it at all, and even mine is not mentioned; rather the enquiry is made only in general terms, and the misconstruction which the judge has put upon the cabinet order is set in such a light on Amelang's part that the court must duly explain the point at issue and remedy the error

In the meantime, however, Amelang advises me to be on my guard and to have at least 3,000 Rthl in state papers in readiness, which I could deposit in case of need, should van der Lahr pursue me here with the execution. But where is one to find bread in the wilderness? Meanwhile I do not now lose heart — if I receive the 100 Friedrich d'or and the hundred ducats which Your Serene Highness need only most graciously promise, then I shall already contrive to make my way to them.

For the assurance of the 600 Centner of iron may God bless you, most gracious Prince — and they shall bring you too, most gracious Prince and Lord, abundant fruits. By it I am freed, and both your credit and mine will greatly gain thereby. I have concluded the contract with Michaelis and have firmly promised him to deliver the 600 Centner / of bar and hoop iron, of which the first sort, four-cornered, must be, I believe, 5/4 of an inch square, and the hoop iron of such length, breadth and thickness as suits it for plating side-walls / by the 1st of May of this year, delivered free at the Ober Baum before Berlin, at 4 Rthl in Courant per Centner. With a trembling hand I signed the contract, and until I had Your Serene Highness's assurance on the matter I could neither rest nor repose. God reward you for it, most gracious Prince, that you have lifted this sorrow.

If it is now in any way possible for Your Serene Highness, then do not send the 600 Centner of bar and hoop iron here to Konotop at the beginning of April; then I shall send it from here to Berlin and the [illegible] is lifted.

Necessity compelled me, in order to escape personal arrest, to conclude the contract at 4 Rthl, so as to obtain money, which is now beyond all measure [uncertain: scarce]. and if papers are bought with it at half or 1/3 of their [uncertain: value] at suitable times, then one pays the debts with them, and the Centner comes to 12 or 15 Rthl, the debts are extinguished and Your Serene Highness is free of cares.

By the next post more concerning the Prince's health, etc. Amelang. God will perhaps find a way in everything — if only I first have the 100 Friedrich d'or and the 100 ducats to buy or redeem the papers, so that I am secured against the claws of Lahr — as to the former, may Your Serene Highness only deign to have it made out as I have stated above, and see to it that I can still dispatch it thither in April, for our credit on both sides is thereby [uncertain: secured]. Your Most Serene Highness's — Today is a fortunate day: just now the justice-burgomaster Hawich and Hecker are come from Zagórów — they bring good news, but the post is about to leave; by the next post I shall most [uncertain: humbly] transmit the report.

humble and faithful servant

von Triebenfeld

Konotop, the 18th of February 1809
