Your Honour,

Most particularly highly honoured Court Councillor!

These last days I have had the justice-burgomaster Hawich and the inspector Hecker from Zagórów here with me, and have made report of everything to His Most Serene Highness by an express courier. As for the 4 matters most kindly communicated to me in the meantime, I answer most devotedly thereupon that

1. the General Moratorium granted by the King of Saxony protects those estates for 3 years from all pressure, if only the interest be duly paid — And to settle this I have bound the people there upon their souls. I am also certain that the same has already been settled by this time, for as Hawich reported to me, Honrichs, who had himself created sequestrator, had already some weeks ago delivered over the monies to the authority for further transmission — The 50,000 Rthl which at that time the Invalids' Fund [text lost] of His Most Serene Highness are entered as attaching to the estates, and, as said before, nothing further is required than that the interest be paid. So far as it is a matter of adhering, no one disputes these monies with the Invalids' Fund, from either the one side or the other, for even the French General Government ordered me to pay back the advanced interest which, by an error, had been exacted from me by military execution and arrest as the Serene Highness's mandatary, because this item of debt belongs to the Invalids' Fund. Nor do I believe that the Invalids' Fund has been threatened that this capital will ever be disputed with it on the part of the King of Saxony, still less of the French.

it seems rather to be a precautionary measure of the curators. Meanwhile the men are not to be blamed [uncertain: if] they do their duty, and they might well be assured on the part of His Most Serene Highness that His Highness would himself intervene in the matter and see to it that the Invalids' Fund should always receive its interest promptly, and also that, in case it should be wished to collect it in error on the part of the King of Saxony, His Highness would intervene for it as far as possible. For the rest, [I said that] the Invalids' Fund has the first mortgage on the estates in question, must take precedence of all other creditors, and may not or cannot be endangered; also that His Serene Highness would willingly pay interest, still less capital, to no one but the Invalids' Fund, the more so as the Jewish banker Oppenheimer has not kept his word given before the court concerning the full satisfaction of the Invalids' Fund, and that on that account a lawsuit has already been commenced some months since in Berlin and just now in Kalisz.

As concerns, 2nd, Meyer's claim on account of buildings, this is as foreign to me as optics to a man born blind; I would also readily swear upon it that Meyer is sooner in debt to His Serene Highness than His Serene Highness to him, for so far as I know this man was never in the service of His Serene Highness, but merely resided on the estate of the building councillor Glenck.

As for what Meyer says of Giese and consorts, the necessary steps have been taken against the fellows, and the lawsuit is pending over the 25,000 Rthl which the rogues owe in arrears. But it is a gross lie

that the fellows did not receive all the lands which were promised them in the contract — the matter stands, as said before, already 4 years in litigation. [uncertain: Royally] the swindlers wished to hide themselves behind the protective shield, and the lands have been re-measured by 2 sworn surveyors, and the matter awaited its course — As to the wood in which the Oleśnica people are to cut timber, that is to be laid to the charge of these devils; if in the course of the war acts of violence were committed thereon through the sequestration, then the Oleśnica people may hold to the sequestrator, according to their contract, and thus His Serene Highness is not bound in any case to grant a remission.

As concerns the matter of von Niedźwiecki, a lawsuit is pending on that account, and certainly everything has been set in train by the [uncertain: Zürich] servant that is required for the fullest possible covering of His Serene Highness; that this wretched man moreover wishes to procure revenues out of the estates is a piece of braggadocio, for so long as the sequestration lasts no one can take a farthing thence without its consent. Nor are all the arrears of interest yet deposited; once so much has been collected / upon which Hawich will now surely insist / then the sequestration ceases at once and the matter comes back into its track — the saddest thing is that everyone complains of the war and the bad times and no one pays — the nobleman and the townsman, on the other hand, now hide themselves behind the Moratorium granted for 3 years / which of course also comes very much to His Serene Highness's advantage / but the coffers remain empty thereby — Meyer, however, is to be told that, according to the answer of von Triebenfeld, Meyer never stood in the service of His Serene Highness, that His Serene Highness owed him nothing, and that no use could be made of his offer to procure monies out of the estates, because according to the laws no one may draw monies out of estates which are placed under sequestration

are said to be, without the knowledge of the curator or sequestrator.

As concerns, finally, the petition of the Augustinow and other colonists, nothing further is to be entered into upon it than to refuse these people in their request in such manner: that they are bound under their hereditary lease contracts to pay the interest without regard to any remission whatever. Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

I have had here with me the justice-burgomaster Hawich from Zagórów, who is appointed as an actual Ducal Warsaw notary public, together with the Chief Inspector Hecker, and with these men I have transacted everything that tends to Your Serene Highness's advantage, and have issued the judicial special powers of attorney for it. Accordingly I have, firstly: pressed for the dismissal of Dąbska in respect of the Trąbczyn estates, and given power of attorney and instruction for it.

Secondly: given the power of attorney for the complete lifting of the sequestration and drafted the introductory steps, the more so as a general indult of 3 years has been granted by the King of Saxony, and since in this matter everything turns upon the absolute payment of the interest, I have thirdly: given Hawich the power of attorney to collect in the interest and to pay it, against receipt, to those creditors who already have judgments having the force of law in their favour, but to remit the remainder to Your Serene Highness. I have also, fourthly: given a power of attorney to bring suit against the Jew Oppenheimer et Wolff in Kalisz, and at once to press for the cancellation of the several sums entered, amounting to more than 72,000 Rthl., a matter in which a lawsuit is likewise already pending in Berlin. Fifthly: I have issued a power of attorney that the deceiver Honrichs, who has had himself appointed as sequester, be forthwith removed and compelled to render account ad Assam, and that Hawich on his side draw up the objections against him and compel him to make good the same, as also to pay the sums still outstanding from him. Likewise I have, sixthly: given a power of attorney to collect from von Niedźwiecki the outstanding lease sum and to seek execution against him. Seventhly: I have issued a power of attorney that all high-handed transactions and

sales of the lands by Honrichs be forthwith annulled, and that the purchasers, if they do not submit to payment into the fund, be evicted with recourse against Honrichs, because he, without being authorised, gave away part of the lands for nothing and in that manner appropriated to himself a little estate of several Hufen, and erected the buildings from the lordship's timber and bricks. Eighthly: I have given a power of attorney for the collection of all arrears of purchase moneys, which are very considerable.

Ninthly: A power of attorney has been issued to compel the Oleśnica hereditary leaseholders to pay the entry-moneys outstanding, the canon included (inclusum), amounting to 23,000 Rthl, or else to be evicted with their dependants, so that the lands and buildings may be let out elsewhere. Also, tenthly: a power of attorney has been given to Hawich for the prosecution of all boundary suits, and the instructions necessary thereto have been imparted.

Eleventhly: that a power of attorney has been given to Hawich, so that he may appear in Your Serene Highness's name at the Diet at Warsaw and in all places, in order to maintain Your Most Serene Highness's rights of possession and property in their due force, the more so as every estate owner is now now to appear in person and reside upon his estates, or else forfeit his possessions.

Twelfthly: besides this I have given Hawich a power of attorney on my own part, together with the original decrees of the French General Government, in order to collect in the interest advanced by me on the Invalids' Fund, together with costs etc., and to remit the same to Your Serene Highness to cover the Lahr sum. Thirteenthly: and finally, a further power of attorney has been made out for Hawich, to collect from the Radzinski heirs the still outstanding hereditary purchase moneys and the canon of several years, which amount to more than 10,000 Rthl, and to refute the unjust claims formerly framed by the deceased.

I have had all this recorded judicially by the justice-burgomaster Schenck from Neusatz, in order to begin this new career right brilliantly; and since by virtue of the bond of 250,000 Rthl I have a right before all the creditors to have a word in the matter, I think this shall surely make an impression and bring about the wished-for outcome. In the meantime, however, Your Serene Highness shall, by my arrangement, faithfully receive the reports on the progress of the business from time to time. In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

faithful and most obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Konotop, the 7th of March 1809.

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

He alone would lay an egg in the Gastheim's nest which should bring forth a birth that would gnaw everything away from him — There exists a will of which he alone knew where it was.

Meanwhile, Your Serene Highness has the 100,000 Rthl bequeathed or lodged to You as good as in [uncertain: hand], for according to the Landrecht

there stands § 165, Tit. XII, Pt. I, almost: "Legacies which probably, or according to the testator's assurance, do not exceed the twentieth part of the estate may be ordered by codicils written and signed in the testator's own hand, without judicial delivery." Now since Your 10,000 Rthl, as well as the other legacies, exceed hardly the 20th, indeed hardly the 30th part, nothing at all any longer stands in Your way, Most gracious Prince and Lord, because 20 witnesses acknowledge and will swear to Colonna's signature. One might, had the stupid Bardthe not let himself be frightened out of his wits and renounced his 50,000 Rthl, have made a handsome profit. I do not even now give up the notion — If You, Most gracious Prince and Lord, guess it, keep it as the deepest secret until I come back. I beg this most earnestly — As for the postmaster Schulz in Strelitz, I hold the fellow to be a windbag. E. maintained that the anonymous letter was from Bardtke and that the letter was in his hand — That is not true; Countess Henckel of Schimanowitz wrote the letter and sent everything to the Princess Sacken. It is the Henckel arms and the Countess's own hand — She had the papers from young Harraszowski, who is much in her house and gladly seen by her. As a kinswoman she had very much counted on a share of the Colonna estate — Now she means to avenge herself — Many further items of intelligence are said to be drawn from this source. Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Since my return from Königsberg I have not had a single quiet hour; sleep and rest have become wholly strangers to me, the most gnawing sorrow accompanies me everywhere, and the greatest distress drives me to the point of despair.

Konotop continues under sequestration; I am short here of about 2,000 Rthl. I cannot raise it, and must suffer that strangers sit upon my estates, draw my revenues, dispose of them arbitrarily and ruin them. On the Świniary estates there is continual execution on account of 2,560 Rthl of interest, and on account of the van der Lahr debt. Could I but raise the 2,560 Rthl, I should be free and my credit restored — To van der Lahr I have sent 300 hundredweight of iron and 14 Schock of boards, where the Schock must measure 1,440 Rhenish feet and each board must be 1 1/2 inches thick and 15 inches broad, at 60 Rthl. This comes together to 2,570 Rthl.

This leech has therefore still 430 Rthl to receive, and the interest and costs, which may amount to 300, and then this fellow is entirely satisfied. To this end I shall have to give a further 1[0?] Schock of boards and send them to Berlin, in order to see myself rescued from the claws of this usurer. The boards are already lying at the water for that purpose, and this famous business will be settled within a few days; meanwhile, through the boards, there escape me again 1,800 Rthl in funds, by which I might have paid my interest, freed this cursed sequestration here, and become master of my estates again. I must yet endure for a time and find other counsel, only God knows

God how this is to be brought about quickly, for to sell produce by private treaty is impossible; the dearth of money has reached its highest peak and increases daily through the exceedingly stupid conduct of the Königsberg people. I have 1,000 bushels of grain to dispose of; in the vault there lie 105 stone of wool. In the forest there stand 2,000 cords of wood. At middling rates this would amount to some 7,000 Rthl. But no man will buy, because in Königsberg they are bushel-stupid enough to permit the Poles to import all these products among us. It is not reckoned that for this our money goes out of the country to them, that the Poles are thereby given the means to keep arming themselves continually and at last to become dangerous to us again. It is not perceived that by this our estate-owners are utterly overthrown and ruined.

I have depicted the danger which must come upon us and all these evils in my reports to Königsberg, and from here as well, and have sought to lay it to the King's heart; but no heed is paid to it, the brood of rats about the King takes it ill into the bargain when one tells the truth, and therefore every honest man must fall silent and look upon his fate buried in dull pain.

My only endeavour now is to obtain the 4,560 Rthl, in order to make my estates free, to be rid of the executions that press upon me. I would gladly give up the products mentioned above for 2/3 of their value, but the sequestration does not permit me to dispose of them until I have paid the 4,560 Rthl; and the want of money is so great that nobody can take and pay for such large lots at once. I must therefore bear this gnawing sorrow yet a while longer and wait upon God's help. These, however, Most Serene Prince and Lord, are the grounds which prevent me from being able to lay myself at your most exalted feet. That I should long since, had I been able to save myself, have hastened to Your Serene Highness, you will surely

believe of me without great protestations. Heaven is my witness that this alone is why I cannot leave the spot; for if I go away, then it is believed I am seeking to [illegible] and there is decreed at once, without all mercy, the compulsory auction of all my estates. Where then should I turn in my old age with my children? To return to Russia, for that I am too old — and my children too stand in my way — Believe me, most gracious Lord, I live here more wretchedly than a day-labourer, for my credit is destroyed and, said among you all, there are many days on which I have not a Groschen, and I have several times gone to bed [uncertain: hungry] so as not to give myself a contradiction — Were one allowed air and some forbearance, were I permitted to dispose of my products, then I should find counsel, pay all[text lost] and remain a man worth at least 400,000 Rthl. In Your Serene Highness's own affairs there remains no other way than that Your Most Exalted Self write directly to the King — For the rest, I believe it is well that Your Serene Highness has not yet done it, for if the honest Major von Pirch is not at Königsberg, then they will seek to twist your business as badly as possible. You have in this commission only the 2 true friends, namely Major von Pirch and von Hache. Gneisenau I do not trust; he behaves very coldly and is said to have declared that Your Serene Highness had never been his friend, and that he wished now to have nothing to do with your business. That Lieutenant Colonel von Knesebak is to be taken back into the ranks I do not find very seemly. This man is too great a hypochondriac; he demanded his discharge at that time with vehemence, and went off sulking. Whoever once goes off in that fashion ought never to come back to me; such capers should be allowed to succeed.

Scharnhorst I do not [uncertain: trust] at all; but his end may be set close before him. From the Friends of Virtue all is now quiet — but thinking, upright men fear a bad explosion from that quarter.

Upon Russia's conduct opinions are much divided; it is feared that Russia too is putting on a mask against us.

God grant only good fortune to Archduke Charles. If this Prince yet now strikes down the monster of the world, then all goes well and we come well out of the affair; but if not, then it is to be feared that Austria will accept the peace, but appropriate to itself [uncertain: Silesia] and Saxony.

Constantine on the other hand will obtain all Poland, Prussia, Pomerania and Silesia as far as the Oder as Emperor of the Sarmatians, in return for which Alexander is to be guaranteed European Turkey.

The Poles will not yet lay themselves to rest — here they recruit and arm, the [illegible] still going on. Honrichs was here yesterday with Cabanis; were he permitted to take the money out, then Your Serene Highness would be helped, and I too could quickly save myself — But it is by no means conceded, notwithstanding that I have handed over the orders of the French Governor General — He is threatened with being declared insecure, and he must deliver all the money to Kalisz [uncertain: um in König] to the sub-prefect Brzechffa, of which he has himself shown the receipts. The hundred and I have accepted with a contrite heart from Lombardini; I am still to pay the duty for iron and boards to my collector here, and there I can carry off nearly the half of it today. In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

most faithful and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Konotop, 11th July 1809.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord, With a bleeding heart I must now nevertheless report to Your Most Serene Highness my exceedingly great misfortune. At Schweiner everything has been sealed up and taken under attachment, in order to sequester the estates.

That usurious van der Lahr had applied for this because the products sent to him, such as iron and boards, were some 6 weeks on the way owing to the [uncertain: lower] water. Now the dog has his payment, but I am ruined, because the other creditors will not desist any sooner than until they have their interest. Since everything there and here has been placed under attachment, I now have [uncertain: little ground] and know of absolutely no way to save myself. My misfortune is now without bounds, and my children will be beggars along with me, for nothing comes out of the sequestration; everything is consumed, the interest piles up and the subhastation follows, so that estates worth 200,000 Rthl. will in these times be squandered for [uncertain: a tree] a third part. Never should I have believed that things could come to this with me — I could once count myself among the most well-to-do men of the State; now already I must regard myself as a beggar, and why? Merely because I was too good, wanted only to help the King and other men, because I never looked to my own but to others' interest — I seem to shun going among men; I live like a savage in solitary corners and lament my own and my children's fate, which before God I do not deserve. Sleep is a stranger to me, and men who only mock me I must flee — what grieves me most is

the wailing and whimpering of my children, from whom I indeed hide myself, but who nonetheless pursue me with the most dreadful lamentations by letter. I can give them nothing, for as God is true I have nothing myself, and my daughters work for money and let it be sold in secret so as not to grieve me. This alone tears my heart the most. I myself endure hunger, thirst and every peril of life; I have few needs, being neither gambler nor philanderer; I would take no heed of all these mishaps, but rather — if I had to bear them alone — would suffer them without confusion; but the reproach that I must see my children working for money, this deranges my senses and dulls my feelings altogether — With 1,860 Rthl I could be saved, but where am I to get them, since here and at Świniary the sequestration has been imposed — My credit is now quite gone; I cannot get 100 Rthl and must go without. I wanted to raise money out of Zagórów upon the decrees of the French General Gouvernement, to take 1,800 Rthl of it for myself and send what more came in to Your Serene Highness — I offered, since ready money is not let out of the country, to accept horses, sheep and spirits; the [uncertain: poor] Honrichs entered into it and wished to see to this. But not only has it been forbidden, Honrichs has been arrested on the spot and they threaten to shoot him — I now have my hands quite full to save the man, who is the father of 7 children. So here too, instead of help, I have costs, sorrow and anxiety.

I should have timber, boards and produce with which to obtain money, but they let me touch nothing and have laid an arrest on everything — I must absolutely first pay the van der Lahr matter, in which the 1,860 Rthl, then they will lift the sequestration and release to me my property again together with all the produce. From that

blood-leech van der Lahr, Grevenitz is sending [uncertain: us] at this moment a receipt and a [uncertain: breast] to Mr von Loen, to the effect that he is satisfied save for a few hundred rt of costs and interest, but that he consents to the lifting of the sequestration and execution. These I am sending this very hour to Wrocław to Loen; but through the rumour the sequestration has now been occasioned on account of the old and new interest of 1,860 Rthl as well, and until I pay these they will not lift the sequestration after all — My fine [uncertain: Fächste], which between brothers were worth 1,000 Rthl., Loen has already had sold for 460 Rthl, and has set off one item of interest against it — O, I could go mad. I should have murdered before I sacrificed myself for King, country and all and gave away such sums — I might then perhaps, as now, [uncertain: have been able to change tragically], but my children ought not to have had to work for money. [uncertain: Aubte Vierchitz] — so I had a friend who would not have let me [illegible], but he is no more — I wrote to Mutius — but he himself is like to starve.

Your Serene Highness is still the only one I now have on this round earth to whom I can pour out my heart. But whether you can help, God knows — It is 1,800 Rthl by which I can be saved; I shall then, it is true, still be in debt to the Köckritz family, but that I can take at once out of produce which lies here under arrest, and satisfy everyone.

Were it possible for Your Serene Highness to raise the 1,800 Rthl there, I would beg that this sum be sent at once to Professor Schade, so that he might immediately pay the interest and press for the lifting of the sequestration — Eternally should I thank Your Serene Highness for it. In this hour I receive a letter from Lombardini — it is of the 29th of July and already 7 days old — that I am to come to Your Serene Highness.

Gladly as I would obey Your Serene Highness's commands, I cannot do so now. I cannot stir from the spot until I am saved and have the estates and the produce free. Then I can travel day and night; gladly will I do it, and were I obliged to go down into hell itself; only just now I am wholly unable to travel 3 miles. My horses are gone to the devil and money I have none. If Your Serene Highness can procure counsel, be pleased to do it soon. But command most graciously that everything be sent by an express. The posts go too slowly, as is proved by the letters I receive from thence. In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Serene Highness's

humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Konotop, the 4th of August 1809.

Your Honour,

Highly Honoured Sir, Court Councillor!

Your Honour's most esteemed letter I received today by express, my joy was at first without bounds to know you as my weather in Wrocław, but on reading your friendly letter further, fresh sorrow stunned my heart, so that I could scarcely compose myself. I have a plan by which I may be rescued from all my embarrassments, only 1,800 Rthl of interest must be paid; before that I cannot come to Wrocław or into those parts. Honour and fortune are still not at stake there; I am for the present dreadfully disgraced by the one accursed van der Lahr affair, and cannot show myself there any sooner than when the 1,800 Rthl of interest are paid. Then I can appear there and carry out my plan. If the Most Serene Lord does not help me with this trifle, then may God stand by my forsaken children; I shall then go to another place, where I shall not require His Serene Highness's help. I have sent His Serene Highness the [uncertain: Bruß] of my daughter, which she wrote in despair, after the distraint over the van der Lahr debt, to my youngest son; and if such a cry of lamentation does not move the Lord, if he does not help me with the trifle, then all gentle feelings have ever been strangers to him. Dear friend — it is 1,800 Rthl that can save me from shame and mockery, indeed from ruin; these decide my choice or dwelling — I must have them, for before that I shall not come thither — If the Prince rescues

me therewith, then I appear there justified, but also not without citation. I then carry out my cause with honour — dismember a part of my estates, assign to my children the interest for their maintenance, and then go to the King, where I remain until much has been done. This is my plan, and these are the consequences, if the Prince provides counsel concerning the 1,800 Rthl — If this last does not happen, then I can no longer present myself there, but shall go to Königsberg and from there perhaps into hell — My heart would burst within me when I consider my misfortune, which I suffer so undeservedly.

Here the estates are sequestered, through the noise (bruit) which I endured in Berlin eternally of the Lahr affair; there, however, [uncertain: swum] — but where am I to turn? Świniary can be saved with 1,800 Rthl, and I be put in a position to carry out all my plans — Here too it would prepare rain-rich consequences. People would deal more sparingly with me if I had Świniary free again; thus everything there depends on the speedy help of His Serene Highness. I would gladly sacrifice for it in return [uncertain: Lebeseeligkeit] and all else, if only the Lord does this for me. Take care of it, Your Honour, then, if it is in any way in the world possible for you, and procure counsel soon, for then I can set out from here on the 12th of September so as to be in Sławięcice by the 16th — but without this help I abandon everything. With a thankful heart, and true high esteem, I shall ever be

Your Honour's

faithfully devoted friend and servant

von Triebenfeld

Konotop, the 31st of August 1809.

Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

The Głogów Landschaft, together with v d Lahr, united with the [illegible] Higher Land Court, have stripped me to the very bones — I am a true Lungenheim and live with my youngest son on Erloffeln, bread, salt and Wester — Yet I am happier than a god, for I now see the end of my sufferings. The day after tomorrow the commission arrives which is to settle me out of the sequestration. Then I shall again be master of my estates — which for so long, through no fault of my own, I have had to look upon with my back turned.

As soon as the commission departs, I too shall take to the road and come to Sławięcice. To that end I am writing to Lombardini that he is to send only 40 Friedrich d'or. Your Serene Highness has permitted 20[uncertain], but I beg him for 40 pieces, because I must make a detour — It does me wohn to take money in this manner, but as God is true I cannot at present help myself otherwise — At the New Year, when my tenant moves in and I receive monies from several quarters, I shall be able to give it back. Now I have a plan by which I mean to make a trial, whether after all the sufferings I have endured I cannot procure myself some advantage. I mean to buy iron for cash money and turn it over against spirits. Nobody buys the iron, but spirits go to Saxony and everywhere else. Now my request is that the Koszęcin ironworks lend me, until the 18th of February[uncertain], 300 Centner of iron against the bill of exchange enclosed herewith. I shall then pay promptly and in cash. I give for the Centner, delivered free as far as

the Bojadła landing-place, 4 Rthl 12 Groschen in coined Courant, that is to say, reckoning the Rthl at 45 fg.

Should Your Serene Highness be willing to show me this favour, may you most graciously be pleased to set the matter in train there in such a way that the 300 Centner of bar and hoop iron be sent to me with all possible speed, carriage paid as far as Bojadła. I shall then pay promptly according to the enclosed bill of exchange. Only I beg most devotedly that there the ship's freight and any costs as far as Bojadła be contracted for and settled, so that there may not again occur a like miscarriage as with the transport of the Einkaufend Leuth, where the boatmen took for the freight and costs so much iron, and sold it, that I received only 751 Centl. God! with a shudder I think back on that forever accursed affair. The claim of the Invalids' Fund amounted all in all to 3,125 Rthl. [uncertain: Wünste] when the French arrested me, to fall into the claws of the usurers, from Lahr 5,040 and from Holz Apfel 1,000 Rthl to take papers, but to give a bond for it in cash — for this whole rubbish-heap I received 2,003 Rthl Courant. My goods I put down, what I laid out in my travel costs, at 1,160 Rthl. Now I was bare and my credit was gone = 3,173 Rthl. The 3 months flew by very swiftly. Zastrow and Grevenitz wished to take precedence; I was to be clapped up da capo; I borrowed from him at cost so[uncertain] 9,000 Rthl in papers and deposited these; these I have indeed given back, but they cost in interest and brokerage 750 Rthl Courant — thereupon came the 3,000 r. from Your Serene Highness, of which I gave Lahr 2,000 r.; the rest went on interest, legal costs and brokerage. I remained 3,000 in debt to Lahr and 1,000 Rthl to Holz Apfel. I was not permitted to leave Berlin, and ate my way through 2,400 Rthl. — all this drew after it the consequence that my creditors went mad,

sequestrated my estates, and Lahr had me distrained upon — The Berlin debt now amounted, without legal costs, for which people now reckon, together with interest, some 700 Rthl., to 7,100 r. Arrears of interest from the estates through the 2 years of war came to 18,000 Rthl., thus together 25,100 Rthl. All this will, with God's help, be discharged by Christmas and I shall be rid of all distress. The feeling is not to be described. Honour, property and all stood at stake. It horrifies me when I think back — faced with the alternative whether I should endure this once more or suffer death, I shall, by God, cry out — Strike away, friend Ham.

For the future I will guard myself against a relapse of this kind, and therefore I seek out sources such as the one overleaf with the iron and spirits trade — Do grant, most gracious Prince and Lord, this my request, and send the 300 Centl. of iron; I shall then truly pay promptly — Five days ago I heard here from several quarters that Your Serene Highness's case had been justly decided, and that His Highness had been appointed General Governor of Silesia. Would to God that this news were ſohnen confirmed. In 1 days the messenger may well be back, and then my commission will likely be concluded, whereupon I can at once set out from here by way of Kłodzko and

f. w. for Sławięcice. Only I should gladly have Your Serene Highness's answer concerning the 300 Rthl of iron — In substance it may be Schien Ersten for me, — to await it here still, and thereafter to make the arrangements for the turnover against spirits. In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

most faithful and humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Konotop, the 9th of October 1809.

I have lain ill for some 7 weeks, half of which time I lived quite happily, for I was robbed of my senses and felt nothing of my cares. For about 8 days now I have again been a thinking man and am labouring to set aside my troubles — whether I shall succeed in this I cannot determine precisely — I do indeed have a tenant for Konotop, but I must first pay 8,000 Rthl. of arrears of interest and debts. Carte of Berlin, who has grown rich through the French deliveries, who from a beggar-dog or dyer's journeyman has raised himself up to be the richest private man and has acquired 1,600000 through the short war, wants to buy timber from me and to pay everything in advance; I expect him daily, and if he does so then I shall at last have a free hand to lease out and to bring everything into its track. 3. Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord, at this moment I can report nothing of consequence to Your Most Serene Highness, because Count Strachwitz is not yet here.

It was only today that I managed, with vexation and displeasure, to get a word with Mr Flesch. He only rails against Goldstücker, for holding the matter to be so easy and for having named the Count outright — He urges all secrecy and caution — Why, I do not know — It seems only, to speak frankly, that a swindle lies at the bottom of it, and as far as I can tell a lawsuit, of which I know nothing, is to be settled along with the business.

For the rest, I must wait here for Count Strachwitz, who is to arrive in Wrocław on the 23rd, in order to be able to take further measures accordingly. This much I know for now, that they are said to be the Oder estates situated near Głubczyce, and their value is put at 900,000 Rthl.

Zackraw[uncertain: Zastrow] does not belong to it; that the Count means to keep for himself — Count Steine it is not, for that belongs to the younger Strachwitz — Today, if my fever abates, I shall speak with Mr von Massow. Meanwhile I know this much, that Massow is not to blame for the purloined lawsuit etc. Merckel has made the noise about it. My Mr Schade, who is his daily and bosom friend, is working upon him today.

I shall report the results most obediently — The war between France, Austria and the Turks is here held to be a settled certainty, and likewise a breach with Russia is believed in.

Our good King is in a [uncertain: mighty] straits. He is absolutely to pay the contribution quickly, or the French will move into our states — Count Schneidniz arrived here from Paris the day before yesterday with this news. Others will have it that Napoleon insists on our joining the war against the Turks, for which we are to furnish 20,000 men at once, and against which he would let ten million rt of the contribution be dropped.

I have delivered all letters and items.

will certainly learn it exactly, for Lahr had solemnly granted me the respite; he may perhaps have omitted to write to his authorised representative about it, and the fellow would have excused himself with ignorance once he had disgraced me along with the Jews. My own affairs are arranged — Richter arrived here from Berlin only the day before yesterday — Köckritz has conducted himself exceedingly handsomely and obligingly, and so has Tesmar, and everyone — I am perfectly satisfied — Köckritz writes that he would send all the Colonna papers himself to Your Serene Highness — He wishes most heartily that something at least might be effected.

Upon Your Serene Highness's own affairs he is wholly silent. Only to Richter, with whom he chatted a full 2 hours, notwithstanding that some 20 officers and other persons were waiting upon him — to him he said: if only the devil would carry off the old business; with the Prince things would then be doubly well. To the Privy Councillor Sa[illegible] he wrote at once that he should be easy concerning the Invalids' interest — he promises to report the effect to me very shortly. or Rückel, Reibnitz's protector — Whereupon the King said: people are always pecking at Triebenfeld, he is certainly an honest fellow. Köckritz answered: of that I am convinced; I believe that if a man were satisfied and set in the right place, he would fetch us the devil out of hell — so Baron von Rhaden also writes to me — likewise a man of the old stamp and fibre — In the so-called wind-blustering there must, then, be not quite so much truth after all.

Be it as it may, however, and let each man permit himself to say whatever he pleases for his amusement, I am content and wish nothing further than to make the acquaintance, for once, of such a windhound; him my pistols shall waken truly frightfully — for on account of the Colonna matter I must pass through hellish stirrup-leathers. Köckritz himself writes to Tesmar: I pity the honest soul, and wish most heartily that something at least may come of it, for the daredevil has poked into a hornets' nest and provoked the B against himself — God grant him fortune — Hardenberg is coming, as Köckritz writes, into full activity, and will arrange the matter of the debts — Tesmar writes this too, and names him as Prime Minister in the same quality as he was at Bartenstein; this is said to be with Bonaparte's approval /O God/. Of Zastrow nothing will now come; to Hardenberg his death is peace — Massow would already be styled minister, only Dohna has hitherto prevented it — from Rhoden Your Serene Highness will doubtless already have full intelligence concerning the 35,000 Rthl., and be reassured.

Grevenitz must have written to Your Serene Highness as well. He will certainly be vigilant and mindful of Your Highness's advantage. The old lady was, as Köckritz writes to me, very ill, but has recovered again; yet her length of life is doubted — In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

most faithful servant

von Triebenfeld

Kąntwicz[?], 8th June 1810.

Two divisions are marching from us against the

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

I have pointed out to him that Stössel, who is now [uncertain: pauren], would let himself be well handled, so that he, Weigel, would recover my claim in a solid manner, and indeed with great advantage, without its being felt by him — and that with his wide acquaintance he could easily [uncertain: gewesen] the estates again. Cörruch], and there, in the very utmost case, a seizure could only be laid upon your share of the revenues — and that would require that Your Serene Highness live another 200 years; the Polish ones alone[?] afforded him a prospect — since, however, a fortunate exchange might be effected thereby, this would be the one moment to be wished for. most humbly faithful servant

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Weigel is now firmly resolved to accept the estates that are to be bargained for in exchange for the lordship of Zagórów, be they the Knobelsdorff or the Poninski ones, and to offset his own and Stössel's claims against them. humble and faithful servant

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

By Your Serene Highness's letter to Mr R. R. Heyne — "that you are willing to cede Koszęcin to Weigel or Stössel" — my fine plan has very nearly come to nothing. I was as though struck to pieces by lightning to hear this news. O God, I had need of every art of dissimulation to make myself appear indifferent. If you mean to give Koszęcin back to Stössel, then I must indeed fall silent, but you lose all the holdings and what you have laid out upon Koszęcin, and get air on no side. humble and obedient servant

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

This morning at 5 o'clock Köckritz departed; I accompanied him as far as his carriage, and the King intended to follow an hour after him — Köckritz commends himself once more to Your Serene Highness's favour. As concerns the exchange transaction, I pursue it with head and heart — I hope it shall succeed — Knobelsdorff wrote some days ago to Fischbach — He said he had a commission from the General Director of the Landschaft; the holding of this commission would last until the 10th, and from the 11th onward he would be at command to set out for Zagórów any day. I have meanwhile written to him yesterday by the express which Lombardini dispatched, and asked him when he means to travel and where we should meet. I await his answer, in order to proceed further accordingly. Weigel is again very well disposed — He says: "If Stössel too would gladly have the Biskupice estates, then I am content, provided I am registered there; gladly will I then give the Prince a receipt and have everything struck out upon Koszęcin." We are thick friends; he visits me often with his children at Świniary, for the Korn — that is his daughter — attaches herself very much to my two daughters — In short, on that side I hope for every possible good, all the more as it is now settled that all monies outstanding in Poland must be paid and may be drawn out of the country.

The widows' fund, the bank, the Maritime Trading Company, the wards' deposit offices and all private persons receive their monies; the Poles are all at one stroke beggars, and it now stands near to this, that they cannot manage and will all go over to the Russians. Nochrich now fears everything and holds the war between France

and Russia to be unavoidable; likewise he believes that the Poles will make the turn; and if that happens, then [uncertain: schließes] West Prussia too joins on to Galicia, and the Poles will throw themselves straight into Russia's arms in order to save themselves — for whence should the poor inhabitants of the small province of Warsaw, which after all makes up only the 10th part of the former Kingdom of Poland, take 27 million rt. There smoulders here a fire beneath the [uncertain: Hegel], which might bring forth a frightful explosion. — Meanwhile a ray of hope dawns here which builds up prospects for Your Most Serene Highness's very self, which I await with a high-beating heart. Private letters from Vienna assure that the peace between Russia and Turkey is at this moment already concluded — God grant that this be confirmed, for then a couple of gloomy clouds which still darken the brightness of our star of fortune would be [uncertain: verwähnt], and we should already see a brighter dawn — Since — as God gives, we [uncertain: Erden Wallen] take it from His hand — the upright man suffers but a short time, then the matter goes better — This very moment the honest Lombardini was with me; he will send [uncertain: einzusetzen]; now I can write more freely — For the present still this — Labage has been sent to Paris, and is to offer linen and iron for the contributions to be paid — half and half this mode of payment has been accepted — should it succeed, then iron would be a new commodity of worth — I learn of it first and tell Your Serene Highness faithfully what profit is to be drawn from it; the Swedish war offers glad prospects, for the iron will be sold at ever higher prices.

Your Most Serene Highness's

faithful, humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Wrocław, the 11th of September 1810.

Kalisz, the 30th September 1810.

Pro Memoria. To Your etc. we have the honour most humbly to report that we have now fully seen to the institution of the Trąbczyn lawsuit here in Kalisz, and that the hearing appointed for it is now set for the 24th October; the reason why this matter has been delayed so long lies in this, that the gentlemen at the Tribunal have had vacation these 8 weeks, which only ended with the present day. Mr Falz[?], Councillor of Justice, has now taken over this lawsuit and has applied his utmost diligence and zeal to it; he has also already given us the sure assurance that the most favourable outcome of this lawsuit would follow on our side at the hearing, where the judgment is always published at once at the hearing. As concerns the honorarium for Mr Falz, he will not demand anything, but leaves this to His Serene Highness's own disposition. The 200 Rthl advance we have handed over to him, with which he was much a stranger [uncertain: contented]. With the administration / it should doubtless read sequestration / upon our estates there is now an entire end, and the rumour goes very strongly here that the King of Prussia will take back to himself all the moneys outstanding here. God grant only that this report may be well founded. With the hereditary leaseholders of Oleśnica it would be best if we were permitted to come to terms; they ask for 12 Hufen of land in hereditary lease at a moderate canon, and you are then again in full possession of Oleśnica. The complaining and lamenting of the Polish peasants and Hollanders is as before, since the grain prices still remain the same and will not rise — with the former we have a hearing on the 12th October on the spot, and the latter are still not content with 3 gulden per Morgen, and suppose they can subsist only at 2 gulden per Morgen. We remain, Your etc., Hecker, Honrichs. NB Mr Friedrich Count Kwilecki asks very much for the promised live stag — My remark — to the peasants and Hollanders something might be remitted of the arrears — for the future nothing — One lets them travel, which now in Poland can easily happen, all the more as Mr von Knobelsdorff would rather have land than interest and reckons it at equal prices. von Triebenfeld

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

I have still not been able to set out on the journey to Poland; the want of money remains for the present the only obstacle standing in my way. Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord, I have this moment received three letters from Your Serene Highness, against which You must also have received three from me.

The business here is of such consequence that it almost robs me of all my senses; I do not know where to turn first. The newer courses of business in the local Zürich and other bureaux were as strange to me when I came here as optics are to a man born blind — Now I know them and it goes better.

Here one sets a term in a case, but then the case is not taken up; rather, the Ups, or the so-called entry in the registers, must first be made. Then, as it pleases the President, he takes up the register, and one must wait from nine in the morning until noon to see whether the matters one has in hand come up. So I still stand with the Trąbczyn one — today it is still the 11th case on the register; it may now come up at any hour, for many times a lawsuit lasts only half an hour, and often too they go per non sunt? and then a new term must again be petitioned for and a new term set, which then always, according to the value of the object, costs, as with Trąbczyn, 237 Rthl. — Now since there are 3 such lawsuits pending here, I must guard the nest

Meanwhile matters stand very well; Trąbczyn I hope quite certainly to vindicate. Falz is a cold man — He is held here to be the cleverest, and the judge listens to his word — He has now received 300 Rthl, and I have promised him much more if we prevail — The President of the Tribunal, a certain Smagorzewski, is an old acquaintance of mine — He has accepted 100 #.

Two assessors who are old friends of the referendary Sommer have each received thirty; there are two more whom I am working upon in another manner, and the wine already costs me some 160 Rthl. By Trąbczyn a very great deal is to be won — for besides the estates we save at once the 22,000 Rthl of dower money registered, and the remaining costs which Dąbska must make good are then indeed twice as high again — this is the judges' own sentiment — She also gives and means to force it through intercession and great [uncertain: fehlen] — But God will help me — The 2nd matter is with the Oleśnica lads.

I must have the fellows out, for they already owe — 16,000 Rthl canon; further, in dues laid out for them, 8,270 Rthl; the remainder of the entry money, 10,000 Rthl; to this the interest and costs with at least 5,000 Rthl; total 39,270 Rthl. They sat in the enjoyment; everything they drew out of the village they gave to the lawyers; the Prefecture has now forbidden that any further rents be given to the [illegible], and now they are checkmated — Unfortunately, however, the fellows have nothing

and the money is lost — now it has been managed that several Polish peasants from Oleśnica have declared themselves willing to enter into the contract and to pay the 10,000 Rthl of entry money, and also to pay the 2,000 Rthl of rent yearly in advance, and perhaps it may succeed that they also undertake to settle a part of the dues in arrears — the matter is in hand and, since I have given 30 ducats to the lower judge before whom it lies, is being briskly pursued; I also hope to obtain the eviction decree here quickly. The 3rd matter is with Niedźwiecki — he owes 6,000 Rthl; he is to pay and to quit, but will have nothing more than 2,000 cords of alder wood, which already lies at the water, likewise 60 head of cattle and a few horses, all of which I have had placed under arrest with the utmost haste. Hawich is the only scoundrel who stirs everything up, especially all the rent peasants, for they have paid nothing yet and will not pay either. Now the Prefecture has granted me military execution, but that avails nothing; they thrash the soldiers out, and so I stand bare and forsaken. Hawich must go now — then I think it will get better. Besides, I have the liberty to throw all the fellows out, provided only that I put other farmers in their place, so that the conscription lists are not [uncertain: Adict]. Now the Oleśnica Pol[ish] peasants offer to bring up as many [uncertain: Poladen] that all the holdings can be occupied and that will gladly pay the rent. This last motive, I think, ought to work. For the German oxen have not believed it — the Poles find themselves honoured that

one has shown them this confidence, and will do their utmost to come into possession of the holdings. The Oleśnica people offer to lay down 4 to 5,000 Rthl. in cash at once — the 5th matter is with the propination tenant — the fellow owes 3,000 Rthl. — he has to pay, but refuses, and wants to have a remission, or to give up the lease, because that is open to him under the Code Napoléon.

I have another already in reserve, who pays in advance, and therefore I sued the rogue the day before yesterday and applied for harsh execution, which will follow within a few days. At present the need is only so great because I am to effect too much with empty hands. But if only Trąbczyn is first vindicated, the tenant will pay 7,000 Rthl at once.

The old Hollanders, upon the contract they entered into with me, which they have solemnly assured me of, 12,000 Rthl. The Oleśnica Pol[es] can do 5,000 Rthl.

For Niedźwiecki's wood and cattle there may come in 3,000 Rthl. The propination lease from Nassalski 3,000 Rthl. The new tenant pays in advance 3,000 Rthl.

From the present Radzinski of Szetlewek 6,000 Rthl. From the outstanding rents at most 5,000 Rthl. Total 44,000 Rthl.

This could come in by New Year if all went happily. By the next post I can, on looking into it, write more on this; the referendary Sommer renders me very good services. May Your Serene Highness be pleased to write with all haste to the President Count Danckelmann at Wrocław, that he grant Sommer a further leave of 4 weeks, for did I not have the man, I should have to go under and return with the business unaccomplished — May Your Serene Highness therefore procure him the leave with the utmost haste. In deep submission I remain, until death,

Serene Highness's

humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Kalisz, the 13th of November 1810

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Of my illness I am cured; my first journey was to Konin, to settle what is owed to the State and at last to [uncertain: been] the oppressive sequestration entirely. On the way, however, I had the misfortune of being overturned and of so crushing my head that on one side I may pass for an African and on the other for a European. In the meantime I hope to be restored in a couple of weeks. For the rest, by the exertion of all human powers I have got so far that the State taxes, on account of which above all the sequestration continues, are paid down to 900 t., and since the suit with the tenant of the propination rights lies before the Kalisz tribunal in a wording whereby Nassalski must at once pay 3,000 r., I hope next week not only to settle the remainder of the taxes but also the interest on the bank capital, and thereby to lift the costly sequestration altogether. With regard to the sums from the Invalids' Fund, Mendel Oppenheimer, Weigelt, Haugt, Seher Thos, etc., etc., I shall set myself on my hind legs, to which end the orders of the tribunal and of the land court, and the attestations in the original, will be despatched tomorrow to Berlin by express courier — for if the Bielski plan, that interest and capital shall be paid over 40 years at 6 per cent, has already, as men say, been accepted, and if on that account the new

arrest has already been laid, then one need give no man a good word any longer. Indeed it were to be wished that a like benefit were granted to the estate-owners in Silesia. Here everything can be made prosperous by this favour. For the rest it is a sad thing here that I must bring everything before the judge and recover every Groschen by way of law; [uncertain: Kühn] by reason of the new ordinances of the Emperor of the French and of the King of Saxony, every man refuses to [uncertain: pay] a single Groschen. Every [uncertain: Cur] says: the Prince is a foreigner, we need pay him nothing; I am therefore of necessity compelled to have all the refractory held to their duty through the judge, and on that account there are now already some 43 suits pending. The most considerable are

1. With Niedźwiecki, for 6,000 Rthl. Here I doubt that one will obtain so much as a [uncertain: deiner].

2. With Nossalski, for 3,000 Rthl. This one will be won in a few days, and he is rich.

3. With the 3 Oleśnica lads, for about 33,000 Rthl. These fellows can pay nothing; if only they can be got out, the Polish peasants will step into the contract, pay 10,000 Rthl. entry-money and the yearly rent of 2,000 r.

4. With the Wrąbczyn peasants, for arrears of rent, 1,200. These fellows say they were cheated at the conclusion of the contract in Wrocław, and will not keep the contract unless they receive an abatement — I shall gladly consent to the annulment of the contract, take everything from the fellows, and, as the laws permit, drive them out to their wages, the more so as I already have people enough, namely Poles, who will give 2,000 Rthl. in cash for the holding and the same rent — this amounts, for 9 whole and 2 half peasant holdings, to 20,000 Rthl.

5. There has long been a suit pending with the Kopojno, Skokum and Świątniki peasants concerning the grounds; this one is already won in the land court and lies before the tribunal for my approval — the people must reimburse 742 Rthl. of costs, which will not come hard to them —

6. With Berda, who has a [uncertain: spiritual] privilege according to which he is to have only 23 Morgen of ground, but who has secretly appropriated to himself some 70 Morgen, and who is to pay some 1,190 Rthl. of arrears of rent. 1,190 Rthl. The fellow refuses to pay; I therefore wish to see the contract annulled; for the holding I shall then at once receive 3,000 Rthl. in cash and a higher rent than now —

7. With 8 Hollanders who owe some 5,000 Rthl. of purchase-monies. 5,000 Rthl. This suit will be won, the holdings taken in and let out elsewhere — whereupon the 5,000 Rthl. come in, but the fellows go away empty.

8. With Ribbeck at Drzewce, for 225 Rthl. of arrears of rent — this suit is compounded; Ribbeck pays the 225 Rthl. on the 1st of April of this year, on pain of losing his goods.

9. With the miller Mex[illegible] of Swięcia, for 500 Rthl. of purchase-money with interest. The suit is somewhat held back because [illegible] promises to pay within 4 weeks.

10. 29 suits with the colonists, who owe 39,000 Rthl. of interest and will pay nothing at all. 89,115 Rthl. The judgments will probably fall out so that the fellows can be removed and others put in their place; I [uncertain: doubt] that more than 6,000 Rthl. will be got out of these arrears, for the people are too obstinate and go off in secret with their goods — There are still many purchase-monies and rents outstanding among good people, but these I must for the present allow time, so that they do not join the wicked ones too, and until I have first wholly overcome the wicked — by Midsummer everything must in the meanwhile be in order, and from then on up to 14,000 Rthl. of clear interest must flow into the treasury. For 3 demesne farms which I am restoring, 9,000 Rthl. a year is offered after the propination rights; this amounts then to some 23,000 Rthl. of clear revenue; the interest, including the amortisation fund, would come to 14,000 Rthl. yearly, and therefore 9,000 Rthl. would flow to Your [Highness's] [uncertain: Causa] from Midsummer onward — 48,467 Rthl. would certainly come in by Midsummer — out of which a part of the arrears, [uncertain: Staunz], the land tax, the costs etc. must still be settled. The deficit is 40,648 Rthl.

The [uncertain: torments], care and sorrow which I endure here in the meantime are not to be described with any pen; I do not know when I shall first hear, or whither I am to turn — The newer ordinances of Napoleon turn everyone's heads; no one gives a Heller willingly. In the 3 months that I have been here, 2,800 Rthl. have been recovered by execution — the suits already cost 1,450 Rthl., of which the Trąbczyn and Meierowitz ones alone, which I omitted to mention overleaf, have eaten up 750 Rthl.; I have had taxes paid to the amount of 1,500 Rthl. This already makes 2,950 Rthl. Now I am again to send in some 600 Rthl. of advances to Konin and Kalisz — if I do not, all is lost; the sequestor liquidates daily, his new account amounts to 2,236 Rthl. He is the favourite of Prefect Garczynski; I must flatter him as far as possible, so that he only does not [uncertain: hiesigt] and vex us, otherwise all is lost — indeed, they will chase me off from here like the cap from the dovecote. Thus Hard[enberg] himself does not know one jot of it, that a fresh arrest has been laid upon all sums conceivable that have been given out of Prussia into Poland, and that the interest and amortisation fund has been fixed at 40 years. Hard[enberg] demands of me proofs concerning the new attachment and the amortisation [uncertain: Platz]; I send him the same tomorrow — I remain, until death, Your Most Serene Highness's most humble

von Triebenfeld

Pro Fisco.

There is the utmost danger in delay. The Councillor of War and Forests von Triebenfeld at Konotop near Zielona Góra in Silesia received, upon his own credit, on the 1st of February 1805, from the General Invalids' Fund here, a loan of 50,000 Rthl Courant according to the coinage standard of 1764, in Maritime Trading Company obligations which at that time could be converted at once into ready money without loss, against 5 per cent interest payable in half-yearly instalments, and repayment of the loan upon six months' notice, free to either party. For this loan he issued to the General Invalids' Fund, under the 28th of January 1805, a judicial bond, and therein, for the security of this loan, not only pledged the whole of his property to the said Fund as surety, but in addition also mortgaged and conditionally ceded to it an obligation which His Serene Highness the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, dated Wrocław the 1st of June 1804, had [uncertain: made out] to him, von Triebenfeld, for the sum of 250,000 Rthl and which was registered against His Serene Highness's Zagórów estates, and likewise granted the said Fund, in respect of its loan, priority over the 200,000 Rthl still remaining to him under the latter obligation. Of the mentioned [uncertain: loan] of the 50,000 Rthl, von Triebenfeld has remained in arrears with the interest at 5 per cent from the 1st of November 1807 to the end of July 1811, that is for 3 3/4 years, amounting to 9,375 Rthl Courant. All means of obtaining payment of this remainder of interest from him have been fruitless, and the General Invalids' Fund has therefore found itself obliged to avail itself of the rights belonging to it, both against von Triebenfeld and against the Zagórów estates of His Serene Highness the Prince of Hohenlohe mortgaged to it, arising out of the above-mentioned instrument of debt and pledge, in respect of this loan and of the interest outstanding thereon; and to this end it has judicially empowered the Royal Saxon and Ducal Warsaw tribunal advocate Mitschke at Kalisz, transmitting to him the original documents concerning that loan, to sue judicially in its name before the competent Ducal Warsaw tribunal, for the present against the possessor of the Zagórów estates, for the interest outstanding on the capital of the 50,000 Rthl, and if necessary to apply for the sequestration of these estates. Apart from the fact that, according to information obtained, the Zagórów estates are very heavily indebted, there arises here the further inconvenience that, according to the letter of von Triebenfeld of the 5th of this month to the General Invalids' Fund, enclosed with the request that it be returned, and according to the resolution of the Kalisz prefecture attached to that letter in certified copy, the capitals owing to the General Invalids' Fund in the Duchy of Warsaw and mortgaged upon estates there have likewise, together with the outstanding interest, been added to the Bayonne sums. In these circumstances, and since, as appears from the mortgage certificate communicated to the General Invalids' Fund by the Głogów Higher Provincial Court by letter of the 21st of September 1810, and likewise enclosed here subject to a request for return, the estate of Konotop near Zielona Góra belonging to von Triebenfeld is indebted almost to the amount of its purchase [uncertain: price] in the year 1800, and further, as that letter of the Głogów Higher Provincial Court shows, the estate of Świniary still belonging to the said von Triebenfeld, situated in the department of the Wrocław Higher Provincial Court, is likewise burdened with considerable debts, the General Invalids' Fund is without any security whatever for the capital of 50,000 Rthl which it has to claim and for the interest outstanding thereon, which, as already noted, already amounts to 9,375 Rthl Courant up to the last day of July of this year. This Fund has meanwhile learnt that His Serene Highness the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen has received, out of the estate of the Prince [uncertain: Selchen] deceased here, the sum of 80,000 Rthl as a legacy, and that he will pay the same over again to the said von Triebenfeld in satisfaction of the sums of money owed to him; and I have been charged by this Fund, by its letter of the 29th of this month, enclosed in the original, which is founded upon the order of the Royal Privy Councillor of State and Chief of the General Police Department in the Ministry of the [uncertain: Interior] of the 28th of this month, enclosed in copy, to lay arrest with all speed upon the aforesaid 80,000 Rthl before a Most Laudable Chamber Court, to cover the loan of the 50,000 Rthl Courant and the interest outstanding thereon from the 1st of November 1807 to the end of July 1811 amounting to 9,375 Rthl Courant, as well as the interest running from that date. This laying of arrest is also well founded in every respect. For the grounding of an arrest in speedy and urgent cases, which is what is in question here, since there is danger in delay, nothing further is required than

1. that the applicant, or party seeking arrest, state his claim and wherein it consists.

2. that he prove, or definitely state, the circumstances from which a present danger admitting of no delay may be gathered, and indicate the means of proof thereof.

3. that he immediately furnish an acceptable security, both to cover the judge and the party arrested, on account of the detriment that may arise to the latter from the attachment.

From the third requisite, concerning the furnishing of security, the treasury, and therefore also the General Invalids' Fund, which enjoys the rights of the treasury, is exempt, pursuant to § 33, Part 1, Title 29 of the Judicial Ordinance. It therefore turns only upon the presence of the other requirements of an application for arrest. The claim of the General Invalids' Fund against von Triebenfeld for 50,000 thalers of capital and the interest outstanding thereon at 5 per cent is, even though the original bond concerning it is not at present at hand, nevertheless attested by the files of the Military Department which concern this business of the loan and which are enclosed subject to a request for return, whereby the requisite under 1 is satisfied. It is further shown, by von Triebenfeld's own letter of the 3rd of July and likewise by the decree of the Kalisz prefecture transmitted with that letter in authenticated copy, that the mortgage upon the Zagórów estates which he pledged and conditionally ceded to the General Invalids' Fund as security for the said 50,000 Rthl and interest has been added to the Bayonne sums, and that the possessor is to be compelled by execution to have the sum owed, together with the outstanding interest, registered anew in court. In this manner the General Invalids' Fund is deprived of the entire security for its claim, and since the state of von Triebenfeld's property is notoriously much entangled and precarious, it is exposed to the danger of losing its capital of the 50,000 Rthl and the interest outstanding thereon, and of being left empty-handed in that regard, unless the aforesaid 80,000 Rthl be laid under arrest; in this way the second requirement of a laying of arrest is also present here. The circumstance that von Triebenfeld is the original debtor of the 50,000 and of the said interest, and that the 80,000 Rthl in question are bequeathed to the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, cannot be prejudicial here. For the Prince, in respect of the 250,000 Rthl against the pledging and conditional cession of which 50,000 Rthl were lent to von Triebenfeld by the General Invalids' Fund, is a debtor of von Triebenfeld, and the General Invalids' Fund is entitled, by virtue of the cession granted to it, to exercise all rights against the Prince which belong to its cedent, the said von Triebenfeld, for by virtue of its cession it has stepped into the place of the latter. The arrest upon these 50,000 Rthl is founded in every respect, whether the Prince be still the owner of them or have already made them over to von Triebenfeld for his satisfaction. Both the Prince and von Triebenfeld are held liable to the General Invalids' Fund, and both are no longer secure for it now. Von Triebenfeld does indeed possess estates in these lands, but they are so heavily indebted that they afford no security, and therefore, pursuant to § 10, Part 1, Title 29 of the Judicial Ordinance, the arrest takes place nonetheless, although he is resident in the Royal lands. I most obediently beg a Most Laudable Chamber Court "most graciously to grant this application for arrest, and, since the General Invalids' Fund has learnt that His Excellency the Minister of Justice von Kircheisen is said to be the executor of the testament of the late Princess von Sacken, not only to cause the requisite order of arrest to issue to him with the utmost speed, but at the same time also to declare the said Fund, by decree, put in possession of these 80,000 Rthl in respect of the capital of the 50,000 Rthl which it has to claim, together with the interest thereon,

as aforesaid."

Berlin, the 30th of July 1811

He, the General, hopes to obtain my estates at 200/m Rthl, and his plan of payment for it, if it were to go according to his wish, is to be as follows:

1. he would gladly bring his estates Seliz and Modzewo into the bargain for 110/m,

2. then he would like to include the small estate of Goła wieś, which

My proposal, without presuming, would be not to reject this plan altogether, and to conclude a contract.

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Right Honourable Sir,

Highly Honoured Sir, Councillor of War and Forests!

Your messenger arrived only this forenoon; he excuses himself for having been so long on the way by saying that he had gone astray. From his march route I see that he was also with the chief district administrator Koenig. He said that the latter was at home and had taken the letters from him himself. Neither Trzciński, Zerboni, nor Koenig lets anything be heard of himself; the first has still paid nothing, the second has likewise fulfilled none of his obligations, Mr Weigelt presses me very hard, and I shall now attempt whether I can quiet him by means of the Trzciński bills of exchange. These monies from Großen I needed for true necessity, since here, unhappily, everything still stands as you know it. Your entire silence has filled me with sorrow, since from it I conclude that all your efforts on my behalf were fruitless. I sent Your Right Honourable a messenger, who however brought only a receipt from the district administrator at Blizanów, which Mr Schenck, after this express had been detained 4 days, expanded to this effect: that you had gone away, would return in 14 days, and that I should then soon receive an answer; this, to my great regret and real disadvantage, did not follow. Only today do I see from Your Right Honourable's dispatch of the 29th of April that you had written to me earlier, which lines I did not receive. I can assure you upon my word that the letter which I here answer is the first that I have received from you since you left Sławięcice; in vain, alas, have I long yearned for it.

I am glad to see from it that I am not wholly erased from your [uncertain: remembrance] — I will believe that the letter, the loss of which the negligence of Mr Koenig has brought upon me, may at least have contained instructive disclosures for me; for that very reason it was inexcusable that he put it into the post at Syców. From the newspapers I see that in the fire at Syców the post house was burnt down along with the rest, and many letters lying there became a prey to the flames. — The [uncertain: worst] of it is now that I know nothing of what you wished me to do; meanwhile I enclose herewith a letter to His Majesty the Russian Emperor under open seal, so that, if you find it suited thereto, the necessary use may be made of it. Most gracious Prince and Lord!

most humble and obedient servant

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

After a toilsome journey, upon which I spent 3 days and 2 nights, I have arrived in Vienna — I found the most exorbitant dearness to be the order of the day here; the dear and sometimes very tattered paper, which as is well known takes the place of ready money, brings the stranger to the verge of ruin, because neither the native nor the foreigner sets it right. But of that a Floro — the honest man may not live without calculation — My text, with which I came hither, was to work and to accomplish. The first thing I heard upon my entry into the famous imperial city was the shattering news that the Congress has been postponed to the first of November, that the sovereigns are travelling to Ofen and Post for several days, there to hold great [uncertain: monreniren] and to return towards the end of this month. Further, that France is resisting our Saxon and Polish acquisition very strongly. My old patriotic heart could have burst over this [uncertain: Neuweke]. — And I hope that this is merely a façon de parler, or rather a feu de paille — Prince Hardenberg, whom I have found in good health and strong, stands firm in his mind and will let nothing be taken from him of his right — so much, meanwhile, on general matters — Now as to the various affairs — The Württemberg affairs go well — the King of W[ürttemberg], who is at bottom very discontented here, will concede much; he will himself draft a constitution and lay the same before the allied monarchies for examination and confirmation

— the estates as a body are storming in upon the good gentleman, and find a satisfied hearing — Prince Mett[ernich] would be the chief opponent of this ruler — but the marriage is held to be certain, and since the title of Royal Highness is to be conferred, this may well bring about a change in the sentiments of Prince M — I have invited the privy councillor von Gärtner to me today at noon, where someone else from the Cabinet will also be with me — He appears to be a man à la [uncertain: fandel], though more settled — the privy councillor Goesch is a fine, courteous and good-natured man, who through the Princess — who for the present, together with her consort, commends herself most cordially to Your Serene Highness — is more effective than the former — Mr von Gärtner is an author, and [text lost] many writings against Württemberg, Baden and Nassau are circulating here — by the next post I shall send over several of them. Your Serene Highness's

most faithful and humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

The monarchs have remained here and the great manoeuvre has taken place here in Vienna; I was unable to take any part in it or to see it, yet it is said to have surpassed everything in elegance — the Emperor as our King. Grand Duke Constantine etc. have received regiments in the Austrian army — which each of them also led forward at the manoeuvre. Only the King of Württemberg was not on horseback and drove / as I myself saw en passant in a carriage drawn by 8 horses, and indeed in an Oriental equipage, after the truly allied sovereigns — In [uncertain: horse] the manoeuvre too was eliminated; the cordiality between the two Emperors and our King, which was shown on every occasion, has surpassed all belief. Our King, after the various [uncertain: toasts], stepped out onto the balcony, had a filled glass of champagne handed to him and drank aloud the health of all brave soldiers — A many-thousandfold thanks, accompanied by many thousands of strangers' tears, was rendered to the King for this even by the oldest bearded warriors, and it seemed that all hatred between Austria and Prussia, which formerly one imbibed with one's mother's milk, was for ever remitted and vanished for good — In unison the 4 [powers] labour for the welfare of mankind, and only the ill-disposed man will gnash his teeth and [text lost] look to the future, which the well-disposed man now regards so hopefully and gladly. the appearance as though he would miss the crossing — Several Princes of the Empire and all 4 estates have agreed among themselves to send a deputation to Prince Metternich and to beg of him that the Emperor of Austria should come forward again as their head, to whom they would willingly and gladly submit themselves if their old rights were restored; they would then form a combined power which would scarcely have an equal in [uncertain: the world] — Prince Metternich has referred the estates to patience in the matter and has informed them that for the time being it is not yet advisable to come forward with it.

Much is spoken concerning Saxony — But it will probably remain with the resolutions long since taken.

Concerning Poland nothing is yet determined; meanwhile the [uncertain: surest] man assures me that, in so far as the matter concerns Your Serene Highness, [text lost] the best; the minister Baron von Humboldt is working here to the best effect, because the matter interests him personally. That, for the rest, Your Serene Highness will yet be able to lead a quiet and happy life in Sławięcice, and that you will shortly see your chief enemy there trodden in the dust — for that, most gracious Prince, I can vouch to you. Only the greatest secrecy is enjoined upon me, because many a stone of offence is still to be cleared out of the way — but the fairest morning is already dawning. The good Privy Councillor von Gärtner, who lays himself most respectfully at Your Serene Highness's feet, has for several days been very ill; as soon as he is [uncertain: better], I shall obtain much essential news from him — [illegible] is everything; on account of the many affairs I must be very watchful. Vienna, the 18th of October 1814.
