(to the Prince State Chancellor von Hardenberg)

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord, I am most submissively [text lost] to lay before Your Most Serene Highness the enclosed letter of the Prince of Hohenlohe, and at the same time to beg that Most High Person for the most gracious permission to depict to Your Most Serene Highness the most pressing distress of the Prince, and therewith to lay at Your Serene Highness's feet a plan for his rescue and for the relief of his sufferings.

From of old the Prince of Ingelfingen was Your Most Serene Highness's most faithful adherent and admirer; this man, who has been brought to misfortune through no fault of his own but merely through his yielding to the influence of others upon his benevolent disposition, throws himself into Your Serene Highness's arms; he begs to be protected from the chicanery of the medical councillor Cosmar, which aims at nothing else than that the good Prince shall go hungry in his old age and perish in misery.

The Sławięcice, Lasowice and Oppurg estates amount in value to a fortune of more than two million Rthl, which, according to the instrument enclosed in copy under A, were confirmed as an entailed estate by His Majesty in 1799, and which today, in the most straitened of times, still yield 79,500 Rthl of income, according to the statement appended under B. Of these considerable estates the Prince, as lord of the entailed estate, is to enjoy the revenues. But by every artifice that can be conceived the medical councillor Cosmar has contrived to nest himself both in the entailed estates and in the estate left by the deceased Princess Sacken, so that he commands everything as though it were his own property, draws in all the revenues, and gives no one a farthing of them. He is called executor of the testament — but what could the Princess Sacken dispose of by way of death? She was of these estates, and that only in part, merely holder of a life interest. The Act A, sanctioned by His Majesty, determines everything: to the [uncertain: divorced] Princess, now married von Sacken, belonged all the estates. After her separation she ceded her whole inheritance of her own free will to her [text lost] wedded lord, the Prince of Hohenlohe, and the Prince founded out of it the trust entail which His Majesty sanctioned. How then could the Princess Sacken still appoint an executor of the testament? Over the ready money she left she might well make testament; but since she has for the greatest part bequeathed everything to her favourite, Prince Adolph, there vanishes every legal ground upon which she, and far less her bosom friend Cosmar, might meddle in the affairs of the entailed estates. But in order to force his way into these affairs notwithstanding the legal barriers standing against it, to [uncertain: dringen] dispose at his own will, and to command the incomes without accountability, as though over his own property, the medical councillor Cosmar has undertaken the most audacious venture of a determined pettifogger. He drew up the far-reaching settlement here enclosed under C at a time when the Princess von Sacken, if indeed she was still living, could not possibly have surveyed the content and the consequences, since she lay at her last gasp, and in the most favourable case was already so weakened in her vital powers that she signed the far-reaching document, instead of with her signature, only with 3 crosses. This settlement is the sum of all intrigues. There are set out in it so many debts and demands which the Princess Sacken would have to claim, that they exceed everything, and which were never thought of in the deed of foundation. The Prince has already made mention of this to His Excellency the Minister of Justice von Kircheisen, as the copy appended under D shows. In his answer under E, however, silence is kept upon it. This settlement further states that Cosmar may command all the incomes of the entailed estates, and needs render no account to anyone — Whether a second executor of the testament of this kind is anywhere to be found in history I doubt; but on that very account the Princess, at the making of the 3 crosses, could not possibly any longer have been in possession of a sound understanding, for the settlement goes to this, to defraud the monarch and all the Prince's creditors, and to deprive the Prince in particular of honour and of everything, and this the deceased Princess cannot have wished! She knew too well what the Prince had endured for her daughter's sake. There could therefore lie at the ground of this contrivance nothing but the most unbounded malice; for the completion of this notorious settlement, wholly contrary to the sanctioned Act of the year 1799, they even knew how to move the Prince to his approval by the most shameful misrepresentations — Now Cosmar had, in his opinion, a game already won; he at once installed his inexperienced under-age son as administrator of the estates. Drew with him all the revenues, paid neither interest nor capital, and, despite all admonitions of the Higher Provincial Court at Brzeg, which he merely put off with defiant sarcastic answers, rendered no account either — The Prince is to draw yearly, according to the 1st agreement, 24/m Rthl, and his son August, now Prince at Öhringen, 18,000 Rthl; also the latter was, immediately after the death of the Princess Sacken, to be paid 100/m Rthl as a "Praedikat" toward the settling of his debts. But 3 years have passed, and the old gentleman has received no more than 2,500 Rthl, and the son, Prince August, not a Groschen; where then do the revenues of yearly 79,500 Rthl remain? where is the possibility of obtaining compensation from Cosmar? But here Cosmar's plan comes to light — whatever is said to him by the Prince, he bears it all without [uncertain: blushing] — The Prince's letter to His Excellency the Minister of Justice [text lost] a proof of it. His Excellency's answer, however,

leaves Cosmar's excuse to be guessed — in fact this man bears every humiliation, only so as not to have to give up his plan and not to have to let go his booty. The foundation of Cosmar's plan rests upon the capital of 300/m Rthl which the Courland heirs have to claim against the Prince, and which with the interest included [uncertain: v] 1805 — amounts to 426,000 Rthl. His Royal Majesty has guaranteed the debt, and the former Princess Hohenlohe signed [text lost] the instrument as principal debtor herself, together with the Prince. In the oft-mentioned settlement of 1811, however, the Prince has bound himself to pay this capital together with interest out of his own means, and to free the former Princess, now married Princess von Sacken, from the payment — A double absurdity — firstly because so considerable a payment is expected of the Prince, who has not ten, let alone hundreds of thousands to pay — secondly, because they believed they could set aside the rights of third interested persons without their consent, — the deceased Princess surely thought too nobly that she should on the brink of the grave still have set herself to defraud her sovereign and more other persons of many hundred thousand Rthl. No one can here mistake the machinery of a self-seeking chicaner, to whom everything had hitherto succeeded — Cosmar knew that the Courland heirs already had a judgment by default in their favour by which the Prince was condemned to pay this considerable sum; he knew that with the Prince, whom he had already for 3 years let go hungry, no object of an execution was to be found — He concluded from this that the monarch would now be applied to by the Courland heirs for payment; and thus he supposed that His Royal Majesty, incensed after this metamorphosis, would disclaim the matter, and out of vexation wholly annul the trust entail founded in 1799, which was sanctioned only without prejudice to the most high interest and to that of any third party. Then, in his opinion, the former Princess, now Countess Sacken, could come forward again, reclaim the estates, have the poor Prince driven out of everything and left to starve — only then would Cosmar's plan have wholly succeeded, and his reward would certainly have been princely — Your Most Serene Highness alone can soon remedy these intrigues and rescue the good Prince out of Cosmar's claws — An agreement has already been reached with the mandataries of the Courland heirs, according to which they will take 112,000 for the whole demand of 426,000 Rthl, give receipt for everything, and hand out all the documents — Just so an agreement has already been reached with all the other creditors, that they will content themselves with a yearly payment on account of 12,000 Rthl, which the Prince has assigned out of the entailed-estate revenues due to him / but which Cosmar, despite all demands even from the Higher Provincial Court at Brzeg, will not pay / — It only depends upon this, that Your Most Serene Highness most graciously grant an advance of 112/m Rthl for the payment of the Courland heirs, even if only for a short time; but especially that you deservedly annul the settlement of 1811 so maliciously forged by Cosmar, which in the manner of its drawing up is more than suspect, is contrary to the Act of 1799 sanctioned by His Royal Majesty himself, irreconcilable with the well-acquired rights of third parties, in short nothing but the presumptuous attempt of an intriguing stranger against the Prince's fortune; that Cosmar be removed from everything, and be held to the strictest rendering of account.

The advance of 112,000 Rthl can, for which I too, if it be permitted, will stand surety with a security of 60,000 Rthl, in the shortest time indeed be discharged in various ways.

Were a payment on account, as such is set out under B, not to be accepted at 25,000 Rthl yearly, then a part of the 100,000 which Prince August is to receive as a "Praedikat" could for the present be applied to it. Only above all the settlement of 1811, so dishonouring even to the Prince, must be annulled, and an honest, expert administrator be appointed in the name of His Royal Majesty, since that Most High Person is interested therein on account of the guarantee. Then nothing stands in the way of the discharge of the advance of 112/m. I further remark most submissively that Cosmar holds behind him over 43,000 Rthl of the moneys which the Prince is to draw for his maintenance, and which the Prince assigned to the general creditors in the settlement — but which Cosmar absolutely will not pay — a further 60,000 Rthl or so of manufactured goods are in stock in the warehouses — these, however, are to be regarded as a working capital — meanwhile these are speaking proofs of the richness of the estates, from which a chicaner draws everything, keeps it behind him for the carrying out of his plan, and in the meanwhile lets the good Prince and those about him go hungry — I must further adduce here that I have included for amortisation the 35,000 Rthl formerly advanced to the Prince out of the B[text lost] treasury. From the benevolence constantly shown by Your Most Serene Highness toward the Prince of Hohenlohe I hope for the granting of my most submissive request, whereby I most obediently implore that a report be required of the Higher Provincial Court at Brzeg, to which His Excellency the Minister of Justice has referred the Prince himself, upon the situation of the Prince, upon all his sufferings which he must endure through the said Cosmar, and indeed that all here is truly and certainly depicted; from which more will be brought to light and the pressing distress of the Prince will be proved.

In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

faithful most humble servant

von Triebenfeld

Vienna, the 20th of October 1814

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Your Serene Highness's most highly esteemed letter of the 9th of this month I received only on the 23rd; if the letters which I send to Your Serene Highness go at a like snail's pace, then it looks sad indeed. — Here things are somewhat quiet at present; the monarchs have after all resolved to go to Hungary, and in fact departed thither today. After their return the Congress will be opened. The ministers have meanwhile remained here and continue to work with the greatest activity. Saxony's [uncertain: Sachſtens] fate is now already decided for ever, Prussia obtains it entirely — Weimar receives [uncertain: erhölt] a small increment, Meiningen [uncertain: Meinungen], Gotha etc. remain as they are, yet all are subordinated to the [illegible: Laug]. Concerning Poland nothing is yet decided. Austria will by no means lay itself to the mark, and Talleyrand too seems to be stirring things up under hand, whence the favourable delay. Yet one hopes [uncertain: haft] the best from the continuing friendship between the Russian Emperor and our King — for the strip from Toruń close past Kalisz towards Kępno would be too slight an equivalent for Prussia's exertions, and this line could never be regarded as a military frontier. Silesia and Prussia would always remain without connection, and in the case of Russia's [uncertain: Huß landt] great power they would have to be regarded as lost provinces, because there are no strongholds or rivers of consequence there.

On the affairs of the Empire I can say little today, for Mr von Gärtner lay very ill for several days, and I too have had to keep to my room for 4 days on account of gouty attacks and a swollen head. But with the first post I shall be able to write much.

From the help of His Serene Highness the State Chancellor I confidently hope very much good for Your Serene Highness — the accompanying piece with all its enclosures I had to submit after altering it twice. The first time I had not adduced Your Serene Highness's letter, which must properly be regarded as a power of attorney.

In the Koszęcin matter nothing essential has yet been done, because B[arbe] and A. do not think it advisable to lay so much before them at once.

In the business of the Polish estates I am to keep quiet until Poland's lot has been cast; for if the district in which the Trąbczyn estates lie should indeed fall to Russia, the Prince Chancellor will certainly at once procure everything with His Majesty the [uncertain: Westen] Emperor for the best of Your Serene Highness.

Zerboni has today received the Order of the Red Eagle, third class, and goes to Warsaw. Heaven dispenses its gifts still as oddly as in 1793. Neuwied, Erbach, Leiningen and several others have gone as deputies to the Emperor Franz on behalf of the [uncertain: aufsstände], and the Emperor most graciously led them forward [uncertain: angeführt] and promised to do what was possible — whereupon these gentlemen also begged an audience with our King; this the King refused, and merely had them told that they might submit their request in writing. Your Most Serene Highness's

254 It is very sad that I must always wait so long for an answer and for support. Since everything is going so exceedingly happily through the honest B[arbe]'s efforts, I do not willingly wish to break off, but rather to bring everything to the desired goal — that this cannot be done here, in these times, with empty hands is surely easy enough to judge — daily I must be together with the men who actually accomplish things, for the Prince Chancellor is too seldom to be seen and in truth has no time to occupy himself with matters of this kind. Only these good men who are always about him must alone do the work and direct everything — no evening passes in which they do not visit me — 20-30 gulden are the way, I do not know where they go — people say a good draught tastes well upon good news, and truly I give it to them gladly, men of that sort deserve it — I thought to be here 4 — 5 weeks, and for that I asked 1,400 Rthl. Now I have already been sitting here some 12 [uncertain: delusions/weeks] and in all that long time I have received 640 Rthl. — today I am already 94 # in debt to Barbe — Even if you now send 100 #, what is left to me, since I must hand Barbe his money over — It then amounts to 940 Rthl that I have received, and that certainly and truly does not suffice for so maddeningly long a time — My own affairs stand badly there, I am abandoning my children and what is mine, for since everything is once going happily, I now wish to bring your affairs too entirely to the desired goal — and to rescue you wholly, as has ever been my wish — after which I may with every right hope for rescue from you in turn, most gracious Prince — It is no small thing that I have already done here and still

must still bring about —

1. You must recover your Polish estates; by that you gain air and throw out Leixner and the S. Jew Meyer Bernhard

2. The Curische debt will be discharged, whereby you will be free of 461,000 Rthl of debts and the King sees you justified

3. you will [uncertain: become/be] Cosmarn and stand again as lord in all your estates, covered with fame and honour

4. The Monarch will have to do you justice, and indemnify you for all your sufferings and remove every stain even from your honour,

5. you need no longer be the mockery of men, still less live on the mercy of your children

6. you come out of the Koszęcin bonds, and that in the most advantageous and most honourable manner — All this I am bringing about here this time, so it would be more than cruel if you were to let me suffer want, [uncertain: starve], and become the mockery of men for it — This would already have happened, I should have had to withdraw like a scoundrel, had the upright Barbe not helped me out so like a brother — six hundred thaler or 200 # I must by force have here within a fortnight at the latest, apart from the 100 # that are said to be on the way, for otherwise the whole mesh stands still — Your distress there must not now be so pressing — Tread on your leeches there now, they will yield up something, for they, B[arbe] — will, after the appointed investigation, surely perceive that it is no longer a sheep and empty sound, and also that their idol's reign will now have an end — Believe me, most gracious Lord, that I would far rather take an emetic than plague you for money — But I cannot do otherwise if I am to go on working with these men. all the amusements and all the mighty processions I know only by the day on which they fell; I therefore need make myself no reproaches that I have squandered the money demanded, or applied it otherwise than in your interest — For the rest, I beg Your Serene Highness to let the letters to be sent to me go entirely under the address of the Royal Prussian Chief Post Director Mr Mann in Vienna; that is to say, the letter to me is duly sealed and provided with the address, and then a cover is made and the full address made out to the Chief Post Director Mann — This is an easy trouble, and the letters go more surely and more swiftly, especially if you send them to Nysa by post twice every week — For from here the Prussian post goes twice weekly to Wrocław and arrives twice — You may well have my horses used for it — now alone is the time, most gracious Prince, now one must bestir oneself and spare nothing; where the blank forms are, where the letter to the Prince is, where the 100 # lie, by God, I sit here and could despair, because I am without any news whatever from Your Serene Highness — this would not need to be so if you always gave the letters to Nysa by the Prussian post and under the above address — Meanwhile I will endure all sufferings, if only a good report comes in from the Brzeg Higher Provincial Court — do see to that there in the best way — of the Koszęcin sale let Your Serene Highness say nothing to anyone too early, for if the creditors [uncertain: scent] a rich purchaser they will be willing to let little of the capital go; this must be settled just as we [text lost] the closing note from Count Portales beforehand, and you can therefore write and seal the written undertaking for B alone in the setting-out — For an honest man this is security enough. von Triebenfeld

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

If Your Most Serene Highness's wishes do not now succeed, then they never will. The upright Prince Chancellor has the best will, and His Excellency the Minister Baron von Humboldt is exceedingly active — The day before yesterday the latter told me that the Curische heirs have applied to the King and have petitioned for their satisfaction.

His Excellency has demanded of me copies of everything I have submitted to His Serene Highness the Prince State Chancellor, so that the answer might be suited to Your Serene Highness's wishes — The King has now had it answered that he would settle the matter after his return. His Excellency is very glad of this and holds the whole game to be won. The monarch perceives that he must pay — and gladly will one gain 314,000 Rthl and advance the 112,000 Rthl — and also annul the settlement — The Prince will, as I know for certain, also bring up the salary due to Your Serene Highness for 9 years, and here too God will help. I have just now come from Count Winzingerode, who showed me a [uncertain: justi-] begun letter to His Majesty, in which he petitions in the name of Prince August that His Majesty might be pleased to command that with the utmost speed 100,000 Rthl be paid to him, pursuant to a testament of his late grandmother the Princess Sacken, out of the revenues of the entailed estates Sławięcice and Lasowice. I have not advised the Count against submitting the matter; meanwhile I told him that His Majesty had firmly determined to have Your Serene Highness's affairs brought to a conclusion first of all, and that the King would perhaps himself have the estates Quest placed under sequestration for years — For the rest, it was striking that the Princess Sakkin should wish to dispose of the entailed estates even after her

death, of which she had been only a life-tenant holder — Here the Count was much taken aback, and said, is that possible —? Oh, what things people do say. I hope that the decision, given through Minister Humboldt, will also be favourable to Your Serene Highness, and will fall out to this effect, that your affairs are to be set right first.

Regarding the Warsaw question nothing has yet come to publicity, although the lot of the Poles has been decided; meanwhile the Trąbczyn and Kamionna matter rests on that account — the affair will not be so easily ended as was believed at Sławięcice — from that quarter everything is being exerted and much sacrificed — added to which our King is all too good — Prince Hardenberg is on that account full of care — The Imperial affairs will end very well; I have heard various things about it in confidence, and communicated what was necessary to the men concerned. Yesterday there was a great Brink here. It was said that France had declared that as soon as Prussia occupied Saxony, France would let 200/m men march over the Rhine. Today, however, I heard from one of my patrons that this is a rumour without any foundation whatever — In the Baden and Württemberg lands things are beginning to grow very unquiet; by the next post I shall write more about it. The departure of the monarchs takes place 18 days from today — In reverence I remain

Your Most Serene Highness's

most faithful and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Vienna, the 5th of November 1814.

Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Your Most Serene Highness's two letters of the 30th of last month and the 4th of this I received on the 15th of November, whereby then a great part of my sufferings was relieved. In the meantime there will be no lack of care, for a great part of it went upon bread already eaten in advance — Enough; here I shall have to get myself through, however wretchedly it may be. Now as concerns the paper of the Court Councillor Hahn, it is simply impossible to add it to that petition, since the same already lies at present before His Majesty. His Majesty is at present very well disposed, and everything depends upon my receiving with all speed the 12,000 Rthl for the Curish plenipotentiaries, in order to conclude with them; the 100,000 Rthl will thereafter be assigned immediately in Berlin. That His Serene Highness the Prince Chancellor is willing faithfully to help Your Serene Highness — of that you may, most gracious Lord, hold yourself assured; and of the sentiments of the Baron von Humboldt the enclosure will convince Your Serene Highness. The fate of Poland is indeed decided, but nothing has yet come to general knowledge. As regards Your Serene Highness's Hohenlohe affairs, everything is indeed fairly well set in train; meanwhile Mr von Gärtner will present a [uncertain: separate]

paper before the Congress upon these abominable grievances, quite separately and at once. So much is certain, that the mediatised houses will throughout regain their old prerogatives, short only of full sovereignty. A few days ago there seemed to prevail here a slight tension, which excited a good deal of whispering — the matter arose from a conference held in the deepest secrecy between Prince Metternich, Wrede and Wessling, to which our Minister was not called in — As yet nothing is known of the subject, nor whether the jealousy is entirely allayed — on the 20th the 3 monarchs go travelling again — They make a tour to Graz and Trieste; one flatters oneself that after their return the Congress will then soonest reach its end.

The Prince of Hohenlohe has, in this matter lying before Your Most Serene Highness, had a further opinion drawn up from the records which lie with the High Provincial Court at Brzeg, by the man of law already made known to Your Serene Highness, in order to see the whole matter quite clearly. The more so, as thereafter the entailed estates must be administered for the royal account. The settlement and the codicil of 1811 — which was forged by Cosmar above all in order to defraud the monarch of 426/m Rthl, and other creditors too of what is theirs — collapse [uncertain: of] themselves. Most [uncertain: Allersebnißest] however I venture to remark that every delay threatens danger, for first, Cosmar spins his web tighter and confuses the matter daily more — secondly, the Prince is about 66 years of age, bowed down and worn out by care; he might well succumb to his misery, as Cosmar and the young Prince wish. Then nothing is registered upon the entailed estates; the Courland heirs, who have on their side the guarantee of His late Royal Majesty (the All-Highest under whom the debts were originally contracted), and who also drew the interest until 1806 out of the royal treasury, would obtain by way of law that His Majesty must pay, and in that manner the monarch would lose, inclusive of the 35,000 Rthl, 461,000 Rthl.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

His Serene Highness the Prince State Chancellor has today for the fifth day kept to his room and his bed. If anyone quietly prays to God for the preservation of this man, then it is truly I who do. Not only would the whole machine come to a standstill, but Your Serene Highness's affairs would be left lying half-way. Concerning Your Serene Highness's military affairs, one is now wholly silent; Barbe, however, says this is being kept in reserve and laid aside until Berlin — That too is well, for there the helpers are more numerous — For the present everything depends only on this, that the Courland matter be brought to an end, that Your Serene Highness be rid of this dreadful business; that Cosmar be thrown out, and that you, as actual lord of the entailed estate, come into possession of the estates, and need no longer live there on the mercy of your own servants. May you also be pleased to send no further letters to me, for on the 11th of [uncertain: next month] I think to lay myself personally at your most exalted feet —

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

The prospects in general have altered very much since my last letters — The departures of the high Allies were, as I had the honour to report in my previous letter, quite certainly fixed for the 8th-9th-10th, but now a course of from 4 to 6 weeks' length is still to be run through — and at this moment, after the turns [uncertain: Tournare] that have occurred, as good as nothing at all has been done — this means that in the matter of the Polish estates nothing can yet be determined with any confidence — Meanwhile Your Serene Highness may hold yourself assured of the best outcome, in view of the truly noble and friendly disposition of his Serene Highness the Chancellor of State [uncertain: Ewr.] — In the principal matter the Prince has charged the privy councillor of state Stägemann to examine everything and to render to [uncertain: so durchlaucht] a report with his opinion — It was resolved today that a supreme command shall go off at once to Berlin, to Mr M. von Kircheisen and his Excellency the Finance Minister von Bulow, pursuant to which a commission is to be appointed which shall investigate in the most thorough manner everything that Cosmar has done — Much, very much is gained. But in the principal matter, that is the settlement with the Curish heirs and the advance of 112/m Rthl, there I still lie at anchor; the enclosed letter will be delivered again tomorrow morning to his Serene Highness the Prince. Anxious and full of doubt whether the Prince of Hardenberg [text lost] could be bought for money, I touched on the matter very softly and from a distance. An abridged answer, that there could be no talk of it at present, kept me between fear and hope. At that time I heard, in secret, that the King will no longer tolerate either exchange or purchase of estates, because a great many estate-holders in Poland would have to abandon their property for the Bayonne sums, out of which in the end nothing but domains were to be created — In my distress I disclosed to Court Councillor Barbe my plan concerning Koszęcin, which however now already turned out otherwise, because I had mixed in the Courland debt, for the discharge of which the King is now advancing the money.

I did not conceal from him that a present of 30,000 Rthl had been demanded from Your Serene Highness for the Prince of Hardenberg, so that the Prince Chancellor should let the matter be done quickly. I told B. that you had agreed with Weigel and Stössel that each would give 10,000 Rthl — Calmly B. rose and asked, who then proposed it, and does the Prince really know of it, and will he accept the 30,000 Rthl?

To all this I could answer nothing further than that of the latter I knew nothing, that I had only been given the instruction from Your Serene Highness to see to the sale of Koszęcin in the aforesaid manner.

Of estates

In the calmest tone B. began: listen, Triebenfeld, you were the one man whom I greatly esteemed; I allowed it to happen that you ceded the papers to my Antonette — but now do not take it ill of me — I must return that to you at once, for you are dealing in neck-breaking matters — Know that if the Prince learns of this you will sit in a dungeon, and if he knew that I had merely brought it forward, he would thrust me from him with his feet and I should be infamously done for — He must indeed be a worse hellish beast than all the devils that are ever painted for us, who would impute such baseness to the most honest of all men, and mean to swindle people on his account — I had to employ every possible eloquence to pacify him again; meanwhile he did not let himself be seen for a couple of days, and only when I showed him the instruction signed in Your Serene Highness's own hand, and had assured him on my honour that I had not yet said a word of the 30/m Rthl to any mortal soul, was the confidential intercourse between us restored —

Oh how unhappy I might have become through this — But now heaven has compensated me for it, and Koszęcin will after all be sold just as well and more securely to a private man — The rich Count Pourtalès, brought up with Barbe in Neuchâtel, has sold his English and French possessions for more than 3 millions in ready money; now he is on the point of disposing of his Schwarzer estates also for ready money, and since the King has treated him at Neuchâtel with such distinguished favour, he wishes to bring his great fortune into our country and to purchase in Silesia — He has asked Barbe to help him to estates of consequence — I have put Koszęcin before Barbe — Barbe has himself made an extract from the valuations and the statistical tables, and has sent it to him by a courier just then despatched thither — Barbe has depicted everything in such a way that the matter may be regarded as done — A [uncertain: Mitlein Einmahl handlet] thousand Rthl has been demanded, whereupon there remain

Your Serene Highness will still come out with 38,000 Rthl, apart from what may perhaps further be gained on the capital deductions, and what I hold to be of consequence in the case of [uncertain: pranzte] ready payment — Barbe has told him that the arrears of interest would lapse in his favour, and also that he would find large stocks on hand, so that the estates would really cost him not much more than 900,000 Rthl in ready money — Barbe has said once again that the matter is as good as concluded — Money these people have in abundance, and they are very enterprising — for the other Pourtalès too wishes to purchase here in our states — I have now promised Barbe, who really deals most honestly in Your Serene Highness's affairs, the 30/m Rthl, as soon as the purchase should come about in that manner with Count Pourtalès — Have the goodness now, gracious Prince, to send me at the very furthest this written undertaking. As soon as the sale of the Koszęcin, Boronów and [uncertain: Cieszowa] estates should come about in the manner agreed with the Lord Count of Pourtalès, I the undersigned shall pay, immediately upon the conclusion of the contract, to any bearer of this written undertaking, the sum of thirty thousand Rthl in Royal Prussian 64-piece Courant — and from the moment of the sale of the above-named estates to Count Pourtalès this written undertaking shall be regarded as a true bill of exchange.

Sławięcice

January 1815 [Locus Sigilli] Friedrich Ludwig, Prince of Hohenlohe

Your Serene Highness's

most faithful and humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Today is the 27th day since Your Serene Highness sent me the latest letter, of 17 December, by the Nysa messenger, which I received on the 21st. Since that time I have not seen a single letter of the alphabet from Your Serene Highness. If, however, Your Serene Highness did indeed dispatch the above letter on 18 December and the money to me on the 25th, and also sent further letters here, then do let the tracking-notes follow after them with all possible speed, and order that these be delivered here to me — For the rest, everything here is still as it was — nothing can yet be determined with certainty — England's too hastily concluded peace with America is causing a sensation — It seems that only now does she mean to have the say here at the Congress. Meanwhile the East Indian and Persian affair appears to be becoming dangerous for the English, and they may well have to adopt a somewhat purer[?] tone — Russia, meanwhile, means absolutely to press our Lord hard concerning Poland. God knows how this will yet end — Prince Bartenstein Stetten has returned from Paris — He had a considerable claim against France. He went there himself and [uncertain: negotiated] with the King, who is having 400,000 Franken paid out to him — If everything here should still go as desired, then Your Serene Highness might also go there yourself

and negotiate directly with the King of Fr[ance]; I believe the outcome would answer to your wishes — The upright Prince Hardenberg is fairly well recovered from his somewhat severe indisposition — God preserve the noble man — for otherwise the whole machine stands still — Once again I beg for the speediest news of what has been accomplished at Brzeg, for the written undertaking, and for money — In deepest reverence I remain, until death, Your Serene Highness's

faithful and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Vienna, 13 January 1815.

Right Honourable Sir,

Most highly revered Sir General, the late King granted me in the year 1796, in the Province of South Prussia, the Kamionna and Trąbczyn estates confiscated from a certain Prusimski. The former lie below Międzyrzecz in the Department of Poznań, the latter however in that of Kalisz, on this side of the Warta, in the Konin district. The administrative commission which assembled in the Province of Warsaw in 1806 took the estates from me by force in 1807, and that fourteen weeks after the Peace of Tilsit, and gave them back to the daughter of Prusimski, now married as Miączyńska. I brought suit over this before the Kalisz tribunal; after a year and a day I received from the said tribunal the resolution that it did not hold itself empowered to set aside the disposition of the commission of that time, and that I should apply in the matter to the Emperor Napoleon — this was against my feeling, and Mrs von Miączyńska possesses the estates to this day. Last year my general attorney, the Councillor of War and Forests von Triebenfeld, applied in this matter to the Prince von Hardenberg. The Prince instructed him to let this business rest until Poland's affairs should be decided. Now, as the [uncertain: rumour] says, this has come about, and as I hear, the Prosna is to hold as the boundary. In that case the district in which the Trąbczyn estates lie falls to His Majesty the [uncertain: Russian] Emperor — being unacquainted with the [illegible] course of business, I now do not know to whom I should apply for the reclaiming of the estates; indeed, still more, I fear the influence which Miączyński is said to have upon the Governor-General Landsko[uncertain: g/y].

In this hard-pressed situation I turn with the most heartfelt request to Your Right Honourable, to let your good word on my behalf be extended to me before His Majesty the Emperor, and to direct the matter so that the Emperor himself shall command that the Trąbczyn estates, together with the eight years' revenues, be given back to me. May Your Right Honourable deign to grant the Councillor of War von Triebenfeld a favourable hearing, and most kindly furnish him with the necessary instructions.

With unbounded gratitude, and with the most especial high esteem, I shall ever remain

Your Right Honourable's

Sławięcice,

the 15th of January 1815.

The General stands in high favour with His Majesty — In general, whatever is to be done must all be done quickly, for here there is very strong talk of war — In the cabinets an unbelievable activity prevails, but everything is kept in the utmost secrecy — the Congress, it is said, may well last another couple of months, but if the thing degenerates into discord it can also be broken off just as quick as lightning — at court, they say, one no longer sees the cheerful faces one saw at first. Our Most Gracious King and Lord dines almost always alone, and likewise he always goes walking alone and solitary. Why the King of Württemberg has left Vienna and the Congress is not to be [uncertain: deciphered] with any certainty. He has, however, already

faithful, humble and obedient servant

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

From the enclosure Your Serene Highness will graciously be pleased to gather what I have written to His Serene Highness the Prince State Chancellor, on presenting the von Kircheisen correspondence, and what I have brought to his remembrance. — Court Councillor B[arbe] handed it to the Prince (since for sad reasons I cannot go out); Fr[?] Serene Highness received it graciously, and in the most well-meaning tone promised everything good. Meanwhile one counts on Prince Hardenberg — who [uncertain: Last / lets himself] not be disconcerted — who says that if they should be unwilling to give the estates back to the Prince, then he must be compensated. — For the rest, I still have no permission from the Prince to apply to the Russian authorities concerning Trąbczyn — the Prince, however, now sees further than all the swindlers. — Minister Wilhelm von Humboldt and Privy State Councillor Beguelin would [text lost] for me as truly upright men. — For the rest, Constantin rages frightfully in Poland; the country is being sucked entirely dry, and every male creature that can so much as bear a weapon is put into the ranks. — To this comes his proclamation that the Poles should hold together and assert their independence. — In what mood this puts our King, Your Serene Highness may easily decipher. — Everyone here speaks of war — may God prevent it. — I wish only that

Your Serene Highness's affairs might first of all be brought to an end here, so that the business does not again lie idle through a war that may break out suddenly. With boundless veneration I am

Your Most Serene Highness's

faithful and most obedient servant

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

If no quite extraordinary events intervene, it is settled that even the town of Kalisz will yet become Russian — I must now work solely on that side to get Trąbczyn back again. But as yet not one of them all has given me any comforting assurance from that quarter; rather, it is said that the Emperor would hardly annul what the Commission of Good Administration had done, and would sooner compensate the Prince in some other way. I am on that account in a desperate position: the Prince Chancellor of State forbids me to make any démarche whatever on that side, and so I must obey, and all the same I fear that everything will be quickly concluded and that the gate of grace will then be shut — Miączyński, husband of the lady née Prusimska, and Count Lanskoy are bosom friends, so not much good is to be hoped for there — Yesterday the great Wellington arrived here as Ambassador Extraordinary [uncertain: eingetrösten]; he is said to look somewhat askance at Kosten, and so something might be suspected there — Meanwhile the harmony between our King and the Emperor continues firmly — whereas the Prince Metternich and the Prince Talleyrand carry on intrigues without end — and on that account there is much talk here of one and of great wars — Today it is said that Dresden and Leipzig, together with the whole tract beyond the Elbe, are to be taken from us again, and the King of Saxony to be reinstated there — If that should happen, then for all our exertions we should have gained nothing, but rather, since Russia takes all Poland, have lost much — It is to be hoped that our King, acknowledged brave as he is, will not let this come to pass.

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

Your Serene Highness's letter of the 28th I received half an hour ago, together with the reply of Mr von Falkenhausen. Since I have known the contents of the report of the Brzeg Higher [uncertain: O. C.] Court these 3 weeks already, I pass over this in silence — Now the shock that Your Serene Highness claims to have received no letters from me since the 13th of last month paralyses my sense and understanding; since that time I have sent 7 letters from here, in which I reported many and important things.

I have informed Your Serene Highness that I wrote to General Schöler on one of the blank forms concerning Trąbczyn, — I have reported that in the same manner I gave a letter of thanks to the privy councillor of state Stägemann. I have informed you that I submitted the correspondence of Minister Kircheisen etc., which had been sent to me, to the Prince, and sent my letter with it in copy. I have faithfully written to you what has happened in this time and what has been said here about Your Serene Highness's affair. I have informed you that even Kalisz is lost to Prussia, and that those districts in which the estates lie fall to Russia — and that it will now cost much trouble to hold the same back, because there everything is done by money and petticoats.

I have further informed Your Serene Highness that now Saxony too — at least the fairest part, that is from Weißenfels onwards by way of Dresden and Leipzig as far as Lauban — is going to the devil. — I have written to you through whom the greatest intrigues are being forged. In my last letter I reported that Wellington has arrived, and that perhaps there is ground to hope

In all the letters I have set out my boundless distress, but above all I have asked, with all the skill and urgency I could, for 200 ducats to be sent, because I must hand over 100 # to the Prince Chancellor and 70 # to Barbe — and this may well be the motive why no letters are supposed to have arrived there — It is hard, more than hard, indeed it is unjust, that Your Serene Highness lets me suffer so dreadfully — I go about here like a beggar's dog, and starve again — Have you then no pity at all for me — do you then wish that I should become an utter laughing-stock — I am to act, and to act with deliberation — Do send someone here who will try the thing too with empty hands, indeed with an empty stomach. Barbe is beginning to look askance. Only yesterday evening he said to me, this does look odd — with those E: words are surely no gospel either — I could still die of shame, and that from [uncertain: Schreitwillen]. And now the Prince first of all: Jordan has already dunned me mockingly for the 100 # — the thing may end tragically — And so I swear before God that I shall not [uncertain: angerahmen] go under — for here everything is at stake — So now to your letter of today — The papers all lie with the privy councillor of state Stägemann; had he not so frightfully much work, everything would already be settled. Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

As regards Poland, matters now stand only so far that the boundary has been accepted from the Thorenſchen territory onward over Słupca near Pyzdry, across the Wartha and down the Prosna as far as Boleslawice, over towards Pitschen. — Likewise the boundary for the Saxony that is to remain has also been settled. The King of Saxony, who was yesterday invited to come here by an Austrian and a Prussian Concir, retains Dresden, Leipzig and Bautzen. — Hereafter the Congress Läute perhaps even sooner than in 3 weeks to have reached its end; but now England is beginning new and quite devilish intrigues — these Waßer hände want to have East Friesland, and we are to compensate Denmark for it. — The Emperor Alexander presses upon our King that a piece of land on our side in Germany should be given to the Viceroy of Italy. Both matters will draw stubborn debates after them, for, as is said, the King will by no means allow this to please him. If next the affairs of the German Empire are still to be arranged in general, when everything must be painted 15 times[uncertain: mahl] upon parchment, then many an hour more of time will yet be required. — Be that as it may, I go on tormenting the Prince Chancellor, yet he still remains good and his patience will not tire. — The papers are still lying with the Privy Councillor of State Stägemann. It is true enough, the work is frightfully great, but I keep on admonishing; thus, for example, I have again submitted to the Prince a petition as the enclosure shows. — He has received it graciously and has certainly promised to help. — Everyone of the good sort of men holds the matter of the 112/m Rthl advance to be quite certain and settled; with Cosmar himself it will probably drag out somewhat, for the Prince will punish the thing severely, the more so as the report of the Brzeg High Provincial Court has turned out so favourably.

B[arbe] is very active and handles the matter wisely and tirelessly. — All upright souls wish that Prince August would only revoke the power of attorney given to Cosmar quickly, and enter into no pour parlez with the pettifogger over it, but rather, as I have already advised, write to the Minister of Justice and to the Brzeg High Provincial Court that he has revoked the power of attorney given to Cosmar. Once this has been done, the 112/m Rthl. given and the Curiſchen heirs satisfied thereby, Cosmar is overthrown. — The Board of Wards, as also the Brzeg High Provincial Court, will bury him outright, once the guardianship in respect of Adolph is taken from him. As regards the Polish estates I await the decision at any moment — whether I am to come from, or whether the Prince Chancellor wishes to settle the matter alone.

Barbe expects the answer from Pourtalès in 10 to 12 days. Barbe wishes that Pourtalès might not come before the end of April, because until then there would still be frightfully much work — and Pourtalès would not gladly settle the matter without him. From the King there lies a letter to Your Serene Highness at the field post office. — It is presumably the answer to your New Year's congratulation. —

With the greatest respect I remain

Your Serene Highness's

most obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Vienna, the 13th of February 1815

273 Your Serene Highness's letter of the 7th of this month I received this very hour. Although it is true that I only wrote to Sławięcice the day before yesterday, the contents of your letter are so important that I hasten to set certain matters in a clear light which threaten even my honour, the more so since in 3 letters received from Your Serene Highness a very cold tone prevails. I therefore give myself the honour of answering first the latter point, point by point. — As regards then, 1st, Mr General Schüler, he will not involve himself in the business, and that in order not to make enemies of the Poles etc. — His last answer was: Should the Emperor ask me, well then I shall see what can be done. — Even Count Nesselrode shrugs his shoulders. I have therefore no other help to expect in this matter than through the State Chancellor and through Mr Minister Humboldt. I have asked Your Serene Highness for 2 French blank forms, in order, if the Prince so commands, to write to the Emperor once more. Mr Court Councillor Barbe will draw it up; he advises, however, that the Prince's commands be punctually complied with. As regards, 2nd, the error concerning the yield of the estates, this — as I have already written to Mr Court Councillor Hahn — will probably have no further consequences than that it marks an ugly contradiction, of which neither the Court Councillor nor I am guilty. Your Serene Highness yourself gives me the revenues as 79,000 Rthl — this I took in the first submission as the standard — but the officials now put them down as low as 36,000 Rthl — and I should have much preferred not to have had this extract appended to the record, because the difference is too striking. That for the rest the officials have either reported incorrectly or managed badly can only be the case. — I am entirely reassured by Mr Court Councillor Hahn's statements, all of which lie before His Serene Highness the State Chancellor from A to Z. He gives the value of the estates as 2 millions and their yield as 60/m Rthl, which in better times would have to turn out much higher. Since indeed the Privy

Councillor of State von Stägemann himself holds him to be an expert man, no further disadvantage is to be feared. — That I should have liked to see Your Serene Highness's statement of the revenues of 79/m Rthl. substantiated in the record at least by 70/m, is surely not to be blamed. Given the distance and the snail-like progress of the posts, I could not know that Mr Court Councillor Hahn had already departed for Brzeg, for otherwise I should not have written at that time at all. — I am content, and am all too glad to be convinced, that the estates have funds enough to discharge the 112/m Rthl in 5 or 6 years — and thus I fall respectfully silent upon this passage, the more so as the oft-mentioned error will now never be of any consequence and everything has already been forestalled. — It does, however, strike me as remarkable why so much fuss is made of this matter. Did I report the revenues? — are they trying to make a beast of burden of me, that I am to bear the blame for it; did I know the yield of the estates? Your Serene Highness gave it to me so. — Your word was sacred to me; upon this foundation I raised the building. — Had I shown Hahn at that time Your Serene Highness's statement, he would perhaps have refuted it, and he, as a straightforward man and as a faithful [uncertain: follower] of Your [text lost] would certainly have advised me faithfully and truly. In short, neither he nor I is at fault for the said error, between which, however, neither I nor Court Councillor Hahn wishes to be left exposed. As regards the advance of the 112/m Rthl., it will be granted. — Unless all are lying — then I have, willy-nilly, lain along with them — only this no one can lie about or say of me, that I wished to settle the matter with the Courland heirs in secret without the knowledge of the mandatories. It is outrageous to me that for all my exertions I should now further

be taken for a filon or a total blockhead.

At bottom I do not know whether it were so great an honour to boast of such a compromise; I have therefore advised that the King himself should never have done this, but that Your Serene Highness should be furnished with the advance of 112/m Rthl. for the purpose

Your Serene Highness appears to wish to burden me with these — this I neither can nor am able to bear. You cause it moreover to be made known to me through a stranger's hand — this is against my sense of honour and humiliates me too greatly. — I have said and done nothing but what stands in the papers given and sent to me. — I have exerted everything to bring the matter to the desired goal. — Much has already succeeded, and the rest would have been attained as well. — That His Serene Highness the Prince State Chancellor does not lay everything else aside and does not answer at once what I submit, for that I cannot be held responsible. — I see him scarcely once a month, which fate thousands share with me. — It has sufficed me hitherto that everything which Barbe hands to him in Your Serene Highness's affairs he has received with goodwill and gracious assurances, and has straightway assigned it to the referee. most obedient servant

Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Lord!

The day before yesterday I was asked what the circumstances were regarding the 100,000 Rthl which Prince August demands; I answered that this is solely a legacy of the late Princess Sakkin, with which Prince August is to pay whatever debts there may be in the Hohenlohe lands. Today a letter goes off from the Prince State Chancellor to Öhringen, in which Prince August is informed that His Majesty has no objection to the delivery of the 100,000 Rthl, and that the Ministry of Justice, Kircheisen, has been directed to let this be done, provided no lawful objections stand against the matter, and to effect it as soon as possible. Your Serene Highness's case still lies with the Privy Councillor of State Stägemann. He has as yet had no occasion to be able to lay a report upon it before His Serene Highness. Everything has been set in train in the most impeccable manner — According to the assurances of Barbe and others, the matter of the advance of 112,000 Rthl is to be regarded as entirely successful. Next to these, Cosmar's removal is a principal object, and it has been resolved upon here; meanwhile this must be made known from Berlin.

As concerns the Polish affairs, I am now to submit the instruments and the records transacted at Kalisz — that which falls or lies within the Grand Duchy of Poznań will not be difficult to obtain, whereas the Trąbczyn matter / which estates lie the Prosna / will be subject to great adversities. Most Serene Prince,

Most gracious Prince and Lord!

His Majesty the late King of Prussia conferred in the year 1796 upon the Prince of Hohenlohe, according to the appended copy of the instrument under Letter A, the estates of Kamionna and Kolno in the Poznań department, likewise the villages of Trąbczyn, Szetlewek, Nowawies, Lazy, Laske, Osiny and Trąbczyner Hauland in the district of Konin, as also the village of Brzyce together with its appurtenances in Cujavia. These estates formerly belonged to a certain von Prusimski, and after his flight they were confiscated and conferred upon the Prince of Hohenlohe.

The Prince possessed these estates, except Brzyce, which the daughter of Prusimski, now the married von Miączyńska, claimed as her maternal inheritance, for over 11 years in the most undisturbed possession. Of these he sold in the year 1804 to the bank director Leixner at Frankfurt an der Oder the Kamionna and Kolno estates, which Leixner likewise possessed undisturbed for 3 years.

Only in 1807, and indeed 14 weeks after the peace of Tilsit, did it occur to the so-called Polish administrative commission to take all the estates from the Prince and from Leixner by force, without any judicial judgment whatever, and to give the same to the married Miączyńska. Prince Hohenlohe, immediately upon his return from the Empire, brought suit before the peace court at Konin, which forum, however, von Miączyńska did not recognise at all. The Prince thereupon caused the complaint here most humbly appended under Letter B to be submitted, in the prescribed manner, through his attorney, to the tribunal at Kalisz, which now also points to everything for further inspection. Von Miączyńska replied thereto through her actuary, according to the enclosure under Letter C, that she was also not not bound to submit herself to the tribunal in this matter. The said tribunal then drew the matter out longer than a year, and at length issued the decree appended under Letter D, in which, after many shallow and unintelligible circumlocutions, it says — that the tribunal did not hold itself empowered to annul the ordinance of the administrative commission, and that this belonged to the King alone — that von Miączyńska should therefore remain seated in the estates, and the Prince pay the costs. So the matter stands even now: Miączyńska sits in the estates, draws in all the revenues, and since 1806 has paid not a Groschen of interest. No one was made more unfortunate by this shameful and violent act of the oft-mentioned administrative commission than the bank director Leixner; this man saw himself not only robbed of his fortune, but he lost his bread and his freedom. After the happy turn which Europe's fate has now taken through Your Serene Highness's foresight and exertion, may Your Most High Self deign to command that Kolno and Kamionna be given back to Leixner, in order that the Royal Bank may be satisfied, and by Your Most High and powerful intercession with His Majesty the Russian Emperor bring it about that to the Prince of Hohenlohe the Trąbczyn estates also, which lie on the far side of the Prosna, must be given back by von Miączyńska, together with the revenues drawn by her through 9 years, which according to the leases amount to 36,500 Rthl.

Your Most Serene Highness will, by the granting of this just request, make happy many persons languishing in misery, and the Royal Bank will likewise receive its money back.

In deepest reverence I remain, until death,

Your Most Serene Highness's

most humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

Vienna, the 2nd of March 1815

Poznań, 2 November 1815.

By the order of 6 June of this year Your Serene Highness transmitted to me two letters of the Prince of Hohenlohe, to Your Serene Highness and to His Excellency the Minister Baron vom Stein, of 12 May

of this year, with the command that I express myself upon the steps which would have to be taken in favour of this Prince with the Imperial Russian cabinet.

The Prince of Hohenlohe received from His Majesty the late King, as a gift, the estates of Kolno and Kamionna in the Poznań country, and the estates of Trąbczyn in the Kalisz department. Both estates were formerly the property of the Starost Prusimski, who had been implicated in the insurrection in the year 1794, and had fallen to the State by confiscation.

The estates of Kolno and Kamionna the Prince sold to the bank cashier Leixner before the year 1806. The Trąbczyn ones, however, he did not. All the estates have, through the political events of the years 1806/7, passed back to the heirs of the former owner, with whom, in these circumstances, they remain under the Vienna treaty of 3 May of this year; against which His Majesty is inclined to compensate the donees for their loss.

After the Prince of Hohenlohe had communicated with me variously concerning this compensation, partly by word of mouth through

[Written by the receiving office:]

c. 3,278 fr: Paris 18 Nov 1815. To Councillor of Legation Balan. The estates of Kolno and Kamionna, which lie in the Grand Duchy of Posen, no longer belong at all to the Prince of Hohenlohe, since he already sold them in the year 1805 for 142,000 Rthl to the bank cashier Leixner, for whom the state of possession has also long since been put in order. There is no ground whatever on which the Prince can be mixed into this affair; his Mandatoris, the deceased von Triebenfeld, also appears to have interested himself in it out of pity for Leixner, who has in the meantime likewise died. that the Royal Ministry of Foreign Affairs for many Princes of Hohenlohe on account of the Trąbczyn estates no [illegible]. Most [uncertain: Meisten]. court; this matter is therefore to issue again to Mr Gericht Jordan, on 13 April St[ä]g[emann].

the councillor of war von Triebenfeld, partly in writing by letters devoid of content, a certain Schenck has at last come forward as his authorised representative, and has deduced to me from a volume of accounts that a compensation of 318,500 Rthl. is due to the Prince for the loss of the Trąbczyn estates, and that this could best be made good by the domain office of Sokolnik, lying in Poland close against the frontier, which pays 15,000 Rthl. a year in rent. To His Excellency Count Bernstorff

The undersigned, Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary of His Majesty the Emperor of All the Russias, King of Poland, has been instructed to communicate to the King's Ministry the enclosed report of the Lieutenant of the Kingdom of Poland concerning a claim which Countess Micheline Miączyńska, née Prusimska, makes against the Prussian Government, and to support it as best he may.

This report contains arguments so conclusive that the undersigned could add nothing to them; and as he has gathered, during the time he has had the honour of being accredited to the King, the most convincing proofs of the impartial justice which His Majesty causes to be administered in His States, he confines himself to begging Count Bernstorff, Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, to recommend the interests of Countess Miączyńska to the authorities who will have to pronounce upon them.

He takes this opportunity to renew to His Excellency the expression of his very high consideration.

David d'Alopeus

Copy

The Commissioners Plenipotentiary for the liquidation of the assets and liabilities of the former Duchy of Warsaw have just made the following statement on the claims addressed to them by Countess Micheline Miączyńska, née Prusimska.

The object of these claims is: that the hereditary estates of the said Countess, confiscated in 1796 from her father, the Starost Prusimski, by the Prussian Government, and into the possession of which she was reinstated by an order of the Governing Commission of the former Duchy of Warsaw of 21 July 1807, made by virtue of a decree of the Emperor of France of 5 July 1807, be relieved of the debts contracted by the donees who had held them temporarily; that the amount of these debts be counted among the liquidated liabilities chargeable to the Prussian Government; and that the said estates be thereby restored to the state in which they were at the time of their confiscation, and the owner protected against the proceedings of the creditors.

In support of her request Madame Miączyńska alleges the following circumstances:

That the Starost Prusimski, her father, possessed hereditary estates, namely:

[Written by the receiving office:]

[chargeable to the Prussian Government:] As if Prussia were answerable to anyone at all for acts of government in former South Prussia!

1. Kamienno and Kolno, district of Międzyrzecz, in the Grand Duchy of Poznań.

2. The estates of Pawłowo, Dzwonowo and Berenkusz, district of Wągrowice, in the same Duchy.

3. Trąbczyn and Szetlowek with their appurtenances, in the district of Konin, Palatinate of Kalisz, in Poland.

The poor state of the health of the said Starost and of that of his wife obliged him in 1794 to go to Italy.

The Prussian Government summoned Mr Prusimski and his wife in October 1795 and in February 1796 to justify the reasons which had led them to leave the country, accusing the former at the same time of having taken part in the insurrection of 1794. Later, on 24 March 1796, that is to say a month after the second summons, without hearing Prusimski's answer, the said Government had all the estates designated above confiscated.

[Written by the receiving office:]

[the health of the said Starost and of that of his wife:] So now he was ill too! She only fell ill at Venice

The Starost Prusimski, who had just then lost his wife, was at Venice. Having had knowledge only very late of the aforesaid summonses, which reached him only some months afterwards, he thought it his duty, in order to justify as soon as possible the reasons for his departure from Poland, to send the Prussian Government a certificate of the

illness and death of his wife, legalised by Count Cathane, Prussian Councillor of Legation to the Republic of Venice, and at the same time begged that the time fixed for his justification be extended; but before he could obtain this he succumbed to the illness from which he was suffering, and which had forced him to seek relief in foreign countries.

Madame Miączyńska, then of tender age and an orphan, deprived of all the help of a legal guardianship, had been unable to pursue her rights to her father's fortune. The Prussian Government meanwhile disposed of it in the following manner. It granted:

To Prince Hohenlohe Ingelfingen the estates of Kolno, Kamionna and Trąbczyn, and others situated in the district of Konin.

To General Sanitz:

The domain of Pawłowo with its appurtenances.

[to the illness from which he was suffering:] 1803. Oct.

At the time of the political changes which came about in 1807, the Emperor of the French, wishing to do justice to the claims of all the Poles whose estates had been confiscated by the Prussian Government, issued a decree by virtue of which all the confiscations were abolished and the lawful owners reinstated in possession of the estates

of which they had been deprived. It is in consequence of this decree that the Senator Palatine (Woywod?) Wybicki recovered possession of his estate called Manieczki, and after him Countess Micheline Miączyńska, then widow of her first husband Dąbski.

General Niemojewski and Wichrowsky were likewise reinstated in their respective properties in consequence of an order of the Government of the Duchy of Warsaw of 21 July 1807.

When the Duchy of Warsaw passed under the sceptre of His Majesty the King of Saxony, the Prussian Government made representations on behalf of General Sanitz, aiming at the restitution to him of the estate of Pawłowo. The King of Saxony asked the opinion of the Council of Ministers of the said Duchy on this matter.

It follows from this that the legitimacy of the rights of Madame Micheline Miączyńska cannot be called in question; and indeed she would have had no ground to make new claims if all her estates had been restored to her, as Pawłowo was, in the same state in which they were at the time of their confiscation. But the estates of Trąbczyn and Szeltowek were burdened by the donee Prince Hohenlohe with a sum of 156,000 Reichsthaler. Madame Miączyńska, referring to the decree of the Government of the Duchy of Warsaw of 21 July 1807, requests that the aforementioned estates be put back in the same state in which her father had left them, that is to say free of every mortgage charge; in support of this request she represents:

[Written by the receiving office:]

[be put back in the same state:] Where is that written? Not even in the Napoleonic decree.

[against all justice:] untrue

1. That the Prussian Government had confiscated the estates of the petitioner against all justice and without regard to the incontestable right she had to them as a minor and an orphan. That although this Government

disposed of the aforesaid estates in favour of Prince Hohenlohe and General Sanitz to reward their services, such a donation could nevertheless only be temporary, as the political events which came about in 1807 proved: in changing the order of things then existing, they produced the same effect on the particular circumstances that arose from it; for in giving existence back to a part of Poland, the private owners were at the same time re-established in possession of the estates which had been unjustly confiscated from them. Now it follows from this that, the donations once annulled, all the transactions deriving from them necessarily had to be annulled in all their effects, so that the debts mortgaged on the aforementioned estates can fall only on the donees who contracted them. It is in consequence of this principle that the Minister of Justice, by his decision of 30 November 1817, referred to the Prussian Government the claims of Leyner, purchaser of the estates of Kolno and Kamienno.

[Written by the receiving office:]

[as the political events ... proved:] but for as long as he possessed it, he possessed it lawfully and with full right of ownership

[unjustly confiscated:] Where is that written?

2. That since the Emperor of the French and the Governing Commission had judged it equitable to give back to the owners the estates unjustly confiscated from them, the effect would not answer to the purpose for which this act of justice

had been done, if the said owners were to be bound to pay the debts with which their estates had been encumbered by the donees; seeing that in such a case they would have recovered only an onerous and purely illusory title of inheritance.

3. The rights of Madame Miączyńska and those of General Niemojewski and of Wichrowski to the estates they claimed being of one and the same nature, the restitution of those estates took place in consequence of decrees issuing from one and the same principle.

Wichrowski recovered possession of his estate of Beskyn free of debt. General Niemojewski took back his own in a like state. And Madame Miączyńska herself was reinstated in her estate of Pawłowo, held by General Sanitz, likewise free of debts; why then should she be bound to discharge those with which Prince Hohenlohe had encumbered the estates granted to him?

[Written by the receiving office:]

[they would have recovered only an onerous title of inheritance:] They got back what was there.

[Prince Hohenlohe had encumbered the estates:] Because here there are debts.

4. The Prussian Government, wishing to reward the services of General Sanitz, made him a gift of the estates confiscated from the parents of Madame Miączyńska; but when these estates were taken back from the donee, the said Government

judged it proper to indemnify him by granting him another estate, called Hetzendorff.

It acted likewise towards General Zastrof, granting him the estate called [uncertain: Lama] in place of that of Manieczki, restored to the Senator Palatine Wybicki.

Now the said Government cannot refuse to indemnify Prince Hohenlohe by undertaking to pay for him the debts with which he burdened the estates now belonging to Madame Miączyńska.

From this historical account of the affair it follows:

That since the Government of the former Duchy of Warsaw had refused to satisfy the claims of the Prussian one as regards the indemnification of the donees for the loss of the estates taken back from them to be returned to their lawful owners, and since the latter recognised it as equitable to indemnify the same donees in its own country and from its own funds, it is consequently beyond doubt, although it has not acted in the same way towards Prince Hohenlohe, that the motives which had determined it to indemnify the former will lead it also to observe the same principle of equity towards the said Prince. In that case

the creditors will settle their claims on the indemnity that will have been granted to him.

That such an opinion could not be appreciated by the Prussian Government once this affair has been laid before it in its true light, the justice of the cause itself seems to be the guarantee, seeing:

1. That the said Government, without waiting for the Starost Prusimski to justify the reasons that had prompted his departure (and which could be none other than those of health, as is proved by the death of his wife, whom he survived only a short time), at once had all his estates confiscated.

2. Madame Miączyńska, of tender age and an orphan, had a right, in conformity with the Prussian laws, to the protection of the Government; as a minor she could not, by the same laws, be held responsible for the conduct of her parents, even had it been recognised as reprehensible. Nor could she be deprived of the fortune of her father, whose lawful heiress she was, all the more since it was the obligation of the said Government to watch over the integrity of the rights of its ward. If the fault lies with the persons charged

with the guardianship of Madame Miączyńska, it is just that the Prussian Government, which had appointed them, should, in redressing the wrongs that their negligence may have done to the interests of its ward, free the estates of Madame Miączyńska from the debts which she had not contracted, and which she is not bound to discharge, either by the principles of all justice or in conformity with the Prussian laws.

Warsaw, 29 April 1818

Berlin, 11 May 1819. No. 2,434 B

To Mr d'Alopeus

Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary of Russia at Berlin

The undersigned, Minister of State and of the Cabinet of His Majesty the King of Prussia, has received the note and the memorial which Mr d'Alopeus, Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary of His Majesty the Emperor of All the Russias, did him the honour of addressing to him under date of 20 February of this year, on the claims of Countess Miączyńska, née Prusimska.

The undersigned thinks it right first to retrace in a few words the state of the question.

The Starost Prusimski took part in 1795 in the insurrection of the Poles against Russia and Prussia. After the insurrection had been put down he fled; his estates were confiscated by virtue of a judicial sentence, and the King having disposed of them in favour of various individuals, these donees borrowed on these landed estates, which served as mortgage security for these debts.

Prusimski died in 1803 in a foreign country without having been able to obtain reinstatement in his possessions; he left a daughter, Countess Miączyńska, as his heiress. After the Peace of Tilsit she was put back in possession of her lands by the Government of the Grand Duchy of Warsaw, and since the dissolution of that state the general amnesty pronounced in the Act of the Congress of Vienna has guaranteed her the enjoyment of her estates.

Today Countess Miączyńska is not content with having recovered her lands in the state in which the donees left them. She asks that the debts which rest on these estates be extinguished.

A subject at once of the Emperor of Russia, by the lands she owns in the Kingdom of Poland, and of the King, by those which belong to her in the Grand Duchy of

Poznań, she had already applied directly to the Prussian Government; but reasons of justice and equity had caused her request to be rejected.

These reasons are still the same. The undersigned has had this affair examined anew, and he has taken into mature consideration the arguments put forward in favour of Countess Miączyńska in the memorial delivered by Mr d'Alopeus. But as these arguments rest in great part on facts which the Countess has presented with more art than truth, this memorial has not been able to weaken the reasoning on which the decision of the Prussian tribunals was founded, and is founded still.

This reasoning is set out in all its force and with the greatest evidence in the memorial which the undersigned has the honour to communicate herewith to Mr d'Alopeus, and he does not doubt that, having read it, this minister will find that the ruling of the Prussian authorities is founded in law and in reason.

The recommendation of the Cabinet of Petersburg laid upon the undersigned the obligation of bringing to the new examination of this affair as much care as impartiality. Having acquitted himself of this duty, he regrets indeed that the result of this examination is not such as Russia desired in favour of Countess Miączyńska; but the love of justice which animates His Majesty the Emperor as it animates the King, and which is one of the finest bonds of the union of Prussia and Russia, gives him the sweet and intimate conviction that the Russian Government will recognise the force of the motives which have dictated to Prussia a fresh refusal.

The undersigned takes this occasion to renew to Mr d'Alopeus the assurance of his high consideration.

Sire, The Minister Secretary of State having, by his official letter of 1/13 April last, transmitted to me the petition of Count Ernest Bethusy, by which the latter asks to be admitted, together with his three sons, to the enjoyment of the benefits stipulated with regard to mixed proprietors by article 18 of the Treaty of Vienna, concluded with Prussia on 21 April / 3 May 1815, I hasten to lay at the foot of Your Imperial and Royal Majesty's throne the explanations which the Commission of the Interior and of Police has just presented to me on this subject.

Count Bethusy possesses lands in the Kingdom of Poland and in Prussian Silesia; now the provisions of the Treaty of Vienna concern only the inhabitants and proprietors of those countries whose separation took

place by virtue of that same Treaty, and in particular the benefits stipulated by article 18 can be applied only to possessions cut through by the frontier line which separates the Kingdom of Poland from the Grand Duchy of Posen.

It follows in consequence that the stipulations of the said Treaty could in no manner be interpreted in favour of the petitioner.

Besides, in claiming the advantages granted to mixed proprietors, Count Bethusy appears to have in view only the liberty of making from time to time transports of the iron ore which he possesses in the Kingdom, for the needs of his forges in Silesia — a liberty which he enjoyed without restriction under the Prussian Government, but which he could not recover in the present state of things, seeing that the exportation of the said materials, as harmful to the interest of the country's manufactories, is absolutely prohibited by our customs regulations.
