Copy

It is with great regret that the undersigned, Envoy Extraordinary, finds himself under the necessity of troubling His Excellency Count Nesselrode with an affair which already in 1818 and 1819 was the subject of an official correspondence between the two Governments, and which — at this moment — has reached such a point that the Prussian Government could not acquiesce in it without compromising its dignity and sacrificing the most evident rights of its subjects.

Referring to the Notes which the King's Mission had the honour of addressing to the Imperial Ministry under date of 10 September/29 August 1819 and of 24/12 May 1820, the undersigned confines himself to recapitulating quite briefly the following facts:

The Starost Prusimski having taken part in the insurrection of 1794, his lands situated in the district of Konin, Palatinate of Kalisz, and namely the lordship of Trąbczyn with its appurtenances, were confiscated in conformity with the laws in force on the crime of high treason.

The ownership of this lordship having been conferred by His Majesty King Frédéric Guillaume II, by means of a donation dated 9 August 1796, on the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, the latter's title of possession was rectified and registered before the Government of former South Prussia.

Some time afterwards the new owner

contracted a debt of 30,000 Reichsthaler to Mr François de Grottowsky, which was registered on the mortgage and afterwards assigned by a judicial act to the merchant Weigel, domiciled at Wrocław.

When in 1807 — in consequence of the political events — Prussia had lost this province, the Governing Commission of the former Duchy of Warsaw gave back the lands of Trąbczyn to the daughter of the late Starost Prusimski, Michalina, then widow of her first husband Mr Dąbski, now married to Count Miączyński; and in conformity with this act of grace the title of possession was changed anew and transferred to this lady. The intabulated claims, however, remained not only intact, but, what is more, it was only then (22 March 1808) that the aforementioned assignment of the 30,000 Reichsthaler was registered.

The interest on this mortgage claim not having been paid since, the merchant Weigel was at last obliged to bring his debtor before the civil tribunal of Kalisz; but, contrary to all expectation, this tribunal, dismissing him entirely, decided at first instance, by a judgment given on 6 March 1819, that Mr Weigel's claim should be extinguished and struck out of the registers.

To justify this decision, the civil tribunal of Kalisz had put forward the following arguments:

1. That the order of the Governing Commission of 1 July 1807, by which the lands in question were given back to Madame de Miączyńska, was alone to serve as the basis of a decision in this affair, without regard to the laws in force on the inviolability of mortgage claims.

2. That, even though it is not said in this order that the mortgage debts contracted on these lands after the confiscation were to be extinguished, this condition must nevertheless be understood, because without it the act of grace of the Governing Commission would have no effect;

3. That the acts of donation made by His Majesty the King of Prussia had been valid only for as long as His dominion had lasted, and that consequently the succeeding Government had been master to annul them just as it pleased.

The merchant Weigel, having lodged an appeal, brought this affair to the knowledge of the Prussian Government, and it was then that the King's Mission had the honour of addressing itself to the Imperial Ministry to ask for its intervention, in order that the judicial decision on the question:

Whether the claim registered on the mortgage of the lands of Trąbczyn was to be extinguished without repayment?

should be discontinued, and that this question should be reserved for diplomatic discussion.

Nine months having passed without the Mission's having received any answer whatever, it had the honour of reminding His Excellency Count Nesselrode of this affair by a note dispatched under date of 24/12 May 1820; but this communication likewise remained without an answer.

Although the undersigned is glad to seek the reason for this as much in the almost inevitable delays in the course of business touching the Kingdom of Poland, in view of the distance between the capitals, as in the Congresses which then required His Excellency's particular attention, it is nevertheless a fact that, without regard to the protests of the Prussian Government, Mr Weigel's suit has meanwhile been judged at 2nd and 3rd instance, and that, although the court of appeal set aside the first sentence, the Supreme Tribunal of Warsaw has just confirmed it in every point.

It would lead too far to enter here into the details of this affair by repeating the arguments put forward on either side; but, after examining them more closely, no one will wish to deny that, judging by the laws in force on the inviolability of mortgage claims in Poland as in Prussia, the merchant Weigel could never have been dismissed from his claim.

Yet the civil tribunal of Kalisz and that of Warsaw saw fit not to keep

to the laws; they admitted as the basis of their judgments only the act of grace of the Regency Commission of the former Duchy of Warsaw, calling this act a privilege belonging to the category of the "constitutiones principum spéciales", and they did not even judge by the terms of this order, but by the sense which it pleased them to find in it, thereby themselves violating the theory of Roman law, to which they appear to refer in order to justify this strange departure from the common law, and which positively prescribes that privileges require a restrictive interpretation where the contrary might prejudice a third party.

In attributing a retroactive effect to the order of the Governing Commission, they have attacked the rights which a Prussian subject had legitimately acquired on an estate whose ownership derived from his Sovereign, and consequently they have taken it upon themselves to contest the validity of a donation made in good and due form by His Majesty the King of Prussia.

Not only have these tribunals exceeded the bounds of their power in seeking to judge a question which belongs to the law of nations, and which, supposing it were in fact doubtful, ought necessarily to have been reserved for political discussion, as Prussia had already asked in 1819 — but, what is more, their judgment is contrary to the clearest stipulations of the

existing treaties, which had long since decided this question in favour of the merchant Weigel and of all those who are in the same category.

The Peace of Tilsit (art. 25) and the convention signed at Vienna on 20 March 1815 furnish evident proof of it, and in particular art. 13 of the convention of 22 May 1819 expressly states the following:

"likewise maintained are every claim and every charge mortgaged on landed property situated in the States of His Majesty the King of Prussia, as also every charge and every claim mortgaged on landed property situated in the Kingdom of Poland, etc. etc."

The undersigned flatters himself with the hope that these observations, which a more detailed examination of the affair cannot but confirm, will suffice to convince His Excellency Count Nesselrode that Prussia has not only the most incontestable right, but even the most sacred duty, to oppose the execution of the said judgment; and it is by express order of his Court that he appeals to the obliging intercession of His Excellency, begging Him kindly to take the necessary steps with the Imperial Government so that the judgment given by the Supreme Tribunal of Warsaw, dated 17 July 1826 and confirming that of the civil tribunal of

Kalisz be annulled, and that the courts of justice of the Kingdom of Poland be enjoined henceforth to respect the mortgage claims legitimately acquired both by the merchant Weigel and by other Prussian subjects, claims which have been solemnly and reciprocally guaranteed by the two Governments.

In the firm conviction that the Imperial Government will not delay in acceding to so just a representation, the undersigned permits himself to add the observation that it matters to his Government that, before all else, the execution of the said judgment be suspended, so that Mr Weigel's claim may not meanwhile be struck out of the mortgage books and replaced by some other claim, which appears to be the design of Countess de Miączyńska, and which could only multiply the difficulties it finds in the recovery of this claim.

The undersigned, charged by his Court to hasten his report on the outcome of this step, likes to believe that His Excellency will be good enough, in consideration of the grave and major interests which are its object, to honour him as soon as possible with an answer, and takes this occasion.

St Petersburg, 10 February/29 January 1827

signed General de Schöler

To His Excellency Count (Karl) Nesselrode

Having heard the conclusions of the Public Ministry, and taking cognisance first of all of the exception of nullity of the summons for want of any mention of the defendants' domicile;

Considering:

That the plaintiff could not, in the summons issued to the defendants, assign them any other domicile than the one they had chosen for themselves in the act of regulation of the mortgage register; and therefore, dismissing this exception on that ground as unfounded, and taking cognisance of the second exception, of nullity of the summons served, on account of the death that had occurred of the defendant Anna née Blachow Grotowska, since this assertion of the advocate Chrystowski is by no credible document

substantiated, because the certificate produced from the Court Office of the Lubliniec estates provides no legal proof either as to form or as to substance, for not only is it not attested by the competent authority, but it speaks moreover of the death of persons having occurred in different places, which could be proved only by the burial record of the authority of the place where the death occurred; for which reason the Tribunal, dismissing this exception too, in the matter itself, after examining the documents produced, the proofs and the state of the case,

Considering:

That it is open to no doubt whatever that the estates of Trąbczyn and Szetlewek with their appurtenances were, before the last

partition of the Polish country, the private and exclusive property of the late Antoni Prusimski, and were held by him by that right until the time of the confiscation of the estates for his belonging to the Insurrection.

That after their confiscation from Prusimski they were granted by a diploma of donation of the Most Serene Fryderyk Wilhelm the Second, King of Prussia, dated the ninth of August of the year one thousand seven hundred and ninety-six, to Fryderyk Ludwik, Reigning Prince of Hohenlohe Ingelfingen,

passed from their true owner to the donee, and it was only on the strength of that act that the latter regulated the mortgage register in his own name.

That after the change of government which followed, the Governing Commission, as the supreme authority in the country, representing the rights of the Monarch, by its decision of the twenty-first of July of the year one thousand eight hundred and seven, issued at Dresden, restored the present plaintiff, Michalina née Prusimska, by her first marriage Dąbska, now Miączyńska, to the estates confiscated from her father

that, therefore, no other consequence follows from all these acts than that, on the one hand, the event of the confiscation of the estates and their grant by a diploma of donation to Prince Hohenlohe, being the effect of the political circumstances of that time, could retain its binding force only for as long as that same state of things lasted, and so, on the other hand, the restoration of the then Dąbska, née Prusimska, to her paternal estates after the change of government is to be regarded in no other way than as a return to the original rights of the owner which were his at the time they were taken from him; in which, from the very nature of the thing,

lies the determination of the same state of things as existed at the time of the confiscation of the estates; and this being so,

Considering therefore:

That since the donee, Prince Hohenlohe, could be regarded only as a conditional possessor, and with the fall of his title the debts contracted by him and burdening the estates likewise ceased to be binding, therefore his creditors too, the present defendants, the brothers Lichnowski and Grotowska née Blachow, being unable to acquire better rights than belonged to the donee himself, to shelter behind his rights in any way

are not able.

nor does the Treaty of Tilsit, namely its Articles 24 and 25, cited by the defendants in their defence, in any way improve their rights, since it cannot at all be applied to estates confiscated from private persons and given back to them again, as is explained more fully by the Opinion of the Council of Ministers in the matter of General Sanitz, laid before the Throne on the fifth of October of the year one thousand eight hundred and ten.

The Minister Presiding in the Government Commission of Revenue and Treasury

I have received Your Honour's letter of 10 Aug. of this year, and its renewal of 14 Sept. of this year, on the subject of compensation to you for the losses you suffered in consequence of the striking-out of your claim of 30.000 thalers from the estates of Trąbczyn, ordered by the courts of this country.

The first of these letters was accompanied by a Liquidation of the compensation Your Honour demands, namely:

in capital 30.000 thalers

in interest 31.800 thalers

in costs 1,300 thalers

Total 63.100 thalers

I found this demand excessive, since under the laws in force with us Your Honour could never have attained such results even in the event of the most favourable conduct of the case. Wishing, on the other hand, to preserve strict justice, with the aim of compensating Your Honour for losses really suffered, and not nominal ones, I was obliged to order that the valuation of the estates formerly burdened with the above claim be ascertained on the spot, and in this way the degree of real value of the capital Your Honour lost be assessed. — This, then, is the reason why I have not been able until now to give Your Honour a detailed answer to your application.

In reply to the high communication of the 22nd of last month, No. 59607/938, I hereby most humbly submit to Your Serene Highness, in certified copy, for the estates of Trąbczyn, Osiny, Łazy, Nowawieś, Zarobna and the Trąbczyn Hollander settlement, with appurtenances,

1. the mortgage certificate of 14 August 1803.

2. the judicial valuation of 6 May 1803.

According to the mortgage certificate the value of these estates is taken at Rthl 160,000.

The items entered ahead of my claim amount to:

1. Section II. Church capitals in all, 7,000 Polish florins or Rthl 1,166. 16 Groschen.

2. Section III. For v. Przepolewski, although paid, ditto 5,000. -

v. Lichnowski ditto 42,000. - = 48,166. 16 Groschen

To cover my item entered in Section III No. 3 for v. Grottowski, now for me, there remained Rthl 111,833. 8 Groschen, and since my claim amounts to only 63,100. -, there is a surplus beyond it of Rthl 48,733. 8 Groschen.

The valuation is drawn up on the low principles that were applied to the estimating of the crown domains. The bushel of wheat is brought into the computation at only 20 good groschen, the bushel of rye at 16 good groschen, the bushel of barley at 12 good groschen and the bushel of oats at 8 good groschen, while on the other hand half the harvest has been deducted, and besides that 15 per cent of the gross income for administration.

By this the assumed value has been calculated at only Rthl 128,917, 17 Groschen. If the 48,166. 16 standing ahead of me are deducted from this, there still remain Rthl 80,751, 1 Groschen to cover me, for which only 63,100. - are required.

From these facts there is surely no doubt that my claim was entirely secure.

So long as legal assistance had not been refused me, I could have paid off the items standing ahead of mine and bid at the forced sale as far as was necessary for my claim.

On the strength of this proof and of the earlier acknowledgement, and finally of the long duration of the matter, I may expect of Your Serene Highness's justice that Your Highness will now most graciously arrange for my satisfaction and fix an early date for the agreement between us, of which there can be no doubt, at which I would appear in person or through an authorised representative.

With the greatest reverence I have the honour to be, etc.

agad118501169-1:
Report of the Commission of Instruction on a conflict of jurisdiction raised by the Commission of Finances against a definitive judgment rendered in [1829] by the Supreme Tribunal, by virtue of which the sum of 30,000 Reichsthaler owed to Sieur Weigel was struck from the mortgage on the Trąbczyn property belonging to the Dame Miączyńska.

The Prussian Government, having in 1796 confiscated the property of Trąbczyn belonging to the Starost Prusimski, gave it in full ownership to Prince Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen.

In 1800, Prince Hohenlohe, having borrowed from a Sieur Grotowski the sum of 30,000 Reichsthaler, this claim was inscribed in the mortgage book of the Trąbczyn estate. Later, in 1807, the daughter of the late Starost Prusimski, Micheline — by her first marriage Dąbska,

by her second Miączyńska — presented to His Majesty the Emperor Napoleon a petition in which she sought the restitution of the property confiscated from her Father.

This petition having at the time been referred to the Governing Commission of the country, the latter rendered, on 5 June of the same year, a decree ordering that the Dame Miączyńska be restored to possession of the Trąbczyn estate, the patrimony of her late father.

The Court of Appeal of the Department of Posen, in carrying this decree into execution, had the title of Ownership of the Dame Miączyńska to the Trąbczyn estate inscribed in the mortgage book, but with the express reservation of the rights of third parties.

In 1808, Sieur Weigel presented himself before the competent mortgage authority as Assignee

of the sum of 30,000 Reichsthaler owed to Grotowski and mortgaged upon the Trąbczyn estate, and obtained the inscription of the said sum in his own name.

In 1808, Prince Hohenlohe, wishing to re-enter into possession of the said property, brought an action before the Tribunal of Kalisz against the Dame Miączyńska. — The Tribunal of Kalisz, having alleged that the examination of the acts of the Sovereign authority was not within the Tribunal's province, and that the matter in question had been decided by the Supreme Authority, declared itself incompetent to judge the case. —

In 1810, the said Weigel brought before the Tribunal of Kalisz a suit against the Dame Miączyńska for the payment of the accumulated interest on the sum of 30,000 Reichsthaler.

The Tribunal, having taken into consideration:

1° that in the matter at issue the decree of the Governing Commission had to be taken as the basis, which, regarded as a special privilege, formed an exception to the general laws;

2° that it follows from the spirit of the said decree that, in causing

the Dame Miączyńska to be reinstated in the possession of her property confiscated by [the] decree, [the intention] was to restore it to her in the state in which it stood at the time of the confiscation; for otherwise the restitution would become an onerous burden, seeing that the debts contracted by the Donee exceed the value of the restored property.

3° that His Majesty the King of Prussia was deemed the legitimate possessor of property confiscated from private individuals only so long as his Authority was in force in the country; but that from the moment it ceased to exist, the new Government of the country, in restoring the property to the original proprietors, has consequently annulled the title of possession attached to the former Sovereign and has in fact regarded him only as a conditional possessor.

4° that the Donee could not acquire more extensive rights than those of his Donor; that thus,

[upon] the cessation of the Authority of His Prussian Majesty in this country, the rights of ownership to the confiscated property likewise ceased, as did their effects; that is to say the donation, and consequently the acts done by the Donee are likewise declared null, and namely the debts contracted upon the fortune of another, and this nullity of rights extended likewise to the creditor of Prince Hohenlohe, Sieur Grotowski, as well as to the assignee of the latter, Sieur Weigel — on these grounds the Tribunal, having rejected Weigel's demand, acquiesced in that of the Dame Miączyńska and consequently had the claim of 30,000 Reichsthaler struck from the mortgage registers of the Trąbczyn property.

The two parties appealed from this judgment. — Both reproduced the submissions they had presented at first instance. Weigel demanded the award

of the interest; the Dame Miączyńska objected to the incompetence of the Tribunal.

By its Ruling of 9 November 1820, the Court of Appeal, in deciding the question of incompetence, rejected it, seeing that the cause, arising from a mortgage obligation, fell within the competence of the Tribunals — all the more so since the Dame Miączyńska, having brought before the Tribunals the demand for the cancellation of the sums claimed by Weigel, had herself recognized them as competent in the matter.

As regards the merits of the case, the same ruling of the Court of Appeal, having annulled the judgment of the Tribunal of Kalisz, ordered the summoning of the personal debtor, namely Prince Hohenlohe.

The Dame Miączyńska, in her memorial brought before the Supreme Court, demanded that Weigel's cause, as infringing

upon the rights of Sovereignty, not be admitted. —

The means of defence having been exhausted on both sides, there intervened, on 15 and 17 July 1826, a ruling of the said Court by which the recourse was admitted and the judgment of the Tribunal of Kalisz confirmed. —

The principal grounds on which the Supreme Court founded its decision are the following:

1° that the effects of the confiscation as well as of the donation, being a consequence of the circumstances of the time, could last only so long as there existed the order of things which produced them.

2° that the spirit and aim of the decree of the former Governing Commission could be none other than that the original proprietor be reinstated in the fullness of the rights he enjoyed at the moment he was dispossessed of them.

3° that the Tribunal, in the grounds

of its judgment, has, in accordance with the real state of things, established that the decree of the former Governing Commission must be taken as the basis of the decision.

4° that the principal aim which the Supreme Authority set itself in restoring the property to the original proprietor would be defeated if these properties remained encumbered with debts he did not contract, which, exceeding the real value of the said property, would render the benefit illusory.

5° finally, that the acts both of the Government of the country and those of the Prussian Government have established this principle, that the original possessor reinstated in his ownership cannot be held responsible for claims that might be raised by third parties bound in their interests.

Such was the course this affair followed in the judicial channel. It remains now to retrace the one it followed in the administrative channel.

In 1811, the Dame Miączyńska petitioned the King of Saxony, then Duke of Warsaw, for an injunction to strike from the mortgage registers of the Trąbczyn estate the debts contracted by Prince Hohenlohe, the former Prussian Donee.

The Minister of Justice, to whom this petition was communicated, declared that:

the examination of the question whether the debts contracted by mortgage by Prince Hohenlohe upon the aforesaid property ought or ought not to be struck from the mortgage registers fell within the province of the Tribunals.

The said Dame, addressing herself later to the Liquidation Commission, framed the demand that the debts encumbering her Trąbczyn estate might be included in the category of debts chargeable to Prussia, which, by placing her beyond the reach of the creditors' pursuits,

would assure her the full and entire enjoyment of her patrimony.

The Liquidation Commission, after having examined in depth the claims of the Dame Prusimska, presented in 1818 its report, in this regard, to the late Prince Czapyski, Minister of the Kingdom, in which, after tracing the history of the affair, it expressed the following opinion:

that the claims of the Dame Miączyńska ought to be set forth in their true light to His Majesty the King of Prussia by diplomatic channels, and if that Sovereign refused to have discharged from his treasury the debts contracted by Prince Hohenlohe and mortgaged upon the Trąbczyn estate, it is only then that the pretensions of the Dame Miączyńska might be brought before the Trilateral Liquidation Commission, to be included there among the passive debts of the Duchy of Warsaw, which fall to the

charge of three high Courts.

Sharing in all points the opinion of the Liquidation Commission, the late Prince Czapski presented an analogous report to His Majesty the Emperor and King.

In 1819, following the aforementioned report, the Minister of State Affairs communicated to the First Lieutenant a reply from the Prussian Ministry, accompanied by a memorandum in which all the allegations of the Dame Miączyńska were refuted and her demand recognized as inadmissible. —

The Lieutenant of the King, by his rescript of 24 September, had this document transmitted to the liquidating Commissioners, and matters rested there.

For his part, Sieur Weigel, independently of the appeal he had lodged from the judgment rendered by the Tribunal of Kalisz, further invoked the assistance of his

Government, requesting its intervention in this regard with the Polish Government.

Indeed, the Ministry of Berlin, interceding in favour of Sieur Weigel, set forth by diplomatic channels that the Tribunal of Kalisz, called by the nature of its attributions to take cognizance solely of questions of Civil law, had exceeded the bounds of its powers in deciding upon a question of political law and of the law of nations, and it demanded in consequence that the question of whether:

the claims encumbering the Trąbczyn estate ought to be struck from the mortgage registers of the aforesaid property without prior discharge —

be withdrawn from the cognizance of the Tribunals to be submitted to decision by diplomatic channels. —

This claim having been

communicated by the Minister Secretary of State to the First Lieutenant of the King, the latter conveyed it to the Commission of Justice, which declared, for its part:

that the affair in question having been brought to the decision of the Court of Appeal, a detailed report in this regard would be premature, for if the said Court reforms the judgment of the Tribunal of Kalisz, by that very fact the claim of the cabinet of Berlin will be satisfied.

Later, the judgment of the Court of Appeal having intervened, the Commission of Justice submits to the First Lieutenant, on 12 January 1821, a report with this observation:

that the ruling of the Court of Appeal had indeed reformed the judgment of the Tribunal of Kalisz, but that nevertheless the affair could not be

regarded as concluded, since it was indispensable to have Prince Hohenlohe summoned as the original debtor.

While these various communications were taking place by diplomatic and administrative channels, there intervened in 1826 the Definitive sentence of the Supreme Tribunal which, confirming the decision of the Court of Appeal, upheld the judgment rendered by the Tribunal of Kalisz. —

This sentence provoked fresh claims on the part of the Prussian Government, following which various opinions were rendered both by the Commission of Finances and by that of Justice. —

Finally, after long debates, the former Council of Administration, adopting the proposal of Mr. the Prince Lubecki, then Minister of Finances, authorized — by a decision taken at the session of 4 October 1829 — the Commission of Finances and of the Treasury to raise a conflict of jurisdiction on the ground of the incompetence of the Tribunals in the affair in question.

It was by virtue of this authorization that the said Commission presented, in July 1830, to the Council of State, a report on the affair in question.

Two principal arguments serve as the basis of the developments it presents therein, namely:

1° that the Tribunals, in pronouncing in the affair in question, gave an ironical interpretation to the decree of the former Governing Commission by virtue of which the Dame Miączyńska was reinstated in her property, and that they thereby infringed upon the Treaty of the State.

2° that the Tribunals, in exceeding the limits of their power, arrogated to themselves cognizance of a matter outside their attributions and thereby encroached upon the rights of the Sovereign.

The Commission of Instruction, as regards the first argument of the Commission of Finances, observes that throughout its exposition it strives to prove only that the Tribunal of Kalisz and the Supreme Tribunal misapplied in their judgments the decree of the former Governing Commission; that the aim of this decree was quite other than that which the said Tribunals ascribed to it, as is shown

more clearly by the Convention of 8/20 February 1822 concluded between the Polish and Prussian Governments; in a word, the Commission of Finances applies itself to proving that the Tribunals judged wrongly and that they ought to have judged otherwise; but it in no way proves that these same Tribunals ought to have abstained entirely from taking cognizance of this affair and rendered no judgment, neither good nor bad; and yet it is this latter assertion which, had it been able to be clearly demonstrated, could alone have given ground for a conflict of jurisdiction; the Commission not having done so, it follows that the whole of the reasoning it deduces cannot justify its conclusion. —

As regards the second argument of the Commission of Finances, namely:

that the Tribunals were competent to decide the affair according to the principles of civil law, but that they were incompetent to

pronounce on the matters by taking as their basis the decree of the former Governing Commission, and that thus, in ruling according to this latter rule, they encroached upon the attributions of the Sovereign authority.

The Commission of Instruction believes it must set forth the following observations.

The Commission of Finances itself acknowledges that the Tribunals were competent to judge the dispute raised between Sieur Weigel and the Dame Miączyńska; but it contests them only the faculty of interpreting the decree of the former Governing Commission, and of taking this decree as the basis of its judgment.

Thus, while striving to prove the contrary, the Commission of Finances could not avoid conceding:

that, as regards the matter, the Civil Tribunals were incontestably competent, but that they merely judged in an improper manner.

And this conviction, so well founded, acquires still more weight from what the Commission of Finances declares

itself:

that the competence of the Tribunal cannot otherwise be established than by the nature of the object in litigation. —

Now, here the object in litigation was mortgage claims; now, claims by their nature are indubitably within the province of the Civil Tribunals, and the latter, being legally invested with the [power] to decide questions arising from mortgage obligations, could no longer become incompetent in the course of the suit, since they did not depart from the matter and since their judgments confine themselves strictly to resolving the question whether a claim ought to be struck from the mortgage book. —

The Commission of Finances itself acknowledges that it is necessarily within the attribution of the Tribunals to have a claim struck from the mortgage book, [and] to declare the obligation as having ceased to exist. —

Now the Tribunals, in pronouncing the cancellation of the claim, acted within the circle of their attributions. What was the basis of their decision is another question.

But once the competence of the Tribunals is recognized according to the principles invoked by the Commission of Finances itself, then in pronouncing in the affair in question they did not exceed the bounds of their attributions, nor did they make any infringement of the prerogative of the Sovereign authority; and irrefutable proof of this is found in the Supreme decision of His Majesty the Emperor Alexander of 4 September 1821, where it is said:

that the course of the proceedings in the affair of Sieur Weigel against the Dame Miączyńska ought not to be impeded.

Could the Tribunals decide, according to the principles of civil law, a question arising from public law? Did they arrogate to themselves the faculty of interpreting public law? In what sense did they understand the latter? All these questions cannot here be the object of any particular examination, for they have no bearing on the question of competence, irrevocably established by the nature of the object in

litigation.

The Commission of Instruction will confine itself merely to observing that the interpretation of Decrees emanating from the Supreme Authority belongs indubitably to the Sovereign whenever [the latter] avail themselves of it and the necessity thereof is recognized, but the application of this Decree in civil relations between private individuals cannot, either, be contested to the Civil Tribunals. —

The interpretation of the Sovereign can only have for its aim to enlighten the Tribunals as to the manner of applying a law or a Decree of the Sovereign; but so long as no such authentic interpretation exists, the Tribunals are bound to apply the law or the Decree in civil relations between private individuals according to the judge's own inmost conviction, arising from the spirit and the letter of the law or of the decree. —

Now the Tribunals must draw the grounds of their judgments solely from the ordinary law, without regard to a special decree which forms

precisely an exception to these laws; this is an assertion that is not tenable, for otherwise the Tribunal, upon the demand of Prince de Hohenlohe — who claimed that the Trąbczyn property be returned to him — would have had to adjudge him the possession of these properties by virtue of civil law, without taking into consideration the Special decree rendered by the former Governing Commission which caused the said property to be restored to the Dame Miączyńska.

The analogy which the Commission of Finances seeks to establish between the affair of Weigel and that of Sieur Godłewski — concerning a dispute over the boundaries between the lands of the latter and those of a domain of the State, and which had likewise given rise to a conflict of jurisdiction — cannot here serve as a precedent, for the reason that the declaration of conflict of jurisdiction had there preceded the judgment of the Tribunal, whereas in the affair of Weigel the conflict of jurisdiction was declared several years after the affair had been definitively judged at third and last instance.

Finally, to justify

the present conflict, the Commission of Finances alleges the following grounds.

a° that a conflict of jurisdiction may be invoked even in the case where the action is prosecuted between two private parties without the Government being interested therein.

b° that a like conflict may be raised even against a ruling of the Supreme Court which has already acquired the force of res judicata.

c° that, in bringing this conflict of jurisdiction to the decision of the Council of State, the Commission does not place itself in contradiction with the Supreme decision providing that in this affair there was no ground to impede the judicial course in the ordinary channel of the Tribunals.

To these three grounds the Commission of Instruction opposes the following observations:

ad a. — To prove that, in a suit between two private parties — one which, without participation or concurrence of the Government, had been judged in the three judicial instances — a conflict of jurisdiction could be raised, the Commission of Finances alleges as an example two fictitious cases in which the Civil Tribunals would have caused to be separated from the landed property the taxes entered as a charge attaching to the person, which would suffice to annihilate the whole collection of revenues, if the treasury had no other means of annulling this judicial ruling than that of the intervention and opposition of a third party.

But from the example alleged above one can infer nothing other than that, if ever, in consequence of the cessation of the collection of taxes, the danger to the treasury were real, [there] would arise the necessity of forming an intervention or a third-party opposition; but when, according to the

provisions of the law, decrees definitively intervened are binding only on the parties who are interested in the suit [and] who are duly summoned to it, this circumstance dispels all fears that such rulings might infringe upon the rights of the treasury, which, on the contrary — without needing to form an intervention or third-party opposition, and without regard to rulings rendered in respect of which it has not intervened — could effect the collection of taxes by the economic-administrative channel. —

The allegation that the Tribunals ought to have recognized their incompetence as soon as the question of civil law changed into a diplomatic question can likewise not be admitted, seeing that the conclusions and reasonings of the Commission of Finances itself prove that the Tribunals, whose competence has already been recognized as to the nature of the object submitted to their cognizance, could not become incompetent when, in their judgments, they did not depart from that nature; and one might here further add that

the imputation made against the Tribunals that it did not belong to them to interpret the decree of the former Governing Commission is mitigated by the Supreme decision of 4 September 1821, which on the contrary upheld the course in the judicial channel of the suit in question.

all the more so since this decision was rendered after the Tribunal of Kalisz had already interpreted the aforesaid decree, and after a claim made by the Prussian Government against the judgment of the said Tribunal.

Moreover, it would be superfluous to seek to prove that a purely civil cause could become diplomatic. —

ad b. — The judgment of the Supreme Tribunal, intervened in 1826, by reason of its being definitive must be regarded as unassailable, since Art. 1 of the former Constitution { then in force } says, presuming that: "This Tribunal is charged with judging at last resort all civil causes."

Neither the former nor the new organization of the Council of State has

conferred upon it the attributions of the Court of Cassation; on the contrary, these attributions are attached to the Supreme Tribunal.

The Commission of Finances, giving a new extension to the provisions of the former Constitution as well as to an article of the former organization of the Council of State, and generalizing them, strives to demonstrate that the powers of the Council of State have no limits, that it can not only prevent the administrative and judicial authorities from encroaching upon their respective attributions, but further quash a judgment rendered on the merits by one authority without opposition on the part of the other, and [has] this power to annul that judgment and consequently to pronounce absolutely as a Court of Cassation. —

To convince oneself how far these assertions — as well as the extensive interpretation of the provisions of the former Constitution and of Art. 31 of the organization of the former Council

of State — are well founded, it suffices to give attention to the origin of a conflict of jurisdiction and to its nature. —

Special regulations have traced certain limits between the power of the Civil Tribunals and that of the administrative Tribunals and authorities, by determining what falls within their respective provinces, that is to say what is the circle of their respective attributions within which they must confine themselves. —

Thus, according to the former and the new organization of the Council of State, a conflict of jurisdiction arises:

when the Civil Tribunal believes that an administrative authority seeks to encroach upon its attributions, or reciprocally when an administrative authority imputes a like encroachment to a Tribunal.

In this case the authority which has a ground for complaint is bound to forewarn the other through its President

by declaring a conflict of jurisdiction. —

If this declaration remains without effect, and the authority forewarned does not declare, within the period of 8 days, that it desists from all further action, then the authority which raised the conflict makes its Report thereof to the respective Governing Commission, which submits the affair to the decision of the Council of State, which, in conformity with the rules indicated, determines which of the authorities — whether judicial or administrative — is competent to pronounce in the affair that gave rise to the conflict. —

Now, for a conflict of jurisdiction to be legitimately raised, the concurrence of the four following conditions is required:

1° a declaration of conflict by the President of the Tribunal before the President of the Instituting Commission, to forewarn the other party that it does not have the power to rule on the matter submitted to its decision

2° to leave to the authorities in conflict the faculty of settling, within the period of 8 days, so as to have the conflict amicably lifted. —

3° to denounce the conflict to the respective Governing Commission, if it could not be amicably settled.

4° to produce to the Council of State the proof that a conflict between two authorities has effectively taken place. —

It remains now to examine whether the case presented by the Commission of Finances as a conflict between the authority of the Throne and the Tribunals is really a conflict of jurisdiction understood in the legal sense, namely: a conflict of jurisdiction between the Tribunals and the administrative authorities. —

The dispute between Sieur Weigel and the Dame Miączyńska had for its object the validity or invalidity

of the claim of the former, mortgaged upon the Trąbczyn property; thus it was a question arising from purely Civil relations. —

The Commission of Finances, while acknowledging the competence of the Tribunals to judge this affair, contests them only the faculty of interpreting the decree of the former Governing Commission and of basing their decision on that same decree. — Now, in fact, the Commission of Finances imputes to them that they pronounced illegally.

The decision of a Tribunal is a final result that cannot be foreseen in advance. — It follows that, since the Tribunal, by reason of the nature of the object in litigation, was recognized as competent, the conflict of jurisdiction could not have been raised, seeing that the decision of the Tribunal could not be foreseen. —

This conflict of jurisdiction not having been able to be declared, and none of the 4 conditions mentioned above having established its existence, and the proof produced by the

Commission of Finances itself, far from demonstrating the existence of a conflict of jurisdiction, demonstrating only that the affair had, several years before, been decided at third and last instance by the Supreme Tribunal — it follows that, in the case at issue, no conflict of jurisdiction had existed, as none exists at present.

But the Commission of Finances, in protesting against a ruling that is definitive and has passed into the force of res judicata, not having been able to have in view a conflict of jurisdiction such as is provided for and determined by the organization of the Council of State — and which has for its aim to cause the decision of an affair to be stayed, for such a conflict would not have answered the aim of annulling a judgment against which the Commission of Finances brings recourse — found itself constrained to give the regulatory provisions an extension analogous to its views, and consequently it took it upon itself to demonstrate that, independently of the conflicts of jurisdiction

such as the organization of the Council determines — namely, conflicts which have for their aim to prevent a decision that would encroach upon the attributions of another authority — there exists yet another conflict, unlimited in its scope and in its consequence, by means of which any definitive judgment having the force of res judicata may be assailed. —

But such an interpretation of the organization of the Council of State demonstrates that, according to the opinion of the Commission of Finances, the consequence of this new species of conflict ought to be:

that the notification of a conflict would no longer be bounded by any period of time; that the jurisdiction of any Tribunal, purely civil or administrative, could be contested even several years after the definitive judgment rendered by it; that rulings rendered whether by the Civil Tribunals or by the Administrative Tribunals could be annulled at all times indefinitely, and the

affairs remitted [to the proper forum] as of right; that the Court which would have to decide such a conflict would be a Court of Cassation with unlimited power; that consequently it could, without regard to prescription, annul all civil relations legally established, efface and abolish the rights legally acquired by each person, whenever the authority of the Tribunal which consolidated them had been contested.

The consequences strictly deduced from the extension given by the Commission of Finances to the provisions of the organization of the Council of State prove that such a species of conflict of jurisdiction, and such a kind of Civil-judicial attribution, are incompatible with the organization of the Council of State regarded as a Supreme administrative Tribunal; that the action which the Commission of Government calls a conflict of jurisdiction is in effect a recourse brought by way of cassation to the Council of State regarded as a Court of Cassation.

ad c. — The Supreme decision of 4 September

1821, which declares that the course of ordinary justice in this affair ought not to be impeded, is so clear and so precise that it admits of no interpretation; and for this it suffices to direct attention to the facts which had preceded this decision. —

The Tribunal of Kalisz, basing its decision on the decree of the former Governing Commission, had the claim of Sieur Weigel struck from the mortgage book of the Trąbczyn estate. The latter, having addressed his claims to the Prussian Government, which by a Ministerial note protested against the competence of the Tribunal and demanded that the affair be referred to the diplomatic channel. —

The Commission of Justice, invited to give its opinion in this regard, declared in its report of 12 January 1821:

"that to resolve this affair there were but two channels, namely the political channel and the judicial. —

"As, however, the Government cannot rule upon the rights

"of a third party (that is to say, of Weigel) to the prejudice of the adverse party, namely the Dame Miączyńska, the Commission of Justice was of opinion that, for the first case — namely a political arrangement — it would be necessary either to engage the Prussian Government to discharge the debts contracted by Prince de Hohenlohe upon the Trąbczyn estate, or that the Government of the Kingdom take this obligation upon itself; that, finally, for the case where the affair could not be arranged by diplomatic channels, its decision had to be left to the civil Tribunals as the sole legal channel."

It is following this report — and while reserving to itself cognizance of what advantages had been granted to other private individuals reinstated in the possession of their confiscated property, [as compared] with those to whom these properties had been conceded by the Prussian Government, as well as of the extent of the obligations that would result for the Treasury of the Kingdom if it were to undertake to satisfy all claims of this kind — that the late His Majesty the Emperor

and King had decided that the judicial course in this affair ought in no way to be impeded.

Now the argument which the Commission of Finances draws from the date of this Supreme decision — that it appeared at the moment when the Court of Appeal annulled the judgment of the Civil Tribunal, in order to conclude therefrom that the said Court had then restored to this affair its purely civil character — gives occasion for the following observations:

The Court of Appeal, in annulling the judgment of the Tribunal of Kalisz solely for the reason that Prince Hohenlohe had not been summoned as debtor, in no way thereby changed the nature of the affair itself; it could not convert it into a suit purely Civil and arising from civil relations, for according to the opinion of the Commission of Government itself this cause was, from the first, purely Civil. — The Court did not rid [it] of extraneous elements other than those arising from the relations of policy, of the right of Sovereignty, and from diplomatic relations. —

for a suit involving a mortgage charge had nothing in common with those relations. — The Court of Appeal ruled only on the necessity of having Prince Hohenlohe summoned as debtor; thus the substance of the affair always remained the same, for it was always a matter of a dispute raised in consequence of a decree of the former Governing Commission. It follows, therefore, that the Supreme decision of 4 September 1821, having upheld the judicial course in the suit in question, is not susceptible of all the restrictions which the Commission of Finances seeks to deduce from it. —

In conformity with this development, and taking into consideration that, according to Arts. 31, 32, 33, 34 and 38 of the former, and under the terms of Arts. 37, 38, 39, 40 and 41 of the New organization of the Council of State, the law knows no conflicts of jurisdiction other than those which precede a definitive judgment of a Tribunal in an affair, and following which the Council of State decides the question whether it is the Tribunal or the administrative authority that must judge

the affair that gave rise to the conflict;

that the imputation of incompetence made by the Commission of Finances against the Tribunals, after the affair between Sieur Weigel and the Dame Miączyńska had been definitively judged at last Instance and without prior declaration in due time of a conflict of jurisdiction, bears none of the characteristics proper to a conflict of jurisdiction. —

that likewise, the case denounced by the Commission of Finances being really a conflict of jurisdiction, even so it could no longer be decided by the Council, having regard to the Supreme decision of 4 September 1821 providing that the judicial course followed in this cause cannot be impeded;

that since, under the denomination of conflict of jurisdiction, the Commission of Finances has presented a recourse by way of cassation tending to quash a judgment of the Supreme Court rendered at last instance and passed into the force of res judicata, it follows that the Council of State, not being invested by its Organization with the attributions of a Court of Cassation, cannot decide such a recourse. —

For these grounds the Commission

of Instruction is of opinion:

That, while acknowledging the non-existence of the conflict of jurisdiction concerning the suit between Sieur Weigel and the Dame Miączyńska, the Council of State set aside the demand of the Commission of Finances as being based on no legal principle.

The Commission of Instruction presents a draft Decree drawn up in conformity with its conclusions.

Done at the Session of the Commission of Instruction, Warsaw, 28 October 1834.

The President

[signed] Faltz

1. That, the actions being joined, the contract concluded on 18 May 1805 between the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen and fourteen colonists of the commune of Trąbczyn, before the Patrimonial Court of the Prince of Hohenlohe at Zagórów, be declared not binding on the counterclaiming plaintiff and lapsed in its effects, and thereby as giving the defendants to the counterclaim no right of free pasture and wood-gathering in the Studzianka district, which belongs to the forests of the Trąbczyn estate.

2. That the servitude of pasture and wood-gathering in the Studzianka district be awarded only to those holdings which were the subject of the contract concluded before the notary Kroszczyński on 21 December 1828 between Michalina née Prusimska, Countess Miączyńska, and seven colonists; and in the alternative:

3. Should the first conclusion be rejected, that the servitude of pasture and wood-gathering be awarded only to the 14 holdings that are named one by one in the contract concluded on 18 May 1805 between the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen and fourteen colonists.

4. That, to find for how many cattle grazing in the Studzianka district is to be allowed for each holding separately, a report of experts be ordered on these questions of fact:

A) For how many cattle, of what kind and in what parts of the Studzianka district, pasture is to be allowed in the district of the Trąbczyn forests called Studzianka for the seven holdings granted by the deed of grant of 21 December 1828, declared by Michalina Countess Miączyńska before the notary Kroszczyński, and in the alternative for the fourteen holdings covered by the contract of 18 May 1805, without regard to the number of settlers now on each of these holdings through their subdivision, having regard to the extent of the holdings, to the meadows and pastures belonging to them, and to the needs of the Trąbczyn estate and the forest management introduced in the Studzianka district.

B) What is to be the greatest quantity of wood that may be gathered, and in what parts of the Studzianka district, on each forest day, for each of the seven holdings granted by the contract of 21 December 1828, and in the alternative for the fourteen holdings granted by the contract of 18 May 1805, having regard to the needs of each single holding as if it were in the sole possession of one settler, and likewise to the needs of the Trąbczyn estate, to the forest management introduced in the Studzianka district, and to the requirements of the Bank of Poland on account of the Treasury loan it has granted, and likewise of the Credit Society on account of the highest loan that is to be taken up.

5. That a member of the Tribunal be delegated to take the experts' oath, and to appoint them by virtue of office should the parties not agree on choosing them freely.

6. That all the other defendants, to whom the right to exercise the servitude of pasture and wood-gathering is not awarded in these proceedings, be forbidden to graze and to gather wood in the Studzianka district.

7. That judgment be given with provisional enforcement. Lastly:

8. That the costs of the proceedings be awarded to the plaintiff against the defendants.

Facts and grounds.

Paweł Prusimski of Kolno and his wife Katarzyna Prusimska, née Rozdrażewska, heirs of the Trąbczyn estate, in the year 1746 granted the Hollanders on the lands of the Trąbczyn estate a privilege settling their mutual relations, in which they said among other things:

“I do not forbid pasture for all their livestock, which they shall enjoy on coming to an agreement.”

By this privilege, then, the right of pasture depended on a particular agreement of each single Hollander with the owner of the Trąbczyn estate.

When, in consequence of political events, the part of the Polish country within which the Trąbczyn estate lay passed under Prussian rule, this estate, then the property of Antoni Prusimski, Starost of Niszczewice, was confiscated and given to the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, who on 18 May 1805 concluded with fourteen Hollanders of the commune of Trąbczyn, named one by one in that contract, a contract of sale of a part of the pine forest and marshes adjoining the lands they held, 42 Hufen of Magdeburg measure in area. In § 4 of that contract it is said:

“They take free pasture, without payment, in the part of the pine forest on the Biskupice boundary called the Zarzyński district, and likewise in that part of theirs the free gathering of wood on the customary forest days.”

The Trąbczyn estate remained in the possession of the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen until the time when, after the change of government that followed, the Governing Commission, as the highest authority in the country, by its resolution of 21 July 1807 restored Michalina Dąbska, née Prusimska, to the ownership of the Trąbczyn estate, which had been confiscated from her father Antoni Prusimski. With Dąbska restored to the rights that were hers after her father, all acts and obligations entered into by the Prince of Hohenlohe were annulled. This question of principle was decided by the judgment of the Court of the Highest Instance given on 7 July 1826 in the case between Michalina née Prusimska, by her first marriage Dąbska, by her second the wife of Stanisław Miączyński, and Bogumił Karol Weigel. In those proceedings Weigel claimed interest on a capital of 200,000 Polish złoty which the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen had raised as a loan on the Trąbczyn estate, and Michalina Countess Miączyńska for her part demanded that this capital be struck out of the mortgage register. The Court of the Highest Instance adopted these principles:

That the passing of the Trąbczyn estate into the ownership of the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen had force only so long as the same state of things lasted as before; that the owner of the estate was restored, by the will and resolution of the Highest Authority, to such rights in respect of his estate as were his when it was taken from him; that a debt contracted by the donee, once he proved to be a conditional possessor, ceased with the fall of his title to bind the estate charged with it — and in consequence of these principles the Court of the Highest Instance dismissed Weigel's demand that interest on the capital of 200,000 Polish złoty be awarded to him, and ordered the capital itself to be struck out.

On the same principles, then, adopted in that judgment, the contract concluded on 18 May 1805 between the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen and the 14 Hollanders did not bind Michalina Countess Miączyńska in the least and must be held to have lapsed in its effects, like all the obligations entered into by the Prince of Hohenlohe in respect of the Trąbczyn estate.

Neither the Hollanders themselves nor Michalina Countess Miączyńska understood the matter otherwise when on 21 December 1828, before the notary Mikołaj Kroszczyński, an agreement settling their mutual relations was concluded between Michalina née Prusimska, Countess Miączyńska, and seven rent-payers holding by purchase, named one by one in that deed. Although in that contract the parties cited the contract of 18 May 1805, they did not confirm it in the least; they only carried some conditions of that contract over into the new agreement. Among these conditions is § III, which reserves the right of common pasture and of gathering wood in the Zarzyński district, or Studzianka, on the side of the Biskupice estate. By this last deed, then, only the settlers named in it had the right to free pasture and the free gathering of wood in the Studzianka district, since for all the other colonists the grant of the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen of 18 May 1805 had lost all force, on the principles adopted in the judgment of the Highest Court of 7 July 1826.

In the alternative: should it be held that the colonists covered by the contract of 18 May 1805 also have the right to exercise pasture and to gather wood in the Studzianka district, this right cannot belong separately to all the

colonists now in being, but only to those holdings which were created by that grant and are named in the contract of the year 1805. For in the contract of the Prince of Hohenlohe a certain number of colonists is set down by number, and so only that number of them ought to exist and only for them could the use of pasture and wood-gathering be awarded; for that contract did not empower the colonists to divide the lands they occupy into parts. Through the subdivision of the holdings an incomparably greater number of hearths, inhabitants and livestock has arisen — and all this has increased the need for pasture and wood, to the evident harm of the manor. Thus the resolution of the Administrative Council in the year 1858 laid down:

1. That perpetual leaseholders ought to occupy themselves with farming alone.

2. That a perpetual leaseholder is not allowed to hold two farms.

3. That a perpetual leaseholder may neither sublet the farm granted to him nor divide it into parts without the express permission of the manor. From this it follows that, at the worst, only those holdings have the right to pasture and wood-gathering which existed at the time of the contract of 18 May 1805, and all the others, which arose through subdivision, cannot enjoy this right; although the plaintiff chiefly maintains that the number of holdings is fixed by the deed of 21 December 1828, and only in the alternative by the contract of 18 May 1805.

With the Trąbczyn forests and their management put in order, the servitude of pasture and wood-gathering, exercised in the manner described above, is exceedingly burdensome. Count Miączyński has the right, under article 4 of the law on servitudes of pasture and felling of 16/28 June 1830, to demand that the number of cattle to be grazed in the Studzianka district be limited to what the land needed when this servitude was established. This servitude can therefore be awarded only to the 7 holdings that acceded to the deed of 21 December 1828, and in the alternative only to the 14 holdings that were the subject of the contract of the year 1805; that is, it can be awarded only in proportion to the need of each of these holdings, and never in proportion to the number of settlers on them and the number of cattle they keep. To establish this number, therefore, a report of experts ought to be ordered on this question of fact:

For how many cattle, of what kind and in what parts of the Studzianka district, pasture is to be allowed in the district of the Trąbczyn forests called Studzianka for the 7 holdings granted by the deed of grant of 21 December 1828, declared by Michalina Countess Miączyńska before the notary Kroszczyński — and in the alternative for the 14 holdings covered by the contract of 18 May 1805, without regard to the number of settlers on each of these holdings through their subdivision, having regard to the extent of the holdings, to the meadows and pastures belonging to them, and to the needs of the Trąbczyn estate and the forest management introduced in the Studzianka district.

The same applies to the right of gathering wood, to determine which the plaintiff proposes the following question of fact:

What is to be the greatest quantity of wood that may be gathered, and in what parts of the Studzianka district, on each forest day, for each of the seven holdings granted by the contract of 21 December 1828, and in the alternative for the 14 holdings granted by the contract of 18 May 1805, having regard to the needs of each single holding as if it were in the sole possession of one settler, and equally to the needs of the Trąbczyn estate, to the forest management introduced in the Studzianka district, and to the requirement of the Bank of Poland on account of the Treasury loan it has granted, and likewise of the Credit Society on account of the highest loan that is to be taken up.

The plaintiff's conclusion is thus fully justified. Costs are due under article 130, and provisional enforcement under article 135, of the Code of Judicial Procedure.

I reserve the development of the grounds, and judgment by default.

Date as above.

Michał Piechowski

Costs

In all 47 silver roubles 21 kopecks.

apl399801333-4:
No. 1805

To the High Commission for Peasant Affairs of the District of Kalisz.

As the attached decision of the Honourable Baron von Rosen shows, a certain Krystian Lippeldt has been granted a servitude of pasturing 2 horses and 7 head of horned cattle on my land [written "majem territorium"], namely on the folwark Włodzimirów, at the places called "smugi". Since Krystjan Lippeldt is from a neighbouring village, I do not wish to take on any obligations towards him — I therefore turn with a request to the High Commission that this decision be annulled, and in support of it I set

out the following facts:

On the folwark Włodzimirów, which belongs to my estate of Trąbczyn, where there is a farming of many fields, I have the only pasture for the young stock. There I sometimes take in the stock of my neighbours, for payment or free of charge. The said Lippeldt, being in touch with the manorial lordship (Dominium), came to me with the request that he be allowed to pasture seven head of cattle and two horses on this pasture for a payment in money or for work at harvest.

In one field on the boundary of Emilienhejm there are three hollows, the so-called "smugi", and since that field had then lain fallow for several years and I had no damage to fear, I allowed him to graze

the said stock in these hollows, but only until 1 November of that year, for a payment in money, which I later changed, at his urgent requests, to labour, and for the information of my administration I gave him my written permission for it.

Since, as I have said, that field lay fallow, in the following years I allowed Lippeldt, who always came to ask in the spring, to graze in these hollows, and now he claims that the Supreme Ukase found him in the use of this pasture. On the contrary, his contract of 1863 ended on 1 November, and so before the Supreme Ukase was issued, and the new written agreement was made on 1 May 1864, and so after the Supreme Ukase was issued.

In that year he also made the attached contract — which he gave up, and returned the original in the presence of the former steward Swiderski. —

From the above account it appears that Lippeldt had no servitudes on my land — that he did indeed use it as pasture, but only by temporary leave — which even for the peasants cannot be a title to a servitude against the owner — and still less for a man from another village — who has done nothing for the land he now wishes to seize — and brought it no benefit —

I hold, therefore, that even if Lippeldt proved his use, a servitude can never be granted to him, for the Supreme Ukase, while extending its benefits to the peasants of the Kingdom as a whole — yet chiefly

works to the advantage of the peasants of the village in which they grew up — and have well deserved it by their labour.

Finally, Lippeldt cannot prove use: — to hold any rights — one must, under articles 1, 5, 11 and others of the Supreme Ukase, have been exercising that right at the time the Ukase was issued. Lippeldt used [the pasture] before the Ukase, made a new contract after the Ukase, from which he withdrew of his own accord, — but he never used it at the moment of the Ukase — and that is precisely the chief principle for obtaining any of the rights the Ukase guaranteed to the peasants. —

Since, then, Lippeldt as a stranger cannot draw favours from the village of Włodzimierów. — Since he likewise at the time

of the Ukase did not graze at the place called "smugi" — I therefore consider — that he can acquire no rights to these "smugi" today either — and I therefore request the High Commission to annul the decision of the Honourable Commissioner. —

W. Miączyński

Trąbczyn, 23 July 1865.

By the decision of 13/25 May 1865, no. 83, on the assessment and confirmation of the rights of the peasants of the Trąbczyn estate, issued by the Honourable Commissioner of the 5th District, six farmsteads in the village of Nowawies, entered in the table of dues of 1846 under nos. 2, 4, 5, 6, 9 and 10, of 5 Morgen each, were recognised as subject to return to the farmers who last held them, or to their successors, together with the crops and buildings that stood on the land when the said farmsteads were abandoned. —

The above decision of the Honourable Commissioner, being too burdensome for the owner of the estate, compels him to come now before the Honourable Commission — with the request that it be set aside — and that the

[Note of the office, in Russian:] On the [exchange?]: to recognise the lands which were formerly held by the peasants as deserted holdings — but since they cannot be returned, to instruct [the Comm…?] [to arrange] a voluntary agreement, and then to assign [them].

[Note in Polish:] I have received the proofs [returned?].

Kalisz, 11 [October?]

[A. Kowal…?]

farmsteads mentioned be left in the ownership of the dominium directum [written "dominii directi"]; in support of which the following grounds are put forward:

The Honourable Commissioner of the 5th District based his ruling on a mistaken account of the facts by the peasants who claim the farmsteads in question, for in the grounds he stated:

1. That the owner removed six peasants from Nowawies of his own will —

2. That he did so in order to join these farmsteads to the folwark lands. —

At the time the Supreme Ukase of 1846 was issued there were eight peasant farmsteads in Nowawies — each of 5 Morgen — one of 5 Morgen 25 rods and one of 5 Morgen 75 rods — which were held by farmers until 1856; this placing of the peasants was at that time very convenient for the owner — and he never thought of any change. It was the peasants of Nowawies themselves who, suffering constant misfortune in their farming because their land lay too low and could not be tilled in wet years, came

with an urgent request to be moved to another place. The owner, therefore, wishing only to better the lot of his peasants, and taking into account how badly they had been settled until then, marked out land elsewhere and put up suitable buildings on it; but already before this happened, that is before 1856, six farmers who had suffered most in the wet years left their farmsteads of their own will, without asking for new ones — and going into service — leaving them deserted; it was then that the owner, in strict compliance with the Supreme Ukase of 1846 — and fulfilling the duty laid on the owner of an estate in article 2 of that law, was compelled to find other people who would take up the abandoned farmsteads within two years; but being unable to find any who would settle in Nowawies — in the old places of the misfortunes and failures of the former holders, he was forced to give them farmsteads in place of those, out of his own folwark land, and to turn the land they were to have taken up — over to the folwark, where crop rotation has now been introduced — and the buildings to the use of the manor servants. Since, then, the peasants who now claim their rights left their farmsteads in Nowawies of their own will (which needs no proof, for the owner could not have evicted them by force), since, further, in accordance with article 2 of the ukase of 1846 — the owner was under the necessary obligation to find new peasants who would take up the abandoned holdings, and these new ones, as wholly representing the former, agreed, indeed expressly demanded, to be moved to the new places, which was done, for to this day they hold them, — and in them they have already

been enfranchised — by what means can the first six, or now their successors (to whom the Honourable Commissioner has granted ownership), have the right to demand the return of farmsteads which, as abandoned, were lawfully given away — and were exchanged by their own will; this exchange, moreover, entered in the supplementary table of 1846 and confirmed by the District Chief and the Commission of Internal Affairs — has binding force. In this way the owner of the estate, for having met the interest of the peasants and come truly to their help, would be forced to give away the same land twice, and what is more, would suffer considerable losses if the Honourable Commission decided to measure out farmsteads in place of the crop-rotation farming that has been introduced. — Article 6 of the Supreme Ukase of 1864 states expressly: that only that land is subject to return which — without exchange for other land — passed into the disposal of the owners; here an exchange took place in accordance with the Ukase of 1846.

Today, under article 8 of the Supreme Ukase of 1864, only those who took the place of the claimants could demand to return to the first holdings; but those who left their farms have no right in any case, if the deserted holdings they left have been lawfully taken up (which has happened), and on the ground of the Supreme Ukases, both of 1846 and of 1864, no right to ownership can be derived for such peasants.

Hence it appears: that the owner of the estate not only committed no arbitrary act, but on the contrary acted lawfully and by the will of the peasants.

Should the facts above be denied, the owner in that case appeals to the testimony of witnesses and names as such: 1. Wawrzeniec Sowiński — 2. Józef Czajka — and many others — whose examination he has the honour to request.

Finally, attention must be drawn to this circumstance: that according to the survey register of the Trąbczyn estate the peasants in all hold more land than falls to them by the table of dues; so where the peasants' rights are recognised and respected, excessive and unlawful demands ought to find no consideration — and therefore the owner of the estate trusts that the Honourable Commission, weighing what is just, will be pleased to grant this request —

As to the pasture — the peasants of Nowawies never had pasture in common with the manor. —

4 proofs are attached.

With deep respect

W. Miączyński

Kalisz, 10/22 August 1865.
apl399801333-5:
No. 19838/4098

Matter of Peasant Affairs

To the Constituent Committee in the Kingdom of Poland

Petition

of the colonists of Łazińsk, in the commune of Trąbczyn, Słupca district, Kalisz governorate, for the recognition of the rights of the privileges granted by the former manorial lordship (Dominium).

As the attached postal receipt shows, we submitted this year a petition to the Constituent Committee for the recognition of the servitudes granted and assured to us by the manorial lordship in former years, that is, free pasture in the Trąbczyn forest, the raking of litter, the digging of stumps, etc., and yet we have so far received no decision; we therefore most humbly ask that an impartial official be delegated from the office of the Słupca district to look more closely into our claims, and then to decide how far this right belongs to us, and to send this decision to the hands of the Honourable Chief of the Słupca District.

With deepest respect, in the name of the others —

faithful subjects —

[three crosses] Daniel Hohm

[three crosses] Wilhelm Moritz

at Łazińsk, 6/18 December 1867.

apl399801333-6:
No. 16658/2133

To the High Constituent Committee in the Kingdom of Poland at Warsaw

Most Humble Petition

of the colonists of the Łazińsk colony, in the commune of Trąbczyn, Słupca district, Kalisz governorate, for the recognition and confirmation of the rights named in the privilege

According to the contract of purchase of the farmsteads from Prince Hohenlohe, the former owner of the Trąbczyn estate, and the privilege of rights he granted us in 1805 — we may graze our stock in the forest, in common with the manor's, in the Studzienka forest section as far as the Bishop's boundary — we may also gajć się [a word not understood] in the forest with carts 2 days a week and rake litter every year — and besides the arable land we had 6 Morgen of clay land for a clay pit for our own needs — and all this His Excellency the Commissioner Baron Rosen recognised as lawful for us, and he obliged the owner to supply the evidence we needed and to produce the mortgage

map of 1805 by 3/15 August — which we can prove at any time by witnesses under oath. But when the owner drew up a new table in 1838, he divided the forest section on which we had our pasture into 3 sections, and on 2 he forbids the grazing of cattle altogether, and on the third part he made 11 clearings and young plantations, and we have no pasture — he does not allow the [ugaj] and the raking of litter, he takes the clay pit away for his own use — and for the drawing up of the new right and table, at the time of the visit of the Honourable Commissioner Władimirow, he brought forward false witnesses and gave them 12 roubles each to testify as he claims — and to this the witnesses are: 1. Marcin Rywarski and 2. Libner, a joiner, living in the village of Trąbczyn — and even one witness of the owner's, Tomasz Janicki, himself declared it.

So as not to be deprived of these servitudes, we brought three petitions to His Excellency the President of the Kalisz Commission for Peasant Affairs, namely on 6/18 June, 30 June/12 July and 3/15 September of

last year, 1867, and then in October to the High Committee, and enclosed a copy of the privilege as evidence, and to that we received an answer dated 31 January 1868 referring us to the Kalisz Commission for Peasant Affairs.

But since to this moment we have received neither the hoped-for result nor any decision, and the copy of the privilege has not been returned to us — we therefore turn in person, with a most humble repeated petition, to the High Constituent Committee, and beg on our knees:

"That the High and Just Government forbid the owner of the Trąbczyn estate to take from us the servitudes written down in the right, order a strict inquiry on the spot, and delegate an official from Warsaw to carry it out — and order that the said clay pit and pasture be given into our possession and use in their former extent and within their former boundaries, forbid him to prevent the [ugaj], the digging of stumps and the raking of litter

— and be pleased graciously to confirm our old right to us."

All the more since, besides our holding the right or privilege, the Supreme Ukases found us in possession of the said things — and should we fail to prove it, we will take on ourselves the costs of conducting the inquiry.

We trust and have strong hope that the High Government, our only hope, will not allow the owner to do us so great a wrong, but will be pleased graciously and mercifully to incline to our imploring petition — will do justice, and by its decision will graciously restore us to the possession and use of the said — servitudes. —

For which we beg in deepest humility. —

Your most humble servants,

Ludwig Hintz

Krystyan Sehr

in the name of all —

Łazińsk colony, 10/22 August 1868.
